p:NGA: The Central Bank of Nigeria issues the naira (NGN). Its exposure score is 41 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; that is more exposed than 83% of the 194 places with a figure. Of six documented cases, the main ones involve former governor Godwin Emefiele, whom the EFCC (Nigeria's anti-corruption agency) charged in 2024 over banknote printing and foreign exchange allocations. He pleaded not guilty to a separate 20-count charge, and none of these is a verdict. President Tinubu suspended him on 9 June 2023, and President Jonathan suspended governor Sanusi in February 2014. Reuters described Olayemi Cardoso, nominated governor on 15 September 2023, as the former head of Citibank in Nigeria. A swap line, an agreement to borrow another central bank's currency, links it to China: CNY 15 billion against NGN 3.28 trillion, dated 27 December 2024.
p:IDN: Bank Indonesia is the central bank of Indonesia and issues the rupiah, printed by Perum Peruri, the state banknote printing firm, at Karawang in West Java. The country scores 34 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. In October 2011 Securency and Note Printing Australia, both subsidiaries of the Reserve Bank of Australia, pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to provide benefits to foreign public officials to win the banknote business of Indonesia's note-issuing authority between 1999 and 2001; the officials are not named. Governor Syahril was released in December 2000 after six months in detention, while the administration was pushing to remove him and install its own candidates; he was sentenced to three years in 2002 over the 546 billion rupiah Bank Bali scandal, and in 2004 the Supreme Court acquitted him on all charges. In October 2008 the Corruption Court sentenced former governor Burhanuddin Abdullah to five years for approving 100 billion rupiah of the bank's funds in 2003 to pay officials' legal fees and bribe legislators over an amendment to the bank's law. In July 2014 the anti-corruption court sentenced Budi Mulya to 10 years over a 689.39 billion rupiah loan to Bank Century. In August 2025 the anti-corruption commission named two members of the House as suspects over alleged misuse of the bank's money for social projects; that is unproven.
p:PHL: Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas issues the Philippine peso, and the Philippines scores 36 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Six cases are recorded. In 2005 an internal audit found 5.955 million pesos missing from the Bacolod City branch, and the Ombudsman, the body that investigates officials, found the manager guilty of dishonesty and dismissed him. An examiner who had audited the Rural Bank of Sapang Dalaga took 103,500 pesos in fees from it through another firm, and the anti-graft court, the Sandiganbayan, upheld his conviction and six to seven years in prison. A former supervision officer took a loan from the Rural Bank of Kiamba in 2006; the Ombudsman cleared him in 2011, but the Supreme Court reversed that and ordered charges, which remain unproven. A 2013 complaint that former governor Amando Tetangco Jr and Monetary Board members favoured Allied Bank in its merger with Philippine National Bank was still pending in September 2025, so it is unproven, as is a January 2021 graft complaint against Governor Benjamin Diokno and six officials over a 1.75-billion-peso identity card contract. Four staff were dismissed in July 2024 for falsifying attendance records, and in August 2025 two supervisors drew the maximum penalties. In December 2016 President Rodrigo Duterte told Tetangco he would give him a whack and threatened criminal charges against the Anti-Money Laundering Council that Tetangco chaired, accusing it of not tracking drug money but giving no details; Deputy Governor Diwa Guinigundo said the bank was independent. The notes are produced at the bank's Security Plant Complex, and Note Printing Australia says it has supplied polymer banknotes to the bank.
p:BRA: Brazil's money is the real, issued by the Central Bank of Brazil. On 3 October 2019 the Federal Police and federal prosecutors in Sao Paulo opened Operation Estrela Cadente into leaks of the bank's interest-rate decisions in 2010, 2011 and 2012, said to have benefited a fund of the bank BTG Pactual; the investigation covered corruption, inside information and money laundering and is still open, so nothing is proven. On 21 June 2024 President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva called the bank's president, Roberto Campos Neto, his political and ideological adversary and said Brazil would return to normality once he could replace him. Three leaders crossed between the bank and private finance: Meirelles, president from 2003 to 2010, held posts at BankBoston, FleetBoston and Lazard Americas; Ilan Goldfajn, governor from May 2016 to February 2019, at Banco Itau Unibanco and Credit Suisse Brazil; and Campos Neto came from Santander and was to join Nubank as vice chairman on 1 July 2025, after a legally required six-month wait. Its notes come from Casa da Moeda, contracted on 13 April 2017 for 980 million notes worth 279.14 million reais. Brazil scores 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:LUX: Luxembourg uses the euro, so the Central Bank of Luxembourg does the country's central banking while the European Central Bank sets interest rates for the 21 euro countries. Its books are checked by outside accountants on fixed terms: Ernst & Young SA covered the financial years 2019 to 2023, and KPMG Audit S.à r.l. was approved on 12 March 2024 for the years 2024 to 2028. Both cases on file belong to the European Central Bank. The European Ombudsman found maladministration and recommended in January 2018 that ECB president Mario Draghi suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, a forum that mixes central bankers with private bankers; the ECB declined and he did not. On 18 May 2015 Cœuré told a private evening event in London that the ECB would bring asset purchases forward, and the speech was published only the next morning, which the ECB put down to an internal procedure error. Luxembourg scores 19 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:FIN: Finland uses the euro, so the Bank of Finland does not set interest rates by itself; the European Central Bank sets them for the 21 countries on the currency. The Finnish bank scores 16 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and no case is recorded against it. Both findings sit at the European Central Bank. The European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, found maladministration and in January 2018 recommended that president Mario Draghi suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, a forum of central bankers and private financiers, saying it did not fit the bank's independence; the bank declined and he did not. On 18 May 2015 board member Benoit Coeure told a private evening event in London that the bank would front-load asset purchases, and the speech was published only the next morning, which the bank called an internal procedure error, Draghi saying nothing market-sensitive was revealed. Finland's gold is stored for it by other central banks rather than managed by them: as of 30 October 2013, 51 per cent at the Bank of England, 20 per cent at Sveriges Riksbank, 18 per cent at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and 7 per cent at the Swiss National Bank. PricewaterhouseCoopers Oy audits the accounts for 2026 to 2031.
p:ZAF: South Africa's money, the rand, is issued by the South African Reserve Bank, which is unusual in having private shareholders: 2,000,000 shares held by just over 800 holders, no holder allowed more than 10,000 shares alone or with associates, voting confined to South African residents at one vote per 200 shares, and no shareholder role in monetary policy, financial stability or regulation. A shareholder list as at 30 June 2022, reported secondhand, names the South African Mutual Life Assurance Society at 20,000 shares and the SA Police Widows' and Orphans' Fund at 10,520, both above that cap, with Absa Bank, Discovery, FirstRand, First National Nominees, Beluga Trust and several other companies, trusts and funds at 10,000 each. An Economic Freedom Fighters bill to have the state buy the shareholders out reached parliament's Standing Committee on Finance, where at public hearings on 2 July 2025 the National Treasury called it a forced takeover; no vote or enactment has followed. The one case against the bank ended with the finding thrown out: in June 2017 the Public Protector ordered the bank Absa to repay 1.125 billion rand over an apartheid-era rescue loan the Reserve Bank had made to Bankorp, and on 16 February 2018 the Pretoria High Court set aside that report and its remedy and ordered the Public Protector to pay part of the Reserve Bank's costs herself. The same report carried a second instruction that went further: it directed Parliament to amend section 224 of the Constitution so as to change the bank's mandate, away from protecting the value of the currency and towards economic growth. Such an instruction binds unless a court sets it aside, so the bank went to court urgently, and the governor called it a gross overreach; the High Court struck the instruction down on 15 August 2017. The Constitutional Court upheld the personal costs order on 22 July 2019 while refusing to declare that she had abused her office. Gill Marcus went from chairing Absa Group to governor from 9 November 2009, having been a deputy governor from 1999 to 2004, and former governor Tito Mboweni joined Goldman Sachs as an international adviser in 2010 and again, as a regional adviser, in February 2022; no ethics finding attaches to either move. Its banknotes are printed by the South African Bank Note Company, which the bank says is its own subsidiary, and a parliamentary reply reported in June 2016 said a large share of the country's gold is stored in the vaults of the Bank of England and other offshore bullion centres, then four million ounces, which is storage rather than management. It scores 38 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:LBN: Banque du Liban issues Lebanon's currency, the Lebanese pound. Riad Salameh ran it for three decades until 2023, arriving from Merrill Lynch, where he worked from 1973 to 1993 and managed the personal portfolio of Rafic Hariri, the prime minister who then appointed him governor. A 2023 forensic audit by Alvarez & Marsal found the bank's foreign-currency position swung from a 7.2 billion US dollar surplus at the end of 2015 to a 50.7 billion dollar deficit at the end of 2020 with no loss shown on the balance sheet, and that Salameh set the accounting standards that concealed the losses and decided which banks benefited from financial engineering, unchallenged by the Central Council. The 2018 accounts, signed off with qualifications by EY and Deloitte, carried a 6.82 billion dollar asset called seigniorage on financial stability while the bank helped fund a widening government deficit. On 18 May 2020 the prosecutor Ali Ibrahim charged Mazen Hamdan, the bank's director of cash operations, with illegally manipulating the exchange rate; that charge is unproven. In May 2023 French prosecutors issued an arrest warrant for Salameh over illicit enrichment and alleged laundering of 330 million dollars, and Germany issued a second a week later; he called the French warrant a violation of the law. Arrested in Beirut in September 2024, held about thirteen months and released in September 2025 on bail of more than 14 million dollars, he was indicted with two lawyers in January 2026 over 44.8 million dollars allegedly taken from a consultancy account. He is also under investigation over allegations that more than 300 million dollars was siphoned off between 2002 and 2015 through Forry Associates, a company controlled by his brother Raja. All of it is unproven, and both brothers deny wrongdoing. The bank holds 286.8 tonnes of gold, 74.5 percent of its reserves, and scores 44 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Press reporting says KPMG was appointed in 2020 to audit the bank's accounts and that its findings have not been made public; this rests on a news report rather than a Banque du Liban document. Where the gold is kept is known only at second hand. The bank publishes no audited accounts, so the split rests on a 2026 policy paper from a research institute at the American University of Beirut, which says roughly two thirds of the holding sits in the bank's own vaults in Beirut and the rest at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The holding, about 287 tonnes, has not changed since 1971.
p:BEL: Belgium uses the euro, and the European Central Bank sets monetary policy for all 21 countries that use it; the National Bank of Belgium is the country's own central bank. Its 400,000 shares are split evenly: 200,000 registered shares are held by the Belgian State, fixed by law since 1948 and not transferable, and the other 200,000 trade on the Euronext Brussels stock exchange. Belgium scores 28 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Two findings stand against the European Central Bank. The European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, found maladministration and in January 2018 recommended that its president, Mario Draghi, suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, a forum whose members include private bankers; the bank declined and Draghi did not suspend it. On 18 May 2015 board member Benoît Cœuré told a private evening event in London that the bank would front-load its asset purchases, and the speech was published only the next morning, which the bank put down to an internal procedure error; Draghi said no market-sensitive information was revealed. Seven career moves between the bank and private finance are recorded, among them Tom Dechaene, who came from Deutsche Bank and the London merchant bank Morgan Grenfell and was made a director by a royal decree of 13 December 2014; those are job changes, not accusations. Most of the bank's 227,402.4 kilograms of gold is stored at the Bank of England, a much smaller portion at the Bank for International Settlements and the Bank of Canada, and a very limited quantity in the bank's own premises — storage, not management of the holding.
p:KEN: The Central Bank of Kenya is the country's central bank and issues its money. Three cases are on file. In the Goldenberg scandal, the government paid cash subsidies for fictitious gold and diamond exports under President Daniel arap Moi. In March 2006 prosecutors indicted five people, including former governor Kotut and former deputy governor Riungu. They are charged, which is unproven. On 23 March 2006 governor Andrew Mullei was charged with four counts of abuse of office, including hiring his son as a consultant. He denied awarding Sh9 million in contracts irregularly, and no court outcome was found. From 2015 to 2018, Kenya's anti-corruption commission investigated current and former officials over the collapse of Imperial Bank, whose directors said bank officers helped embezzle Sh34 billion. That is under investigation and unproven. One career move is on record. A Kenyan government sector profile says Sheila M'mbijjewe was appointed deputy governor by the President in June 2015 and sat on the bank's Monetary Policy Committee for nine years, and that she had served on the boards of several companies, as a director of Standard Chartered Bank, a non-executive director of Ecobank and a board member of PricewaterhouseCoopers; it gives no dates for those roles. Kenya scores 38 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:ARG: Argentina's money is the peso, issued by the Central Bank of the Argentine Republic, which scores 39 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Luis Caputo, its president from June 2018 until he resigned on 25 September 2018, had headed bond and equity trading at JP Morgan Argentina in the 1990s and presided over Deutsche Bank in Argentina from 2003 to 2008. In January 2010 the government called on governor Martin Redrado to resign after he refused to back a decree releasing 6.6 billion dollars of reserves, then fired him; he resigned that month, the reserves stayed frozen and a court held that the full Congress had to approve their use. Fifteen people, among them Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner and economy minister Axel Kicillof, were tried over the bank's 2015 dollar-futures sales, and the case against all of them was dismissed on 13 April 2021. In May 2023, an election year, the bank advanced a further 140 billion pesos to the Treasury, using 99.2 per cent of the limit agreed with the International Monetary Fund. It is examining at least 900 million dollars bought at the official rate in 2022 and 2023 that allegedly reached the parallel market; the firms deny it and nothing is proven. Its notes have moved around: the state mint, Casa de Moneda, printed 1,000- and 2,000-peso notes under contracts of November 2021, September 2022 and February 2023, the bank partly cancelled them and the mint stopped printing at 10pm on 28 October 2024. Production of the 2,000-peso note had gone to Spain's Fábrica Nacional de Moneda y Timbre, and 20,000-peso notes were imported from China. In July 2026 President Javier Milei announced a bill to bar the bank from funding the state.
p:MEX: Mexico's money is the Mexican peso, and its central bank is the Bank of Mexico, known as Banxico, one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Mexico scores 32 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. On 9 December 2020 the Senate approved a bill from Morena's Senate leader Ricardo Monreal obliging the bank to buy foreign banknotes and coins that commercial banks collect and cannot send back to the country they came from. The bank said the same day that this would violate the autonomy the Constitution gives it, because the law itself would fix the active operations it must carry out, and that those operations are high risk and could compromise its holdings of international reserves. It answered the premise with figures: foreign cash is less than 1 per cent of remittances sent to Mexico, and of the foreign cash that entered the country in the first nine months of 2020 the banks placed or repatriated 98 per cent themselves. Governor Alejandro Diaz de Leon said the bank could challenge the law in the Supreme Court, and that foreign authorities could bar it from transacting with counterparts abroad or freeze and confiscate reserves. Monreal said it was no attack on the bank's autonomy. The lower house never carried it. On 23 March 2022 President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador announced the bank's unanimous rate rise, from 6 to 6.5 per cent, before the bank published it; on 25 March he said finance minister Rogelio Ramirez de la O, who sits in on board meetings, had told him the evening before, and he apologised to the governor and accepted that the Bank of Mexico law had been violated. Deputy governor Gerardo Esquivel called it an error rather than a leak. People also move between the bank and private finance: Agustin Carstens came from deputy managing director of the International Monetary Fund to be governor from 1 January 2010 to 31 December 2015, and former governor Guillermo Ortiz became chairman of BTG Pactual's Mexico business from 1 January 2016. The bank makes its own notes in every denomination, at two factories of its own in Mexico City and El Salto, Jalisco; the notes it first circulated in 1925 were made by the American Bank Note Company of New York, and printing moved in-house in 1969. Note Printing Australia also says it has supplied the bank with polymer banknotes.
p:IND: India's money is the rupee and its central bank is the Reserve Bank of India, which scores 32 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. One case is recorded and unproven: in December 2016, while 500 and 1,000 rupee notes were being withdrawn from circulation, the Central Bureau of Investigation arrested bank official K. Michael in Bangalore and charged him with converting 15 million rupees of withdrawn notes into 100 rupee notes without legal documentation, with a state bank employee. On 10 December 2018 governor Urjit Patel resigned, giving only personal reasons; media reports said he was annoyed by repeated government efforts to influence policy after a public spat. In September 2010 banknote paper supplier De La Rue said some employees had deliberately falsified paper test certificates, which was reportedly followed by suspension of supply to the bank. Three leaders came from elsewhere: Duvvuri Subbarao, governor from 2008 to 2013, had been a lead economist at the World Bank; Raghuram Rajan was the International Monetary Fund's chief economist from 2003 to 2006 before his appointment in 2013; and Patel arrived as deputy governor in January 2013 from the Fund, Reliance Industries and Boston Consulting Group. Part of India's gold is kept in safe custody with the Bank of England and the Bank for International Settlements, which is storage, not management of the money.
p:EST: Estonia uses the euro, so interest rates are set not by the Bank of Estonia but by the European Central Bank, for the 21 European Union countries that use the currency. The one Estonian case ended in acquittal: on 5 March 1999 the Tallinn City Court found Siim Kallas, a former head of the bank, and Kaju not guilty of abuse of power and of submitting false information over the loss of 10 million US dollars from the North Estonian Bank, a charge of preparing to embezzle having been dropped two weeks earlier; the prosecutor, Jaan Naaber, appealed ten days later. Two findings concern the European Central Bank. In January 2018 the European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, found maladministration and recommended that President Mario Draghi give up his membership of the Group of Thirty, a private forum of central bankers and bank executives; the bank declined and he kept it. And on 18 May 2015 board member Benoît Cœuré told a private London event that the bank would front-load its asset purchases, the speech appearing only the next morning, which the bank put down to an internal procedure error. Six career moves between that bank and private finance are recorded, among them Jorg Asmussen going to the bank Lazard. The Estonian bank's other ties are to the auditors Ernst & Young Baltic AS and Forvis Mazars and to the fund managers BlackRock, PIMCO, Informed Portfolio Management, Goldman Sachs Asset Management and Schroder Investment Management. Its Annual Report for 2019 says that at the end of that year the bank had four external asset managers, that the programme runs on overlay mandates with the managers expressing most strategies through derivative instruments, and that PIMCO had worked for it since 2005, Informed Portfolio Management since 2007, and the other two since 2017. No mandate size and no share of the reserves is given, and that position is as at 31 December 2019. It scores 19 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. At the end of September 2017 five members of the Riigikogu, from the EKRE, Vabaerakond and Keskerakond groups, initiated a bill to compensate holders of VEB Fund certificates out of Eesti Pank's profit distributions, under which parliament would direct 50 per cent of the bank's annual distribution, 10 to 15 million euros, to the certificate holders. Eesti Pank replied that its own council decides how its profit is distributed.
p:MLT: Malta uses the euro, so its interest rates are set by the European Central Bank, in which the Central Bank of Malta takes part. Its own case concerns governor Edward Scicluna, a former finance minister: on 29 May 2024 he pleaded not guilty to fraud over the government's handling of a private hospital contract, the Vitals concession, while he was minister, and the charges remain unproven. He stepped aside in July 2024, deputy governor Alexander Demarco replacing him, after a cabinet meeting appeared to reach a compromise; he had insisted he would not resign, Prime Minister Robert Abela insisted on the presumption of innocence, and he kept his salary, reported at 138,000 euros. He was reinstated in July 2025 after the European Central Bank was consulted and raised no objections. Two further findings sit at the European Central Bank: the European Ombudsman found maladministration over president Mario Draghi's membership of the Group of Thirty, a club of central bankers and private bankers, and recommended in January 2018 that he suspend it, which the bank declined and he did not; and a speech of 18 May 2015 to a private London event was published only the next morning, which the bank put down to an internal procedure error. Malta's own share of the European Central Bank's US dollar pooled reserves is not run from Malta: the Central Bank of Ireland has managed it since 1 January 2008, at Malta's own request. Each euro-area country transferred foreign reserves to the ECB in proportion to its shareholding, and the ECB says those reserves are managed in a decentralised way by the national central banks on a disclosed agency basis; Malta is the one that handed the job to another country's central bank. Its books have been checked from outside by two firms: KPMG for the financial years 2019 to 2025 and Deloitte Audit Ltd for 2023 to 2027. Malta scores 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed.
p:JPN: The Bank of Japan issues the yen and has capital of 100 million yen, of which the government holds 55 percent and private investors 45 percent through subscription certificates traded on the Tokyo Stock Exchange. Those holders have no say in running it, and the bank does not name them. One case is on file: in June 2006 governor Fukui apologised and took a 30 percent pay cut for six months after disclosing that he had kept a 10 million yen investment, made in 1999, in a fund run by Yoshiaki Murakami, who was arrested for insider trading; by then the stake was worth 22 million yen. The bank said he broke no law or internal rule, and he did not resign. Nine people have moved between its Policy Board and private finance, among them Atsushi Mizuno, who joined Credit Suisse the month after his term. Japan scores 39 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. The sharpest pressure on the bank was legal rather than personal. From December 2012 Prime Minister Shinzo Abe repeatedly said his government would revise the 1998 law that guarantees the bank's independence unless it adopted a 2 percent inflation target, and his coalition held enough seats to pass such a bill. The bank adopted the target and an open-ended asset purchase commitment on 22 January 2013, in a joint statement with the government, and the government then said there was less need to change the law. Officials inside the bank described the outcome as fending off the most serious threat to its independence in fifteen years.
p:BGR: Bulgaria's central bank is the Bulgarian National Bank. On 1 January 2026 the country swapped the lev for the euro at 1.95583 lev to the euro and joined the Eurosystem, the group of national central banks that works with the European Central Bank, so its governor now sits on the body that sets interest rates. Its own large case concerns Corporate Commercial Bank, Corpbank, which collapsed in June 2014: prosecutors charged two former deputy governors responsible for supervision with failing, from February 2010, to take the measures the law required against the bank, allegedly to benefit its shareholders. Gounev was charged in June 2014 and removed from office by court order that December, and Simeonov about ten months later; neither charge is proven, and the accusation that Corpbank's majority owner embezzled 206 million leva is likewise unproven. The state's Bulgarian National Audit Office checks the books under a continuing legal mandate, Oberthur Fiduciaire AD has handled banknote production since 2014, and Louisenthal supplied the thread, foil and watermark for the 100-lev note that became legal tender on 28 December 2018. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, and belongs to the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, which offers advice, training or asset management without the page saying which Bulgaria uses. About 60 per cent of its 41 tonnes of gold sits outside its own vaults, stored at the Bank of England, which stores the metal rather than managing it. Two findings sit at the European Central Bank: the European Ombudsman found maladministration over President Mario Draghi's membership of the Group of Thirty, a forum whose members include private bankers, and recommended in January 2018 that he suspend it, which the ECB declined; and a speech by Coeure to a private London event on 18 May 2015 about front-loading asset purchases was published only the following morning, which the ECB called an internal procedure error. Kalin Hristov, long a member of the Governing Council and deputy governor for the Issue Department, joined the supervisory board of the commercial DSK Bank in August 2025; no ethics finding is recorded. Bulgaria scores 32 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. On 5 March 2015 Parliament voted 84 to 0 to set up an ad hoc committee of inquiry into the collapse of Corporate Commercial Bank, to examine the conduct of the state bodies and institutions meant by law to exercise the control that should have prevented the bank being drained, over the years 2009 to 2014. The Bulgarian National Bank's banking supervision arm is named among those bodies. Before that, on 10 December 2014, the bank published a letter from the European Central Bank signed by Mario Draghi warning that proposed amendments to the deposit insurance law could infringe its independence. The amendments would have obliged the bank to cover any shortfall in the deposit guarantee fund. The letter said the draft would stop the bank investing and managing its own reserves, that transfers to the fund could cut its own resources enough to hinder the work it does within the European System of Central Banks, and that such a transfer could put the stability of Bulgaria's currency board at risk.
p:AUT: Austria uses the euro: the European Central Bank sets its interest rates, for the 21 euro countries together, with the Oesterreichische Nationalbank taking part; the ECB is one of 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. The national bank owns its banknote printer, OeBS, which cooperates with two other central-bank-owned printers. Managers of OeBS paid kickbacks to win orders, overcharging Azerbaijan's central bank by 20 percent and Syria's by 14 percent, about 14 million euros. Seven were convicted in October 2014; after a retrial, a Vienna court in February 2018 gave Wolf and Miller 18-month suspended sentences and Meyer 21 months suspended, and acquitted former deputy governor Duchatczek. In January 2018 the European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, ruled that ECB president Draghi's membership of the Group of Thirty, a club of central bankers and private bankers, was maladministration; the ECB declined to drop it. In 2015 a speech by board member Coeure on front-loading asset purchases reached a private London audience the evening before publication; the ECB called this an internal procedure error. BDO Assurance, elected on 23 March 2023, audited the bank's 2025 accounts. The government that took office in 2017, the People's Party with the Freedom Party, planned to take banking supervision away from the bank. In April 2019 the bank said publicly that this threatened its financial independence: the draft law would have paid 95 percent of its profits to the federal government instead of the 90 percent then in force, which it said cuts its ability to build reserves, and it expected supervision costs to rise under more complicated structures that included three new sections inside the Finance Ministry. The Finance Ministry answered that it was following European best practice, that a payout rate of 95 percent or more existed in countries including the Netherlands, and that the change was structural and aimed at efficiency rather than personal. The reform did not take effect and the bank still supervises banks. Austria scores 24 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Its gold is kept in two places inside the country: the bank says that of Austria's total gold reserves of 280 tons, 140 tons are stored in Austria, 90 tons in its own vaults, and 50 tons sit in the vaults of one of its subsidiaries, Münze Österreich AG, the Austrian Mint; the 280 tons correspond to some 22,400 gold bars. Seven career moves are recorded between the bank or the ECB and private finance: Ewald Nowotny went from chief executive of BAWAG P.S.K. to governor of the Oesterreichische Nationalbank from 2008; Otmar Issing, the ECB's former chief economist, accepted an offer in October 2006 to act as an international adviser to Goldman Sachs; Jörg Asmussen sat on the ECB Executive Board from 2012 to 2013 and moved in 2016 to the investment bank Lazard; José Manuel González-Páramo served on the ECB Executive Board from 2004 to 2012 and was appointed an Executive Board member of BBVA in June 2013; Lorenzo Bini Smaghi sat on the ECB Executive Board from June 2005 to December 2011 and has chaired the board of Société Générale since 2015; Luis de Guindos was Chief Executive Officer Iberia at Lehman Brothers and Chief Executive Officer at Nomura Securities from 2006 to 2008 and has been ECB Vice-President from 2018; and Peter Praet was Chief Economist of Générale de Banque and Fortis Bank from 1988 to 1999 before joining the ECB Executive Board in 2011.
p:IRL: Ireland uses the euro, so its interest rates are set not by the Central Bank of Ireland but by the European Central Bank, for the 21 European Union states that use the currency; Bulgaria joined on 1 January 2026, at 1.95583 lev per euro, and its governor took a seat on the ECB's Governing Council. The Irish bank's books are checked from outside by Grant Thornton Ireland, under a term covering 2023 to 2027, with the Comptroller and Auditor General also auditing the accounts. Its gold bars are held at the Bank of England, which stores them rather than manages them, and the remaining coin stocks stay at the Central Bank of Ireland. The bank also pays outside firms to run its own portfolio of shares, and the contracts are public. A tender with reference 2016P038, for equity management services, went to Amundi Asset Management of 90 Boulevard Pasteur in Paris, for a contract valued at 700,000 euro excluding value added tax. The next round, reference 2022P012, appointed UBS Asset Management (UK) Ltd of 5 Broadgate, London, for a contract valued at 10 million euro excluding value added tax. In 2008 and 2009 the financial regulator, Neary, said he would retire early over the regulator's handling of 87 million euros in secret directors' loans at Anglo Irish Bank; an internal committee found the matter, discovered in January 2008, was not pursued, partly because a letter from Anglo went missing, and Neary said he was not told until the finance minister raised it in December 2008. Two further findings sit at the European Central Bank. In case 1697/2016/ANA the European Ombudsman found maladministration and in January 2018 recommended that president Mario Draghi suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, a club whose members include central bankers and private bankers, saying it was not in keeping with the ECB's independence; the bank declined and he kept it. And a speech of 18 May 2015, in which Coeure told a private evening event in London that the bank would front-load asset purchases, was published only the next morning, which the bank put down to an internal procedure error; Draghi said no market-sensitive information was revealed. Seven career moves run between these banks and private finance, among them Matthew Elderfield, the Irish deputy governor and financial regulator, hired by Lloyds Banking Group as director for conduct and compliance from October 2013, and Otmar Issing, a former ECB chief economist who became an international adviser to Goldman Sachs in 2006. The sharpest pressure on Ireland's central bank came from outside the country. Emergency lending to banks is paid out by the Central Bank of Ireland but has to be allowed by the European Central Bank's governing council, and on 19 November 2010 the ECB's president, Jean-Claude Trichet, wrote to the finance minister, Brian Lenihan, in a letter marked secret, saying that further emergency lending would be authorised only if Ireland committed in writing to apply for an international rescue programme, along with commitments on austerity, bank recapitalisation and repayment of the liquidity. Support to Irish banks had passed 50 billion euros by then. Lenihan, who had insisted publicly the week before that Ireland needed no bailout, wrote back accepting that Sunday, and Ireland applied on 21 November. The ECB refused to publish the letter for four years and released it on 6 November 2014, after the European Ombudsman and an Irish member of the European Parliament pressed for it and after The Irish Times had obtained and printed it; the ECB's statement with the release said documentation showed domestic factors pushed Ireland towards the programme. Ireland scores 25 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, less exposed than 85 percent of the 194 places with a figure.
p:LTU: Lithuania uses the euro, so the Bank of Lithuania does not set interest rates itself: the European Central Bank sets them for the 21 countries that share the currency. Lithuania's own case ended in acquittal. An official who monitored the commercial bank Snoras was sacked in November 2011 and charged with letting Snoras keep information from the bank's leadership, including on assets in Swiss banks; a guilty verdict in March 2014 was annulled by a Vilnius court, which found that no crime had been committed, and that ruling can still be appealed to the Supreme Court. The closing of Snoras was faulted too: in May 2012 a parliamentary commission chaired by Valentinas Mazuronis found the bank had acted too fast and with too little reasoning, the takeover of the shares in the public interest and the start of bankruptcy proceedings both hasty. Two further cases sit at the European Central Bank. In case 1697/2016/ANA the European Ombudsman found maladministration and in January 2018 recommended that president Mario Draghi suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, a forum where central bankers sit alongside private financiers such as Citi's chief executive Jane Fraser; the bank declined. On 18 May 2015 one of its officials, Coeure, told a private evening event in London that it would bring forward its asset purchases, and the speech was published only the next morning, which the bank put down to an internal procedure error; Draghi said no market-sensitive information had been revealed. Six of that bank's officials have moved to or from private finance, among them Otmar Issing, its former chief economist, who in 2006 took what he called a loose advisory position with Goldman Sachs. Lithuania's 5.8 tonnes of gold, 466 bars, are all held at the Bank of England as custodian, none at home. UAB ROSK Consulting audits its accounts for 2025 to 2027, and it scores 22 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:HRV: Croatia uses the euro, so the European Central Bank sets its monetary policy, for 21 countries in all; the ECB is also one of 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. The country's own central bank is the Croatian National Bank. In January 2022, after media reports, the Zagreb prosecution and the financial regulator HANFA opened inquiries into whether senior bank officials had traded securities of commercial banks they supervise on inside information. The bank said its executives sold shares before the ban took effect and that trading bonds was not prohibited; the inquiries remain open and nothing is proven. Two further cases concern the ECB: between 2016 and 2018 the European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, found maladministration over ECB president Draghi's membership of the Group of Thirty, a private forum of bankers, and the ECB declined its recommendation that he give it up; and in 2015 a speech on asset purchases was published only the morning after a private London event, which the ECB called an internal procedure error. Ernst & Young d.o.o. audits the Croatian bank's accounts for 2025 to 2027. Croatia scores 29 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. On 4 October 2016 the Ministry of Finance asked the European Central Bank for an opinion on a draft act amending the Act on the Croatian National Bank, and the ECB replied on 28 October 2016 in Opinion CON/2016/52. The draft would have let the State Audit Office carry out an annual audit of the bank's business operations and made the bank's reports subject to a parliamentary adoption vote. The ECB said the parliamentary vote would affect the bank's institutional independence, and that the draft was unclear, contradictory and failed to satisfy the requirements and safeguards it set out.
p:SVK: Slovakia uses the euro, so the National Bank of Slovakia does not set interest rates; the European Central Bank does that for the 21 euro countries. The Slovak bank is also one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, whose capital is held by central banks alone. Slovakia's own case ended in a conviction: on 29 May 2025 the Specialised Criminal Court found the sitting governor, Kazimir, guilty of paying a 48,000 euro bribe in 2017 and 2018, while he was finance minister, to the head of the tax office in connection with audits of private companies, and fined him 200,000 euros. He denied wrongdoing and said he would appeal, and the offence predates his central bank post. Two findings concern the European Central Bank. The European Ombudsman found maladministration over president Draghi's membership of the Group of Thirty, a private forum of central bankers and bank executives, and recommended in January 2018 that he suspend it; the ECB declined and he did not. And Coeure's remark to a private London event on 18 May 2015 that the ECB would front-load asset purchases was published only the next morning, which the ECB put down to an internal procedure error. The Slovak bank owns 31.694 tonnes of gold in bars, stored for it by the Bank of England as depositary, which safekeeps rather than manages it. Deloitte Audit s.r.o. audited its accounts and Grant Thornton Audit, s.r.o. is the approved auditor for 2024 to 2027. Governor Jozef Makuch told the bank's Banking Council on 27 November 2018 that he would leave in March 2019, two years before his term ended, so that his successor would be chosen before the 2020 general election rather than by the parliament that followed it; he argued that appointing a governor early would strengthen the bank's independence, and no source reports anyone pressing him to go. He stayed until Kazimir was appointed on 1 June 2019. Slovakia scores 25 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Part of its reserves is run from outside, in one fund. The bank's Annual Report for 2020 says its renminbi investment is made through the BISIP CNY, which footnote 3 describes as an open-ended fund of Chinese government bonds managed by the Bank for International Settlements in Basel, with a market value of about 47 million US dollars at the end of 2020 and a balance-sheet line of its own. The audited statements say the same from the other side, valuing the holding on data the Bank for International Settlements supplies monthly. The bank's separate equity portfolio of exchange-traded funds, 236 million euros at the same date, names no manager and is not counted here.
p:LVA: Latvia uses the euro, so policy is set by the European Central Bank for the 21 countries on the currency, and the Bank of Latvia takes part in it; the Latvian bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the bank central banks use among themselves. Former governor Ilmars Rimsevics was convicted of taking a bribe and other material inducements by the Riga District Court on 20 December 2023, sentenced to six years in prison with a five-year ban on public office, and lost about 25,000 euro and several properties to confiscation; he was tried alongside the businessman Maris Martinsons. Parliament had moved on the bank's rules while he was still in post: on 22 February 2018 the Saeima sent draft amendments to the Law on the Bank of Latvia to its committees, proposed by lawmakers of the Unity faction, which would limit the governor to two successive terms and would allow the bank's top officials to be suspended if they become suspects or defendants in criminal proceedings. The proposal came days after the Corruption Prevention and Combating Bureau detained Rimsevics, who denied the allegations and refused to resign. Two further matters concern the European Central Bank. From 2016 to 2018 the European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, found maladministration and in January 2018 recommended that president Mario Draghi suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, a private forum of central bankers and bank executives; the bank declined and he did not. On 18 May 2015 Cœuré told a private London event the bank would front-load asset purchases, and the speech appeared only the next morning, which the bank called an internal procedure error; Draghi said no market-sensitive information was revealed. Six officials have moved between that bank and private finance, among them Otmar Issing, who became an international adviser to Goldman Sachs in 2006, with no ethics finding attached. Latvia's gold is stored at the Bank of England, which is custody of a reserve asset rather than management of money, and the bank manages its yen share of euro reserves jointly with the Oesterreichische Nationalbank. KPMG Baltics SIA audits its accounts for 2025 to 2029; Forvis Mazars audits the European Central Bank for 2025 to 2029, where BlackRock was also hired to help design asset-backed securities purchases. Latvia scores 23 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed.
p:SVN: Slovenia uses the euro, so the Bank of Slovenia does not set interest rates itself; the European Central Bank sets them for the 21 countries using the euro. Both are among the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. The main local matter is the 2013 bank bailout, in which a 960 million euro bail-in, meaning losses forced on investors, hit about 100,000 junior bondholders and shareholders. Police have filed a second criminal complaint alleging abuse of office over it, after a 2016 attempt hit a dead end over procedural errors; the specialised prosecutor has asked the court to investigate, so nothing is proven. That inquiry included a search of the bank's premises on 6 July 2016, over which the European Central Bank's President wrote to Slovenia's prosecutor general and to the European Commission about information seized. The police took all communications from the governor's email account, every electronic document in his workspace and on his laptop dated between 2012 and 2014 whatever its content, part of the paper files in his office from those years and documents from the bank's central IT server, and went ahead without involving the European Central Bank after the bank objected. On 17 December 2020 the Court of Justice of the European Union held, in Commission v Slovenia, that the material seized must have included documents forming part of the European Central Bank's archives and that Slovenia had infringed their inviolability; it also held that Slovenia then failed to cooperate, by not letting the bank identify which seized documents related to central bank tasks and by not returning even those the authorities themselves regarded as irrelevant to the investigation. Two findings concern the European Central Bank itself: on 18 May 2015 Benoit Coeure told a private London event it would front-load asset purchases before the speech was published; and in January 2018 the European Ombudsman found maladministration and asked Mario Draghi to suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, a private forum of central bankers and financiers, which the bank declined. Six career moves are recorded between that board and private finance, among them Otmar Issing advising Goldman Sachs and Lorenzo Bini Smaghi leaving to chair Societe Generale, with no ethics finding on them. Slovenia scores 24 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:MYS: Bank Negara Malaysia is the country's central bank and issues the ringgit. Malaysia scores 32 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Two bribery cases are recorded, both from banknote printing. In July 2011 the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission charged former official Mohamad Daud with taking two bribes of 50,000 ringgit in 2004 and 2005 over a 95 million ringgit contract for the five-ringgit polymer note, won by Note Printing Australia; the court acquitted him on 6 December 2015 and the Attorney-General withdrew the appeal in February 2016. In October 2011 Securency and Note Printing Australia, both belonging to the Reserve Bank of Australia, pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to provide benefits to foreign public officials to win banknote business with Malaysia's note-issuing authority between October 2001 and December 2003; no Malaysian official was named, and they paid 19,809,772 and 1,856,710 Australian dollars. Zeti Akhtar Aziz, governor for 16 years until 2016, became group chairman of the fund manager Permodalan Nasional Bhd. The bank's leadership changed hands under political conflict once. In late August 1998, during the Asian financial crisis, governor Ahmad Mohd Don and his deputy Fong Weng Phak resigned in disagreement with the government's currency plans. He had favoured tight monetary policy and was backed by the finance minister, while the prime minister and his special functions minister wanted an expansionary course and had attacked the governor publicly over it. A row over how the new currency controls were to be carried out prompted both resignations. The finance minister was sacked days later; Zeti Akhtar Aziz was appointed acting governor on 31 August 1998, and capital controls and a ringgit peg to the dollar followed the next day.
p:HUN: The Magyar Nemzeti Bank issues Hungary's forint and owns outright the company that prints the notes. Hungary scores 32 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. In July 2010 the cabinet went ahead with a bill cutting governor Andras Simor's monthly pay by 75 percent, from about 8 million to 2 million forints, under a cap on all public pay; the European Central Bank said such changes should apply only to future appointments. In December 2011 parliament's constitutional committee tabled an amendment merging the bank with the financial regulator under a head appointed by President Pal Schmitt on Prime Minister Viktor Orban's nomination, cutting Simor to deputy, and Simor said he refused what he called bullying. On 12 March 2024 the bank said a proposed law widening its supervisory board's control could erode its independence. The Constitutional Court ruled on 31 March 2016 that the foundations the bank endowed in 2014 with over 267 billion forints were managing public money, and the Public Procurement Board fined six of them 200,000 forints each. In March 2025 the State Audit Office found mismanagement and losses of hundreds of billions of forints there and filed a criminal complaint. On 21 October 2026 former governor Gyorgy Matolcsy was detained on suspicion of economic fraud and use of a forged private document, which is unproven.
p:GRC: Greece uses the euro, so its interest rates are set by the European Central Bank. The Bank of Greece is unusual in being a listed company: 19,864,886 of its shares trade in Athens. The Greek State holds 1,774,088 of them, 8.93 percent, after taking over 1,309,210 shares from DEKA S.A. when that body was dissolved under a law of 2011. A social security fund, e-EFKA, is listed at 12.4402 percent as of 7 August 2020, but that figure comes from Wikipedia and is not confirmed in a filing by the bank. From the spring of 2015 the SYRIZA government and the party press attacked the governor, Yannis Stournaras, who had been finance minister in the previous conservative-led government. The party's parliamentary spokesman, Nikos Filis, said on party radio that Stournaras was undermining the negotiations with creditors; the party-affiliated newspaper Avgi called the bank an organ working against the government; and the government issued a non-paper telling the bank to investigate a leak to a journalist. Handelsblatt reported that Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras wanted to replace him with someone he trusted, and Bloomberg reported on 13 May 2015 that the European Central Bank was concerned about the pressure and publicly backed him. The Speaker of Parliament, Zoi Konstantopoulou, returned his June 2015 monetary policy report as unacceptable. In September 2016 corruption prosecutors raided his home over his wife's alleged role in an advertising case, and in February 2019 a deputy health minister, Pavlos Polakis, leaked a recording of a telephone call in which he had raised his own bank loan with the governor; Stournaras called that a preposterous attempt to interfere and asked Tsipras to protect the bank's independence. The bribery case against him collapsed: on 29 August 2019 prosecutors dropped charges that he had taken bribes from the drug company Novartis while he was finance minister, along with charges against six other former senior officials; the allegations reached back to 2001 and predated his central bank post. Two findings concern the European Central Bank, where the European Ombudsman found maladministration and recommended in January 2018 that President Mario Draghi give up his membership of the Group of Thirty, a private forum of central bankers and bank executives, which the bank declined to do, and where a speech of 18 May 2015 told a private London audience about front-loaded asset purchases before it was published. Georgios Provopoulos, governor from June 2008 to 2014, came straight from Greek private banking, having advised Alpha Bank from 1993, held a management role at Emporiki Bank from 2004 and been vice president and chief executive of Piraeus Bank from 2006 to 2008. Greece scores 32 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:TUR: Turkiye's money is the Turkish lira, issued by the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkiye, which has shareholders: at the end of 2025 the Ministry of Treasury and Finance held 55.12 per cent, a share the law bars from falling below 51, the state-owned Ziraat Bankasi 19.22 per cent and Mervak Ic ve Dis Ticaret 5.12 per cent. Four governors have been removed by presidential decree: Murat Cetinkaya in July 2019, after the bank held its rate at 24 per cent; Murat Uysal on 7 November 2020, after the lira lost 30 per cent of its value that year; Naci Agbal on 20 March 2021, four months in and after a rate rise; and Sahap Kavcioglu on 8 June 2023, having cut rates from 19 to 8.5 per cent. His replacement, Hafize Gaye Erkan, joined Goldman Sachs in 2005, was a managing director by 2011 and went to First Republic Bank in 2014, becoming co-chief executive in 2021. Government pressure was reported in 23 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, all of it for lower rates and 21 of those quarters in election periods. In October 2025 Istanbul prosecutors took former deputy governor Sener and six others into custody and arrested him, in an investigation into corruption and tender-rigging in two 2023 tenders at the Interbank Card Center, the national payment network the bank majority-owns; that investigation is open and nothing is proven. The notes are printed at the Banknote Printing Plant, which operates under the bank itself. About 34 tonnes of its gold sit in its own vaults, about 382.9 tonnes are stored at the Turkish exchange company Borsa Istanbul and about 119.2 tonnes at the Bank of England, all safekeeping rather than management. It scores 48 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:BGD: Bangladesh Bank issues the taka, printed at Gazipur by the Security Printing Corporation (Bangladesh) Ltd, known locally as Takshal. On the night of 4 February 2016 attackers used the bank's access to SWIFT, the network banks use to send payment instructions, to take reserves from its account at the New York Federal Reserve: 101 million dollars by The Daily Star's figure, 81 million extracted by Prothom Alo's. A government inquiry's final report of 30 May 2016 hinted that central bank officials were involved, but it was never published and no one had been punished as of 2019. Governor Atiur Rahman resigned on 15 March 2016, having been criticised for not telling Finance Minister Abul Maal Abdul Muhith, who called the bank's handling very incompetent. The Anti-Corruption Commission prosecuted Atiur in February 2025 over the AnonTex loan scam and in June 2025 opened an investigation into him over alleged abuse of power and the Hallmark and S Alam Group frauds; former deputy governor SK Sur was arrested on 14 January 2025 for failing to submit an asset statement, after a 2022 investigation into allegations he helped and gained from PK Halder's loan scam. Neither is proven. Governor Abdur Rouf Talukder resigned on 9 August 2024 citing health, three days after more than a hundred of the bank's own staff stormed his office demanding he go. Its gold is stored abroad rather than managed for it: the Bank of England holds about 188,927 troy ounces, used in lending, Standard Chartered 92,739 ounces and HSBC 93,535. One career move runs out of the bank into private banking: Md. Khurshid Alam joined Bangladesh Bank as an assistant director in 1988, worked in banking regulation, bank inspection and small-business programmes, was made deputy governor in February 2024 on a three-year contract and forced to resign that August after the political transition, and was appointed chairman of Islami Bank Bangladesh PLC, which the report calls a private sector bank, on 24 May 2026. Bangladesh scores 41 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed. Bangladesh Bank's own accounts are audited by two Dhaka firms together, Howladar Yunus & Co. and ACNABIN, whose joint report for 2024-2025 was signed on 26 August 2025 and is addressed to the Government rather than to the bank's board.
p:CYP: Cyprus uses the euro, so interest rates for the Central Bank of Cyprus are set by the European Central Bank, for the 21 countries on the currency. It scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Former governor Christodoulos Christodoulou and five others were charged with corruption, money laundering and abuse of office over a payment of 1 million euros made in 2007 by a Greek businessman through Focus Maritime Corporation; on 31 July 2020 judges dismissed the case, ruling he should not be tried twice, and he said he was not bribed. In 2014 he pleaded guilty to six tax offences over the undeclared payment and was jailed for five months, and he faced 29 further charges, none proven, over a payment said to have been made so he would overlook Andreas Vgenopoulos and Marfin Investment Group taking control of Laiki Bank. Governor Panicos Demetriades resigned in March 2014, giving no reason, after the President of Cyprus said he would start proceedings to remove him for not doing his job properly; PricewaterhouseCoopers Limited checked the accounts from outside for 2018 to 2022, and Baker Tilly Klitou and Partners Limited holds that work for 2023 to 2027.
p:NLD: The Netherlands uses the euro, whose rates the European Central Bank sets for the 21 countries on it, and De Nederlandsche Bank is the Dutch central bank inside that system; it scores 23 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. In June 2010 the Scheltema committee, set up by finance minister Wouter Bos, found that the bank had fallen seriously short in supervising DSB bank, missing flaws when licensing DSB in 2005 and being too patient afterwards, though it thought a different approach probably would not have prevented DSB's collapse. Parliament pressed the bank hard after that report: members called for a major overhaul of how it operates, the Christian Democrats said it had seriously fallen short as a regulator and that president Nout Wellink should explain publicly how he would restore its credibility, the GroenLinks member Jolande Sap said it would be very difficult to keep him on, and Roland van Vliet of the Freedom Party asked finance minister Jan Kees de Jager to sack him with a year of his term still to run. On 1 July 2010 the lower house voted on a motion of no confidence in Wellink and he survived it. He accepted the report's conclusions, which several members said was enough for them, and left at the end of his term in 2011. Two further findings sit at the European Central Bank: the European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, found maladministration over president Mario Draghi's membership of the Group of Thirty, a forum of central bankers and private financiers, and in January 2018 recommended he suspend it, which the bank declined and he did not; and a board member's 18 May 2015 remarks in London that the bank would front-load asset purchases were published only the next morning, which the bank put down to an internal procedure error. Wim Duisenberg joined the Dutch bank in 1981 and became chairman in 1982, after three years at the International Monetary Fund and a seat on Rabobank's board. Most of its gold is stored for it rather than managed: 32 per cent at the Bank of England, 18.5 per cent at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and 18.5 per cent at the Royal Canadian Mint in Ottawa. EY Accountants B.V. audits the accounts for 2026 to 2032. The bank is unusually open about where its gold is. Its own website gives the split in plain words: 31 per cent, about 200,000 kilograms, at its own Cash Centre at Zeist, 32 per cent in the vaults of the Bank of England in London, 18.5 per cent at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and 18.5 per cent at the Royal Canadian Mint in Ottawa, out of more than 612 tonnes worth 72.2 billion euros at the end of 2025. Most central banks disclose nothing of the sort, or bury a single line in a note to the accounts.
p:FRA: France uses the euro, so the Bank of France does not set rates on its own; the European Central Bank does that for the 21 countries using the currency. France scores 20 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Jean-Claude Trichet, while governor, was charged with spreading false information and publishing inexact accounts of the state-owned bank Crédit Lyonnais for 1991 to mid-1993, and prosecutors asked for a ten-month suspended sentence; in June 2003 judges cleared him, writing that he had only imprecise or incorrect information about the losses. Jacques de Larosière, a Banque de France governor at the time, was accused alongside him, and the verdict for him is not stated. Two findings stand against the European Central Bank: the European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, found maladministration and in January 2018 recommended that Mario Draghi suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, which the bank declined and he did not do; and on 18 May 2015 Benoît Cœuré told a private London event that the bank would front-load asset purchases, the speech appearing only the next morning, which the bank called an internal procedure error and which Draghi said revealed nothing market-sensitive. François Villeroy de Galhau was chief operating officer of the BNP Paribas group until 1 May 2015 and took office as governor on 1 November 2015. The bank prints more than 2.5 billion notes a year at its own works at Chamalières, and stores its gold, 2,436.8 tonnes at the end of May 2023, mainly in its own vault 27 metres underground.
p:LKA: The Central Bank of Sri Lanka issues the rupee. It scores 34 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, its weakest side being corruption and secrecy around it, at 63. On 14 November 2023 a majority of a five-judge Supreme Court bench ruled that the three Rajapaksa brothers, former governors Cabraal and Lakshman and members of the bank's Monetary Board violated the public trust in their handling of the economy, leading to the 2022 crisis. In June 2019 the Attorney General filed a 23-count indictment against former governor Arjuna Mahendran and nine others over a February 2015 treasury bond auction; these are charges, not findings. Mahendran's term ended on 30 June, and he told the Monetary Board he would not seek reappointment until the parliamentary committee COPE finished its bond inquiry. President Maithripala Sirisena, who had said in June 2015 that he should resign, tweeted that he would name a new governor within hours; Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe said Mahendran could not be removed because the charges had never been proved, and nobody was named that day. Sirisena said in 2017 that he personally removed him, and the Auditor General found a loss of 1.6 billion rupees. The notes are printed at De La Rue Lanka Currency & Security Print (Pvt) Ltd in Biyagama, and Note Printing Australia says it has supplied polymer banknotes to the bank.
p:ITA: The Bank of Italy is Italy's central bank, and because Italy uses the euro its interest rates are set by the European Central Bank. It has shareholders: capital of 7.5 billion euro in 300,000 quotas of 25,000 euro each, held by Italian banks, insurers, social security bodies, pension funds and banking foundations, 173 holders on 30 April 2026, with no holder allowed above 5 per cent since 1 January 2022, up from 3 per cent under Law 5/2014. UniCredit sits at that cap with 15,000 quotas, the pension bodies INARCASSA, ENPAM and Cassa Forense hold 14,800 each, Intesa Sanpaolo 14,736, CNPADC 11,000 and BPER Banca 9,765. On 28 May 2011 a Milan court sentenced former governor Antonio Fazio to four years and a 1.5 million euro fine for market rigging in the 2005 attempt by Banca Popolare di Lodi to take over Antonveneta, prosecutors arguing he had favoured Gianpiero Fiorani's bank over ABN Amro; the appeal court cut that to two years and six months on 28 May 2012, and the Court of Cassation made the conviction final on 28 November 2012. Over Unipol's attempted takeover of BNL he was sentenced to three and a half years in October 2011 and then acquitted, with twelve other defendants, on 30 May 2012. Two findings concern the European Central Bank: the European Ombudsman found maladministration and in January 2018 asked Mario Draghi to suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, a private forum of central bankers and bank executives, and the ECB declined, so he kept it; and Coeure's remark to a private London event on 18 May 2015 that the ECB would front-load asset purchases was published only the next morning, which the ECB put down to an internal procedure error. Draghi was vice chairman and managing director of Goldman Sachs International from 2002 to 2005 before becoming governor in 2006. Of its 2,452 tonnes of gold, 1,100 tonnes are stored in the bank's own security rooms at Via Nazionale. Deloitte audits the accounts. Antonio Fazio's departure from the bank in 2005 was itself a case of a government forcing out a governor it could not dismiss. Under the law as it then stood he held office for life, and the government said it had no power to remove him, so he refused for months to go despite calls from across the political spectrum, including from the prime minister. The economy minister resigned in protest in September 2005 at the government's failure to act; his successor said on the day Fazio finally quit, 19 December 2005, that he wanted parliament to change the laws governing the bank so the governor could be replaced, and legislation to that effect was being prepared when the resignation came. The reform that followed ended the open-ended tenure and put a fixed term in its place. Italy scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:POL: Poland's money is the zloty, issued by the National Bank of Poland. Six matters are recorded. In the ArtB cheque-float affair of 1991, those arrested after the company's owners fled included the bank's president, Grzegorz Wojtowicz, who was charged with unintentionally causing bank losses of about 72 billion old zloty; the court acquitted him. In February 2009 the Central Anti-Corruption Bureau detained eight people in a case against the head of a division in the bank's IT and telecommunications department, accused of taking at least 350,000 zloty in bribes to rig tenders between 2001 and 2008; he was charged and nothing is proven. Warsaw's district prosecutors are investigating the disclosure of material classified as secret from the closed part of a Monetary Policy Council meeting on 8 September 2023, and on 12 June 2025 secured documents at the bank's head office after it had twice refused to hand them over. In March 2024 ruling-coalition members of parliament filed a motion to bring the bank's president, Adam Glapinski, before the State Tribunal, the court that hears cases against senior officials, on eight charges, among them bond purchases in 2020 and 2021 said to have indirectly financed the budget deficit by at least 144 billion zloty, and breaching the bank's political neutrality. On 20 August 2024 the Constitutional Tribunal dismissed that attempt, ruling the enabling law unconstitutional; it had earlier held, on 12 January 2024, that a three-fifths majority was needed, where the coalition held 241 of 460 seats against a threshold of 276. A Sejm committee then upheld all eight charges on 9 October 2026, with the full vote still to come in the second half of November 2026; Glapinski and the bank call the accusations groundless, and nothing is proven. Dariusz Filar went from chief economist of Bank Pekao to the Monetary Policy Council, with no ethics finding recorded. Leszek Balcerowicz, governor from 2001 to 2007, is a member of the Group of Thirty, sitting alongside private-sector members including Jane Fraser of Citi, Philipp Hildebrand of BlackRock, Gail Kelly of the UBS Group board, Maria Ramos of Standard Chartered and Guillermo Ortiz of BTG Pactual. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, whose capital is held by central banks alone since private shares were bought back in 2001, and KPMG Audyt Spółka z ograniczoną odpowiedzialnością sp.k. audited its 2025 accounts. The notes are made to the bank's order by Polska Wytwornia Papierow Wartosciowych, and of the 448 tonnes of gold held at the end of December 2024 about three quarters sits abroad, in roughly similar portions in the vaults of the Bank of England and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, which store the bars rather than manage the holding. A bank publication says it moved 100 tons of gold in 2019 from the Bank of England to the domestic vaults, finishing in November that year, and that almost 124 tons were left in the Bank of England after the move; the bank's own text names only domestic vaults, while a research report, In Gold We Trust, says they are in Warsaw and Poznan, which is that report's claim and the bank has not confirmed it. It scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:AUS: The Reserve Bank of Australia issues the Australian dollar, which floats freely. It scores 25 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and no government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. On 14 July 2023 the government announced that governor Philip Lowe would not be reappointed when his term ended that September, breaking the custom by which the two previous governors were each given a second term. Lowe had been widely criticised after telling the public rates were unlikely to rise before 2024 and then raising the cash rate from 0.1 to 4.1 percent; that criticism led the treasurer to commission an independent review of the bank, whose recommendations to change how it is run and how policy is made the government accepted in full. Its one case came out of its own banknote businesses: in October 2011 the subsidiaries Securency and Note Printing Australia pleaded guilty to conspiring to bribe foreign officials to win banknote work from the note-issuing authorities of Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam and Nepal, paying proceeds-of-crime penalties of 19.8 million and 1.86 million Australian dollars and fines of 480,000 and 450,000. Securency's former chief financial officer got a suspended six-month sentence for false accounting in 2012, the agent Radius Christanto a suspended two-year sentence in 2013. Three governors went into private finance on leaving: Ian Macfarlane to the ANZ board in 2007, Glenn Stevens to Macquarie Group in 2017 and Philip Lowe to Barrenjoey in 2024. Almost all its gold, 80 tonnes as at 30 June 2026, sits at the Bank of England, which holds it as bailee: storage, not management, with title staying with the Reserve Bank.
p:ISR: Israel's money is the shekel and its central bank is the Bank of Israel. It scores 26 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and no government pressure was reported between 2010 and 2018. Ministerial pressure came later. Through 2025 finance minister Bezalel Smotrich publicly pressed governor Amir Yaron to cut interest rates, calling the February decision to hold the rate at 4 percent wrong and asking him to reverse it, and on 4 September 2025 telling business leaders that if the governor would not lower rates he would lower taxes instead. The bank answered that the governor and the Monetary Committee decide on professional grounds alone; Smotrich said in the same remarks that the bank's independence was critical and that he had no intention of interfering. On 29 April 2002 State Comptroller Eliezer Goldberg reported that former governor Jacob Frenkel unlawfully received hundreds of thousands of shekels when he resigned, approved by a senior official who reported to him; Goldberg did not say whether the money should be demanded back. On 3 February 2009 Globes reported that a draft comptroller report alleged flaws in the bank's supervision of Bank Hapoalim's sub-prime investments, on which Hapoalim wrote off 1.5 billion dollars; the bank said it had responses to all the points, and this is unproven. A comptroller report on 17 October 2012 found supervision of the bank's reserves dealing deficient as those reserves grew from 28 to 75 billion dollars, with no control over the receipt of bids and the Governor's two committees working without written procedures; the bank said some issues had been corrected during the audit. Four officials have moved between the bank and private finance or international lenders. Frenkel, governor from 1991 to 2000, came from the International Monetary Fund and afterwards chaired Merrill Lynch International, became a vice-chairman of AIG and chaired JPMorgan Chase International; he sits in the Group of Thirty alongside private-sector members such as Jane Fraser of Citi. Stanley Fischer, governor from 2005 to 2013, came from the World Bank, the IMF and Citigroup. Karnit Flug joined the IMF in 1984, the bank's research department in 1988, and became deputy governor in July 2011 and governor on 13 November 2013. BlackRock is an outside manager for the equities and corporate parts of the bank's portfolio and helped build its strategic asset allocation methodology. Ernst & Young's Israeli firm, Kost Forer Gabbay & Kasierer, audits the accounts, and the bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Who prints the shekel rests on an encyclopaedia entry rather than anything the bank publishes: it names Orell Fussli Security Printing of Switzerland, while the bank's own currency pages name no printer.
p:ESP: Spain uses the euro, so the Bank of Spain follows interest rates set by the European Central Bank for 21 countries. It owns four fifths of Imprenta de Billetes S.A., or IMBISA, which prints the euro notes allotted to Spain. In 2002 a Madrid court sentenced De la Concha to six years in prison for falsifying public documents linked to a securities account of former governor Mariano Rubio; a wound-up company, NALVI, had hidden Rubio as the investor from at least 1986, and the ruling could be appealed. On 15 September 2017 the National Court decided not to prosecute the former governor over the 2012 failure of the commercial bank Bankia, and the case was dismissed, a decision described as final. Two further cases sit at the European Central Bank: the European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints watchdog, found maladministration and recommended in January 2018 that Mario Draghi give up his membership of the Group of Thirty, which the bank declined and he did not; and a speech by Benoit Coeure to a private London event on 18 May 2015 was published only the next morning. Miguel Angel Fernandez Ordonez left the bank early under political fire: on 29 May 2012 he told the prime minister he would go on 10 June, a month before his term ended, four days after the BFA-Bankia group said it would need record public support and after figures in the governing party had blamed him publicly for the banking crisis. The day after announcing it he told the Senate he would not give the bank's account of the Bankia collapse because the government wanted him to stay silent, the governing majority having declined to approve his appearance before the Congress. Spain scores 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:PRT: Portugal uses the euro, so interest rates are set by the European Central Bank for all 21 European Union countries on the currency rather than by the Banco de Portugal, which has its notes printed by Valora S.A., a printer it owns. It scores 30 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Governor Carlos Costa says prime minister Antonio Costa telephoned him on 12 April 2016, while the bank was stripping Isabel dos Santos of her fitness to sit on the board of EuroBic, and said the daughter of the president of a country friendly to Portugal could not be treated badly. The two sides agree the call happened and disagree what it was: Observador reported a written message in which the prime minister confirmed the call and said he had considered the removal inopportune, while the prime minister told parliament he had never made any approach in her favour, called the account false and filed a civil action, which the former governor answered with one of his own; both were dropped by agreement in May 2025. The bank did not change the decision and Isabel dos Santos was removed from the board.
