A 600-page report by a committee the bank itself appointed, with technical support from Boston Consulting Group, pointed to failures in its supervision of Banco Espirito Santo going back to the start of the previous decade, and said information on the Espirito Santo group and on the bank's operations in Angola was reportedly not used; the Banco de Portugal twice refused parliament's request for the report. On 20 July 2021 Fernando Anastacio, rapporteur of parliament's inquiry into losses at Novo Banco, presented a draft report saying supervision had failed across the board, which remained a draft that the PSD said its deputies would vote against. The committee approved its final report on 27 July 2021, concluding that the rescue of Banco Espirito Santo and the first capitalisation of Novo Banco, of 4,900 million euros, were a political fraud, with criticism of the Banco de Portugal and the European Commission and no officials named. In April 2019, after an EY audit of the management of Caixa Geral de Depositos, the bank's ethics committee examined governor Carlos Costa's request to be excused from matters concerning that bank, where he had been a board member from 2004 to 2006; no conclusion was published. Two findings concern the European Central Bank itself: the European Ombudsman found maladministration over President Mario Draghi's membership of the Group of Thirty, a forum that includes private financiers, and recommended in January 2018 that he suspend it, which the bank declined; and a speech by Coeure to a private London event on 18 May 2015, saying asset purchases would be front-loaded, was published only the next morning, which the ECB put down to an internal procedure error. Vitor Constancio was governor from 1985 to 1986, an executive director of Banco Portugues de Investimento from 1995 to 2000, governor again until May 2010 and then ECB Vice-President, with no ethics finding recorded. PricewaterhouseCoopers & Associados audits the accounts for 2022 to 2026. Of 382.7 tonnes of gold, about 45 per cent was kept in the bank's own vaults in 2023, 49 per cent at the Bank of England, 5 per cent at the Bank for International Settlements and 1 per cent at the Banque de France; those institutions store the metal, they do not manage it.
p:RUS: The Bank of Russia issues the ruble, and is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the central banks' own bank. It scores 40 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weakest side being corruption and secrecy around it. Government pressure was reported in 5 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, every time to cut rates or loosen policy, with one threat to replace its leaders, one to change its law and one demand that it print money. In October 1994 President Boris Yeltsin fired chairman Viktor Gerashchenko over his part in the Black Tuesday ruble crash and named Tatyana Paramonova in his place; the State Duma rejected her by secret ballot, 107 to 127, opponents saying the constitution barred hiring or firing the bank's chief without the Duma's approval. On 19 October 2005 the Moscow prosecutor's office indicted Alexei Mishin, chief legal expert at the bank's Moscow directorate, and a deputy department head of the Federal Tax Service, for taking a bribe of 1 million US dollars; at the Moscow City Court on 17 April 2007 prosecutors asked for 15 years in a strict-regime colony for Mishin, plus a fraud conviction over an apartment, and 12 years for the tax official Oleg Alekseev, but no verdict has been reported, so nothing is proven. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Western countries immobilised the bank's assets held in their jurisdictions, put at around 300 billion euros worldwide, and on 12 December 2025 the European Union agreed to freeze 210 billion euros of them indefinitely, using Article 122 of the EU treaty in place of six-monthly renewals that Hungary or Slovakia could veto. The Financial Stability Board, the international body that watches for risks to the financial system, lists the bank as a member but notes that the Russian authorities have agreed not to take part in its meetings at present. It holds 2,283 tonnes of gold, the sixth largest holding on the map, and its own statement, quoted by Interfax, is that all of it sits in its own vaults on Russian territory. It has swap lines, standing arrangements to lend each other currency, with China, for 150 billion yuan, and with Kazakhstan, signed on 28 May 2026 for up to three years and worth 35 billion rubles or 225 billion tenge. Oleg Vyugin, a First Deputy Chairman of the bank who was also First Deputy Minister of Finance, held private finance posts as executive vice president of Troika Dialog, senior adviser for Russia and the CIS at Morgan Stanley Bank, chairman of the board of MDM Bank, a board member of Binbank and chairman of the board of Safmar Financial Investments; the CV listing them gives no dates, so the order of the moves is not established, and no ethics finding is recorded. Its accounts are audited by B1 - Audit LLC and by the Accounts Chamber of the Russian Federation. Goznak, owned entirely by the federal government under the Ministry of Finance, prints Russian money, though the page describing it does not name the bank as its customer.
p:PAK: The State Bank of Pakistan is the country's central bank. It scores 34 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. One case from 2025 is alleged and unproven. In August 2025 Pakistan Observer reported, citing internal memos and cash slips, that senior officials including an executive director issued bulk fresh banknotes directly to private brokers, who resold them at premiums, with each transaction netting officials at least 2 million rupees in kickbacks. It said no probe had been opened. The state has also turned its own auditors on the bank: on 8 August 2023 the National Assembly's Public Accounts Committee, chaired by Noor Alam Khan, directed the Auditor General to audit the State Bank over the disbursement of about 1,145 billion rupees in TERF concessional loans, and directed an inquiry into whether those loans went out on merit. In January 2014 governor Yaseen Anwar resigned; the Finance Ministry spokesman said he cited personal reasons, while unnamed senior officials said it covered differences with Finance Minister Ishaq Dar over inflation and reserves. Anwar had come to the bank from private finance, and the bank's own profile of him gives the dates: he trained at JPMorgan Chase in New York from 1973 to 1975, spent about fifteen years at Bank of America from 1976 to 1991 ending as a vice president in its global export finance group, was a vice president at Merrill Lynch in New York and London from 1992 to 2001, and was a non-executive director of United National Bank Ltd. (U.K.) from 2000 to 2006, before being appointed deputy governor on 29 March 2007 and governor on 19 October 2011. Two governors came from the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund: Ishrat Husain, appointed in December 1999, and Reza Baqir, appointed in May 2019 after leading the IMF's Debt Policy Division. KPMG and BDO audit its accounts.
p:CHL: Chile's central bank is the Central Bank of Chile, which issues the Chilean peso. It scores 24 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and no government pressure was reported between 2010 and 2018. The Constitutional Convention elected to write a replacement for the 1980 constitution drafted new articles on the bank, and on 5 April 2022 its president Rosanna Costa wrote to the Convention on the Council's behalf. The main objection was the removal provision: one third of the members of Congress could have asked the Supreme Court to remove councillors, which the bank said exposed it to political judgements that would diminish its autonomy. It asked that the power be limited to a majority of councillors or the President of the Republic, and that productive diversification be struck from its objectives as not a monetary task. Voters rejected the draft on 4 September 2022. Two cases are recorded, both still under investigation. On 24 July 2012 three staff allegedly tried to take about 38 million pesos in banknotes being processed for destruction, and a fourth was detained the next day. In March 2022 someone posing as the finance chief of the US firm RVK sent a false invoice for 205,000 dollars from an address one letter off the real one, and the bank paid; it complained to prosecutors and dismissed its accounting management head on 23 June 2022, who sued in December seeking 267 million pesos. Three officials moved in from finance or international lenders: Joaquin Vial from BBVA, Mario Marcel from the World Bank, and Rodrigo Valdes from BTG Pactual and Barclays Capital. The bank picks and supervises the outside firms running parts of the state's sovereign wealth funds, among them BlackRock, Nomura Asset Management, UBS Asset Management, Mellon Investments Corporation and BNP Paribas Asset Management. Note Printing Australia listed it among its export orders in 2006/07 and KPMG audits the accounts. Its swap line with China, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency, was renewed on 23 October 2026 at about 7.5 billion US dollars equivalent for five years.
p:ZWE: The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe issues the ZiG, which circulates alongside foreign currency. From 2003 to 2013, under governor Gideon Gono, it ran quasi-fiscal activities, handing out cash and farm equipment at events presided over by President Mugabe and raiding private foreign-currency accounts to fund state operations, leaving debts of close to 1.3 billion dollars that a 2014 government bill moved onto taxpayers. In 2009 the Movement for Democratic Change demanded Gono be replaced, saying Western donors would not fund reconstruction until he went; Mugabe said he would stay, and he was not removed. Gono stepped down in December 2013, and in March 2014 finance minister Patrick Chinamasa, citing President Robert Mugabe, announced the appointment of John Mangudya, then chief executive of the Harare-based commercial bank CBZ, to head the bank from 1 May 2014. At a parliamentary Public Accounts Committee hearing in September 2019, deputy governor Mlambo confirmed the bank had issued 663.8 million US dollars in Treasury Bills in 2017 and 2018 to Sakunda Holdings, owned by presidential ally Kudakwashe Tagwirei, on Finance Ministry instruction; the committee also cited a 1.37 billion dollar overdraft issued without parliamentary approval. Both matters stand as official findings. Government pressure was reported in 8 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, always to ease policy. The country's notes are made by a company the bank itself owns: Fidelity Printers and Refiners of Harare, whose own corporate history says it began printing secure banknotes in 1966 in the basement of the old Reserve Bank building on Samora Machel Avenue and moved to purpose-built premises at Msasa in 1978-82. In 2021 the printing side was split off into a separate company, the Printing and Minting Company of Zimbabwe. Zimbabwe scores 34 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:DEU: Germany uses the euro, and its central bank, the Deutsche Bundesbank, applies the interest rates the European Central Bank sets for the 21 countries using the currency. Bundesbank president Ernst Welteke resigned on 16 April 2004 after criticism for accepting a free New Year stay at Berlin's Hotel Adlon, paid two years earlier by the commercial bank Dresdner Bank, which the Bundesbank supervises; prosecutors and the Bundesbank both opened inquiries. Two further matters concern the European Central Bank. The European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, found maladministration and in January 2018 recommended that president Mario Draghi suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, a forum including private bankers; the ECB declined and he did not. And on 18 May 2015 board member Cœuré told a private London event the ECB would bring forward asset purchases, in a speech published only the next morning, which the ECB called an internal procedure error. Leaders have moved into private finance: Axel Weber to the chairmanship of UBS, Jens Weidmann to chairman of Commerzbank's supervisory board in May 2023. Most of the gold is stored abroad rather than managed by others: of 3,381 tonnes at the end of 2015, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York held 1,347.4 tonnes, the Bank of England 434.7 and the Banque de France 196.4. In May 1997 the finance minister proposed changing the Bundesbank law to revalue the bank's gold and hand part of the paper profit to the federal government that year, which would have helped Germany meet the deficit criterion for joining the euro. The Bundesbank's council rejected it in public, saying the plan could be construed as an attack on the bank's independence, and the bank had to break its usual silence to deny that its president was resigning. The chancellor and the coalition said at first that they would change the law regardless. They backed down in early June: the gold could be revalued, but not counted towards that year's figures. Germany scores 24 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:LBY: The Central Bank of Libya issues the dinar, and Britain's De La Rue prints the notes. Another run came from elsewhere: Goznak, the Russian state printer, printed dinars for the parallel eastern central bank in Benghazi, which is not internationally recognised, and Russian customs data cited by Reuters showed 4.5 billion dinars shipped between February and June 2019; Malta seized two containers on 1 November 2019, citing United Nations resolutions that recognise only the Tripoli government. The bank has signed a cooperation agreement under the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, aimed at better returns on its foreign currency reserves, which it describes as an exchange of expertise and capacity building rather than handing its reserves over to be managed. Four cases are recorded. The Misrata Criminal Court convicted two people of belonging to an organisation set up to seize 128 million US dollars and 5 million euros from the bank's Sirte branch in 2013 through coercion; one received 15 years in prison and a 2.5 million dinar fine, the other 13 years and a 50,000 dinar fine, and the Attorney General's Office reported the ruling in October 2023. In November 2022 the bank accused its deputy governor, Ali al-Hibri, of signing forged 50-dinar notes it said were printed in Russia and bore his signature, and Governor Saddek Elkaber asked the Attorney-General to pursue a complaint; that allegation is unproven. Two further matters come from Global Witness. Its investigation published on 19 February 2021 found that senior central bank officials hold paid directorships abroad and that Elkaber chairs a London bank indirectly owned by the central bank, which the report calls a conflict of interest; it cited nearly 2.5 billion dollars of private sector letters of credit approved between April and July 2020 and a 110 million dollar letter of credit for power equipment diverted to a company in the United Arab Emirates with a name almost identical to the original contractor's, and it states that it makes no allegation that any individual or bank broke the law. A companion report named that London bank as ABC International Bank, through which most Libyan letters of credit enter the international system, and said sources described mispricing, laundering and procurement fraud; no official finding of fraud followed. Both of those remain allegations. One long career runs through the bank: Saleh Ahmed Keshlaf began in its research department in 1985, was Director of the Governor's Office from 1999 to 2012, advised the research and statistics department from 2012 to 2024 and was reappointed Director of the Governor's Office in 2024. Alongside that he sat on the board of Arab Italian Bank (UBAE) from 2005 to 2012, on the Libyan Foreign Bank's supervisory committee from 2007 to 2012, as Deputy Chairman of the Libyan Financial Services Company from 2009 to 2024 and on Joumhourria Bank's supervisory committee from 2012 to 2022. The Libyan Foreign Bank and Joumhourria Bank are state institutions, so the move is filed as one inside the public sector and is not counted as a move into private finance. On 18 August 2024 the Tripoli-based Presidential Council decreed that Sadiq al-Kabir, governor since October 2011, be replaced by former deputy governor Mohamed Abdul Salam al-Shukri. The decree gave no official reason, and the east-based House of Representatives and the Supreme Council of State, both mandated to appoint governors under the constitutional document, called the firing illegitimate. A delegation from Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah's government then took over the governor's office, al-Kabir said he and other senior staff had fled the country because of militia threats, and banking operations were suspended. Deloitte audited the bank's accounts for 2021, and the United Nations Support Mission in Libya delivered the final reports of that audit through its Special Envoy, Kubis. Libya scores 50 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, more exposed than 96 percent of the 194 places with a figure, and 2.5 of 15 on how much it tells the public. One governor held a seat in private finance while in office. Farhat Bengdara was Deputy Governor and then Governor from 2006 to 2011, and from 29 April 2009 he also sat on the board of the Italian bank UniCredit as a member and vice-chairman, so the two roles overlapped. UniCredit's own shareholder page shows a mixed register: Aabar Luxembourg 5.039 per cent, BlackRock 4.993 per cent in non-discretional asset management, the Verona foundation 3.460 per cent, the Central Bank of Libya itself 2.923 per cent and the Turin foundation 2.517 per cent. So the bank he governed was among the shareholders of the bank whose board he sat on. The career side rests on an encyclopaedia entry. It holds 146.7 tonnes of gold, 20.5 percent of its reserves.
p:CHE: Switzerland's money is the Swiss franc, issued by the Swiss National Bank, a joint-stock company listed on the SIX Swiss Exchange with 100,000 shares and 25 million francs of capital. At the end of 2025 the 26 cantons held 38.995 per cent, 24 cantonal banks 11.966 per cent, 19 municipalities 0.265 per cent and private shareholders 48.774 per cent; the largest single holders were the Canton of Berne with 6.63 per cent, the Canton of Zurich with 5.23 per cent and one private holder, Theo Siegert, with 5.01 per cent. Holders outside the public sector may vote no more than 100 shares each, and the Confederation owns none. Orell Fussli Security Printing prints the notes, KPMG has audited the accounts since 2015, and the bank part-owns the Bank for International Settlements. About 70 per cent of its gold is stored in Switzerland, some 20 per cent at the Bank of England and roughly 10 per cent at the Bank of Canada; those two store the gold and do not manage its money. It scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. One case and one episode of pressure are recorded, and both are the same affair. Chairman Philipp Hildebrand resigned on 9 January 2012, with immediate effect, less than two years into the job. His wife Kashya, a former currency trader, had bought 504,000 dollars in August 2011 and sold the position three weeks later for a profit of 75,000 francs, after the bank had intervened to weaken the franc. Details of the family's private bank transactions were leaked by an IT worker at Bank Sarasin to a lawyer sitting in the Thurgau cantonal parliament for the Swiss People's Party, and Switzerland's highest court later imposed suspended fines on both men. Christoph Blocher, the party's leading figure, had long called for Hildebrand to go and passed documents on the trades to the government; the party weekly Weltwoche said it had proof the trades were Hildebrand's own. The party was at the time campaigning against the bank's policy of buying euros to hold the franc at 1.20. Hildebrand denied wrongdoing on 5 January and refused to resign; four days later he resigned, saying he could not prove beyond doubt that he had been unaware of his wife's transactions, and he gave the profits to charity. A later inquiry cleared him of insider trading, a criminal investigation was dropped, and the bank tightened its rules on staff financial dealings. He joined BlackRock as vice chairman in 2012. Jean-Pierre Roth, chairman of the Governing Board from 2001 to 2009, was elected to the board of the reinsurer Swiss Re in 2010. Neither move carries an ethics finding.
p:SWE: Sveriges Riksbank is Sweden's central bank and issues the krona. It scores 15 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, less exposed than 99 per cent of the 194 places with a figure. The Riksdag adopted a new Sveriges Riksbank Act on 23 November 2022, in force from 1 January 2023. The inquiry that preceded it proposed limits on what the Riksbank may do in monetary policy, which its Executive Board objected to in its consultation response and some of which were dropped from the final Act. What stayed includes a requirement of exceptional grounds before the bank may buy or sell financial instruments other than Swedish government securities for monetary policy purposes, on the reasoning that such trading carries much greater financial risk for the bank and for state finances; limits on its equity and a cap on borrowing for the foreign exchange reserve; and an obligation to ask the Riksdag to restore its equity when that falls below the floor, which it had to do after the bond purchases it made earlier lost money as rates rose. The Riksdag also now approves the specification of the inflation target. The bank's own account is two-sided: it says the Act leaves it a strong and clear mandate and carries the ban on taking instructions over unchanged, while governor Erik Thedeen said after a year of it that the governance is too strong on strengthening the foreign exchange reserve and on buying securities for financial stability purposes. Two linked cases run from 2020 to 2021. On 18 June 2021 the Riksbank said a routine check of staff securities dealings had found a few employees making transactions that did not fit its ethics rules, including share trades close to monetary policy decisions and trades in companies whose corporate bonds it was buying; it called this inappropriate, held talks with those involved and began revising the rules. After media reports that Stefan Ingves and Skingsley had conflicts of interest from shares they held while deciding on corporate bond purchases, the bank's General Council reviewed the matter and on 17 December 2021 concluded the link was too weak to amount to a conflict of interest, finding no shortcoming in their conduct. Ingves was appointed governor in October 2005, having headed a department at the International Monetary Fund since 1999. The Riksbank's own published CV shows a move the other way: Anna Breman was a senior economist at Swedbank from 2013 to 2015 and its group chief economist from 2015 to 2019, then became deputy governor of the Riksbank in 2019 and first deputy governor in 2022. Swedbank is a commercial bank listed on the Stockholm exchange rather than a state body. Its 125.7 tonnes of gold sit partly at the Riksbank and partly abroad, 61.4 tonnes at the Bank of England, 33.2 at the Bank of Canada, 13.2 at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and 2.8 at the Swiss National Bank, which is storage of the gold and not management of its money. Crane AB printed the notes at Tumba until the Riksbank gave notice to end the contract on 19 June 2018 because Crane was moving printing to Malta; De La Rue replaced it under an agreement announced on 19 September 2018.
p:GHA: The Bank of Ghana issues the cedi, and Ghana scores 32 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Governors keep being pushed out. In March 2016 the MP Kwasi Ameyaw-Cheremeh said the government had forced out Henry Kofi Wampah; Wampah said he had agreed with President Mahama to leave early, and no government response is reported. Abdul Nashiru Issahaku resigned with effect after 1 April 2017 citing personal reasons, under an agreement with the government that month, after the New Patriotic Party won the 2016 election and the party's Anthony Akoto Osei said he should step down; a governor's four-year term is protected by the 1992 constitution. In December 2017 the government pushed for second deputy governor Johnson Asiama to go; he said he had not resigned, and nothing further was reported. In November 2022 Isaac Adongo, for the Minority in Parliament, called governor Ernest Addison incompetent over the cedi's fall and said he should resign or be sacked, with no answer reported. The bank said in February 2023 that its claims on the government at the end of 2022 included a 37.9 billion cedi overdraft covering auction shortfalls and maturing bonds, 7.2 billion cedis of treasury bonds bought from banks and 8.9 billion cedis of International Monetary Fund money passed on, after government, bank and Fund had adopted zero deficit financing. In February 2020 the Attorney-General charged Kwabena Duffuor, a former finance minister and governor, and seven others with 68 counts over uniBank's collapse: Duffuor with dishonestly receiving 663.28 million cedis and money laundering, Asiama with approving a 300 million cedi unsecured facility from the distressed uniBank to Universal Merchant Bank. Asiama's charges were withdrawn around 30 January 2025 and the case against Duffuor and the others was ended on 22 July 2025 after more than 60 per cent of the funds allegedly lost had been recovered; none of it was proven. Duffuor had gone from governor between 1997 and 2001 to founder and president of HODA Holdings, whose largest holding was uniBank. De La Rue, a security printer in the United Kingdom, prints the notes and charges in British pounds, and KPMG audits the accounts. On the 2020 accounts, gold held with the Bank of England and the US Federal Reserve came to 2.05 billion cedis between them, with 907 million cedis with the Swiss firm UBS Gold Investment and 111.7 million in its own vault: storage of gold, not management of its money.
p:MOZ: The Bank of Mozambique is the country's central bank, and it scores 43 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Four of its records come out of the 'hidden debts', more than two billion US dollars of loans from Credit Suisse and VTB of Russia. Letters from 2013 shown at a trial in the United States had the bank authorising the company Proindicus to seek 372 million dollars, later 622 million, and Ematum 850 million; board member Silvia de Abreu signed them after an instruction from governor Ernesto Gove, who in 2016 denied responsibility and said he had never heard of Proindicus. That strand is still under investigation, so nothing in it is proven. At the Maputo City Court on 23 November 2021 Gove testified that he had signed on grounds of sovereignty and national security and admitted irregularities, and judge Efigenio Baptista rejected his argument that the law barring such approvals did not apply; the same day the bank's administrator Silvina de Abreu testified that it should not have authorised the loans and that Gove told her to keep technical staff out. Both of those stand as official findings. In April 2023 the daily Noticias reported Gove and two other board members among four people accused in a second trial then being prepared, with no date set and no charges listed, which is unproven. President Filipe Nyusi fired deputy governor Antonio Pinto de Abreu on 26 January 2016 without giving a reason, and on 31 August 2016 replaced Gove with Rogerio Zandamela, an International Monetary Fund official. On 2 September 2026 President Daniel Chapo revoked Waldemar Fernando de Sousa's appointment as governor, citing circumstances he did not specify, and named Felisberto Dinis Navalha; the Attorney General's Office accuses De Sousa over the hidden debts, though he was not tried in the main case. One career move is recorded. Teotonio Jaime dos Anjos Comiche spent 1976 to 1992 at the Banco de Mocambique, running its accounting department and then its accounting directorate before joining its board of administration from 1989 to 1992, and then became an executive director of Banco Comercial de Mocambique from 1992 to 2000 and of Banco Internacional de Mocambique, the bank trading as Millennium bim, from 2000 to 2015. The holdings in that bank are stated and mixed: 66.69 per cent BCP Internacional II, described as a subsidiary of a privately owned Portuguese bank, 17.76 per cent the Mozambican state, 4.95 per cent the national social security institute, 4.15 per cent the state insurer EMOSE, 1.08 per cent a development foundation and 5.37 per cent managers, technicians and staff. The bank also uses outside managers for its reserves and names none of them: its 2022 annual report says it contracts external managers, sets a benchmark for each externally managed portfolio and takes a monthly custodian breach report, without naming a firm. Crane Currency printed its 500-metical note and BDO audited its 2019 accounts.
p:GEO: The National Bank of Georgia issues the lari. Its law scores 0.847 of 1 for independence from government, and it scores 27 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. On 17 July 2015 parliament voted 80 to 19 to move banking supervision out of the bank to a new Financial Supervisory Agency, on a draft from two Georgian Dream members of parliament; one of them, Tamaz Mechiauri, argued that the composition of the bank's board was against the current leadership's interests, and Bidzina Ivanishvili blamed the bank and its chairman Giorgi Kadagidze for the lari's fall. In September 2023 the bank unfroze assets tied to Otar Partskhaladze, a former Prosecutor General sanctioned by the US Treasury, arguing that Georgian citizens cannot be sanctioned without a conviction in a Georgian court. At a briefing on 20 September 2023 acting president Natia Turnava confirmed that she had single-handedly adopted the change to the procedure for carrying out sanctions, made on 19 September and effective the next day, saying it fell within the discretion of the bank's president and that she had told Council members in advance; TBC Bank and Bank of Georgia had frozen Partskhaladze's accounts, and she said they had not broken the law because the amendment only took effect that day. Three of the four vice presidents and an adviser resigned, among them Papuna Lezhava, and no court verdict or official finding followed. In 2026 the Prosecutor's Office began investigating Council member Nana Keinishvili over possible unlawful involvement in business by a public official, after complaints from the crypto firm Bitexchange LLC, which the bank had fined and whose complaints the bank passed on; RFE/RL put the fine at 572 million lari and the bank did not disclose the amount. The investigation was still open in October 2026 and nothing is proven. The World Bank's Reserves Advisory and Management Partnership advises the bank on its reserves investment strategy and gold policy rather than managing the money. KPMG Georgia LLC audited the bank's accounts for 2020. Two careers run in from outside. Koba Gvenetadze was picked as president by the bank's board on 16 March 2016 and approved by the President of Georgia the next day, replacing Giorgi Kadagidze; he had joined the International Monetary Fund in 2002 and was its resident representative in Azerbaijan from early 2008 to late 2009 and in Kyrgyzstan from 2010 to 2014, and he was Georgia's Deputy Finance Minister in 2000 and 2001. The bank's own profile of Vice-Governor Nino Jeladze, in post since 10 February 2025 for a term to February 2032, gives eighteen dated years at ProCredit: account manager at ProCredit Bank Georgia in 2003, head of customer service from 2004 to 2005, branch manager including of the central branch from 2006 to 2014, operational risk manager from 2014 to 2015, the same work at ProCredit Holding in Frankfurt from 2015 to 2017, and head of anti-money-laundering and compliance back in Georgia from 2017 to 2021, before she became head of the bank's Supervisory Policy Department in 2024. ProCredit Holding's own shareholder page names Zeitinger Invest, the German state development bank KfW, the DOEN foundation and the EBRD, so the ownership is mixed rather than plainly private. One printer is named, and for one note only: at the bank's own presentation of the 200 lari note on 31 March 2007, Giesecke & Devrient's executive director Walter Schlebusch said the note had been produced at his company.
p:NPL: Nepal Rastra Bank issues Nepal's rupee and holds it at a fixed rate against India's rupee, and scores 31 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. In 2007 the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority charged sitting governor Bhattarai and executive director Pradhan with embezzlement over the hiring of American consultants; Bhattarai was suspended, and the Supreme Court later cleared both. In October 2011 Note Printing Australia, owned by the Reserve Bank of Australia, pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to provide benefits to foreign public officials to obtain banknote business with Nepal's note-issuing authority between February 2000 and May 2002, and paid 1,856,710 Australian dollars. On 8 April 2022 the government suspended governor Adhikari over charges, still unproven, of leaking sensitive government decisions; the Supreme Court stayed the suspension on 19 April and he returned to work. Adhikari retired as the bank's deputy governor in December 2015 after three decades there, then became chief executive officer of the Nepal Investment Board, and was appointed the bank's 17th governor on 6 April 2020 for five years.
p:IRN: The Central Bank of the Islamic Republic of Iran issues the rial, which is in free fall. Its law leaves most power with government, 0.448 of 1 where 1 means the bank holds it. Its notes and coins come from the Security Printing and Minting Organization, a state printing works owned by the bank since 1962; before 1982 the notes were printed abroad. The governor appointed in August 2013 came in from private banking: the bank's general assembly appointed Valiollah Seif, described in local press as having been managing director of the privately owned Karafarin Bank, in place of Mahmud Bahmani, and that report is what states the employer's private ownership. The government then replaced Seif on 25 July 2018 with no reason given, and dismissed his successor Abdolnasser Hemmati on 30 May 2021 because he was standing in the 18 June presidential election, naming deputy Akbar Komijani in his place. In October 2021 a Tehran court sentenced Seif to ten years in prison, his former deputy Araghchi to eight and the intermediary Salar Aghakhani to thirteen over an illegal foreign-currency distribution scheme in 2017 and 2018, in which the judiciary said ten people were identified; the Supreme Court overturned the verdicts in 2023, citing insufficient evidence and authorisation by higher authorities, and the judiciary dropped the prosecution of Seif and Araghchi in March 2025. Abroad, Bahrain's High Criminal Court in November 2020 fined the bank and other Iran-owned banks, including Future Bank, one million Bahraini dinars each and jailed three Future Bank officials for five years; prosecutors said the Central Bank of Iran planned to launder billions of dollars through Future Bank, which handled suspicious transfers favouring Iranian entities without reporting them. Bahrain's top court upheld the conviction in 2021, with five Future Bank officials given ten-year sentences and a sixth five years, and confiscation of remittances estimated at 184 million US dollars, 967 million euros, 53 million dirhams and 235 billion Iranian riyals. Iran scores 43 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, 24th of 194.
p:MWI: The Reserve Bank of Malawi issues the kwacha, and presidents have removed its leaders again and again. President Joyce Banda removed governor Perks Ligoya, according to two unnamed sources, with Charles Chuka reportedly chosen to succeed him and no official reason given; the date is not stated. Newly elected president Lazarus Chakwera dismissed governor Dalitso Kabambe and appointed Wilson Banda on 8 July 2020. After a forensic audit of the bank's payments between January 2019 and June 2020, the state charged Kabambe and three others with abuse of office, negligence, money laundering and causing loss of public funds, alleging that 4.3 billion kwacha went to FDH Bank without board approval; pleas were not taken because the charges were subject to change, and nothing is proven. In December 2021 police arrested Kabambe and Joseph Mwanamvekha, saying the two procured and masterminded the falsification of gross liability and net reserve base returns to make the International Monetary Fund believe Malawi was meeting the conditions of its Extended Credit Facility loan; that too stands only as an accusation. Chakwera then dismissed the governor he had himself installed, removing Wilson Banda in early January 2025 and moving up the deputy governor, MacDonald Mafuta Mwale, with immediate effect, subject to confirmation by Parliament's Public Appointments Committee. Mafuta Mwale's own path is the one career move recorded: he had served as Secretary to the Treasury, the senior civil service post in the finance ministry, with no years given for it, and was redeployed back to the Reserve Bank in January of the previous year, two years after that post. The government's statement thanked Banda for his service and gave no reason; Nyasa Times reported that the President had been demanding monetary reforms since June of the previous year and quoted a source close to State House saying the results were painfully slow. Banda had devalued the kwacha by 25 to 27 percent in May 2022, calling it a necessary evil to align the supply of foreign exchange with the fundamentals, and by a further 44 percent in November 2023, and the gap with the parallel market widened after both. A disputed episode runs alongside that removal. Two Malawian civil society organisations, the Black Economic Empowerment Movement and the Forum for National Development, said in January 2026 that the dismissal of the whole board at the time, senior executives included, breached the Reserve Bank of Malawi Act's requirement of continuity in leadership, that they had warned the government the mass dismissal was illegal and left the bank open to manipulation, and that one of those removed, Henry Mathanga, was targeted for perceived political associations rather than misconduct. Nyasa Times reported instead that Mathanga had been removed after a formal disciplinary inquiry under the Act and was facing criminal charges in the Financial Crimes Division of the High Court. The two accounts have not been reconciled. In January 2026 President Peter Mutharika appointed Mathanga deputy governor, and critics say that appointment breaches section 16(2) of the Reserve Bank of Malawi Act. Its 2,000-kwacha note is printed by Giesecke & Devrient, and its accounts for the year ended 31 December 2025, in reports signed on 30 June 2026, were audited by Deloitte in Malawi together with Deloitte & Touche in South Africa. Malawi scores 37 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Part of the foreign reserves is run by an outside firm. The bank's audited statements for the year ended 31 December 2025 say it sets a benchmark of the Merrill Lynch 1-3 Year US Government Bond Index at 80 per cent and the Merrill Lynch 3-month US dollar deposit rate at 20 per cent for foreign reserves being managed by external fund managers, allocates those managers a risk budget expressed as an acceptable level of underperformance against that benchmark, and put the value of the externally managed funds at 3,880 million kwacha at that date, against 3,740 million a year earlier. The counterparty table names the firm, as Crown Agents Fund manager of the United Kingdom, against the same 3,880 million figure and separately from the bank's three banking lines with Crown Agents Bank Limited.
p:VNM: The State Bank of Vietnam issues the dong and moves its rate against the dollar in small steps rather than leaving it to the market. On paper its law gives it almost no independence, 0.301 of 1 and 154th of 155 places, and government pressure was reported in 6 of 37 quarters up to 2018. That weakness is written into the statute itself and is still in force. Under the Law on the State Bank of Vietnam of 16 June 2010, in force from 1 January 2011, the bank is a ministerial-level agency of the Government as well as the central bank; the National Assembly decides the annual inflation target, on the Government's proposal, and the Prime Minister or the Governor then decides which tools to use, following rules the Government sets. There is no episode and no end date here: the bank carries out a target set above it. In April 2024 the Ho Chi Minh City People's Court sentenced Truong My Lan, chair of Van Thinh Phat, to death for fraud at Saigon Commercial Bank, finding that she had ordered subordinates to bribe State Bank inspectors; state media reported that head banking inspector Do Thi Nhan took 5.2 million US dollars and deputy chief inspector Nguyen Van Hung 300,000. In October 2011 Securency, a subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of Australia, pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to give benefits to foreign public officials to win banknote business with Vietnam's note-issuing authority between 2001 and 2004; the officials are not named. The bank's notes are printed by the state-owned National Banknote Printing Factory, whose chairman the Governor appoints. Cao Si Kiem, governor from 1989 to 1997, joined the board of the joint-stock commercial DongA Bank in March 2012 and became its chairman on 26 April 2014. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, and Vietnam scores 35 of 100 on exposure to outside influence.
p:IRQ: The Central Bank of Iraq issues the dinar and keeps it within a band of 2 percent or less against the US dollar. It scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and 0.733 of 1 for the independence written into its law, where 1 means the bank holds the power and 0 the government. In 2012 Iraq's Board of Supreme Audit examined the bank's daily auctions of dollars to banks and found that most transactions rested on fraudulent paperwork; the country's top auditor told US officials that up to 800 million dollars a week was leaving Iraq illegally, as reported by the US Special Inspector General for Iraq Reconstruction. In October 2012 the cabinet removed governor Sinan al-Shabibi and named a successor while a parliamentary committee was examining possible manipulation of the dinar and charging that bank officials were abusing the dollar sales. A committee member said arrest warrants had been issued for 30 people, including al-Shabibi and his deputy Mudher Saleh, and the Supreme Judicial Council confirmed warrants without saying what the charges were. The integrity committee's chairman said the inquiry was not about money but about procedures, while a member of the finance committee called it a political decision and not professional; al-Shabibi's defence called the case politically motivated. No court outcome was ever reported, so nothing was proven; he died on 8 January 2022, and the bank mourned him as a distinguished former governor. One career move is on record, and it stays inside the public sector: on 14 March 2023 the governor appointed Faisal Wisam al-Heims as deputy governor, from the post of Director-General of the Trade Bank of Iraq, which the report describes as a state-owned bank, and he had also chaired the Iraq Securities Commission, a regulator. It holds 175.6 tonnes of gold, about a quarter of its reserves. Its own accounts for the year ended 31 December 2025 split that holding into three lines, gold held abroad, gold at the bank's own vault and gold coins at that vault, so the only place named for any of it is the bank's vault in Baghdad. The Board of Supreme Audit audits its accounts. Who prints the dinar rests on an encyclopaedia entry rather than anything the bank publishes: it says the 2003 series, still the basis of circulating notes, was printed by De La Rue.
p:KOR: South Korea's money is the won, issued by the Bank of Korea, which scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. One episode of government pressure is recorded. Choi Kyung-hwan became deputy prime minister for the economy and finance minister in July 2014 and pressed publicly for lower interest rates, saying he had not mentioned the base rate and that the central bank should get the hint. On 14 August 2014 the bank cut its base rate by a quarter point to 2.25 percent, the first move in fifteen months, and cut again to 2.0 percent on 15 October; reporting at the time described both cuts as made under government pressure. Governor Lee Ju-yeol said the decision was his committee's and its independence guaranteed. Two cases are recorded, both ending in conviction. Between 2022 and 2023 a currency-exchange employee at the Daejeon Sejong-Chungnam headquarters broke the rule that older coins leave the vault first, at a coin collector's request, letting 240,000 one-hundred-won coins from 2018 and 2019 go out ahead of 2017 coins; the collector made about 180 million won selling them and gave the employee about 55 million, and the Daejeon District Court imposed two years and six months in prison, a fine and confiscation. Between 2013 and 2015 an employee handling publication sales receipts diverted about 56 million won to a personal account and spent about 12 million won on commemorative banknote sheets with a corporate card; the Seoul Central District Court gave eight months suspended for two years, the money having been repaid. Four officials have moved between the bank and outside institutions. Hwang Geon-il came to the rate-setting Monetary Policy Committee from two years as an executive director of the World Bank. Rhee Chang-yong was running the International Monetary Fund's Asia and Pacific department when he was nominated governor on 23 March 2022. Lim Ji-won worked at JP Morgan's Seoul branch from 1999 until she took office on the committee on 17 May 2018, and sold her remaining 6,486 JP Morgan shares that summer, within the law as it then stood, which limited holdings of domestic shares and not overseas ones; critics said not selling before taking office was inappropriate, and Lee Ju-yeol said the question was legal rather than ethical. Jeong Gyu-il joined the bank in 1987 and rose through its economic research institute, international cooperation and economic statistics posts to deputy governor, and in an announcement of 2 July 2021 Seoul Foreign Exchange Brokerage made him its chief executive and president. The notes and coins are made by the state-run Korea Minting and Security Printing Corporation, the country's only maker of banknotes and coins, and the Board of Audit and Inspection audits the accounts alongside an auditor appointed by the President. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements and sits on the Financial Stability Board. A newspaper report of 12 February 2025 says all 104.4 tonnes of South Korea's gold, bought between 2011 and 2013, is stored at the Bank of England; that is the paper's own wording, so it is reported rather than confirmed by the bank.
p:VEN: The bolivar is issued by the Central Bank of Venezuela. On paper the bank is protected, scoring 0.816 of 1 on an index of 42 legal rules where 1 means the bank rather than the government holds the power, but government pressure was reported in 18 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, including 13 demands to print money. In January 2017 President Nicolas Maduro announced the firing of bank chief Nelson Merentes, who the report says handed in his resignation, and named Ricardo Sanguino to succeed him; no reason was given. Merentes had moved the other way before that: he had been president of the central bank since 2009 when Maduro named him finance minister on 22 April 2013, two days after being sworn in as Hugo Chavez's successor, replacing Jorge Giordani, and the report calls it his third stint as finance minister without saying when the first two were. In January 2020 the prosecutor Tarek William Saab said a payments head at the bank and others had forged purchase files so the bank paid about 1.7 million US dollars to three companies it had never contracted, for goods never delivered. Eight arrest warrants were sought, the case began with a complaint by the bank's president, Calixto Ortega, and no trial or conviction is reported, so the accusations are unproven. On 29 July 2022 London's High Court ruled that Venezuelan supreme court judgments backing the Maduro-appointed board should be disregarded, keeping more than 1 billion US dollars of Venezuelan gold held at the Bank of England out of Maduro's control. Russia's state printer Goznak signed a contract to print the bank's notes in November 2019. Venezuela scores 37 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:BOL: The Central Bank of Bolivia issues the boliviano, and the state audit office, the Contraloria General de la Republica, audits its accounts under the 1995 central bank law. On 17 December 2019 Guillermo Aponte took over as interim president from Pablo Ramos, who was under investigation over alleged favouring of illicit enrichment, with questions about armoured trucks said to have carried foreign currency out at unusual hours and about some 75 million US dollars in loans to state firms; that is where the matter stands, and nothing is proven. On 5 March 2021 the bank let go more than a dozen senior managers, among them the manager for international operations, the principal adviser on political economy and subdirectors of several departments, and a former governor said the change of government had likely influenced the dismissals. On 28 April 2026 La Paz prosecutors had former president Edwin Rojas and three other former senior officials detained over seven debt-swap operations with local financial entities in June and July 2024 at inflated prices, said to have cost the state 142.3 million US dollars, with the transparency vice ministry saying price records were later altered on internal email instructions to hide the overvaluation; prosecutors, investigating breach of duties and uneconomic conduct over a 2024 regulation they say allowed irregular sovereign bond transactions, put the alleged damage at 124 million US dollars. The suspects deny wrongdoing, seven people are under investigation, and Rojas invoked his right to silence. Banco Mercantil Santa Cruz, Banco Bisa, La Vitalicia Seguros y Reaseguros, La Boliviana Ciacruz and Gestora Publica are named alongside the central bank in that matter. One career move is recorded: Jaime Valencia Valencia, general manager of the bank from 1996 to 2006 and again from 16 January 2020, had earlier worked at three Bolivian financial firms, Banco de la Union S.A., Banco de Cochabamba S.A. and Compania Boliviana de Seguros S.A.; the first of those was set up by the Bolivian government by public deed on 28 July 1979, with the National Treasury taking a 97 per cent stake. Bolivia holds 22.5 tonnes of gold, almost all of its reserves. About 2.62 tonnes of it sat in the bank's own vaults at 31 December 2024, and the other 19.91 tonnes was deposited and invested in gold accounts at financial institutions in London: 6.48 tonnes at UBS, 5.50 at Toronto-Dominion, 3.89 at BNP Paribas, 2.77 at JPMorgan Chase, 1.00 at the Bank of Montreal and 0.27 at the Bank for International Settlements, which is an interest-earning deposit rather than storage. On 27 July 2023 the bank awarded its banknote tender to Oberthur Fiduciaire SAS for 25,945,787 US dollars, for 321.5 million notes of 10, 20, 50, 100 and 200 bolivianos. Three outside firms manage money the bank holds. Its 2018 reserves report names Amundi of France, BlackRock Financial Management of the United States and UBS Asset Management (Americas), also of the United States, as delegated managers of the Fondo RAL-ME, which stood at 1,052 million US dollars at the end of 2018. That fund is not the country's international reserves, which annexes to the same report show the bank runs itself: it is the foreign-currency reserve that Bolivian banks are required to hold at the central bank, and the report says the bank manages it in a way analogous to the international reserves. The report also logs three compliance breaches by Amundi in 2018, two trades put through a broker that had not been approved and one breach of the limit on exposure to a single bank. Bolivia scores 31 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:SMR: San Marino uses the euro, and its central bank is the Central Bank of the Republic of San Marino. It scores 47 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, mainly because its money is issued or backed from abroad. The bank is owned mostly by the state: the Eccellentissima Camera della Repubblica di San Marino holds 72%, four banks hold the rest: Cassa di Risparmio della Repubblica di San Marino 16%, Banca di San Marino 6%, Banca Agricola Commerciale Istituto Bancario Sammarinese 5% and Banca Sammarinese di Investimento 1%, as of 31 December 2025. One case is recorded, from 2019 to 2020, over a 220,000 euro payment from the bank to Sandro Gozi for a consultancy that investigators suspected was fictitious. The case, against Gozi and bank president Catia Tomasetti, became public in April 2019. The Tribunal of San Marino dismissed it in 2020, finding no relevant conduct by either suspect; the article reports the consultancy was real. Who fills its governing bodies is set by its Statute, Law no. 96 of 29 June 2005, in the text in force from 30 November 2025: the Consiglio Grande e Generale, San Marino's parliament, appoints the President and the five Councillors of the Governing Council, and the Director General the Council appoints takes office subject to the parliament's approval. Article 48 puts the Committee for Credit and Savings under the Secretary of State for Finance, who chairs it alongside two to four members of the Congress of State, and gives that committee the function of directing and orienting banking, financial and insurance supervision; the Statute does not say its directions bind the bank. The bank's accounts are audited by Solution S.r.l. of Borgo Maggiore, a San Marino firm belonging to no international network, which signed its report on the 2025 accounts on 5 May 2026 and reports to the shareholders rather than to the board. San Marino's government publishes the curriculum vitae of Luca Beccari, who served inside the central bank from 10 November 1997 to 8 January 2020, latterly heading its Organisation, Human Resources and General Services Service from 1 April 2019. Every outside employer on it is public: he coordinated the Finance and Budget Department at the Secretariat of State for Finance and Budget from 1 January to 30 June 2006 and again from 15 December 2008 to 31 December 2012, both expressly on leave from his central bank post, and held a short-term consultant post at the World Bank. The one private employer comes before the central bank and is not financial, Exim S.r.l., described on the CV as a San Marino maker and seller of pharmacy furniture and equipment, where he was administrative manager from 1 October 1993 to 30 September 1997, so none of it is counted on the revolving-door layer.
p:UKR: The National Bank of Ukraine issues the hryvnia and prints the notes itself, at the Banknote Printing and Minting Works that is part of the bank. Its independence written into law is high, 0.893 of 1, but its governors have been pushed. In January 2009 parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, voted no confidence in governor Volodymyr Stelmakh, 227 of 450 seats in favour, as the hryvnia lost nearly half its value; President Viktor Yushchenko's office called the vote illegal and kept backing him, and he was not removed. In July 2020 governor Yakiv Smolii resigned, telling President Volodymyr Zelensky that systematic political pressure had been exerted on the bank. One case is open: on 11 November 2019 the National Anti-Corruption Bureau detained seven people, including former first deputy governor Pysaruk, on suspicion of embezzling 1.2 billion hryvnia, about 49 million US dollars, from a 2014 loan the bank made to prop up VAB Bank, which was declared insolvent that November; it is unproven. Valeria Gontareva, governor from 2014 to 2017, had worked at Societe Generale, ING Bank and the Ukrainian financial services group Investment Capital Ukraine. Ukraine scores 29 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:PRY: The Central Bank of Paraguay issues the country's money, the guaraní, and scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Impeachment proceedings opened in January 2003 against President Luis González Macchi over an alleged 26 million US dollar embezzlement from the bank, and the Senate vote fell short that February. On 6 June 2006 a court in Asunción sentenced him to six years for breach of trust over 16 million US dollars diverted from Unión and Orienta, two private banks the central bank had taken over, and former banking superintendent José Pecci to eight years; an appeals court later cleared González Macchi for insufficient evidence. In February 2007 President Nicanor Duarte Frutos dismissed bank president Mónica Pérez over her disagreements with the economic team. Police searched the bank on 13 July 2021 over embezzlement and money laundering, an open investigation. On 3 November 2026 governor Carlos Carvallo resigned at President Santiago Peña's request, after a prosecutor sought an investigation around ueno, a digital lender Carvallo had headed until August 2023. Its accounts are audited by a consortium of Deloitte & Co S.A. and Deloitte Paraguay S.R.L., which the bank's board awarded the work on 7 November 2025 under an international public tender covering the financial years 2025, 2026 and 2027. An earlier head of the bank went the other way: Carlos Fernandez Valdovinos led it for five years, from 2013 to 2018, after being appointed by Horacio Manuel Cartes, and in October 2018 he joined the board of directors of the commercial bank Banco Basa.
p:NOR: Norges Bank issues the Norwegian krone and is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, whose capital has been held by central banks alone since private shares were bought back in 2001. Both recorded cases come out of one hiring. On 24 March 2020 the Executive Board appointed Nicolai Tangen, who had started the hedge fund AKO Capital in 2005, to run Norges Bank Investment Management, which manages the country's oil fund. The bank's Supervisory Council warned that the hire risked breaking laws, rules and guidelines, saying Tangen still appeared to be AKO Capital's main owner with voting control, although the bank said he had cut those ties. After the Storting's finance committee raised the same concern, the Executive Board revised his terms in August 2020: he would give up his holding in AKO Capital LLP and hand it and its dividend rights to the charitable AKO Foundation, and hold his personal fund assets as bank deposits. Supervisory Board chair Julie Brodtkorb said guidelines, regulations and laws had been breached; Executive Board chair Oystein Olsen said the board had thought the existing contract was enough but accepted that the Storting took a different view. Tangen could take office on 1 September. Ernst & Young audits the bank from the 2022 financial year for six years, and at the end of 2025 103 organisations ran outside mandates worth 1,062 billion kroner. Notes were printed by Oberthur Fiduciaire in France from 2016 to 2019 and, from 2020, by Crane NXT in Malta. A commission appointed by the Ministry of Finance and chaired by Svein Gjedrem, a former governor of the bank, proposed in late June 2017 that the oil fund be managed by a separate statutory entity outside Norges Bank, which would have taken away the largest thing the bank does. Its reasoning was that central banking and investment management differ in nature, that both had grown and now placed greater demands on the board, senior management and the organisation, and that separate bodies could tailor their skills to each task. The bank's own leadership and the fund's split in public: governor Oystein Olsen wanted the fund kept inside Norges Bank, while the fund's chief executive Yngve Slyngstad was reported as believing it should be taken out. The Ministry of Finance rejected the proposal and decided the management should stay in the central bank, on the reasoning that Norges Bank enjoyed a high level of trust in Norway and internationally and that its performance in both roles had been good over time; the Central Bank Act the Storting passed on 28 May 2019, in force from 1 January 2020, left the bank both responsibilities. Norway scores 22 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:CHN: China's money, the renminbi, is issued by the People's Bank of China. The country scores 37 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and the weakest part is corruption and secrecy around the bank. Written independence scores 0.659 of 1 on an index of 42 legal rules, but the part covering the governor and the board scores only 0.04, meaning the government holds nearly all of that power; pressure from government was reported in 2 of 37 quarters surveyed between 2010 and 2018. One case is documented: in October 2024 the Huanggang Intermediate People's Court sentenced Fan Yifei, a former deputy governor, to death with a two-year reprieve, to be commuted to life without parole, for accepting property worth more than 386 million yuan through his posts at the central bank and other institutions including China Construction Bank. A year before that sentence, in September 2023, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, the Communist Party's own disciplinary body, announced that Fan Yifei had been expelled from the party and dismissed from public office for serious violation of discipline and law. The commission alleged that he accepted banquets, travel, golf and private club access against the rules, took gifts and cash, had relatives paid without working, traded his position for personal gain and sex, interfered in law enforcement, used his financial role to obtain loans for others and illegally accepted large amounts of property, and it said his illegal gains would be confiscated and that he would be prosecuted in accordance with the law; these were the commission's own findings and allegations, which had not at that point been tested in court. Its notes and coins are made by the China Banknote Printing and Minting Corporation, described as a state company inside the bank, though only Wikipedia was found saying so, and the National Audit Office audits the accounts. One career move is documented: Zhou Xiaochuan spent two years as president of China Construction Bank, a large state commercial bank, then was chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission, the state securities regulator, from 2000 to 2002, and then became governor of the People's Bank of China; no years are given for the China Construction Bank post. The governor, Pan Gongsheng, two former governors and a monetary policy committee member sit in the Group of Thirty, a private forum alongside the chief executive of Citi and a vice chairman of BlackRock. Its reach is wide: 89 swap lines, which are standing agreements to lend its currency to another central bank, 8.6 percent of world currency trading and 2,346.4 tonnes of gold.
p:AZE: The Central Bank of the Republic of Azerbaijan issues the manat, held at a de facto fixed rate against the US dollar. It scores 31 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, with corruption and secrecy around it at 62. On 12 April 2022 parliament approved President Ilham Aliyev's proposal to replace governor Elman Rustamov, in post since 1995, with Taleh Kazimov, head of Pasha Bank; Rustamov became adviser to the prime minister, and no official reason and no statement from him were reported. One career move is documented, and it is Kazimov's: at the private PASHA Bank, set up in 2007, he rose from risk manager to chief executive officer and then chairman, with no years given for those posts, and he then became governor of the central bank on the parliamentary vote reported on 18 April 2022. Two cases are documented. A Vienna court found that the Austrian banknote printer OeBS had overcharged the bank by 20 per cent on banknote contracts and that the kickback went back to local decision makers; OeBS managers were convicted in 2014 and again on retrial in 2018, and no Azerbaijani official was named or tried. Austrian prosecutors also told a court that former OeBS employees had paid bribes to officials at Syrian and Azerbaijani banks for printing contracts, which stands as a prosecution allegation. In September 2009 a Baku court sentenced six former officers of the bank to between a two-year suspended sentence and eight years for abuse of power and embezzling 1.4 million manat between 2003 and 2008. Who prints the money now is reported rather than confirmed by the bank: an industry association's per-note profile of the renewed 50-manat banknote lists G+D Currency Development GmbH, part of Giesecke+Devrient, as the printer and Papierfabrik Louisenthal GmbH as the supplier of the paper it is printed on. KPMG Audit Azerbaijan LLC audits the accounts for 2025, and the bank holds no gold.
p:THA: The Bank of Thailand issues the baht and prints its own notes: its history records that the Cabinet authorised it to set up the Note Printing Works in 1961, built for Thai banknote production. It is also one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, and Thailand scores 39 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. On 29 May 2001 the government fired governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul after Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said he was not satisfied with the bank's low interest rates, and Finance Minister Kittiratt Na-Ranong later pressed for governor Prasarn Trairatvorakul to be replaced over the 2.75 percent rate. More recently Pheu Thai leader Paetongtarn Shinawatra said the law keeping the bank independent gets in the way of solving economic problems, and Prime Minister Srettha Thavisin said he had no plan to remove Governor Sethaput Suthiwartnarueput. A case brought in 2001 against former governor Rerngchai Marakanond, over using the reserves to defend the baht during the Asian financial crisis, ended on 5 October 2016 when the Supreme Court upheld a ruling that he had not acted improperly, so he was acquitted. Former finance minister Surapong Suebwonglee was convicted of malfeasance for putting three representatives of banks the Bank of Thailand supervises on the committee that selects its board in 2008; he was given a one-year jail term suspended for a year and fined 20,000 baht.
p:SUR: The Central Bank of Suriname issues the Suriname dollar, which it lets move within a managed range against the US dollar. It scores 32 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side, at 63, is corruption and secrecy around it. Two cases ended in convictions. On 31 January 2022 a court convicted former governor van Trikt of breaking the Anti-Corruption Act and of forgery, embezzlement, money laundering and taking part in a criminal enterprise, in a matter involving more than 800,000 US dollars taken at the bank's expense, and sentenced him to eight years in prison and a 500,000 Suriname dollar fine; the bank's legal director and others were convicted too, and on appeal in January 2026 his sentence was cut to six years. On 17 December 2021 a court sentenced Hoefdraad, who was not present, to 12 years and a fine of the same size for conspiring to defraud the bank while he was finance minister; on appeal on 19 January 2026 the court imposed 10 years for breaking the anti-corruption law and for embezzlement, and dropped the criminal-organisation count. Hoefdraad, who left Suriname in 2020, calls the case a political show trial. One career move is documented, and it is his: Gillmore Hoefdraad began working for the International Monetary Fund in Washington DC in 1999, with no job title given, was Governor of the Central Bank of Suriname from 2010 to 2015, and then served as Suriname's Minister of Finance from 2015 to 2020 under President Desi Bouterse. The government also took money out of the bank. In February 2020 it admitted taking 197 million US dollars from the central bank for imports, debt payments and other purposes it did not specify. The money came from term deposits and from the foreign currency cash reserves that commercial banks held at the bank, and was reportedly used without their permission or knowledge; the commercial banks had been told in 2019 to deposit half the foreign currency they held for customers there. On 3 February 2020 the Surinamese Bankers' Association said the bank had misled them for months with incorrect and incomplete information about the state of that reserve, and named the then governor as mainly responsible for the disappearance of more than 100 million dollars out of a 426 million dollar reserve. Opposition parties demanded that President Desi Bouterse explain himself in Parliament and said the government should resign if he could not, accusing it of using the money to service foreign debts; the Vice President said the government had made agreements with the commercial banks about the use of their cash reserves and that the bank had not kept its end. Van Trikt was removed in January 2020 and resigned on 4 February. On 22 March 2020 the government passed a law temporarily blocking foreign exchange transactions as the currency fell. The bank holds 1.2 tonnes of gold and has three agreements with China to exchange currencies, signed on 18 March 2015, in 2017 and on 11 February 2019, though whether any of them is still in force is not known; one source records drawings of 988,182,600 renminbi in 2020. BDO Assurance NV audited its 2020 accounts, and notes have been printed by Giesecke+Devrient, an expansion of the initials the source gives rather than its own wording.
p:LBR: Liberia's money is the Liberian dollar, issued by the Central Bank of Liberia, which scores 32 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. In March 2019 a Monrovia court ordered former deputy governor Sirleaf, former governor Weeks and official Hagba held for trial on charges of economic sabotage, theft or misuse of public money and criminal conspiracy, over banknotes printed in 2016 to 2018 that could not be accounted for. The Justice Minister later dropped the charges against Sirleaf and three others, while Weeks remained under indictment, so nothing was proven against him. Crane Currency printed those notes under two contracts totalling 15 billion Liberian dollars, and a Presidential Investigation Team alleged it conspired with bank officials to print 18,151,000,000, beyond what was contracted; Crane denied wrongdoing and kickbacks and said it had not been charged, and the allegation is not a court finding. In July 2024 Liberia suspended governor Tarlue indefinitely after the General Auditing Commission reported on 2018 to 2023 and found irregularities in lending to the government, including more than 80 million US dollars in apparently unauthorised financing for salary payments, irregular contract awards and spending beyond approved limits; that stands as an official finding. His own career before the bank is documented in the bank's published profile of him: J. Aloysius Tarlue, Jr. was a compliance analyst at HSBC Bank NA from 2001 to 2004, a compliance officer at Merrill Lynch from 2004 to 2007, a senior risk officer at Deutsche Bank NA from 2007 to 2008, a compliance officer at BNY Mellon NA from 2008 to 2013 and a compliance officer at J.P. Morgan Chase from 2013 to 2018, then executive chairman of the board of commissioners of the Liberia Electricity Regulatory Commission from 2018 to 2020, and has been Executive Governor and chairman of the board of governors since 2020. A governor also left at the president's request. In May 2019 President George Weah announced that Executive Governor Nathaniel Patray was stepping down because of his age, which surprised the public and the banking sector, and Patray resigned that October. That he went at the President's request is the bank's own account, given to FrontPage Africa in 2024, where it said his resignation in October 2019, following the former President's request, marked a crucial turning point for the institution. No wrongdoing by him was alleged, the reason given at the time was his age, and the request is stated by the bank in retrospect rather than by the presidency at the time. The bank joined the World Bank's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership under a technical assistance agreement, described as training and advice rather than the partnership managing its assets. Deloitte & Touche in Accra and Baker Tilly Liberia in Monrovia audited the 2024 accounts.
p:COL: The Bank of the Republic issues Colombia's peso and prints it itself, at its own banknote works, with a coin plant at Ibagué in Tolima; it is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the bank used by central banks themselves. One case is recorded and it ended in the officials' favour: two of them were investigated in 2011 for allegedly giving reserved information about people and companies to officials of the DAS security agency and received a one-month suspension, but in January 2011 the bank reported that the Procuraduría's second-instance ruling revoked the suspension, recognising that they had broken no rule. Government pressure was reported in 2 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, each time to cut rates. On 31 July 2025, after the board voted 4 to 3 to hold the rate at 9.25 percent, President Gustavo Petro accused the bank of wanting to finish off the economy and of having an electoral bet. Much of the work of investing Colombia's international reserves, the foreign money the central bank keeps in hand, is given to outside firms. The bank's reserves management report counts seven of them each running a dedicated, actively managed portfolio of those reserves at 31 December 2024, among them JPMorgan Asset Management (UK) Limited, Wellington Management Company LLP, Goldman Sachs Asset Management L.P., State Street Global Advisors Trust Co., UBS Asset Management (Americas) Inc. and Pacific Investment Management Company LLC, known as Pimco. Beyond those private managers, on the same date the bank held 914.79 million US dollars in the Bank for International Settlements' Chinese government and central bank bond pools and 287.59 million in its global corporate debt pool, funds open only to central banks. Amundi won a mandate in 2023, as one of eight outside managers, running an active fixed income programme covering Treasuries, mortgage-backed securities and G10 currencies for 1.7 billion US dollars of assets; the central bank was impressed by Amundi's knowledge-transfer proposal when screening managers. The reserve gold, 4.7 tonnes or 1 percent of reserves, is in the custody of the Bank of England, which stores it rather than manages it. Two career moves are recorded. Leonardo Villar became general manager in January 2021, after serving as an Executive Director at the International Monetary Fund from November 2018 to October 2020 and alternate Executive Director in November and December 2020. Gerardo Hernández Correa spent sixteen years at the Bank of the Republic as a board member, executive manager and secretary of the board, was Colombia's financial superintendent for six years, became vice-president for legal affairs at Banco de Bogotá in 2021, and on 27 June 2024 was named president of Banco AV Villas, replacing Juan Camilo Ángel; both are commercial banks, and the same report states that Grupo Aval, a private financial conglomerate rather than a state body, holds controlling stakes in financial entities including Banco AV Villas. The accounts for the year ended 31 December 2024 were checked by the Auditor General del Banco de la República, an office inside the bank, in a report dated 27 January 2025. Colombia scores 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, less exposed than 82 percent of the 194 places with a figure, and 8 of 15 on how much it tells the public. There have been two systemic banking crises since 1970.
p:MNE: The Central Bank of Montenegro does not issue money. Montenegro took the euro on its own: the Deutsche Mark became sole legal tender on 1 January 2001 and the euro replaced it in March 2002. The bank issues no euros and is not a member of the European System of Central Banks, but has a repo line, a short-term loan arrangement, of up to 250 million euros with the Eurosystem. It scores 34 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Three cases are documented, all alleged and unproven. In July 2018 the bank's Council reportedly found that deputy governor Irena Radovic put personal interest ahead of the public interest and disclosed business secrets, and the bank asked parliament to dismiss her; she called the decision illegal retaliation and said she would sue, and no court has ruled. The NGO MANS said five payments totalling 4,100 euros went to relatives of governor Radoje Zugic in 2017 and 2018; he reportedly said he did not act illegally. In July 2012 MANS alleged to a prosecutor that First Bank got a 44 million euro state loan in 2008 it could not repay; no charge has been brought. “Ernst&Young Montenegro” Ltd Podgorica audits the bank's accounts. Zugic has moved between the bank and the government several times: he was Deputy Director General for Payment System Operations at the bank from 2001 to 2004, director of Montenegro's Pension and Disability Insurance Fund from 2004 to 2010, Governor from 2010 to 2012, Minister of Finance from 2012 to 2016, Advisor to the Prime Minister from May to October 2016, and Governor again since October 2016; he also sat as a board member representing state capital at the commercial banks Podgoricka banka, before its privatisation, and Prva banka Crne Gore. In October 2022 Dejan Djurovic, a member of parliament for the Democratic Front, tabled amendments to the Central Bank of Montenegro Law that would have cut short the six-year mandates of vice-governor Zorica Kalezic and three members of the bank's Council. The bank said in writing that the proposal directly undermines the independence guaranteed to it, and the IMF's mission chief, Srikant Seshadri, said the Fund had told Parliament directly that the existing system should not change.
p:COD: The Central Bank of the Congo issues the country's money.
