In April 2021 a report by Congo's state finance inspectorate, the IGF, called a 43 million US dollar transfer from a central bank account at BGFI Bank to the food importer Egal an embezzlement of public funds, and said the bank kept false accounts to cover it: its 2013 accounts showed about 43.1 million dollars in that account when the real balance was about 119,000 dollars. The former governor Deogratias Mutombo, the bank and PricewaterhouseCoopers did not respond to the journalists who reported this from leaked BGFI documents. On 25 October 2023 the accounts of Mutombo and of Albert Yuma, former board chairman of the mining company Gecamines, were frozen over an alleged embezzlement of 25.521 million dollars, with both men required to remain available to the national audit court; that allegation is unproven and still under investigation. Belgium's federal prosecutor also opened a money laundering investigation into Mutombo and five others over hundreds of thousands of dollars allegedly moved through Belgium, with searches in September 2023; as of October 2024 the prosecutor said no suspect had been charged. A career move out of the bank is also recorded: Leny Ilondo's career at the bank included the position of Director before he retired, and he joined the board of Rawbank in 2024 as a non-executive director sitting on its risk and audit committees; the only description of who owns Rawbank is its own annual report's chairman's letter, which calls the shareholding family and entrepreneurial, names no individual shareholders and does not call it a private commercial bank. The bank scores 35 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Giesecke+Devrient printed the 200-franc note issued on 31 July 2007, and its imprint on the 100-franc note is the only record of who printed that one. The bank's accounts are audited by Ernst & Young RDC of Kinshasa for 2024. In a communique that reached the state news agency ACP on Wednesday 23 September 2026 the Cour des comptes, Congo's audit court, announced an audit mission at the Central Bank of the Congo to examine the bank's treasury operations for the 2025 financial year, as part of checking how the 2025 finance law was carried out. The court's First President, Jimmy Munganga, instructed the bank's services to hand the auditors the documents they need. No start or end date is given, and parliament's review of the 2025 accounts-settlement bill and of the 2027 finance bill waits on the court filing its report.
p:NZL: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand issues the New Zealand dollar. It scores 24 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, less exposed than 89% of the 194 places scored, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it. On 10 March 2016 the decision on the Official Cash Rate, the interest rate the bank sets, leaked from its media lock-up before release. Deloitte, engaged on 11 March 2016 and reporting on 12 April 2016, traced it to a Mediaworks employee: one journalist emailed a draft story out of the lock-up, and another emailed the economics blogger Michael Reddell at 8.04am, before the 9am announcement. Mediaworks reported itself on 5 April 2016, and the bank ended embargoed lock-ups. Adrian Orr, governor from 27 March 2018, was chief economist at the bank Westpac in New Zealand from 2000 to 2003, joined the Reserve Bank as deputy governor in 2003, and ran the New Zealand Superannuation Fund from 2007 until his appointment. It part-owns the Bank for International Settlements, and Note Printing Australia prints its banknotes. Orr resigned on 5 March 2025 with three years of his second term left, which the board chair put down to a personal decision. Documents released that June under the Official Information Act showed the cause was a deadlock over the bank's next five-year funding agreement: Orr argued that what the finance minister and the Treasury proposed was well below what the bank needed, and the board was willing to settle for less than he was. He had sought $1.031 billion and the settled package was close to $776 million. In August the Ombudsman forced the bank to disclose that Orr had stepped down temporarily on 27 February and agreed to resign on the basis that a letter of concerns from the board was withdrawn. The board chair resigned at the end of that month. A small part of the reserves is run from outside. The bank's own page on managing foreign reserves says a small portion of the portfolio is invested in investment funds managed by the Bank for International Settlements, and names three of them: the Asian Bond Fund, the Chinese Yuan Bond Fund and the US Dollar Green Bond Fund. It gives no amount and no share of the reserves. A separate Reserve Bank announcement of September 2019 confirms the third of those, saying the bank funded its green bond investment from its foreign reserves portfolio and that the fund invests in green bonds under the Bank for International Settlements' investment pool structure.
p:AFG: Da Afghanistan Bank is Afghanistan's central bank and issues the afghani. It scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weakest side being corruption and secrecy around it, mainly corruption in the country, while the independence written into its law scores 0.87 of 1, where 1 means the bank holds the power. In May 2011 Afghanistan's High Office of Oversight and Anticorruption reported that the central bank had monitored Kabul Bank poorly; Kabul Bank had 925 million dollars in loans outstanding, many of them undocumented and given to powerful figures, before the central bank took it over in 2010. One career move is recorded: Ajmal Ahmady came to the bank from money management, as a fixed income analyst at T. Rowe Price from 2008 to 2009, a sovereign analyst at Acadian Asset Management from 2009 to 2012 and in emerging market trading at Fortress Investment Group from 2012 to 2014, with a role at the emerging markets private equity group ACAP Partners, then government posts in Kabul, and was made acting governor by presidential decree in June 2020, serving until 15 August 2021. That dated career rests on Wikipedia, the only source that gives it; Harvard Kennedy School's own page for him, which is not Wikipedia, says that before his government work he held a variety of positions in the asset management industry and names Fortress Investment Group, Acadian Asset Management and T. Rowe Price. After the Taliban took power, the United States froze nearly 9.5 billion dollars of the bank's assets on 17 August 2021, much of it held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and stopped shipments of cash. On 11 February 2022 President Joe Biden signed an order splitting 7 billion dollars of the frozen money in two: 3.5 billion for relief in Afghanistan and 3.5 billion kept in the United States for lawsuits by US victims of terrorism. The bank holds 21.9 tonnes of gold, and its 2018 accounts were audited by Ernst & Young Ford Rhodes Sidat Hyder. A news report of 6 January 2020 said the bank had awarded the Polish Security Printing Works a contract for new 10, 20, 50 and 100 afghani notes, and on 1 February 2021 the Polish embassy in New Delhi announced that the works had delivered 380 million printed banknotes; no contract value is given and nothing says the arrangement continues.
p:UGA: The Bank of Uganda issues the Ugandan shilling, and the Auditor General audits its accounts under section 43 of the Bank of Uganda Act. One case is recorded. A confidential 2018 Auditor General report to parliament said bank managers, including governor Mutebile, acted without guidelines, regulations or policies and may have intentionally neglected aspects of the closure and sale of at least seven commercial banks between 1993 and 2017, including Crane Bank in 2016 and 2017. These are the findings of a report, not court verdicts. Sudhir Ruparelia, dfcu Bank and Nile River Acquisition Company are named in the case, the last two as having received money, favours or contracts from the central bank. Parliament then put the bank through a public inquiry over the same closures. The Auditor General, John Muwanga, presented his special audit to the Speaker of Parliament on 27 August 2018; it had been requested on 28 November 2017 by the chairman of Parliament's Committee on Commissions, Statutory Authorities and State Enterprises, and the bank had tried to stop it. It found no documented rules for identifying the buyers of three of the banks sold, and questioned how the bank spent over 400 billion shillings closing Crane Bank, half of it not recovered. The committee, chaired by Abdu Katuntu, took evidence from the governor, Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile, his deputy Louis Kasekende and other officials from late 2018 into 2019, and on 1 November 2018 Katuntu sent the governor and deputy governor away for arriving without the documents. Mutebile told the committee on 12 November that the seven banks were put under resolution largely because they were insolvent, said he had never delegated his powers to agree the sale of Global Trust Bank to DFCU Bank, and said liquidation reports had been kept from him by junior staff, which raised the question in public of whether he was in charge of his own institution. The committee's report, finalised in February 2019, recommended individual accountability for the officials implicated; demands in Parliament for action against them later stalled. One career move is recorded: Stephen Mpuuga Kaboyo held senior executive positions at the Bank of Uganda and is the founder and managing director of Alpha Capital Partners. The bank's banknote printing contract is with Oberthur Fiduciaire, signed on 26 July 2018. Northern Trust supplies compliance, performance and risk analysis and a dashboard for watching the outside firms that invest its money, which is analysis and advice rather than management of the money. Uganda scores 37 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and on paper the bank is among the less independent, 0.467 of 1 on a 42-rule measure of independence written into law.
p:MDV: The Maldives Monetary Authority issues the Maldivian rufiyaa, and its record turns on one scandal: the embezzlement of 1.3 billion rufiyaa from the Maldives Marketing and Public Relations Corporation. An Anti-Corruption Commission report made public in February 2019 found the authority negligent. Its Financial Intelligence Unit, the office that watches for suspicious money, was told in 2014 of a 59 million US dollar cheque from that company to a firm called SOF but did not look into it properly, did not examine SOF's large transactions through the Bank of Maldives and the Bank of Ceylon, and did not pass suspected money-laundering cases on. The unit's former head, Ibrahim Athif Shakoor, said governor Azeema Adam objected to filing a police report, citing too few staff and resources; Azeema said she had told him to investigate SOF's transactions and gave no specific instructions because the unit decided its own actions. In March 2019 police summoned governor Ahmed Naseer and confirmed he was being investigated for obstruction of justice, with no charge or court outcome named. He resigned in July 2019 amid allegations that he had got around the authority's rules and interfered in the unit's inquiries, one of them into a 22.5 million rufiyaa deposit to then-President Abdulla Yameen's account shortly before the 2018 election; Naseer denied influencing the unit and made counter-allegations, and no charges or findings followed. In February 2020 the Prosecutor General's Office charged Shakoor with negligence and failing to act appropriately on the case; he denied the allegations, and on 14 October 2025 that office withdrew the charge, citing how long it had been in court, with no conviction reported. One career move is documented: Ali Hashim, who was finance minister under former president Mohamed Nasheed from November 2008 to December 2010 and who also chaired the Addu International Airport Company during the previous MDP government, with no years given for that, was nominated by President Ibrahim Mohamed Solih for the vacant post of governor of the authority, as reported on 29 August 2019. Deloitte Partners in Male' audited the 2024 accounts. On 7 October 2024 India agreed a currency-borrowing line of 400 million US dollars and 30 billion Indian rupees. The authority scores 38 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Its notes are printed abroad. De La Rue's launch release says the family of six notes introduced on 1 November 2015, from 10 to 1,000 rufiyaa, was designed by local designer Abdullah Nashaath and printed by De La Rue on polymer, in close association with the Monetary Authority. Parliament has also opened the bank's own balance sheet to the government. On 23 November 2021 the People's Majlis approved the Finance Ministry's request to extend to the end of 2023 the overdraft of the public account at the Monetary Authority, by 42 votes; it had earlier suspended parts of the Fiscal Responsibility Act to allow 4.4 billion rufiyaa to be overdrawn, of which 2.5 billion was converted into a fifty-year amortising bond held by the Authority at 2.5 per cent.
p:SGP: The Monetary Authority of Singapore is the central bank that issues the Singapore dollar. It scores 24 of 100 for outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed, making it less exposed than 92% of 194 places scored; its weakest side is that the country's laws hide who owns money. No documented case was found. Who chairs it is a matter of record, and it is the cabinet: the Authority announced that from 8 July 2023 the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance would chair its Board of Directors, with the Minister for Trade and Industry as Deputy Chairman, succeeding a chairman who had held the post for twelve years while serving as a Senior Minister. The arrangement continues; the Authority's own board page now lists the Chairman as the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry and the Deputy Chairman as the Minister for National Development, with a Minister of State and the Attorney-General also on the board. Under a 1967 agreement, Brunei and Singapore accept each other's notes and coins at par. The bank is part-owner of the Bank for International Settlements, which 63 central banks own, and belongs to the Financial Stability Board. Former chairman Tharman Shanmugaratnam is a member of the Group of Thirty. It has 16 swap lines (agreements to borrow another central bank's currency). Note Printing Australia prints its banknotes. Ong Chong Tee, a Deputy Managing Director of the authority, was appointed a director of the commercial United Overseas Bank on 1 January 2023 and chairs its audit committee; he is also a director of AIA Group.
p:SRB: The National Bank of Serbia issues the Serbian dinar, and makes its own notes and coins at its Institute for Manufacturing Banknotes and Coins at Topčider, which was built from 1927, began operating in December 1929 as the institute of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, gained a mint in 1937 and also produces for foreign countries. A bill, expected to pass on 15 July, would have placed the bank under government control and allowed the dismissal of governor Mladjan Dinkic: Prime Minister Zoran Djindjic wanted a devaluation Dinkic resisted, and members of the DOS coalition said a party official cannot be governor. Dinkic said the law would make the bank dependent on government and parliament; the authorities said his claims had no foundation. On 18 July 2003 he resigned, with two of the bank's three deputy governors, after parliament passed a law letting members of parliament nominate and appoint the bank's top officials; Energy Minister Kori Udovicki was nominated to succeed him. On 11 January 2006 police arrested vice-governor Dejan Simić, along with Vladimir Zagrađanin, on suspicion of taking bribes; an investigation was ordered and the bank's Council removed him on 16 January 2006, but no indictment, verdict or acquittal followed, so the suspicion is unproven. On 10 May 2011 Erste Bank Hungary named a former governor, Radovan Jelašić, its chairman and chief executive, to start on 1 June 2011 subject to approval by the Hungarian market regulators. Serbia keeps its gold at home rather than with a custodian abroad. It holds 54.6 tonnes in all, 20.9 percent of its reserves. The bank's annual report for 2024 sets out the make-up of the foreign exchange reserves at 31 December 2024 as foreign securities at 59.16 percent, money in accounts abroad at 22.04 percent, gold in the bank's own vaults at 13.26 percent, and foreign cash and special drawing rights; the whole holding sits in those vaults in Belgrade, with no foreign custodian, which is storage rather than management. Ernst & Young d.o.o. Beograd audited the accounts for 2025. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the bank used by central banks themselves, and has two currency swap lines with China, one re-signed on 28 May 2026 for 5 billion yuan against 74 billion dinars and running five years from the re-signing, and an earlier agreement of June 2016 for 1.5 billion yuan. Serbia scores 29 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, less exposed than 65 percent of the 194 places with a figure.
p:MNG: The Bank of Mongolia issues the tugrik. Two cases and two departures centre on N. Zoljargal, governor from 2012, who was replaced on 20 July 2016, two years before his term was due to end and with no reason given. The anti-corruption agency IAAC arrested him on 29 November 2017 over the Chinggis bond and a price-stabilising programme, part of a wider look at how the bank was run from 2012 to 2016; a court released him with a travel ban, prosecutors had not formally charged him and no later outcome was found, so nothing there is proven. In April 2020 he and three politicians were reported charged with abuse of power over illegally transferring 49 per cent of the Erdenet Mining Company; no outcome is recorded and those charges are unproven too. Lawmakers accepted the resignation of his successor, Nadmid Bayartsaikhan, on 21 November 2019, after the Financial Action Task Force, which sets international rules against money laundering, put Mongolia on its grey list over enforcement. The present governor, B. Lkhagvasuren, came from the World Bank in Washington to the bank as adviser to the governor in 2000, and the rest of his career is in Mongolian public bodies. Two more careers run between the bank and the banks it supervises. Khosjargal Undraa joined the Supervisory Board in 2025 after thirteen years at Golomt Bank, from branch teller in 2006 to project director of its business process re-engineering project in 2018 and 2019, then deputy director of MIG LLC and chief executive of BPM Mongolia; Golomt's own account of itself says it was set up in 1995 as a subsidiary of Bodi International and became a joint-stock company at its 2022 listing, naming no state shareholder. Enkhjargal Danzanbaljir's career stays inside the public sector and so is listed without being counted: chief economist and adviser to the governor, London representative, Deputy Governor from 2007 to 2010, then the Asian Development Bank, the AIIB, the World Bank, an EU and GIZ project, the intergovernmental International Investment Bank and the state-owned State Bank of Mongolia, before rejoining the Supervisory Board in 2025. Ernst & Young Mongolia Audit LLC audited the accounts for the 2020 financial year, and Giesecke & Devrient printed the new 5,000-togrog note. It holds two currency swap lines with China, arrangements to lend each other money, one renewed on 26 June 2026 at 15 billion yuan against 7.85 trillion tugrik, and scores 31 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Where its gold is kept is disclosed, and the disclosure is going backwards. The bank's audited accounts for 2021 say its monetary gold and silver are mainly placed at the Bank of England and at JPMorgan Chase Bank, a commercial bank. The same note in the 2024 accounts drops both names and says only that the gold is held in foreign banks and in the vault of the Bank, so part of it is kept at home and the foreign holders are no longer named.
p:ECU: Ecuador's money is the US dollar, adopted in January 2000 at 25,000 sucres to the dollar, so the Central Bank of Ecuador issues no currency of its own. It does not set policy either. The 1998 constitution had given the bank independence; the constitution that replaced it, sponsored by Rafael Correa's government and published on 20 October 2008, took it away. Article 303 makes the drafting of monetary, credit, foreign exchange and financial policy the exclusive power of the Executive, to be carried out through the Central Bank, and the bank's own website describes its job in those terms. The monetary board was replaced by a board of five members appointed by the president and confirmed by Congress. A monetary and fiscal history of Ecuador prepared for the University of Chicago lists 2008 as the suppression of central bank independence and says the constitution made the bank dependent on the executive branch, which became responsible for designing fiscal and monetary policy. Article 303 is still in force, so this is the standing arrangement rather than an episode with an end. Ecuador scores 35 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weakest side being corruption in the country and the risk of money laundering in its banks. One case is recorded and it ended in conviction: on 8 January 2019 the National Court of Justice sentenced Pedro Delgado, a former president of the bank, to five years in prison, restitution of 788,855.94 dollars, forfeiture of assets and public apologies. Prosecutors described the crime as unlawful association while the court's own post called it illicit enrichment; the same source reports an earlier embezzlement conviction in 2015 carrying eight years, and says he allegedly allowed large loans without proper documents or guarantees while leading the bank, which is unproven. One career move is counted. Juan Diego Mosquera Pesantes was a delegate and member of the Monetary Board at the Banco Central del Ecuador in 1981, and has been a director and board member of Produbanco, formally Banco de la Produccion S.A., since 2014; the curriculum vitae Produbanco publishes for him also lists posts at Citibank Quito, where he was founding manager, Banco del Pichincha, Banco del Azuay, where he was a manager, the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and BAC Corp Securities. Government pressure was reported in 2 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, pressing the bank to loosen policy, change the law and print money. The bank joined the World Bank's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, which gives it advice, executive training and asset-management expertise rather than a mandate to run Ecuador's reserves. Its 2021 accounts were audited by Kreston Audit Services Ecuador. It holds 26.3 tonnes of gold, 27.7 percent of its reserves, and the country has had two systemic banking crises since 1970.
p:CMR: Cameroon's money, the Central African CFA franc, is issued by the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), which sets monetary policy for 6 members. The franc is fixed at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs, France guarantees its convertibility, and the BEAC must keep at least 50% of its foreign reserves at the French Treasury. The bank scores 44 of 100 for outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed. One case is recorded: a November 2009 internal report found about 20 billion CFA francs diverted from the bank's Paris office to 139 beneficiaries between 2004 and 2008. On 28 September 2012 a court in Mfoundi sentenced Kemadjou to life imprisonment and ordered him to pay BEAC 26.4 billion CFA francs. Jean-Pierre Oyiba, chief of staff to Gabon's president, is named as a recipient of the money; he resigned on 9 November 2009 after the report said he received about 100,000 euros, which he denies. Philibert Andzembe, a Gabonese national, had been the bank's governor since July 2007, and in October 2009 Gabon's president Ali Bongo fired him in response to a scandal in which 28.3 million US dollars went missing from the bank's Paris branch; Gabon held the right to appoint the governor at the time, and Lucas Abaga Nchama of Equatorial Guinea took the post in 2010. A separate leaked US diplomatic cable, made public in December 2010, alleged that Gabonese officials working at the bank had taken about 36 million US dollars from the pooled reserves over roughly five years. The reserves the BEAC must keep at the French Treasury sit in an operations account (compte d'operations) opened in the BEAC's name. The required share earns interest at the European Central Bank's marginal lending facility rate, 0.25 per cent since 16 March 2016, and anything the BEAC chooses to deposit above that share earns the ECB's minimum rate on main refinancing operations, 0 per cent since 16 March 2016. KPMG Afrique Centrale and Mazars Cameroun audit the accounts jointly. Its money is printed in France. The French foreign ministry's own page on the Franc Zone says the African central banks place the orders for notes and coins under a contract with a manufacturer, in this case the Banque de France, and that CFA franc notes and coins have been made at its works at Chamalieres since 1945; the heads of state and government of the Franc Zone may decide together to change where they are printed. The BEAC's own site cannot be read by automated requests, so this does not rest on a BEAC document. The governor's career is published, and it reaches Cameroon through the union. Abbas Mahamat Tolli was Chad's Minister of Finance and Budget from 2005 to 2008 and President of the Development Bank of Central African States, the BDEAC. On 31 July 2016 CEMAC heads of state, meeting in Malabo, appointed Chad's former finance minister as the new BEAC governor, to take office in January 2017 in succession to Lucas Abaga Nchama; he held the post until 2024.
p:HKG: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority runs the Hong Kong dollar as a currency board, meaning it is tied to another currency: the monetary base is fully backed by US dollar assets in the Exchange Fund. The link began on 17 October 1983 at 7.80 Hong Kong dollars per US dollar, and since May 2005 the authority sells Hong Kong dollars at 7.75 and buys at 7.85. It scores 35 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. One case is recorded: in 2012 a Legislative Council subcommittee found that former chief Joseph Yam Chi-kwong should bear “ultimate responsibility” for investors' losses on Lehman's minibonds. The authority replied that the report had not fully taken into account the information it submitted, and some members prepared a minority report. One career move is recorded, and it is his: Joseph Yam headed the Office of the Exchange Fund from 1991 to 1993 and ran the authority from 1 April 1993 to 30 September 2009, and after leaving he was an independent non-executive director of China Construction Bank from 2010 until 23 October 2013, was elected in April 2011 to the board of the Swiss bank UBS AG, where he sat on its risk committee and its corporate culture and responsibility committee from 2011, and sat on the UBS Group AG board from November 2014 to May 2017. Banknotes are printed in Hong Kong by Hong Kong Note Printing Limited, in which the government keeps management control and a majority stake. The authority's relationship to the government is its founding design rather than something later taken from an independent bank, and it is a standing arrangement with no end date. The HKMA's own annual report describes how the Legislative Council passed amendments to the Exchange Fund Ordinance in 1992 empowering the Financial Secretary to appoint a Monetary Authority, and the HKMA began work on 1 April 1993. The Monetary Authority is appointed to assist the Financial Secretary, the Exchange Fund is under his control, and the powers are exercised by his delegation.
p:SSD: South Sudan's money is the South Sudanese pound, issued by the Bank of South Sudan, and its notes are printed by De La Rue, which won a contract for 2.8 billion banknotes in 2011. The country scores 39 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, almost all of it from corruption in the country. A United Nations Human Rights Council commission report said De La Rue transferred about 1.4 million US dollars between 2016 and September 2017 into an Equity Bank account in Nairobi held by a consultant to the bank, against a banknote contract worth about 144 million dollars, and noted suspected corruption. That report stands as an official finding, but the United Kingdom's Serious Fraud Office, which opened its own investigation in July 2019, closed it in June 2020, saying the case did not meet the test for prosecution. On 9 June 2025 President Salva Kiir Mayardit removed Johnny Ohisa Domian as governor by presidential decree, broadcast on state-run media, and no reason was given; the first deputy governor, Addis Ababa Othow, was named to replace him. Othow's own career is the one move recorded here, and it runs in and out of a commercial bank: he joined the Central Bank of Sudan as a banking inspector in 1997, joined Ivory Bank in 1998, came to the Bank of South Sudan in 2010 as head of its non-banking division, headed its planning, regulation and licensing division in 2013, then in 2015 joined Equity Bank's Nairobi headquarters as general manager of operations, becoming managing director of Equity Bank South Sudan in 2018, a step his profile describes as moving back to the private sector; he was first deputy governor from 2022 to October 2023, returned briefly to Equity Bank, was reappointed first deputy governor in February 2025 and appointed governor in June 2025. In February and March 2026 security forces detained former governor Manguak, placed under house arrest, with former finance ministers and other officials, and the information minister said a committee was investigating financial malpractices; no charges had been announced as of March 2026, so nothing is proven, and Manguak denies the allegations. The Auditor General audits the accounts.
p:ROU: The National Bank of Romania issues the Romanian leu, which in practice tracks the euro. It scores 25 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and no government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. On 28 December 2018 the government imposed a tax of 0.3 percent on banks' financial assets and set the rate of that tax by reference to ROBOR, the interbank money market rate, so the tax rose as the bank raised rates. Appearing with the whole board before Senate committees in February 2019, Governor Mugur Isarescu called it a tax on monetary policy that ties the central bank's hands and said that linking the asset tax to ROBOR is an attack on the independence of the National Bank. The European Central Bank wrote to the finance minister on 5 February 2019 saying it had not been consulted, contrary to its obligation under EU rules, and that the measure came with no impact assessment. The government published amendments removing the link to ROBOR on 26 March 2019. One case is recorded. In 2014 the High Court of Cassation and Justice placed the sitting deputy governor, Olteanu, under 30-day house arrest in a National Anticorruption Directorate case alleging that in 2008, while parliament speaker, he asked for and received a 1 million euro bribe from the businessman Sorin Ovidiu Vantu. He was convicted of influence peddling and given a final five-year sentence in October 2020, but on 31 March 2023 the Bucharest Court of Appeal confirmed the case closed as time-barred and annulled the conviction, while ordering the money confiscated. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Nicolae Danila ran Banca Comerciala Romana from 1999 to 2008, then sat on the bank's board until September 2014 and later chaired First Bank SA; no ethics finding is recorded. The bank said on 10 September 2024 that it is the holder of an account at the Bank of England where about 60 of its 103.6 tonnes of gold sit, that the custodian cannot use that gold in any form, and that transactions happen only on the bank's instruction; 42.4 tonnes are held in Romania. That account comes from a newspaper quoting the statement rather than from a document on the bank's own site. Part of its reserves is run from outside. Note 8 to its audited accounts for 2023 says that under a technical assistance and asset management contract signed with the World Bank in 2017, the World Bank continued during 2023 to manage the US dollar denominated asset portfolio the bank allocated to the Reserves Advisory and Management Program. It gives the holdings at 31 December 2023 as deposits of 85,083 thousand lei and securities of 2,663,330 thousand lei, 2,748,413 thousand lei in all, against 2,710,628 thousand lei a year earlier, and no share of total reserves.
p:MMR: The Central Bank of Myanmar issues the kyat, and the military has taken hold of its leadership. Three days after the coup of 1 February 2021 the military's State Administration Council made Than Than Swe a deputy governor; she later became governor in place of Than Nyein. On 24 August 2022 the junta replaced Than Nyein and a vice chairman with Than Than Swe and Major General Zaw Myint Naing, two months after installing six lieutenant colonels as deputy directors, a shake-up Radio Free Asia reported as a bid to control the country's financial sector. The former deputy governor Bo Bo Nge, arrested on the morning of the coup, was sentenced by a junta court in December 2022 to 20 years in prison after a months-long secret trial, which sources said concerned mismanagement of banks trading foreign currency; the junta-backed Anti-Corruption Commission accused him of not collecting tax on a 5 million US dollar Open Society deposit and of placing a 350 million dollar loan in a lower-interest account, with alleged losses of 102, 360 and 655 million kyats. Those accusations are the commission's own, and the economist Sean Turnell called Bo Bo Nge someone fighting against corruption. Two people have left senior posts at the bank for private banks. Than Lwin was an economist at the bank from 1966, a director in 1997 and deputy governor and controller of foreign exchange from 1997 to 2003, and in 2004 he joined Kanbawza Bank as a consultant, later becoming its deputy chairman; an interview with Kanbawza's senior managing director calls it Myanmar's largest privately owned financial institution and the largest of 19 privately owned banks in the country, which is what establishes the employer's private ownership. Khin Saw Oo, a former deputy governor for whom no central bank dates are given, joined AYA Bank as vice-chairman in 2018 and was re-designated executive chairman in May 2021; AYA's own corporate profile calls it a leading private sector bank in Myanmar and says it was registered as a private company limited by shares on 14 July 2010 and reincorporated as a public company limited on 30 December 2022. No documented case at the bank was found, which is not proof that none happened: Reporters Without Borders rates the situation for journalists here as very serious in its 2026 index, so the court reports and press coverage a case would be found in may not exist or may not be publishable. Government pressure was reported in 18 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, mostly pressing the bank to ease and to print money. Giesecke+Devrient of Munich, which had supplied raw materials, supplies and system components for printing kyat notes, suspended all deliveries to the state-owned Security Print Works after the military crackdown. The bank's own printing works at Wazi printed a 20,000-kyat commemorative note introduced on 31 July 2023, which is not the circulating series, and the Union Auditor General Office audits the accounts under the 2013 central bank law. Myanmar scores 38 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:KNA: St Kitts and Nevis does not issue its own money. The East Caribbean dollar is issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, set up under an agreement signed on 5 July 1983, for eight member places, and the rate has been held at 2.70 East Caribbean dollars to one US dollar since July 1976, when the peg moved from sterling. The country scores 31 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weakest side being corruption and secrecy around it, and no government pressure on the bank was reported in any of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case concerns the bank: after it seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued it in Dallas in 2013, alleging it had fraudulently taken assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors; on 17 August 2018 a US federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, without ruling on whether the allegations were true. In a letter dated 17 February 2025 to Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who chairs the ECCU Monetary Council, St Vincent and the Grenadines Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves objected to the EC$22 million spent on an official residence for Governor Timothy Antoine, called the spending outrageous and the roughly 10,000 square foot house a mansion of veritable palace proportions, wrote that the governor may wish to consider whether his continued occupancy of the office is tenable and that the spending invites disciplinary action, and proposed that the Monetary Council sell the residence to the government of St Kitts and Nevis; on 5 March 2025 Gonsalves told NBC Radio he would neither confirm nor deny sending the letter. Trevor Brathwaite, an accountant who earlier worked for KPMG Peat Marwick, was deputy governor from April 2006 to September 2021 and sat on the board of East Caribbean Financial Holding Co. Ltd, a financial holding company; no dates are given for that seat. De La Rue prints the notes and PricewaterhouseCoopers Eastern Caribbean audits the accounts. The bank's 2020/2021 annual report says it continued its engagement with the World Bank's Reserves Advisory Management Partnership (RAMP), and that a second engagement was judged appropriate to go on building up its newly formed Risk and Analytics Unit, the unit that reports on the reserves portfolio; the same report says the investment guidelines for its external managers were reviewed and updated and that the foreign reserve portfolio had grown to about EC$4.6 billion. The annual report for 2024/2025 and the audited accounts to 31 March 2025 do not repeat the RAMP engagement, so it stands as a 2020/2021 fact.
p:GTM: The Bank of Guatemala issues the quetzal and in practice holds it close to a fixed rate against the US dollar. One case is recorded. In May 2015 the bank's president, Julio Suarez, was arrested along with other members of the board of the social security institute, the IGSS. Prosecutors said the group took part in the irregular award of a 116 million quetzal IGSS contract, about 14.5 million US dollars, to the drug company Pisa de Guatemala, on charges of unlawful association, influence peddling, illegal commissions and active bribery. He was acquitted on appeal in June 2019, and the Supreme Court's Criminal Chamber upheld that acquittal, as reported in October 2021. An earlier president of the bank was prosecuted and sentenced: Guatemala's Public Ministry and the UN-backed International Commission Against Impunity in Guatemala, CICIG, charged Edgar Barquin, a former president of the bank and a 2015 vice-presidential candidate, with influence trafficking, after investigators found he had warned Francisco Edgar Morales Guerra, known as Chico Dolar, of a coming investigation and later helped him evade scrutiny for monetary gain. On 16 September 2016 Barquin was sentenced to 30 months in prison, which the judge suspended on the attorney general's recommendation as part of a plea bargain in which Barquin admitted guilt and agreed to cooperate; he was barred for five years from public office and from exercising his political rights, and the report says he admitted involvement in laundering 30 million US dollars. One career move is documented: Alvaro Gonzalez Ricci was Guatemala's Minister of Public Finance from January 2020 and then became president of the Bank of Guatemala for a four-year term reported on 1 October 2022 and running to 20 September 2026. No government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. The bank keeps coined gold worth about 315.5 million US dollars at the end of 2024 in its own vaults, and gold worth about 263.1 million dollars in storage at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, which holds it while Guatemala still owns it. Its smaller notes are printed abroad: on 20 August 2018 the bank agreed with the Polish printer Polska Wytwornia Papierow Wartosciowych to produce 5- and 10-quetzal notes on a material containing synthetic fibres. It is also a member of the World Bank Treasury's RAMP network, which offers advice, training and asset management, without saying which of those Guatemala gets. Most of one tranche of its reserves is run by outside firms. The bank's quarterly statement of international reserves at 31 March 2026 breaks the investment tranche's portfolio sub-tranche, 17,731.0 million US dollars, between UBS Asset Management (UK) at 2,843.8 million, Allianz Global Investors through PIMCO at 2,744.8 million, JPMorgan Asset Management (UK) at 2,644.9 million, the World Bank's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership at 1,716.3 million, Allianz Global Investors itself at 1,502.3 million, and the Bank of Guatemala in-house at 6,278.9 million, against total reserves of 33,049.9 million. Guatemala scores 34 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:CIV: Côte d'Ivoire uses the West African CFA franc, issued by the Central Bank of West African States, the BCEAO, which sets monetary policy for eight member countries. The franc is pegged — held at a fixed rate — at 655.957 to the euro, and France promises to advance euros if the bank's reserves run out; a 2019 agreement ended the rule that it keep at least half its reserves at the French Treasury. The country scores 43 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Two cases come out of the post-election crisis of December 2010 to April 2011. On 18 January 2018 a court sentenced Laurent Gbagbo, Aké N'Gbo, Katinan and Dallo to 20 years and a fine of 329 billion CFA francs for offences including group theft by break-in of BCEAO vaults and cash; seven bailiffs got 36 months and a 700,000 CFA franc fine, Katinan was absent throughout, Gbagbo always denied the charges, and on 6 August 2022 President Ouattara pardoned him. Earlier, in January 2011, a summit of UEMOA heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation, after he was criticized for ignoring a 23 December decision by UEMOA finance ministers that gave Alassane Ouattara power over the institution; the account says the bank paid 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime after that date, and Senegal's President Abdoulaye Wade asked for an audit and alleged 500 billion CFA francs had been moved, with no audit result given. The bank's own statement said the resignation resulted from pressure from the region's leaders, and Dacoury-Tabley said afterwards that he agreed to hand it in because that is what was asked of him. Days later Gbagbo ordered the seizure of the bank's Ivorian branches, after it said it would no longer honour his signature; Ouattara ordered those branches closed and said anyone following Gbagbo's orders would be prosecuted. His prime minister, Guillaume Soro, said that when Gbagbo goes to the BCEAO in Abidjan with tanks and Kalashnikovs he cannot but trigger bank closures and halt cash flow. On 9 February 2011 the Gbagbo administration also seized the regional stock exchange, the Bourse Regionale des Valeurs Mobilieres, which then stopped operating in Abidjan, and international banks left the country. Its money is printed in France. The French foreign ministry's own page on the Franc Zone says the African central banks place the orders for notes and coins under a contract with a manufacturer, in this case the Banque de France, and that CFA franc notes and coins have been made at its works at Chamalieres since 1945; the heads of state and government of the Franc Zone may decide together to change where they are printed. The Banque de France's own director general of banknote manufacturing has called the BCEAO its largest export customer. The BCEAO's published accounts do not name the maker. Its gold is mostly not in Africa. Note 6 of the BCEAO's own financial statements for 2024 lists three places: the bank's head office, the Banque de France and the Bank for International Settlements. On deposit at the Banque de France are 1,054,479.65 ounces, valued at 1,756,111 million CFA francs, out of a stock of about 1.52 million ounces worth 2,531,800 million, which is about 70 per cent; press reporting places it in the Banque de France's underground vault in the first arrondissement of Paris. The Bank for International Settlements holds close to 106,000 ounces, and only about 120,000 ounces, under 8 per cent, sit physically at the head office in Dakar. In the 2018 statements the Paris deposit was 85 per cent of holdings; the share has fallen because the rest of the stock grew, not because gold left Paris. Answering Senator Pierre Laurent on 20 October 2022, the French economy ministry said the rules for the deposit are set by a specific convention covering the services the Banque de France provides to the BCEAO, and that the gold, like the union's foreign exchange reserves, is pooled at the BCEAO rather than apportioned by country. The concentration is contested: pan-Africanist currents and some economists read it as a continuing post-colonial dependence and ask whether the gold will be repatriated as the member states' operating account deposits at the French Treasury were. Part of the reserves is run by outside institutions. The BCEAO's own audited accounts for 2025 say it has bought units in an investment fund called BISIP K, managed by the Bank for International Settlements, worth 205,811 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 222,297 million FCFA a year earlier, and that it has joined the RAMP fund, the Reserve Advisory Management Program managed by the World Bank, worth 138,800 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 149,873 million FCFA a year earlier. Together the two sets of fund units came to 344,611 million FCFA at the end of 2025, and the accounts group the BISIP K units with the holdings kept for immediate liquidity. The accounts are audited by firms appointed in pairs, one doing the work and one standing in: Deloitte Cote d'Ivoire with Mazars Cote d'Ivoire for Cote d'Ivoire, and Deloitte Cote d'Ivoire with Mazars Senegal for the BCEAO itself. The governors' careers are published, and they reach Cote d'Ivoire through the union. Jean-Claude Kassi Brou joined the International Monetary Fund in 1982, worked as an economist and senior economist in several African countries, was the IMF's resident representative in Senegal from 1990 to 1991 and the World Bank's representative for Chad; he worked at the BCEAO from 2000 to 2008, was President of the ECOWAS Commission from 1 March 2018 to 3 July 2022, and became governor on 3 July 2022. Tiemoko Meyliet Kone joined the bank in 1975 and was its National Director and Alternate Governor at the IMF from 1991 to 1998, was chief of staff to Prime Minister Guillaume Soro from 2007 to 2010 and Minister of Construction, Urban Planning and Housing in 2010, was governor from 2011 to 2022, and has been Vice-President of Cote d'Ivoire since April 2022, appointed on 19 April 2022. The ministry he held was construction and housing, not finance.
p:SEN: Senegal uses the West African CFA franc, issued for eight countries by the Central Bank of West African States, the BCEAO, which is based in Senegal. The franc is fixed at 655.957 to the euro, and the French Treasury promises to advance euros if the bank's reserves run out; an agreement signed on 21 December 2019 ended the rule that at least half those reserves sit at the Treasury. One case is recorded. In January 2011 a summit of UEMOA heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation, after he was criticized for ignoring a 23 December decision by UEMOA finance ministers that gave Alassane Ouattara power over the institution; the report says the BCEAO paid out 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime afterwards. The bank's own statement said the resignation resulted from pressure from the region's leaders, and Dacoury-Tabley said afterwards that he agreed to hand it in because that is what was asked of him. President Abdoulaye Wade asked for an audit and alleged the former governor moved 500 billion CFA francs to Gbagbo; that is unproven, and no audit result is given. Its money is printed in France. The French foreign ministry's own page on the Franc Zone says the African central banks place the orders for notes and coins under a contract with a manufacturer, in this case the Banque de France, and that CFA franc notes and coins have been made at its works at Chamalieres since 1945; the heads of state and government of the Franc Zone may decide together to change where they are printed. The Banque de France's own director general of banknote manufacturing has called the BCEAO its largest export customer. The BCEAO's published accounts do not name the maker. Its gold is mostly not in Africa. Note 6 of the BCEAO's own financial statements for 2024 lists three places: the bank's head office, the Banque de France and the Bank for International Settlements. On deposit at the Banque de France are 1,054,479.65 ounces, valued at 1,756,111 million CFA francs, out of a stock of about 1.52 million ounces worth 2,531,800 million, which is about 70 per cent; press reporting places it in the Banque de France's underground vault in the first arrondissement of Paris. The Bank for International Settlements holds close to 106,000 ounces, and only about 120,000 ounces, under 8 per cent, sit physically at the head office in Dakar. In the 2018 statements the Paris deposit was 85 per cent of holdings; the share has fallen because the rest of the stock grew, not because gold left Paris. Answering Senator Pierre Laurent on 20 October 2022, the French economy ministry said the rules for the deposit are set by a specific convention covering the services the Banque de France provides to the BCEAO, and that the gold, like the union's foreign exchange reserves, is pooled at the BCEAO rather than apportioned by country. The concentration is contested: pan-Africanist currents and some economists read it as a continuing post-colonial dependence and ask whether the gold will be repatriated as the member states' operating account deposits at the French Treasury were. Part of its reserves sits in two funds run by other institutions. The BCEAO's own audited accounts for 2025 say it bought units in a fund called BISIP K, managed by the Bank for International Settlements, worth 205,811 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 222,297 million FCFA a year earlier, and grouped with the holdings kept for immediate liquidity. The same accounts say the bank joined the RAMP fund, the Reserve Advisory Management Program, managed by the World Bank, whose units were worth 138,800 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 149,873 million FCFA a year earlier. Together the two came to 344,611 million FCFA at the end of 2025. The governors' careers are published, and they reach Senegal through the union. Jean-Claude Kassi Brou joined the International Monetary Fund in 1982, worked as an economist and senior economist in several African countries, was the IMF's resident representative in Senegal from 1990 to 1991 and the World Bank's representative for Chad; he worked at the BCEAO from 2000 to 2008, was President of the ECOWAS Commission from 1 March 2018 to 3 July 2022, and became governor on 3 July 2022. Tiemoko Meyliet Kone joined the bank in 1975 and was its National Director and Alternate Governor at the IMF from 1991 to 1998, was chief of staff to Prime Minister Guillaume Soro from 2007 to 2010 and Minister of Construction, Urban Planning and Housing in 2010, was governor from 2011 to 2022, and has been Vice-President of Cote d'Ivoire since April 2022, appointed on 19 April 2022. The ministry he held was construction and housing, not finance.
p:CAN: The Bank of Canada issues the Canadian dollar, which moves within a band of 2% or less against the US dollar. Canada scores 24 of 100 on exposure to influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed; that is 179th of 194, less exposed than 88 percent of the places with a figure. One case is documented, and it ended in an official finding: two internal audits of the bank from 2004, released under the Access to Information Act, one of them dated 15 October, criticised it for slack financial practices, finding that employees paid invoices without authorization, did not evaluate whether they got good value from suppliers, and violated a fail-safe system meant to guard against cheque fraud. No government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. Pressure came later and from the opposition rather than the government: at a Conservative leadership debate in Edmonton on 11 May 2022, Pierre Poilievre pledged to fire governor Tiff Macklem if he became prime minister, having called the bank financially illiterate the month before, and also promised to have it audited and to bar it from issuing a digital currency; he repeated the pledge as party leader in December 2022. Macklem had been appointed in 2020 to a seven-year term, and the Bank of Canada Act says the governor is appointed for seven years during good behaviour, so removing one would require Parliament's involvement. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and Finance Minister Chrystia Freeland both defended the bank's independence and former governor David Dodge rejected the criticism; the party's own finance critic, Ed Fast, was removed from that role after saying the pledge was deeply troubling and hurt the party's economic credibility. The bank's own profile of Mark Carney, governor from 1 February 2008 to 1 June 2013, describes a thirteen-year career at the investment bank Goldman Sachs, in its London, Tokyo, New York and Toronto offices, before he entered the public service; he joined the bank as Deputy Governor in August 2003, moved to the Department of Finance in November 2004 and returned as Governor, and no ethics finding is recorded for the move. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Ernst & Young and PricewaterhouseCoopers audit its accounts, Canadian Bank Note Company and BA International print its notes, and Securency International supplies the polymer the notes are made of. The Canadian dollar is 5.76% of world currency trading and 2.47% of foreign reserves, and the bank has 9 swap lines, which are agreements to borrow another central bank's currency.
p:AGO: The National Bank of Angola issues the kwanza (AOA). Angola scores 42 of 100 on exposure to influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is secrecy about who owns money and corruption (index score 32 of 100). Government pressure was reported in 29 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, nearly all pressing the bank to cut rates or ease, with 8 threats to replace leaders. On 14 August 2020 the Supreme Court convicted former governor Valter Filipe (eight years), BNA manager Samalia (five years), José Filomeno dos Santos (five years) and businessman Sebastião (six years) of embezzlement, fraud and influence peddling over an attempted transfer of $500 million to a London account, which a British bank blocked. The Constitutional Court is also named in the case. Goznak, the Russian state printer, printed the 5,000-kwanza note. KPMG audits the bank's accounts, and signed off on the 2021 accounts with one reservation and seven emphases, against three reservations and six emphases the year before. The London firm Gemcorp Capital held 56 percent of the bank's external assets at the end of 2023, 601,697 million kwanzas or about 725 million US dollars. For the 2019 and 2020 accounts Gemcorp did not say what it had invested the central bank's money in, so the bank had to carry the holding at nil, and it then renewed the investment for a further six years. Both facts come from the newspaper Expansao reading the bank's accounts rather than from the accounts themselves: the bank's own website publishes no documents a reader can open. On Friday 27 October 2017 President Joao Lourenco exonerated Valter Filipe as governor of the Banco Nacional de Angola and named Jose de Lima Massano in his place, returning Massano to the post he had held until January 2015 and taking him from the chairmanship of the executive board of Banco Angolano de Investimentos. A note from the President's Civil House says the exoneration was at Filipe's own request, and no other official reason is given; the exit came eleven days after the President criticised the bank in a speech on 16 October, and no connection between the two is reported. Massano's own career is on record: he was governor for close to ten years between 2010 and 2023, became a Senior Minister in the President's office in June 2023, and had earlier been chief executive of Banco BAI and an executive director of the state-owned BPC. His biography gives no dates for either bank. BAI's ownership is now on record from the bank's own corporate page, which says it was founded on 14 November 1996 as the first private bank with national capital established in Angola, so that side of the career is private finance. The move back is dated too: BAI's general assembly elected Massano to its board of directors on 18 August 2015, duties he had held there before, and he was due to take office on 1 September 2015.
p:PER: The Central Reserve Bank of Peru issues the sol, managed within a band of about 5 per cent against the US dollar, and Peru scores 28 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Congress passed law 31143 against usury by insistence on 11 March 2021, overriding the executive's objection. It requires the bank to set maximum and minimum interest rates every six months for consumer loans up to two tax units, about 8,800 soles, and for loans to small and micro enterprises. The bank had opposed rate ceilings in public and said so again in the announcement setting the first ceiling at 83.4 percent a year: ceilings are not the most appropriate mechanism, because they ration credit away from borrowers whose credit risk sits above the cap. Its own study of the period from May 2021 to March 2024 estimated more than 542,000 people affected, 40 percent of them borrowers who left the financial system. In November 2021 the justice minister, Anibal Torres, criticised Governor Julio Velarde for having come out against the law. Congress reached into the design of the money as well. Law 32251, published on 19 January 2025 and following a Constitutional Court ruling, requires the bank's coins and banknotes to carry the full national coat of arms, the words Republica del Peru and the motto Firme y feliz por la union. A bank official, Abraham de la Melena, said the bank was not consulted in drafting the law or in approving it, and the bank set out what the change costs in practical terms: the full coat of arms shrinks the central part of a coin's obverse, which makes it harder to strike and makes the coin's security features harder for the public to recognise; fitting the motto in means cutting the bank's own name from the design; and on banknotes the coat of arms cannot go on the front without disturbing the security elements, watermarks and fluorescent zones among them. On the Ministry of Defence's draft regulation of July 2025 the bank added that coin-handling machines nationwide would need recalibrating, that two versions of one denomination in circulation would confuse users and open a door to counterfeiters, and that redesigning, tendering, printing and distributing new notes would take 14 to 15 months at high cost. Velarde said the bank would comply but that the change introduces costs, and that the arms the bank uses predate the bank's own 102 years. Congress then moved to undo it: bills 10738 and 10769 cleared the constitution committee, and in March 2026 Congress approved an amendment making the use of the coat of arms and the motto conditional on the bank's own board approving it, which the committee framed as preserving the bank's technical and operational autonomy. One matter, from 1986 to 1991, is alleged and unproven. A New York grand-jury indictment of the Bank of Credit and Commerce International in 1991 alleged three million US dollars in bribes in return for depositing part of Peru's 1986-87 reserves in that bank's Panama branch, after the Peruvian board approved moving 100 million dollars and later doubling it. The indictment named no officials of the Peruvian bank; the Christian Science Monitor identified Figueroa and Neyra, and both strenuously denied the charges, Neyra calling the decision purely technical. All Peruvian deposits were withdrawn by the end of 1987, and a Peruvian parliamentary commission also looked into the bank. Separately, Eduardo Torres-Llosa spent 21 years at BBVA in Peru, left in June 2019 as its managing director, sat on the boards of Financiera Confianza and BBVA in Uruguay and chaired the engineering firm Cosapi, and became the central bank's general manager in March 2022; no ethics finding is recorded. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Perum Peruri won the tender to print the 10, 20 and 50 nuevo sol notes, reported as still unsigned in January 2020 and as secured by December 2022, with no value given, and a member firm of PricewaterhouseCoopers audits the accounts.
p:SLE: The Bank of Sierra Leone issues the leone and scores 36 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is corruption and secrecy, at 66. Under the 2019 Bank of Sierra Leone Act, sacking the governor needs a two-thirds majority in parliament. In August 2018 the recently elected president dismissed the governor, and Kelfala Kallon was appointed on 15 August as the bank's third governor in 17 months; neither the dismissed governor nor either side's reason is named. On 22 November 2021 Kallon told parliament that he had bribed people hoarding the leone to bring it back into the banking system. The Anti-Corruption Commission investigated and said in May 2022 that he had meant cash swap operations in which the bank sold about 68.6 million United States dollars of foreign currency in 2021, that the word was used in error, and that it had closed the investigation after advising him to choose his words more carefully. On 13 March 2023 President Julius Maada Bio sent Kallon on indefinite leave and named his deputy, Ibrahim Stevens, interim head; no official reason was given, Kallon did not respond, and the president was reported to be bypassing the 2019 Act. De La Rue printed the 10-leone note of the redenominated series introduced on 1 July 2022, and the West African Monetary Institute manages the Stabilization and Cooperation Fund, in which the bank holds 63.59 million new leone. One career is on file, and every outside employer in it is public or academic. The Bank of Sierra Leone's own board page gives names, roles and appointment dates and no employers at all, so this comes from a university biography: Ibrahim L. Stevens spent a decade at the Bank of England, including as Senior Adviser at its Centre for Central Banking Studies, was Director of Research at the Bank of Sierra Leone from 2008 to 2010 on secondment from the Bank of England, worked with the International Growth Centre at the London School of Economics and advised Rwanda's finance ministry on a project funded by GIZ, became Deputy Governor in July 2014 and was reappointed in 2019, became First Deputy Governor after the 2019 Act, and has been Governor since November 2023.
p:TZA: The Bank of Tanzania issues the Tanzanian shilling. It scores 33 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and government pressure on it was reported in 2 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018. An audit by Ernst & Young of the bank's External Payment Arrears account found about 133 billion shillings paid out wrongly in 2005 and 2006 to 22 local companies, many phoney or using fake documents. President Jakaya Kikwete dismissed governor Ballali in January 2008, the companies were ordered to refund the money, and some lower-level defendants were jailed. In the first court cases to follow, reported on 27 May 2011, the Kisutu Resident Magistrate's Court in Dar es Salaam convicted the businessmen Farijala Hussein and Rajabu Maranda of offences related to financial impropriety, forgery and obtaining credit under false pretences, jailed them for five years and ordered them to return what they had taken. The bank is also audited by the Controller and Auditor General, and in 2024 the printing firms De La Rue and Crane Currency won its tender to reprint its banknotes. Part of its reserves is run from outside. The Bank of Tanzania's 2020/21 annual report, note 20 with the accounting policy at note 3, records a portfolio externally managed by the World Bank Treasury under its Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership; the note totals 6,255.0 billion shillings at 30 June 2021, of which the policy note identifies the 690.5 billion held at fair value through profit or loss as the externally managed designation and 5,540.7 billion as managed internally. Emmanuel Tutuba was appointed governor on 7 January 2023, succeeding Florens Luoga; he came from the finance ministry, where he had been made permanent secretary to the treasury in April 2021, its most senior civil servant, a role in which he already sat on the bank's board, and he had earlier been the ministry's budget commissioner.
p:YEM: The Central Bank of Yemen issues the rial, held close to a fixed rate against the US dollar. It scores 43 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and the corruption and secrecy around it stand at 86. Government pressure was reported in 6 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, all of it pressing for easier money or for printing money. On 18 September 2016 President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi, announcing from Saudi Arabia, sacked central bank head Mohammed bin Hammam, named Mansar al-Kaiti in his place and ordered the bank moved to Aden, with no official reason given. A UN Panel of Experts report in January 2021 said the Aden-based bank broke its foreign-exchange rules and laundered 'a substantial part' of a 2 billion dollar Saudi deposit, giving traders a 423 million dollar windfall. The bank rejected the claims, and on 25 March 2021, after an internal review, the panel withdrew the money-laundering and corruption accusations. On 6 December 2021 Hadi dismissed the governor and his deputy, naming Ahmed bin Ahmed Ghaleb Al-Maabq governor and Muhammad Omar Banaja deputy, with no reason given; it was the fourth such sacking since the civil war began. Ernst & Young audits the accounts, a record that rests on the announcement of the appointment on 7 February 2021 and states no financial year. Its money is printed in Russia. The Russian foreign ministry confirmed in June 2020 that the state printer Goznak had been printing notes for Yemen's government under a commercial contract signed in 2017, after separatists in Aden seized a convoy carrying 64 billion rials, about 255 million US dollars, of Russian-printed banknotes. The bank's governor has a career list, and every employer on it is public. Al Arabiya's profile of Ahmed Ghaleb Al-Maabaqi, appointed Governor by presidential decree reported on 7 December 2021 alongside Mohammed Omar Banajah as his deputy, gives it dated: the Ministry of Finance from 1985 to 2005, ending as Undersecretary for External Financial Relations; the Tax Authority from 2005 to June 2014, as deputy head and then head; two terms on the executive board of the Arab Monetary Fund in Abu Dhabi, from 1996 to 2002 and from 2007 to 2010; and the chairmanship of the state General Holding Corporation for Real Estate Development and Investment immediately before the decree. No commercial or private bank appears anywhere in it, so the move is listed here and not counted on the revolving-door layer.
p:TUN: The Central Bank of Tunisia issues the dinar, which follows a slowly adjusted fixed rate against the euro. On 27 June 2012 President Moncef Marzouki fired the governor, Mustapha Kamel Nabli, saying he had refused to bring monetary policy in line with the country's economic needs; the elected assembly approved the removal in July 2012. In February 2018 Tunisian prosecutors said five of the bank's agents had been arrested, two of them jailed, in a currency-trafficking investigation. They were accused of money laundering, corruption and abuse of power for exchanging small euro notes for 200- and 500-euro notes without recording the exchanges, and the bank said it had referred the operations to the courts itself. They stand charged and the accusations are unproven. One career move is documented: Marouane Abassi, a former World Bank economist who had been the World Bank's representative in Libya since 2010, became governor after parliament approved him, as reported on 16 February 2018. The bank's 2025 accounts were audited jointly by FMBZ - KPMG Tunisie and Cabinet C.M.C, it holds 6.8 tonnes of gold, and Tunisia scores 32 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Oberthur Fiduciaire, printed in the source under its former name Oberthur Technologies, printed the 20-dinar note.
p:LSO: Lesotho issues the loti, and the South African rand circulates alongside it. The Rand Monetary Area agreement was signed in December 1974 by South Africa, Swaziland and Lesotho, replaced by the Common Monetary Area in July 1986 and then by a Multilateral Monetary Agreement in February 1992, when Namibia formally joined; member currencies are pegged to the rand at par and are legal tender only in the country that issues them, Lesotho must back what it issues fully with rand assets, and South Africa pays it an imputed return on rand circulating there as legal tender. All five of its current notes, introduced on 23 December 2021, are printed by De La Rue. In February 2024 three South Africans appeared in the Ficksburg Magistrates Court on fraud and money laundering charges over 57 million rand said to have been stolen from the Central Bank of Lesotho. The Hawks, a South African police unit, said Lesotho officials intercepted vouchers meant for service providers and diverted the payments to co-conspirators in South Africa, and that some officials were already before court in Lesotho. The charges are unproven. Two career moves are recorded, and neither is an accusation. Mr. O. 'Nete, a non-executive director on the bank's board, came from Standard Bank of Lesotho, where he was Senior Finance Manager, Finance Manager and Senior Manager Personal Credit, and earlier from Stanlib, where he was Tax Manager, with no dates given; Standard Bank Group's own structure page lists Standard Lesotho Bank Limited at 80 per cent among its holdings as at 30 June 2026, so that employer is majority owned by the Johannesburg-listed group rather than by the state. Mrs M. Mohasoa, also a non-executive director, was a board member and chairman of the audit and risk committee of the insurer Liberty Life Lesotho from 2017 to 2021, an insurer whose ownership is established through two further pages, the South African Reserve Bank's list of designated entities placing Liberty Life Lesotho Ltd within the Liberty Insurance Group and Liberty Holdings' own 2019 annual report stating that the stock-exchange-listed Standard Bank Group Limited holds 53.6 per cent of Liberty's issued ordinary share capital. Its 2023 accounts were audited by Moteane, Quashie & Associates with SizweNtsalubaGobodo Grant Thornton. Lesotho scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and corruption and secrecy around the bank is its weakest side, at 60. At a hearing on Monday 8 June 2026, at which the Auditor General presented consolidated financial statements for 31 March 2023 and 2024, the parliamentary Public Accounts Committee called for a forensic audit of the Central Bank of Lesotho to trace missing public money. Its chairperson, 'Machabana Lemphane-Letsie, said the bank must undergo a forensic audit and say who the money had been paid to. The figures in the report do not agree with each other: its headline puts the gap at M3.9 billion, while the statements it describes show government cash of M5.91 billion at 31 March 2024 against M2.82 billion in the consolidated accounts, a difference of M3.09 billion, which a quotation in the same piece also gives. The committee resolved that the Auditor General's office submit a budget for the audit by 30 June so it could go into the supplementary budget; that office said it has neither the expertise nor any budget allocated for one. The bank resisted, citing its own 2000 Act, which provides for an external auditor and limits the Auditor General to auditing currency balances rather than government payments the bank makes for the state.
p:KGZ: The National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic issues the som and holds it within 2 per cent of the US dollar. One case is recorded. In September 2005 prosecutors placed the governor, Ulan Sarbanov, under house arrest, accusing him of abuse of power for handing more than 400,000 US dollars to the deposed president Askar Akayev in 1999. Sarbanov denied wrongdoing, and Euromoney reported that his position had been insecure since Akayev was ousted in March 2005 and that politicians close to the new leader, Kurmanbek Bakiyev, had pressed for his dismissal. On 26 April 2006 Judge Esenjan Abylkasymov acquitted him and four other former finance officials, ruling that there was no crime because they had acted in the interests of the state; the prosecutor's office said it would appeal, and no appeal outcome was found. Two heads have left since: parliament approved the early resignation of Kubanychbek Bokontaev on 26 June 2024, and Melis Turgunbaev, chairman from that same day, resigned on 18 March 2026, which the report calls voluntary. Neither article gives a reason. One career move runs the other way, out of the bank and into commercial banking: Maksat Ishenbaev, a deputy chairman of the bank's board until 2007, took office on 15 January 2025 as chairman of the board of MBANK, the commercial bank OJSC Commercial Bank Kyrgyzstan, whose audited accounts filed with the Kyrgyz Stock Exchange state that a private individual, O. T. Babanov, held 97.97 per cent at 31 December 2024, with A. T. Babanova holding the same stake a year earlier, 2.03 per cent held by other physical and legal persons and no state body listed. His earlier posts include Energo Bank from 2000 to 2004, the representative office of OJSC Bank CenterCredit from 2007 to 2010, Zalkar Bank from 2010 to 2012, a leasing company and an insurance company, Bai-Tushum bank from December 2017 and the supervisory board of the Kyrgyz Stock Exchange from May 2018; the ownership of those earlier employers is not stated. Crane Currency printed the 5,000-som note introduced on 10 May 2024; Central Asian Secure Printing Typography began printing at home in September 2026, with 20- and 50-som notes entering circulation on 27 October, while an earlier attempt by Uchkun in March 2025 produced 10-som notes that never circulated. Baker Tilly Bishkek LLC audits the accounts for 2025. Kyrgyzstan scores 31 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:NAM: The Bank of Namibia is the country's central bank. Namibia belongs to the Common Monetary Area with South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini, joining under the agreement of February 1992: the Namibian dollar is pegged to the South African rand one for one, and every Namibian dollar issued must be fully backed by rand assets. The bank scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weakest side corruption and secrecy around it, and the law gives it middling independence, 0.637 of 1 and 103rd of 155 countries. In 2002 court papers in a suit by Nambib Resources against the Minister of Mines listed governor Tom Alweendo as a 10 per cent shareholder in Trade Line Namibia, which held an exclusive licence to prospect on the Skeleton Coast. Alweendo said he had been made a director without his knowledge, and no finding or outcome is reported, so the allegation is unproven. Johannes !Gawaxab came from a private-sector banking career to the governorship on 1 June 2020, succeeding Ipumbu Shiimi; the headline of the article is the only place that describes him as coming from the private sector, and no firm, role or dates are named, and the bank's board page now shows Ebson Uanguta as governor from 1 January 2026. On 13 April 2026, in the question-and-answer session after her State of the Nation Address, President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah said the reported losses at the Bank of Namibia, together with missing Government Institutions Pension Fund money, were smelling of corruption and must be investigated. Affirmative Repositioning leader Job Amupanda said the central bank had made a loss close to a billion dollars for unexplained reasons. No investigation is reported as having been ordered, and no body is named as the one that would carry it out. Deloitte Namibia and Grand Namibia audit its accounts, and De La Rue printed its new 50-dollar note.
p:KHM: The National Bank of Cambodia is the country's central bank. It scores 38 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and neither matter on record was ever confirmed. The Phnom Penh Post reported that governor Thor Peng Leath lent three million US dollars of central bank money on 31 May 1994 so Credit Bank of Cambodia could meet its minimum capital, which bank officials admitted was highly irregular, and that on 8 May 1995 the bank released 145,000 dollars from former commerce minister Var Huot's frozen account. Preferential treatment was claimed, but Var Huot said there was none, and no charges or findings followed. In November 2013 Chea Serey, daughter of governor Chea Chanto, was promoted to director-general; former deputy governor Tioulong Saumura said being the governor's daughter should exclude her, Nguon Sokha called her a skilled technocrat, and no investigation followed. Who holds the bank's leadership is set out in its founding law and has no end date.
