Under the Law on the Organization and Conduct of the National Bank of Cambodia of 26 January 1996, the Governor and Deputy Governor are appointed, replaced and dismissed by royal decree on the recommendation of the Royal Government, with that article naming no grounds a dismissal must meet; the other board members are appointed and dismissed by sub-decree; the seven-member board seats both a representative of the Ministry of Economy and Finance and a representative of the head of the Royal Government; and the bank may not withdraw currency from circulation without the Royal Government's consent. Policy itself is set by the board, which the law requires only to consult the government. Its accounts have no private auditor either. Article 57-New, added by a law of 29 December 2006, says the bank's financial records are verified by its own Board and by the National Audit Authority, the state's supreme audit institution, with no financial year set. The riel is made in-house, by the bank's own Banknote Printing Works, which printed the 200,000-riel note issued on 16 October 2024 for the twentieth anniversary of King Norodom Sihamoni's coronation. The bank belongs to the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, which central banks join for help with their reserves. BNY Mellon supplies it with reporting systems and staff training.
p:BLR: The National Bank of the Republic of Belarus issues the Belarusian ruble and holds it within 2 percent of a mix of the euro, the Russian ruble and the US dollar. It scores 34 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. On 18 July 2011 the state news agency Belta reported that President Alyaksandr Lukashenka had relieved Pyotr Prokopovich of his duties as chief of the National Bank of Belarus by decree, with no official reason given; Prokopovich had led the bank since 1998, had heart surgery in April 2011 and had been replaced on an acting basis in June by Yury Alymov while he recovered, and the dismissal came during an economic crisis marked by rising inflation, a sharp currency devaluation and government price controls on some key goods. In December 2016 the state security service, the KGB, said a directorate head at the bank and his deputy had been arrested over a bribe, reported as 13,000 dollars, for choosing the company BelAVM as an equipment supplier; the bribes were said to have been paid in October and November 2016 through intermediaries, and the matter is unproven. At a trial reported in March 2020 prosecutors charged Feliks Kasperovich and Andrei Podgorny of the bank's information technology directorate with taking at least $868,750 in bribes, starting with $10,000 in 2007 and including $260,000 paid in 2016, and Igor Kudasov, head of its payment systems directorate, with taking $30,000; Kudasov had been held in custody since 29 December 2018. Kasperovich admitted the charges in full; the rest remains unproven. Two career moves are recorded. One runs from the central bank into private banking: an official who served at the National Bank from 1998 to 2005, finishing as a deputy head of department, then spent 2005 to 2016 at Priorbank in roles including head of the project management office, chief digital officer and head of retail banking. A separate report on Priorbank's sale calls it the largest private bank in Belarus and says 87.74 per cent of its shares, held until then through a subsidiary of the Austrian group Raiffeisen Bank International, were to be transferred to a buyer named SOVEN 1. The other move is public on both sides. Nadezhda Yermakova chaired the board of Belarusbank, then chaired the National Bank of Belarus from 2011 to 2014, ran Belgazprombank's interim administration from 15 June to 11 December 2020, and on 15 January 2021 was made head of Belgazprombank's board of directors. Belgazprombank's ownership is mixed and mostly Russian: the Russian companies Gazprom PJSC and Gazprombank JSC hold 49.66 per cent each, Gazprom Transgaz Belarus 0.49 per cent and the Republic of Belarus, through its Ministry of Energy, 0.097 per cent. Belarus also has two agreements with China, from 2010 and 2015, to borrow its currency, and holds 53.9 tonnes of gold, just under half its reserves. The China Banknote Printing and Minting Corporation printed the 80-ruble commemorative note introduced on 31 March 2025.
p:GMB: The Central Bank of The Gambia issues the dalasi and scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. The Janneh Commission, a public inquiry into the finances of former president Yahya Jammeh, found that governor Amadou Colley had let Jammeh and General Sulayman Badjie take money out without proper authorisation, including millions of dollars by Badjie. Appearing before that commission on 19 September 2017, Colley said accounts controlled by the Office of the President had been opened at the bank, that an account for sand mining was opened at that office's request, which he called irregular, and that withdrawals followed instructions from an individual in that office without the account signatory's approval. The government's White Paper on the inquiry accepted that between September 2015 and January 2017 Badjie, purportedly acting for Jammeh, instructed the governor or his deputies to release US dollars, and that cash was handed over by the governor to soldiers and loaded into vehicles. It held Badjie accountable for $15,785,601, 300,000 euros and 9,606,000 dalasi and ordered the money recovered by forfeiting and selling his properties, and it also records $28.5 million illegally granted in one bank account in 2000 and 2001 and $268,000 stolen from the bank and used to buy the Observer newspaper. Colley was banned from holding public office for life and held jointly liable for the money taken in breach of the bank's procedures. He had already lost the job by then. On Tuesday 9 May 2017 President Adama Barrow dismissed him along with his deputies Basiru Njai and Oumie Savage-Samba and the bank's director of finance, Ousainou Corr, and no reason was given; Colley said they received their letters that day stating only that their services had been terminated with immediate effect, and that he was surprised at his unceremonious removal after more than three decades of service. The commission was established only in June 2017, a month later, so the dismissal was not a consequence of its findings. Barrow had taken office in January, after Jammeh lost the December 2016 election and left the country under weeks of diplomatic pressure, and had been replacing officials in key positions across a state still largely staffed by Jammeh's allies. The bank's own research economist, Bakary Jammeh, was named governor, and the dismissals came while inflation was high and the dalasi was depreciating. One career move is recorded: Alassan Jabby joined the bank in late 2004 as the accountant in charge of its treasury unit and is now Executive Director and Business Development Manager of FirstBank Gambia Limited, which its own pages describe as a subsidiary of FirstBank of Nigeria Limited, listed on the Nigeria Stock Exchange with over 1.3 million shareholders, so a stock-exchange-listed parent with private shareholders rather than a state bank. De La Rue has printed notes for the bank, and PKF Gambia and PKF Nigeria audited the 2021 accounts.
p:MUS: The Bank of Mauritius issues the Mauritian rupee and holds it within about 2 per cent of the United States dollar. Mauritius scores 27 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and 0.733 of 1 on an index of independence in law, where 1 means the bank rather than the government holds the power. On 9 and 10 April 2025 the country's Financial Crimes Commission arrested the former governor, Seegolam, for fraud by abuse of position; he was charged with fraud and released on bail. The investigation concerns the alleged taking of 300 million rupees, about 6.7 million United States dollars, from the Mauritius Investment Corporation, a vehicle owned by the central bank and set up during the COVID pandemic. Seegolam and Renganaden Padayachy deny wrongdoing, and the charge is unproven. Rama Krishna Sithanen became governor on 16 November 2024, the day after he stopped chairing the fund administration firm Apex Group (Mauritius); he had chaired Sanne Mauritius from 2017 to 2022 and International Financial Services from 2011 to 2016. An earlier governor was dismissed outright. Rundheersing Bheenick took the post in February 2007; his first term was not renewed when it expired in February 2010 while allegations of abuse of power were investigated, he was cleared and reinstated on 21 May 2010, and was given a further term in 2013. Days after the general election of December 2014 brought in a new government, he received a letter from the secretary of the President of the Republic terminating his contract with immediate effect, and said the next day that he would consult his lawyers about whether the newly elected government had the constitutional right to dismiss the central bank governor. No reason was made clear at the time. Under section 13 of the Bank of Mauritius Act 2004 the governor is appointed by the President on the recommendation of the Prime Minister, and the bank is accountable to the Minister of Finance. Ramesh Basant Roi took over on 30 December 2014. Bheenick later sued the bank for 270 million rupees after settlement talks failed, saying he had been paid a nominal 10 rupees a month across his 91 months in office; the bank's deputy secretary confirmed that about 51.6 million rupees remained owed to him. The bank holds 12.4 tonnes of gold, with bars in storage at the Bank of England.
p:ISL: The Central Bank of Iceland issues the króna and keeps it within 2 per cent or less of the euro. It scores 18 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, lower than 97 per cent of the 194 places with a figure, and it ranks 9th of 112 for what it tells the public. No government pressure on it was reported in any of the 37 quarters covered between 2010 and 2018. One case is on its record, an official finding: in April 2010, after the 2008 collapse of Iceland's three largest banks, parliament's Special Investigation Commission found that seven officials, among them central bank head Oddsson and officials Gudnason and Fridriksson, had acted with gross negligence by failing to act on information about the banks' condition. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the bank for central banks. The bank's leadership was changed by statute after the collapse. The incoming prime minister wrote to the three governors on 2 February 2009 asking them to resign so the bank could be restructured; Davíð Oddsson, a former prime minister who chaired the board, refused in public and called the demand interference with the bank's independence. Parliament then passed a bill on 26 February, by 33 votes to 18, replacing the three-person board with a single governor and a deputy, which removed him. A Norwegian economist was named interim governor the next day. Asgeir Jonsson was named governor by Prime Minister Katrin Jakobsdottir for a five-year term starting 20 August 2019, succeeding Mar Gudmundsson; he had been chief economist and head of the research department at Kaupthing Bank, later Arion Bank, from 2004 to 2011, worked as an economic consultant for the finance companies Virding and Gamma, and has taught at the University of Iceland since 2004.
p:DNK: Danmarks Nationalbank issues the Danish krone and holds it at a rate against the euro that is announced in advance. At the end of 2025 it held assets of 109.8 billion US dollars. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the bank used by central banks, and PwC signed the auditor's report on its 2025 accounts. Oberthur Fiduciaire was chosen as banknote supplier under a four-year framework, with the first notes in circulation in 2020, and the bank has since agreed with De La Rue to produce a new Danish series at De La Rue's plant outside London, due for launch in 2028 under a contract running at least six years. It can borrow foreign currency under two swap lines: up to 30 billion US dollars from the United States, agreed on 19 March 2020 as a temporary pandemic facility and expired on 31 December 2021, and a standing 24,000 million euros from the European Central Bank. Since 2002 about 97 per cent of its roughly 66.5 tonnes of gold has been kept at the Bank of England in London and about 0.5 per cent at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, with about 2.5 per cent in Copenhagen; those are storage arrangements, not management. Lars Rohde, who chaired the Board of Governors from 2013 to 2023, had worked at the mortgage bank Realkredit Danmark until 1998 and then ran the statutory pension body ATP; he joined the board of the bank Nordea in 2024, and no ethics finding is recorded. Denmark scores 16 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:BWA: The Bank of Botswana issues the pula, which it manages against the South African rand within a narrow band. One case is recorded and it ended in acquittal: a woman arrested on 17 October 2019 was accused, with others including former president Ian Khama and former intelligence head Isaac Kgosi, of stealing 100 billion pula from the bank. High Court judge Zein Kebonang acquitted her, the state withdrew a terrorism financing charge, and he found the accusations fabricated and referred the investigator to police for perjury prosecution; the accusations against the others remain unproven. In January 2020 the Directorate of Public Prosecutions, headed by Stephen Tiroyakgosi, called in governor Moses Pelaelo over that sum, and Tiroyakgosi said Pelaelo told them there is no money missing from the bank, with the investigation continuing. In May 2019 the Directorate on Corruption and Economic Crime confirmed it was investigating unaccounted-for funds on government accounts at the bank, after the Auditor General reported 22 billion pula unaccounted for, and the Financial Intelligence Agency was reported to have opened its own investigation. Linah Kelebogile Mohohlo, Governor from 20 October 1999 until she retired in October 2016, worked at the International Monetary Fund from 1994 to 1996 under its Special Appointee Programme. De La Rue printed the 10 pula polymer note issued on 1 February 2018, EY audits the accounts, and Botswana scores 26 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:KWT: The Central Bank of Kuwait issues the Kuwaiti dinar and holds it at a fixed rate against the US dollar announced in advance. Its assets were 36.4 billion US dollars at the end of 2025, and it is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Two accounting firms check its books, Al-Aiban, Al-Osaimi & Partners of Ernst & Young and KPMG, Safi Al-Mutawa & Partners, which signed off the accounts for the fiscal year ended 31 March 2013, and Note Printing Australia's customer list says it has produced and supplied polymer banknotes to the bank. One case is recorded and it is unproven: the Kuwaiti newspaper Al Jarida, citing unnamed sources, reported that the securities regulator had decided to refer Governor Mohammad Al Hashel to prosecutors over a suspected breach of investment rules involving shares in a local bank. He denied it, saying he had never traded shares in a listed company while in senior posts; the regulator did not answer Reuters' calls. Governor Basel Al-Haroon, in post since April 2022, worked at the bank from 1989 to 2006 and from late 2006 to 2012, and in between and afterwards led a Kuwaiti investment company and was vice chairman of a Kuwaiti bank from 2016 to 2018. No ethics finding is recorded. Kuwait scores 34 of 100, and 3 of 15 on how much it tells the public. The law the bank runs under lets the executive direct it, and this is a standing arrangement with no end date rather than an episode. Article 38 of Law No. 32 of 1968, as the Central Bank of Kuwait publishes it in English, provides that the Minister of Finance may issue directives to the bank and that such directives become binding on it, with a decision of the Council of Ministers final.
p:EGY: The Central Bank of Egypt issues the Egyptian pound, which it keeps within 2 percent or less of the US dollar, and prints its own notes at its Banknote Printing House in the New Administrative Capital. Egypt scores 31 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Government pressure was reported in 1 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, a threat to replace leaders. In October 2015 Daily News Egypt reported that severe pressure, from no named source, pushed governor Hisham Ramez out a month early; that is unconfirmed. On 17 August 2022 governor Tarek Amer, whose term was due to run to 2023, resigned; President al-Sisi accepted it and made him a presidential adviser, with the pound at 19.1 to the dollar. His successor Hassan Abdalla had been vice chairman and managing director of the Arab African International Bank from 2002 to 2018. No documented case of wrongdoing was found.
p:SOM: Somalia's money is the Somali shilling, and the Central Bank of Somalia issues it, though the notes are printed abroad: the circulating 2,000-shilling note comes from Sudan's state currency printing works. Two cases are recorded, and both run through one short governorship. Yussur A. F. Abrar came to the bank in 2013 out of private finance, the one career move recorded here: she had worked at a number of international banks, none of them named in that account, held positions at the African Development Bank and was managing director of TLG Financial Services, and reporting on the day she took office calls her a former banker at Citigroup and AIG, which is what establishes the private employers; the ownership of TLG Financial Services is stated nowhere. She replaced Abdusalam Omer and resigned after seven weeks, writing to the president that from the moment of her appointment she had continuously been asked to sanction deals and violate her fiduciary responsibility to the Somali people; she had refused to sanction a contract over frozen government assets with the United States law firm Shulman Rogers, which denied wrongdoing. She resigned about a month before Bashir Ise Ali was reappointed on an interim basis. A July 2013 report by the United Nations Monitoring Group for Somalia and Eritrea, an official finding, said 80 per cent of withdrawals from the bank were made for private purposes, that the governor was key to the irregularities, and that 12 million of 16.9 million US dollars transferred by the accounting firm PricewaterhouseCoopers could not be traced; the bank rejected the allegations. The bank later became a member of the World Bank's Reserves Advisory and Management Program at the IMF-World Bank annual meetings, which its own newsletter describes as technical support, advisory services and a network of global institutions rather than management of its assets, and Deloitte & Touche, Certified Public Accountants in Tanzania, audited the 2024 accounts. Somalia scores 39 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:GNQ: Equatorial Guinea uses the Central African CFA franc (XAF), issued by the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), which sets monetary policy for 6 members. The franc is fixed at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs. France guarantees convertibility without limit, and the BEAC must deposit at least 50% of its foreign exchange reserves at the French Treasury (lowered from 65% in 2007). Exposure score is 49 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. The BEAC scores 0.5 of 15 on transparency, last of 112, and government pressure to cut rates or ease was reported in 3 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case: a November 2009 internal report found about 20 billion CFA francs diverted from the Paris office to 139 beneficiaries between 2004 and 2008. On 28 September 2012 a court in Mfoundi, Cameroon, sentenced Kemadjou to life imprisonment and ordered him to pay BEAC 26.4 billion CFA francs. A governor lost his job over the same affair: Philibert Andzembe, a Gabonese national, had led the bank since July 2007, and in October 2009 Gabon's president Ali Bongo fired him in response to a scandal in which 28.3 million US dollars went missing from the bank's Paris branch; Gabon held the right to appoint the governor at the time, and Lucas Abaga Nchama of Equatorial Guinea took the post in 2010. A leaked US diplomatic cable made public in December 2010 alleged that Gabonese officials working at the bank had taken about 36 million US dollars from the pooled reserves over roughly five years. The reserves the BEAC must keep at the French Treasury sit in an operations account (compte d'operations) opened in the BEAC's name. The required share earns interest at the European Central Bank's marginal lending facility rate, 0.25 per cent since 16 March 2016, and anything the BEAC chooses to deposit above that share earns the ECB's minimum rate on main refinancing operations, 0 per cent since 16 March 2016. KPMG Afrique Centrale and Mazars Cameroun audit the accounts jointly. Its money is printed in France. The French foreign ministry's own page on the Franc Zone says the African central banks place the orders for notes and coins under a contract with a manufacturer, in this case the Banque de France, and that CFA franc notes and coins have been made at its works at Chamalieres since 1945; the heads of state and government of the Franc Zone may decide together to change where they are printed. The BEAC's own site cannot be read by automated requests, so this does not rest on a BEAC document. The governor's career is published, and it reaches Equatorial Guinea through the union. Abbas Mahamat Tolli was Chad's Minister of Finance and Budget from 2005 to 2008 and President of the Development Bank of Central African States, the BDEAC. On 31 July 2016 CEMAC heads of state, meeting in Malabo, appointed Chad's former finance minister as the new BEAC governor, to take office in January 2017 in succession to Lucas Abaga Nchama; he held the post until 2024.
p:NIC: Nicaragua's money is issued by the Central Bank of Nicaragua, which scores 33 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. One case runs from 2000 to 2008 and ended in an official finding. In 2007 the country's Comptroller General, the state auditor, concluded that the bank's board sold CENI certificates, paper issued to cover the collapse of banks, for less than market value and then raised interest rates to the benefit of the main buyer, Bancentro; the fraud is described as 500 million dollars. The Comptroller alleged criminal involvement by six men, among them former finance minister Eduardo Montealegre, who denied wrongdoing and called it a political witch hunt, and in July 2008 a special prosecutor filed charges against 39 people including him. No central bank officials are named among the accused and no court ruling is given, though former bank president Francisco Mayorga had already been found guilty in the banking scandal. Two career moves are recorded. Luis Rivas Anduray was an economic adviser at the bank from 2001 to 2002, ran the finance ministry's fiscal affairs office from 2002 to 2003, and became general manager of Banpro at the end of 2004, where he is now chief executive and a director; Banpro's majority shareholder is Grupo Promerica, of Panamanian origin, described as the second Central American financial group of private capital, and Banpro was owned by the Nicaraguan businessman Ramiro Ortiz Mayorga, which is how that employer's private ownership is established. The man who now runs the bank came to it from the government: Ovidio Reyes was Chief Economist at the Ministry of Finance from 2004 to 2012, became the bank's General Manager in 2012-13 and its President in January 2014, a move between two public bodies, with no private employer named. At the end of 2024 the statute governing the bank was rewritten in a week. The presidency sent the National Assembly the Ley de Administracion del Sistema Monetario y Financiero on 19 December 2024; it went to committee on 23 December during the legislative recess, was approved on 26 December and published in La Gaceta on 30 December. It repealed the bank's own organic law and the law governing the Superintendency of Banks and Other Financial Institutions, and put the two institutions, until then independent of each other, under one statute and one common board chaired by Reyes, abolishing the Superintendency's own board; Reyes was also given coordination of the Financial Analysis Unit and the deposit fund. The law's own text says the institutions keep organic, functional, administrative, financial and budgetary autonomy and their institutional specialisation. Divergentes read it the other way, writing that the law eliminates the autonomy of the monetary and financial institutions and gives plenipotentiary powers to Reyes and to the Executive, and that removing the cross-checks between supervisor and central bank removes a safeguard against political and economic bias. Article 24 obliges every person resident or domiciled in Nicaragua, national or foreign, to give the bank and the Superintendency whatever economic, financial, statistical and regulatory information they ask for. The bank did not object publicly and its president gained authority rather than losing it; what changed was that the law governing the bank was rewritten by the Executive, without consultation. Baker Tilly Nicaragua, S.A. audited the accounts for 2024, and on 27 March 2024 the printer Orell Fussli was reported to have been partly awarded a tender to print and supply the bank's banknotes, with no value or quantity given.

p:GNB: Guinea-Bissau uses the West African CFA franc, issued by the Central Bank of West African States, the BCEAO, which sets monetary policy for eight member countries. The franc is pegged — held at a fixed rate — at one euro to 655.957 CFA francs, and France gives an unconditional, unlimited promise to advance euros if the bank's reserves run out. An agreement signed in Abidjan on 21 December 2019 replaced the 1973 one: it ended the requirement that the bank keep at least half its reserves at the French Treasury, and France withdrew its representatives from the board, the Monetary Policy Committee and the banking commission, though one independent committee member is still appointed in consultation with the French government. Guinea-Bissau scores 46 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, mostly because of corruption in the country and money-laundering risk in its banks. One case is documented: in January 2011 a summit of UEMOA heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation, after he was criticized for ignoring a 23 December decision by UEMOA finance ministers that gave Alassane Ouattara power over the institution; the account says the bank paid 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime after that date, and Senegal's President Abdoulaye Wade asked for an audit and alleged the former governor moved 500 billion CFA francs to Gbagbo after being dismissed, with no audit result given. The bank's own statement said the resignation resulted from pressure from the region's leaders, and Dacoury-Tabley said afterwards that he agreed to hand it in because that is what was asked of him. Its money is printed in France. The French foreign ministry's own page on the Franc Zone says the African central banks place the orders for notes and coins under a contract with a manufacturer, in this case the Banque de France, and that CFA franc notes and coins have been made at its works at Chamalieres since 1945; the heads of state and government of the Franc Zone may decide together to change where they are printed. The Banque de France's own director general of banknote manufacturing has called the BCEAO its largest export customer. The BCEAO's published accounts do not name the maker. Its gold is mostly not in Africa. Note 6 of the BCEAO's own financial statements for 2024 lists three places: the bank's head office, the Banque de France and the Bank for International Settlements. On deposit at the Banque de France are 1,054,479.65 ounces, valued at 1,756,111 million CFA francs, out of a stock of about 1.52 million ounces worth 2,531,800 million, which is about 70 per cent; press reporting places it in the Banque de France's underground vault in the first arrondissement of Paris. The Bank for International Settlements holds close to 106,000 ounces, and only about 120,000 ounces, under 8 per cent, sit physically at the head office in Dakar. In the 2018 statements the Paris deposit was 85 per cent of holdings; the share has fallen because the rest of the stock grew, not because gold left Paris. Answering Senator Pierre Laurent on 20 October 2022, the French economy ministry said the rules for the deposit are set by a specific convention covering the services the Banque de France provides to the BCEAO, and that the gold, like the union's foreign exchange reserves, is pooled at the BCEAO rather than apportioned by country. The concentration is contested: pan-Africanist currents and some economists read it as a continuing post-colonial dependence and ask whether the gold will be repatriated as the member states' operating account deposits at the French Treasury were. Part of the reserves is run by outside institutions. The BCEAO's own audited accounts for 2025 say it has bought units in an investment fund called BISIP K, managed by the Bank for International Settlements, worth 205,811 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 222,297 million FCFA a year earlier, and that it has joined the RAMP fund, the Reserve Advisory Management Program managed by the World Bank, worth 138,800 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 149,873 million FCFA a year earlier. Together the two sets of fund units came to 344,611 million FCFA at the end of 2025, and the accounts group the BISIP K units with the holdings kept for immediate liquidity. The accounts are audited by firms appointed in pairs, one doing the work and one standing in: Mazars Senegal with Grant Thornton Senegal for Guinea-Bissau, and Deloitte Cote d'Ivoire with Mazars Senegal for the BCEAO itself. The governors' careers are published, and they reach Guinea-Bissau through the union. Jean-Claude Kassi Brou joined the International Monetary Fund in 1982, worked as an economist and senior economist in several African countries, was the IMF's resident representative in Senegal from 1990 to 1991 and the World Bank's representative for Chad; he worked at the BCEAO from 2000 to 2008, was President of the ECOWAS Commission from 1 March 2018 to 3 July 2022, and became governor on 3 July 2022. Tiemoko Meyliet Kone joined the bank in 1975 and was its National Director and Alternate Governor at the IMF from 1991 to 1998, was chief of staff to Prime Minister Guillaume Soro from 2007 to 2010 and Minister of Construction, Urban Planning and Housing in 2010, was governor from 2011 to 2022, and has been Vice-President of Cote d'Ivoire since April 2022, appointed on 19 April 2022. The ministry he held was construction and housing, not finance.
p:MLI: Mali's money is the CFA franc, issued not by a national central bank but by the Central Bank of West African States, known as the BCEAO, which sets monetary policy for eight member countries. The rate is fixed at 1 euro to 655.957 CFA francs, and France gives an unconditional, unlimited guarantee that the currency can be exchanged, advancing money to the bank if its foreign currency reserves run out. A cooperation agreement signed in Abidjan on 21 December 2019 replaced the 1973 one and ended the requirement that the bank keep at least half its reserves at the French Treasury; the bank's account there was closed in April 2021 according to a French Senate report, while the Treasury's own page says there has been no such account since January 2020. France approved the agreement by a law of 3 February 2021 and withdrew its representatives from the bank's board, its Monetary Policy Committee and the regional banking commission, though one independent member of that committee is still appointed in consultation with the French government. The agreement provides for the currency to be renamed the eco, and a West African meeting on 7 September 2026 kept 2027 as the target year for launching a single currency of that name. Mali scores 43 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, mainly because of corruption in the country and the risk of money laundering. One case is recorded at the bank: a summit of heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation in January 2011 after he was criticised for ignoring a decision of 23 December by the union's finance ministers that handed control of the institution to Alassane Ouattara, and the report says the bank paid out 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime after that date. The bank's own statement said the resignation resulted from pressure from the region's leaders, and Dacoury-Tabley said afterwards that he agreed to hand it in because that is what was asked of him. Senegal's President Abdoulaye Wade called for an audit and alleged that the former governor moved 500 billion CFA francs to Gbagbo after being dismissed; another figure given is 300 billion, and no audit result is reported. Its accounts are checked by firms appointed in pairs, one the titulaire that does the audit and the other the suppléant that stands in: Grant Thornton Senegal with a grouping of PKF BAGE and Crowe TG ICAAF behind it, and Deloitte Côte d'Ivoire with Mazars Senegal behind it for 2024 to 2029. Its money is printed in France. The French foreign ministry's own page on the Franc Zone says the African central banks place the orders for notes and coins under a contract with a manufacturer, in this case the Banque de France, and that CFA franc notes and coins have been made at its works at Chamalieres since 1945; the heads of state and government of the Franc Zone may decide together to change where they are printed. Its gold is mostly not in Africa. Note 6 of the BCEAO's own financial statements for 2024 lists three places: the bank's head office, the Banque de France and the Bank for International Settlements. On deposit at the Banque de France are 1,054,479.65 ounces, valued at 1,756,111 million CFA francs, out of a stock of about 1.52 million ounces worth 2,531,800 million, which is about 70 per cent; press reporting places it in the Banque de France's underground vault in the first arrondissement of Paris. The Bank for International Settlements holds close to 106,000 ounces, and only about 120,000 ounces, under 8 per cent, sit physically at the head office in Dakar. In the 2018 statements the Paris deposit was 85 per cent of holdings; the share has fallen because the rest of the stock grew, not because gold left Paris. Answering Senator Pierre Laurent on 20 October 2022, the French economy ministry said the rules for the deposit are set by a specific convention covering the services the Banque de France provides to the BCEAO, and that the gold, like the union's foreign exchange reserves, is pooled at the BCEAO rather than apportioned by country. The concentration is contested: pan-Africanist currents and some economists read it as a continuing post-colonial dependence and ask whether the gold will be repatriated as the member states' operating account deposits at the French Treasury were. Part of its reserves sits in two funds run by other institutions. The BCEAO's own audited accounts for 2025 say it bought units in a fund called BISIP K, managed by the Bank for International Settlements, worth 205,811 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 222,297 million FCFA a year earlier, and grouped with the holdings kept for immediate liquidity. The same accounts say the bank joined the RAMP fund, the Reserve Advisory Management Program, managed by the World Bank, whose units were worth 138,800 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 149,873 million FCFA a year earlier. Together the two came to 344,611 million FCFA at the end of 2025. The governors' careers are published, and they reach Mali through the union. Jean-Claude Kassi Brou joined the International Monetary Fund in 1982, worked as an economist and senior economist in several African countries, was the IMF's resident representative in Senegal from 1990 to 1991 and the World Bank's representative for Chad; he worked at the BCEAO from 2000 to 2008, was President of the ECOWAS Commission from 1 March 2018 to 3 July 2022, and became governor on 3 July 2022. Tiemoko Meyliet Kone joined the bank in 1975 and was its National Director and Alternate Governor at the IMF from 1991 to 1998, was chief of staff to Prime Minister Guillaume Soro from 2007 to 2010 and Minister of Construction, Urban Planning and Housing in 2010, was governor from 2011 to 2022, and has been Vice-President of Cote d'Ivoire since April 2022, appointed on 19 April 2022. The ministry he held was construction and housing, not finance.
p:BFA: Burkina Faso uses the West African CFA franc, issued by the Central Bank of West African States, the BCEAO, which sets monetary policy for eight member countries. The franc is pegged, meaning held at a fixed rate, at one euro to 655.957 CFA francs, and France promises to advance euros if the bank's reserves run out; an agreement signed on 21 December 2019 ended the requirement that at least half those reserves sit at the French Treasury. One case is recorded: a summit of UEMOA heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation in January 2011, after he was criticized for ignoring a 23 December decision by UEMOA finance ministers that gave Alassane Ouattara power over the institution, and the article says the BCEAO paid out 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime afterwards. The bank's own statement said the resignation resulted from pressure from the region's leaders, and Dacoury-Tabley said afterwards that he agreed to hand it in because that is what was asked of him. Abdoulaye Wade asked for an audit and alleged the former governor moved 500 billion CFA francs to Gbagbo; that is unproven. Its money is printed in France. The French foreign ministry's own page on the Franc Zone says the African central banks place the orders for notes and coins under a contract with a manufacturer, in this case the Banque de France, and that CFA franc notes and coins have been made at its works at Chamalieres since 1945; the heads of state and government of the Franc Zone may decide together to change where they are printed. The Banque de France's own director general of banknote manufacturing has called the BCEAO its largest export customer. The BCEAO's published accounts do not name the maker. Its gold is mostly not in Africa. Note 6 of the BCEAO's own financial statements for 2024 lists three places: the bank's head office, the Banque de France and the Bank for International Settlements. On deposit at the Banque de France are 1,054,479.65 ounces, valued at 1,756,111 million CFA francs, out of a stock of about 1.52 million ounces worth 2,531,800 million, which is about 70 per cent; press reporting places it in the Banque de France's underground vault in the first arrondissement of Paris. The Bank for International Settlements holds close to 106,000 ounces, and only about 120,000 ounces, under 8 per cent, sit physically at the head office in Dakar. In the 2018 statements the Paris deposit was 85 per cent of holdings; the share has fallen because the rest of the stock grew, not because gold left Paris. Answering Senator Pierre Laurent on 20 October 2022, the French economy ministry said the rules for the deposit are set by a specific convention covering the services the Banque de France provides to the BCEAO, and that the gold, like the union's foreign exchange reserves, is pooled at the BCEAO rather than apportioned by country. The concentration is contested: pan-Africanist currents and some economists read it as a continuing post-colonial dependence and ask whether the gold will be repatriated as the member states' operating account deposits at the French Treasury were. Part of the reserves is run by outside institutions. The BCEAO's own audited accounts for 2025 say it has bought units in an investment fund called BISIP K, managed by the Bank for International Settlements, worth 205,811 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 222,297 million FCFA a year earlier, and that it has joined the RAMP fund, the Reserve Advisory Management Program managed by the World Bank, worth 138,800 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 149,873 million FCFA a year earlier. p:BIH: The convertible mark is issued by the Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina under a currency board: marks are put into circulation only against convertible foreign currency the bank holds, at 1.95583 marks to the euro, and its monetary liabilities may never exceed its foreign currency assets. Its law scores 0.899 of 1 for independence, 11th of 155 countries, and no government pressure was reported in the quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is documented: in 2023 a criminal complaint accused governor Senad Softic of suspected wrongdoing in several matters, including a project to acquire an office building in Pale and a procedure to buy land in Sarajevo. The prosecutor's office said in February 2023 that it had opened a case and was verifying the allegations, which remain unproven, while the bank said examining allegations is not an investigation and that reports of one were untrue. The state has twice acted on the bank. On 25 June 2019 two of the five members of its Governing Board were dismissed by the country's tripartite Presidency, the collective head of state, with the reasons unclear. And in April 2025 the Council of Ministers adopted a revised state budget that settled the liability from the Viaduct arbitration out of the bank's profits; the bank suspended the transfer of 244.3 million marks, part of its 412.6 million marks of 2024 net profit, to the Ministry of Finance and Treasury, saying the move would endanger its assets and the country's financial stability. One career move is recorded: the bank's own page gives Jasmina Selimovic as an independent member of the Supervisory Board of Raiffeisen Bank Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2018, president of the board of the Sarajevo Canton Institute of Health Insurance since 2021, and appointed to the bank's Governing Board on 3 January 2024. Who prints the mark rests on an encyclopaedia entry rather than anything the bank publishes: it reports that Oberthur Fiduciaire prints every denomination except the 200-mark note, and that OeBS was chosen after an international tender to print the 200. Grant Thornton d.o.o. Banja Luka audited the 2016 accounts. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, and it has joined the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, which offers advice, training and asset management, the announcement stating the membership rather than which services the bank takes. It scores 39 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:MDA: The National Bank of Moldova issues the leu, which is held within 2 percent of the euro. Its law scores 0.861 of 1 for independence, where 1 means the bank holds the power, and it scores 30 of 100 for exposure to outside influence. Dorin Dragutanu resigned as governor on 21 September 2015 after criticism for failing to prevent about 1 billion dollars disappearing from three Moldovan banks; he blamed pressure from politicians and denied responsibility, and President Nicolae Timofti and Prime Minister Valeriu Strelet had both said he should go. The Associated Press reported the same resignation after weeks of street protests over 1.5 billion dollars that disappeared from three banks before a parliamentary election the previous November, with protesters camping in a Chisinau square since 6 September; Dragutanu accused politicians of interfering in the bank's internal affairs. On 5 March 2020 prosecutors searched the bank's headquarters and detained deputy governor Cincilei, former deputy governor Tabirta and a division head on suspicion of fraud and money laundering tied to that theft, which surfaced in 2014 and 2015 after the bank made a 13 billion leu emergency loan later turned into public debt; they also moved to arrest Dragutanu. None of it is proven. On the evening of 21 December parliament dismissed governor Octavian Armasu by 81 votes, citing insufficient and defective work on the fraud case. Armasu had come to the bank from the government: he became Governor on 30 November 2018, appointed for a seven-year term, having served before that as Moldova's Minister of Finance. A second career runs in from the auditors rather than from a bank. The bank's own biography of Constantin Schendra, appointed Deputy Governor by a parliamentary decision of 4 November 2021, records more than eight years in international audit companies: senior auditor at Ernst & Young Moldova from 2010 to 2015 and at Ernst & Young Cyprus from 2013 to 2014, then executive director at Baker Tilly Moldova from 2015 to 2018, before joining the bank as director of banking supervision in 2018. Those are private firms in professional services rather than banks or insurers. On its reserves, the bank's own page on external technical cooperation says the World Bank assists it through the Reserve Advisory and Management Program, described as technical assistance to improve management of the state's foreign exchange reserves and knowledge sharing among member states; the arrangement is advice and training rather than the management of a portfolio. KPMG Moldova SRL checks the bank's accounts from outside, for 2024 and 2023.
p:ZMB: The Bank of Zambia issues the kwacha, which floats within a band of about 5 percent against the US dollar. Denny Kalyalya came to the governorship in February 2015 from the World Bank Group, where he had been executive director for the Africa Group One constituency. On 22 August 2020 President Edgar Lungu dismissed him, less than a week after he warned of economic difficulties, and appointed Christopher Mvunga from the finance ministry; Kalyalya returned as governor in October 2021. In October 2015 the Drug Enforcement Commission arrested a section officer for theft by a public servant and money laundering, accusing him of taking 43,660 US dollars and 20,335 kwacha in cash between January and September 2015; he was charged, and no court outcome is given, so the accusation is unproven. Of three career moves on record, one runs into a commercial bank: Dr Austin Mwape went from deputy governor of operations to chairman of the board of Stanbic Bank Zambia, part of the Standard Bank Group, from December 2016 until 1 September 2020. Dr Richard K. E. Chembe, who had held senior management posts at the bank and the International Monetary Fund, was announced on 16 April 2015 as managing director of Investrust Bank, whose largest shareholder was already ZCCM Investments Holdings, which describes itself as state owned. The Heritage Series of six notes and six coins was launched on 31 March 2025, with the 10 and 20 kwacha notes on Landqart's Durasafe composite substrate; who printed the series is not published. The Auditor General audits the accounts each year under the Bank of Zambia Act No. 5 of 2022, and Zambia scores 32 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:MAR: Bank Al-Maghrib issues Morocco's dirham, held to a pre-announced peg, meaning a fixed rate, against the euro. It prints the notes and mints the coins at its own unit, Dar As-Sikkah, founded in 1987, and is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Morocco scores 28 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and no government pressure was reported between 2010 and 2018. Two cases are on record, both under investigation and unproven. In 2022 the bank complained to the prosecutor's office about one of its own staff and a service provider over suspected corruption in awarding contracts, with no amounts, charges or ruling given. On 4 July 2019 it said 1.2 million dirhams, about 125,000 US dollars, had been stolen while cash was moved from the Dar As-Sikkah mint to northern cities, and opened an investigation, with no findings reported. Abdellatif Jouahri was named wali, or governor, in 2003, coming from the presidency of the CIMR, a private-sector employers' pension body. On 24 March 2023 Driss Sentissi, president of the Mouvement Populaire's parliamentary group, wrote to the presidency of the parliamentary commission on finance and economic development asking that wali Abdellatif Jouahri be summoned before parliament to explain the rise in the key rate from 2.5 per cent to 3 per cent. The Mouvement Populaire is an opposition party, and whether the commission agreed to summon him is not reported, so what is documented is the demand and not a decision of parliament.
p:LAO: The Bank of the Lao P.D.R. is the central bank of Laos, which uses the kip; its top-denomination 100,000-kip note is printed by Goznak, the Russian state currency works. One case is recorded and it ended in convictions. On 8 September 2026 the Vientiane People's Court sentenced two former directors general to life imprisonment for abusing their positions to withdraw foreign currency from the bank's reserves and exchange unlimited amounts; one of them, Aod, was sentenced in his absence because he died during the proceedings. In a related case nine bank employees were convicted of corruption and money laundering, including trading currency at special rates. Losses across the cases exceeded 2.29 trillion kip, about 102.6 million US dollars. Government pressure was reported in 1 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, and that instance was a demand to print money. The government's hold on the bank is in its founding law and has no end date. Under the Law on the National Bank of the Lao P.D.R., approved on 14 October 1995, a Deputy Prime Minister chairs the bank's Board of Management, with the Governor and the Minister of Finance as vice-chairs; the Prime Minister appoints and removes board members; and the Governor proposes monetary, interest rate and exchange rate policy to that board and then submits it to the Government, which decides whether to adopt and proclaim it. The bank has two swap lines with China, arrangements to borrow each other's currency: one of 6 billion yuan, and one from January 2020 with no amount stated. One career move is recorded. Joint Development Bank's own history lists Somphao Phaisith among the presidents of its management board from 2007 to 2009, and he became Governor of the Bank of the Lao PDR in 2009. The same page sets out who owned the bank while he ran it: Thai investors held 70 per cent of the shares and the Lao side, represented by the Bank of the Lao PDR itself, the remaining 30 per cent; on 15 June 2010 the central bank transferred all of its shares to a Thai investor, leaving the bank wholly in private hands. So he ran a bank the central bank part owned, and then ran the central bank. Laos scores 39 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:TON: The National Reserve Bank of Tonga issues the pa'anga, which follows a crawling peg or a band of 1 per cent or less against the US dollar. The National Reserve Bank of Tonga Act, Chapter 16.12 in its 2020 revised edition, sets out how the government may steer it. Section 10(1) has the Minister, with Cabinet's consent, appoint five directors and the Chairman and Deputy Chairman, and section 11(1) has the Governor appointed by Cabinet on the Minister's recommendation. Section 50(1) lets the Minister, with Cabinet's consent, issue the bank written directives, and section 50(4) requires him to put any disagreement with the Board over a policy it has determined to Cabinet, which then determines the policy the bank adopts. The Governor is protected in office: under section 11(3) he may be removed by Cabinet, on the Minister's recommendation made at the Board's request, only for permanent incapacity, serious misconduct or failure to perform his duties. Two careers run in from other public bodies. The present Governor, Tatafu Moeaki, was appointed on 20 December after an open recruitment process, on the Finance Minister's recommendation in consultation with the Reserve Bank Board; he was a director of the National Reserve Bank Board from 2013 to 2016, during which he was also the Government's chief economic adviser and chief executive of the Ministry of Finance, and he had been chief executive of the Ministry of Trade and Economic Development, World Bank liaison, Asian Development Bank Tonga country head, a Member of Parliament and Minister for Finance until 10 August 2022. Joyce Mafi, who was Governor for ten years until July 2013, was an economist at the Tonga Ministry of Finance before she joined the Reserve Bank in 1993. No commercial bank or private financial firm is named for either. Two cases are documented. In 2024 and 2025 Tonga's Anti-Corruption Commissioner sued the bank and its directors, alleging that a 2024 staff payment, for example $6,600 to each of 73 staff, was an unlawful bonus linked to record profit, a breach of trust and misfeasance in public office; the board had described it as a one-off anniversary payout, and on 20 November 2025 the Court of Appeal dismissed the proceedings, finding no reasonable cause of action against the bank and that the claim against the directors also failed. Between 2017 and 2019 a Senior Exchange Control Officer forged a Government bond to support another person's New Zealand visa application and asked for $2,500 pa'anga; she pleaded guilty, her employment was terminated, and on 21 May 2019 the Supreme Court of Tonga gave her a two-year sentence, fully suspended, and ordered $800 compensation. Coopers & Lybrand audited the 1993 accounts, and De La Rue printed the 100-pa'anga note in the family introduced on 4 December 2023. Tonga scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and 5.5 of 15 on what it tells the public.
p:ALB: The Bank of Albania is Albania's central bank and issues the lek, kept close to the euro without any formal promise to do so; it scores 25 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. In July 2014 one of its employees was found to have stolen 713 million lek, nearly seven million US dollars, from the reserves. On 5 September 2014 prosecutors arrested governor Fullani and the bank's senior auditor and charged them with abuse of office over alleged mismanagement linked to that theft; the board dismissed Fullani, and the charges remain unproven, with no verdict reported. In September 2014 parliament voted 72 to 6 to dismiss Ardian Fullani, who had been appointed in 2004 and was serving a second seven-year term, after the bank's executive board argued that he posed a grave threat to the bank's interests. He was jailed earlier that month and later moved to house arrest, and seventeen other central bank employees were arrested; Fullani denied wrongdoing and was not accused of personally profiting, and Elisabeta Gjoni served as acting governor. No government pressure was reported in 37 quarters to 2018. The bank signed a swap line with China for 2 billion yuan on 3 April 2018, letting the two central banks lend each other their currencies; a borrowing line with the European Central Bank expired on 15 January 2024. Gent Sejko has been Governor and Chairman of the Supervisory Council since 5 February 2015 and was re-elected for a second term on 24 February 2022; immediately before that appointment he was Deputy General Manager of Societe Generale Albania, a commercial bank, and earlier he held senior posts at the National Commercial Bank, the American Bank of Albania and Raiffeisen Bank.
p:KAZ: The National Bank of Kazakhstan issues the tenge, which floats within a de facto band of about 5 per cent against the US dollar, and gold makes up 77 per cent of its reserves, 368.4 tonnes. On 2 November 2015 President Nursultan Nazarbayev replaced chairman Kayrat Kelimbetov with presidential adviser Daniyar Akishev, telling parliament that confidence in the bank and the tenge had fallen and that tenge liquidity was short; Kelimbetov is not quoted. It prints its own money through the Banknote Factory of the National Bank, one of its subsidiaries, which also makes passports, identity and payment cards and has released three series of tenge notes. Landqart AG says the bank's 20,000 tenge note, issued for the 30th anniversary of independence, is printed on its Durasafe material, the second such note the bank has issued. PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP audited the accounts for the year ended 31 December 2025. It has five swap lines, arrangements to borrow another central bank's currency: Turkiye for 28.0 billion Turkish lira in 2025, Russia for 35 billion roubles on 28 May 2026 and China for 7 billion yuan on 14 December 2014. Kazakhstan scores 29 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Grigory Marchenko chaired the bank from October 1999 until 2004, then chaired Halyk Bank, the country's third-biggest financial institution, from January 2005, and was appointed chairman of the National Bank a second time, replacing Anvar Saidenov, as reported on 30 January 2009.
