The Banque de France's own director general of banknote manufacturing has called the BCEAO its largest export customer. The BCEAO's published accounts do not name the maker. Its gold is mostly not in Africa. Note 6 of the BCEAO's own financial statements for 2024 lists three places: the bank's head office, the Banque de France and the Bank for International Settlements. On deposit at the Banque de France are 1,054,479.65 ounces, valued at 1,756,111 million CFA francs, out of a stock of about 1.52 million ounces worth 2,531,800 million, which is about 70 per cent; press reporting places it in the Banque de France's underground vault in the first arrondissement of Paris. The Bank for International Settlements holds close to 106,000 ounces, and only about 120,000 ounces, under 8 per cent, sit physically at the head office in Dakar. In the 2018 statements the Paris deposit was 85 per cent of holdings; the share has fallen because the rest of the stock grew, not because gold left Paris. Answering Senator Pierre Laurent on 20 October 2022, the French economy ministry said the rules for the deposit are set by a specific convention covering the services the Banque de France provides to the BCEAO, and that the gold, like the union's foreign exchange reserves, is pooled at the BCEAO rather than apportioned by country. The concentration is contested: pan-Africanist currents and some economists read it as a continuing post-colonial dependence and ask whether the gold will be repatriated as the member states' operating account deposits at the French Treasury were. Part of its reserves sits in two funds run by other institutions. The BCEAO's own audited accounts for 2025 say it bought units in a fund called BISIP K, managed by the Bank for International Settlements, worth 205,811 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 222,297 million FCFA a year earlier, and grouped with the holdings kept for immediate liquidity. The same accounts say the bank joined the RAMP fund, the Reserve Advisory Management Program, managed by the World Bank, whose units were worth 138,800 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 149,873 million FCFA a year earlier. Together the two came to 344,611 million FCFA at the end of 2025. The governors' careers are published, and they reach Togo through the union. Jean-Claude Kassi Brou joined the International Monetary Fund in 1982, worked as an economist and senior economist in several African countries, was the IMF's resident representative in Senegal from 1990 to 1991 and the World Bank's representative for Chad; he worked at the BCEAO from 2000 to 2008, was President of the ECOWAS Commission from 1 March 2018 to 3 July 2022, and became governor on 3 July 2022. Tiemoko Meyliet Kone joined the bank in 1975 and was its National Director and Alternate Governor at the IMF from 1991 to 1998, was chief of staff to Prime Minister Guillaume Soro from 2007 to 2010 and Minister of Construction, Urban Planning and Housing in 2010, was governor from 2011 to 2022, and has been Vice-President of Cote d'Ivoire since April 2022, appointed on 19 April 2022. The ministry he held was construction and housing, not finance.
p:CZE: The Czech National Bank issues the koruna and scores 23 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, leaving it less exposed than 93 percent of the places measured. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the bank used by central banks themselves. Ales Michl was an economist and investment strategist at Raiffeisenbank from 2006 to 2015 and an external economic adviser to the finance ministry from 2014 to 2018 and later to Prime Minister Andrej Babis, joined the bank's board in December 2018 and was then appointed governor in succession to Jiri Rusnok. Czech Television reports that he founded Michl Fund Management in 2016, which co-founded the qualified-investor fund Robot Asset Management SICAV, that he later placed the company in a trust, and that some experts believe he may still have influence over it, which he denies; no ethics finding is recorded. In 2026 police arrested a long-serving employee accused of misappropriating tens of millions of koruna, after suspicious transactions on his account were flagged; the bank confirmed the theft was being investigated at its Brno branch, and the accusation is unproven. Government pressure was reported in 3 of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, all of it pressing for tighter policy, alongside three threats to replace leaders. The president of the Czech Republic appoints all seven members of the bank board alone, and on 18 February 2015 President Milos Zeman said he would appoint nobody who favoured devaluing the koruna and would name members who backed adopting the euro, at a time when the bank was holding the koruna weak against the euro; Andrej Babis, then finance minister, called that an unacceptable interference with the bank's independence. Zeman had five of the seven seats to fill before March 2018, and the bank kept the policy. State Street Global Advisors has held an equity mandate from the bank since 2007, since raised to 7.5 billion US dollars, and also advises it on alternatives to its reserve strategies; BNP Paribas Asset Management agreed a 500 million dollar mortgage-backed securities mandate in November 2019; and Ernst & Young Audit, s.r.o. audits the accounts. Some of the gold is kept in the bank's own high-security vault in Prague, mostly for making its gold coins, with most of the reserve stored in London under no named institution, which is storage rather than management. A commemorative banknote marking the establishment of the Czechoslovak currency, which entered circulation on 30 March 2022, carries the imprint of Statni tiskarna cenin; who prints the circulating notes is not stated.
p:ETH: The National Bank of Ethiopia issues the birr. It scores 34 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 58% of the 194 places scored. Its legal independence is low: 0.495 of 1 on one index of 42 rules and 0.291 of 1 on another, rank 176 of 191. Government pressure was reported in 3 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, mostly pressing to cut rates or ease. One case is recorded. In March 2008 Ethiopian anti-corruption officials arrested 26 people after 90 kilos of fake gold were found in the bank's vaults: 7 from the bank, 4 from the Ethiopian Geological Survey and 15 businessmen and collaborators. What is known covers the arrests only, not charges or court outcomes. Some of the notes are made abroad: the bank awarded Francois-Charles Oberthur Fiduciaire of France a 19.6 million birr share of a 206 million birr banknote printing deal, covering the 50 birr note. Mamo Mihretu was appointed governor in January 2023, in an announcement dated 20 January, replacing Yinager Dessie; at the time he was chief executive officer of the state-owned company Ethiopian Investment Holdings, and before that he had been a senior private sector specialist at the World Bank, a senior policy adviser to the Prime Minister and Ethiopia's chief trade negotiator. On 30 November 2023 the standing parliamentary committee for Planning, Budget and Finance Affairs questioned governor Mamo Mihretu for nearly four hours. Its chair, Desalegn Wodaje, called for renewed efforts against the parallel currency market and said the bank has to use all policy options including devaluation, if it is necessary to bridge the widening gap. That is a parliamentary committee telling the bank which policy to adopt, in public, rather than an inquiry into how the bank has behaved.
p:GBR: The Bank of England is the central bank of the United Kingdom and issues the pound sterling. It scores 25 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, 169th of the 194 places with a figure, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it. In the 2022 Conservative leadership contest Liz Truss said she would review the bank's mandate if she became prime minister, her campaign saying she would be more directive in setting it, and an ally said the review would consider the bank's independence. Governor Andrew Bailey defended independence publicly while saying he was open to a review of the mandate. Truss dropped the proposal once in office. A group of 44 Conservative MPs later called for a Treasury-led review of the bank's mandate and independence over its handling of inflation and of the unwinding of its bond holdings. Two cases are recorded. Deputy governor Charlotte Hogg resigned on 14 March 2017 after the House of Commons Treasury Committee called it a very serious breach that she had repeatedly failed, since joining the Bank in 2013, to declare that her brother was director of group strategy at the bank Barclays; she said she had also unintentionally misled the committee. The Bank itself passed material on its 2007 and 2008 liquidity auctions to the Serious Fraud Office, which investigated from 2015 and closed the matter in June 2017, finding no evidence of criminality. Eighteen career moves between the Bank and private finance are on file. Mervyn King joined Citigroup as a senior adviser after retiring as governor in 2013, and Katharine Braddick moves from Barclays to deputy governor for prudential regulation on 1 July 2026, barred for six months from decisions on Barclays.
p:USA: The US dollar is issued through the Federal Reserve System. Banks that join hold stock in their district's Reserve Bank, and at the end of 2018 Citibank held 42.8 per cent of the New York Fed and JPMorgan Chase 29.5 per cent; member banks elect six of each Reserve Bank's nine directors, though the Board says the System is not owned by anyone. It scores 54 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, more than 98 per cent of the 194 places with a figure, and its weakest side is influence from inside. Many moves between the Fed and private finance are recorded, and none is an accusation: Alfred Hayes came to the New York Fed presidency from the New York Trust Company in 1956 and became chairman of Morgan Stanley International in November 1975; Allan Sproul left that presidency in 1956 for a Wells Fargo Bank directorship; Timothy Geithner was made president of the private equity firm Warburg Pincus in November 2013; Brian Sack ran the New York Fed's Markets Group until 2012 and joined the hedge fund manager the D. E. Shaw group; Loretta Mester joined the board of the reinsurer RenaissanceRe Holdings in November 2024; and Alberto Musalem became St. Louis Fed president in April 2024, having worked at Tudor Investment Corporation, the New York Fed and Evince Asset Management. Janet Yellen's disclosures show more than 7 million dollars of speaking income, including 952,200 dollars from Citigroup. On trading by officials, the Fed's Inspector General found in September 2024 that trades made for Raphael Bostic from 2017 broke ethics rules but no insider trading law; in January 2024 that Robert Kaplan's 2020 trades looked like acting on confidential policy information, with Eric Rosengren having failed to report his; and on 15 November 2025 that Adriana Kugler's 2024 trades broke Fed rules. Jerome Powell's and Richard Clarida's trades were cleared, and Jeffrey Lacker resigned in April 2017 over a 2012 leak, without charges. President Donald Trump has said Powell should resign, the Justice Department subpoenaed the Fed in January 2026, and after he moved to fire Governor Lisa Cook the Supreme Court ruled on 29 June 2026 that she stays.
p:VUT: Vanuatu's money, the vatu, is issued by the Reserve Bank of Vanuatu, created in 1980 and held within a band of 2 percent or less against the Australian dollar. The country scores 36 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around the bank; independence written into its law scores 0.498 of 1. One case is on record. An Ombudsman report of 3 July 1996 found that governor Samson Ngwele improperly signed ten bank guarantees worth 100 million US dollars in total, without the board's approval and under pressure from Finance Minister Barak Sope, breaching the Reserve Bank Act and the Leadership Code. The guarantees went to Peter Harold Swanson for a trading programme the Ombudsman called a scam, and were still in circulation when the report was written. No governor was removed over it: what the finding describes is a minister pressing the governor into committing the bank. The report commended Ngwele's later attempts to put things right; he disagreed with its adverse comments about him. Two people came to the bank from other public bodies. The newly appointed Governor, August Letlet, had been Director General of the Ministry of Finance and Economic Management. Marakon Alilee, appointed to the board on 12 September 2014, was then Director General of the Ministry of Trade, Commerce, Industry and Tourism, and had held senior posts at the Vanuatu Chamber of Commerce, Airports Vanuatu Limited, VANAIR and the Vanuatu National Provident Fund; Jimmy Nipo was re-appointed in the same announcement, from the New Zealand High Commission and the post of Director General of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. The bank's own board page names no commercial bank or private financial firm for Letlet or for the other three board members, whose careers it places in government, regional organisations and donor-funded programmes. Note Printing Australia's customer list says it has produced and supplied polymer banknotes to the bank, without a date or contract value, and the 2019 accounts were audited by KPMG, a Fiji partnership. One fuller career has since been published for a Reserve Bank director. A Sista profile of Sereana Moira Marum gives a first job in 2003 as a trainee accountant at Equity Investment Group, sixteen years inside the Reserve Bank from May 2006 ending as Director of Support Services, a move in 2022 to the donor-funded Vanuatu-Australia Health Partnership, and from February 2023 a seat on the National Bank of Vanuatu board held as the representative of the Vanuatu National Provident Fund, with the chairship from October 2024. The profile states no ownership for Equity Investment Group, and the bank seat is held for a statutory provident fund, so the move is listed here and not counted on the revolving-door layer. It rests on a profile rather than on a bank document.
p:JAM: The Bank of Jamaica issues the Jamaican dollar and moves its rate against the US dollar in small announced steps. It scores 27 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and no government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters to 2018. One case is recorded and unproven: governor Derick Latibeaudiere borrowed 51 million dollars from the bank for a house, furnishings and landscaping. At a Public Accounts Committee hearing on 26 May 2009, Auditor General Pamela Monroe Ellis said she had no documents showing the loans were secured and that 25 million of it was still unsecured; the bank's lawyer said 30 million was fully secured against the governor's house, and the committee told both sides to resolve their differences and report back. That contract is also why he lost the job. On Friday 30 October 2009 the Minister of Finance terminated his services, after thirteen years as governor. Prime Minister Bruce Golding told the House of Representatives that the government found the terms unacceptable, embarrassing and repugnant: a basic salary starting at 11,226,271 dollars, rising each year by whatever increase public sector employees were granted and by further incremental and performance adjustments, which had carried it to 14,545,000 dollars by the day of his dismissal, inside a package reported at about 38 million dollars a year - more, Golding said, than the Chairman of the United States Federal Reserve was paid, and set against a government that had not met nurses' demand for reclassification. Latibeaudiere had held that the bank's obligations to him must be met, writing to the minister on the day itself that if the principle governing the sanctity of contracts was to mean anything, the contract he had signed with the minister under statute had to be honoured. He was at that moment Jamaica's lead negotiator for a standby agreement with the International Monetary Fund and said he was in those talks until two hours before he was dismissed. Standard and Poor's downgraded Jamaica's sovereign bonds the next day, which Golding called a knee-jerk reaction. The National Workers Union questioned the legality of the decision and said the government should have consulted him first; the Economist reported talk in Kingston of a policy disagreement with the finance minister. Brian Wynter took over on 1 December 2009. Richard Byles became governor on 19 August 2019, after running Pan Caribbean Merchant Bank from 1988, the Pan Jam group from 1991 for thirteen years and Sagicor Jamaica from 2004 until he retired in 2017. Crown Agents Investment Management manages the bank's investments of special drawing rights, which began at 250 million US dollars and have since doubled, with the bank leaving the investment decisions to the firm. De La Rue prints the banknotes. The Independent Auditor's Report in the bank's Annual Report 2025 is issued by Ernst & Young Chartered Accountants of Kingston and signed on 4 March 2026.
p:DZA: The Bank of Algeria issues the dinar and holds it within a band of 2 per cent or less against the euro. Algeria scores 29 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, less exposed than 68 per cent of the 194 places with a figure, its weakest side corruption and secrecy around the bank, mainly laws that hide who owns money and money-laundering risk in its banks. Government pressure was reported in 3 of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, every time a demand to print money. One case is recorded, and it ended in acquittal: in the Khalifa Bank case the Blida criminal court sentenced former governor Abdelwahab Keramane in absentia to 20 years in prison in 2007, and on 7 June 2022 the same court acquitted him; the pages opened do not state the specific charges. On Monday 23 May 2022 Algeria's president Abdelmadjid Tebboune ended the duties of Rostom Fadhli as governor, with a statement from the presidency citing article 91 paragraph 7 and article 92 paragraph 7 of the constitution and giving no official reason; Fadhli had been appointed in June 2020 and had been expected to overhaul the 1990 money and credit law, a project that was not completed, and Salah Eddine Taleb, until then secretary of the Money and Credit Council, replaced him. One career move is on record: Mohamed Lamine Lebbou, appointed governor in February 2026, began his career at BNP Paribas El Djazair from 2004 to 2006, a bank its own 2018 annual report says is 100 per cent owned by BNP Paribas France, and that is the private employer in his career; the banks he ran later are public, the state-owned Banque nationale d'Algerie from 2021 to 2024 and, from May 2025, BEA International Bank, the French subsidiary of the state Banque exterieure d'Algerie. The bank holds 173.6 tonnes of gold and is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Who checks its books is a state body rather than a firm, and the arrangement sits close to having no outside auditor at all. Under the money and credit law of 21 June 2023, a Censorat of two full-time censeurs, appointed by presidential decree and required to have central bank accounting expertise, verifies the end-of-year accounts, reports to the bank's board and sends a report to the Minister of Finance within four months of the year end. The censeurs are put there by the head of state rather than chosen by the bank, and they answer to a minister; but the Censorat is created by the bank's own charter law and its members sit in its board sessions, which is why this is recorded with the doubt attached. No private firm is named anywhere in the law for the bank's own accounts.
p:RWA: The National Bank of Rwanda issues the Rwandan franc, which in practice follows a crawling peg against the US dollar, meaning the rate is allowed to drift slowly in a managed way. In November 2012 the Senate summoned governor Claver Gatete, who appeared with finance minister John Rwangombwa, over the franc's slide after it weakened 1.3 percent against the dollar in the first half of the year; Gatete put it down to speculation by investors who had heard donors were cutting aid, and said the bank had put 327.8 million US dollars into the foreign exchange market since 2011. One case is recorded: the bank lost 63 million Rwandan francs from deposit accounts in early 2014 in a fraud reported to involve its own staff, and its information technology director said the suspects had manipulated the internal security system before taking the cash. One person was arrested and the file went to the Prosecutor General, while police said the main suspect was believed to have fled to Uganda; the matter is under investigation, so nothing in it is proven. De La Rue printed the 2,000-franc note introduced on 3 September 2024. Rwangombwa was Governor from 2013 until February 2025 and came from government: Minister of Finance and Economic Planning from 2009, earlier Rwanda's first Accountant General and then Secretary to the Treasury. It scores 29 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:CUW: The Central Bank of Curacao and Sint Maarten issues the Caribbean guilder, pegged to the US dollar. It scores 50 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 96 per cent of the 194 places with a figure, its weakest side the local laws that hide who owns money, which score 78.2 of 100 for financial secrecy. Neither independence index codes it. Crane Currency, headquartered in Massachusetts with plants in Malta and Sweden and a supplier to more than 50 central banks, was contracted to print the new banknotes, with the Royal Canadian Mint making the coins. The bank's supervisory board came under pressure in May 2017. A report published on 26 May 2017 said the board had voted three to two to extend a managing director's term, short of the supermajority required, and that the finance minister, Richard Gibson, had written to the board members Robert Pietersz, Tom Kok, Miriela Carolina, Vance Williams and Hubert Lopez asking them to work on a solution; it quotes him saying that if a solution could not be found there would be no other choice but dismissal of the board, without naming who would carry it out. One case is recorded. In July 2024 a court found former president Tromp and former deputy director Laurents guilty of document forgery over a backdated 2009 loan agreement under which over 400,000 dollars went to Tromp's pension account. It acquitted them of official bribery and money laundering, including over a 1.5 million dollar payment in 2015 from the Venezuelan company Enpiso, which prosecutors linked to Girobank takeover talks. Two career moves are documented. Bob Traa became president with effect from 13 June 2019 after working for the International Monetary Fund for over 34 years, a temporary appointment by the Supervisory Board pending official appointment by Curacao and Sint Maarten, with no private employer named. Jose Jardim, a board member and Financial Economic Director from 2017 responsible for financial and economic supervision and monetary policy, left on 30 June 2025 after eight years and became chief executive of Banco di Caribe, a commercial bank the central bank supervises, with effect from 1 July 2025; Banco di Caribe has been wholly owned since 2022 by United Group Holdings, a privately held group headed by the Curacao businessman Gregory Elias. The Supervisory Board's own announcement of his departure said only that he would take a leadership position at a commercial bank, without naming it.
p:BRN: Brunei Darussalam Central Bank issues the Brunei dollar and runs it as a currency board, meaning the dollar is held at a fixed rate against the Singapore dollar. Under an agreement set up in 1967, the Brunei bank and Singapore's monetary authority each take in the other's notes and coins from banks and exchange them at par without charge. The bank has one swap line, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency, through the ASEAN+3 regional scheme, to which Brunei contributes 0.06 billion US dollars against a maximum arrangement of 0.3 billion, though the factsheet says the member is the country, not necessarily the central bank. Note Printing Australia has printed notes for Brunei: the Reserve Bank of Australia's 2007 report lists the Brunei Currency and Monetary Board among that printer's export orders in 2006/07, without giving a number of notes. PricewaterhouseCoopers Services audits the accounts. No case at the bank is documented. Who sits on its board is a matter of record, and it is the government: the bank announced on 21 October 2025 that His Majesty the Sultan had consented to the appointment of its directors, naming the Minister of Primary Resources and Tourism as Chairman and the Deputy Minister of Finance and Economy as Deputy Chairman, with the Deputy State Mufti, two permanent secretaries, the Solicitor General and the bank's own managing director as the other members. The announcement gives no term. This rests on the bank's own announcement rather than on the Central Bank Order of 2010, which it does not publish anywhere a reader can reach. Its law scores 0.704 of 1 for independence from government, and it scores 50 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:SAU: Saudi Arabia's money is the riyal, issued by the Saudi Central Bank and held at a fixed rate against the United States dollar. It scores 30 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. The independence the law gives it is thinner: 0.501 of 1 on an index of 42 rules, rank 138 of 155, where 1 would mean the bank rather than the government holds the power, and 0 on the part covering control of its own money and budget. It tells the public little, 5.5 of 15 on a transparency measure, and no case at the bank is documented, which is not proof that none happened. The arrangement that matters here is in the law. Under the Saudi Central Bank Law, issued by Royal Decree M/36 of 26 November 2020 and shown as in force on the bank's own rulebook, the bank reports to the King; its five non-government board members are nominated jointly by the Governor and the Minister of Finance and appointed by royal order, and their pay is set by royal order on the Minister of Finance's recommendation. The rulebook's own footnotes record the Council of Ministers amending one of its articles by resolution. The bank part-owns the Bank for International Settlements, the bank for central banks in Basel; its officials also sit on the Financial Stability Board, and it holds 323.1 tonnes of gold. It has one swap line, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency, signed with China on 20 November 2023 for three years and worth 50 billion yuan or 26 billion riyals. Governor Fahad Al-Mubarak came from private finance: general manager of Rana Investment Company from 1992 to 1999, then chairman and managing director of Morgan Stanley Saudi Arabia. He was governor from 2011 to 2016, and King Salman named him governor again by royal decree on 24 January 2021; no ethics finding is recorded against him. Banknotes are reported to be printed at home by the Saudi Central Bank Printing Works. PricewaterhouseCoopers and Ernst & Young Professional Services audited the accounts for the year ended 30 June 2023.
p:LCA: St. Lucia has no central bank of its own: it uses the EC dollar, issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank for eight members, among them Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada and Saint Lucia. The currency has been fixed at EC$2.70 to one US dollar since July 1976, and the law requires reserves of at least 60 per cent of currency in circulation; the agreement was signed on 5 July 1983. One case is recorded. After the bank seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued it in Dallas in 2013, alleging it fraudulently misappropriated assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors. On 17 August 2018 a US federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, without ruling on whether the allegations were true. In a letter dated 17 February 2025 to Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who chairs the ECCU Monetary Council, St Vincent and the Grenadines Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves objected to the EC$22 million spent on an official residence for Governor Timothy Antoine, calling the spending outrageous and the roughly 10,000 square foot house a mansion of veritable palace proportions; he wrote that the governor may wish to consider whether his continued occupancy of the office is tenable and that the spending invites disciplinary action, and proposed that the Monetary Council sell the residence to the government of St Kitts and Nevis. On 5 March 2025 Gonsalves told NBC Radio he would neither confirm nor deny sending the letter. For St. Lucia the arrangement scores 29 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. De La Rue supplies the polymer the notes are made of, and a report on the updated 2027 banknote family says the notes are printed on Safeguard polymer by De La Rue; PricewaterhouseCoopers Eastern Caribbean audits the accounts. The bank's 2020/2021 annual report says it continued its engagement with the World Bank's Reserves Advisory Management Partnership (RAMP), and that a second engagement was judged appropriate to go on building up its newly formed Risk and Analytics Unit, the unit that reports on the reserves portfolio; the same report says the investment guidelines for its external managers were reviewed and updated and that the foreign reserve portfolio had grown to about EC$4.6 billion. The annual report for 2024/2025 and the audited accounts to 31 March 2025 do not repeat the RAMP engagement, so it stands as a 2020/2021 fact. The careers of the people who have run the bank are published, and they reach Saint Lucia through the union rather than through a central bank of its own. The ECCB's own pages on its former governors and deputy governors give dated careers. K Dwight Venner was Director of Finance and Planning in the Government of Saint Lucia from 1981 to 1989 and then governor from 1989 to 2015. Cecil Jacobs was appointed on transfer as Financial Secretary of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, having acted in that post in St Kitts from 1958 to 1961, and ran the institution from 1973 to 1989. Trevor Brathwaite was Permanent Secretary in Saint Lucia's Ministry of Finance, International Financial Services and Economic Affairs from 2002 to 2006 and deputy governor from 2006 to 2021; before entering the public sector in 1992 he was employed by KPMG Peat Marwick. Timothy Antoine had a 22-year career with the Government of Grenada, fourteen years of it as Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Finance, and advised the World Bank Group's executive director for Canada, Ireland and the Caribbean, before taking over as governor on 1 February 2016. Errol Allen, deputy governor from 1983, sits on the boards of the Bank of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and the National Commercial Bank of Anguilla and spent a year at the International Monetary Fund as a special appointee, and the page gives no years for those seats.
p:DMA: Dominica's money is the East Caribbean dollar, issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, which sets monetary policy for eight members: Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Montserrat, St Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. The rate has been fixed at EC$2.70 to one US dollar since July 1976, when the peg moved from sterling, and the founding agreement of 5 July 1983 requires reserves of at least 60 per cent of currency in circulation and other demand liabilities. One case is recorded, and it was dismissed. After the bank seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued it in Dallas in 2013, alleging it had fraudulently misappropriated assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors. On 17 August 2018 a United States federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, without ruling on whether the allegations were true. No government pressure was reported in any of the 37 quarters surveyed from 2010 to 2018. In a letter dated 17 February 2025 to Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who chairs the ECCU Monetary Council, St Vincent and the Grenadines Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves objected to the EC$22 million spent on an official residence for Governor Timothy Antoine, calling the spending outrageous and the roughly 10,000 square foot house a mansion of veritable palace proportions. Gonsalves wrote that the governor may wish to consider whether his continued occupancy of the office is tenable, and that the spending invites disciplinary action; he proposed that the Monetary Council, which is made up of the member states' finance ministers, sell the residence to the government of St Kitts and Nevis, and said he had supported Antoine's appointment but wanted suitable and comfortable accommodation for him instead. On 5 March 2025 Gonsalves told NBC Radio he would neither confirm nor deny sending the letter. De La Rue supplies the polymer the notes are made of and, by one report on the updated family announced on 9 July 2026, prints them; PricewaterhouseCoopers Eastern Caribbean audits the accounts. Dominica scores 27 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, less than 83 per cent of the 194 places scored. The World Bank has a hand in running the reserves: the bank's 2020/2021 annual report says it continued its engagement with the World Bank's Reserves Advisory Management Partnership (RAMP), and that a second engagement was judged appropriate to go on building up its newly formed Risk and Analytics Unit, the unit that reports on the reserves portfolio. The same report says the investment guidelines for the bank's external managers were reviewed and updated, and that the foreign reserve portfolio had grown to about EC$4.6 billion. The engagement is not repeated in the later annual report for 2024/2025 or in the audited accounts to 31 March 2025, so it stands as a 2020/2021 fact. The careers of the people who have run the bank are published, and they reach Dominica through the union rather than through a central bank of its own. The ECCB's own pages on its former governors and deputy governors give dated careers. K Dwight Venner was Director of Finance and Planning in the Government of Saint Lucia from 1981 to 1989 and then governor from 1989 to 2015. Cecil Jacobs was appointed on transfer as Financial Secretary of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, having acted in that post in St Kitts from 1958 to 1961, and ran the institution from 1973 to 1989. Trevor Brathwaite was Permanent Secretary in Saint Lucia's Ministry of Finance, International Financial Services and Economic Affairs from 2002 to 2006 and deputy governor from 2006 to 2021; before entering the public sector in 1992 he was employed by KPMG Peat Marwick. Timothy Antoine had a 22-year career with the Government of Grenada, fourteen years of it as Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Finance, and advised the World Bank Group's executive director for Canada, Ireland and the Caribbean, before taking over as governor on 1 February 2016. Errol Allen, deputy governor from 1983, sits on the boards of the Bank of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and the National Commercial Bank of Anguilla and spent a year at the International Monetary Fund as a special appointee, and the page gives no years for those seats.
p:VCT: St Vincent and the Grenadines shares the East Caribbean dollar with seven other places, all served by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, set up under an agreement signed on 5 July 1983. The rate has been fixed at 2.70 East Caribbean dollars to one US dollar since July 1976, and the law requires reserves worth at least 60 per cent of the currency in circulation. The bank's legal independence is 0.549 of 1 on an index of 42 rules, where 1 means the bank rather than the government holds the power, and government pressure was reported in none of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is recorded. After the bank seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued it in Dallas in 2013, alleging it misappropriated assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors; on 17 August 2018 a US federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, and did not decide whether the allegations were true. The country's own prime minister has since pressed the bank's governor. In a letter dated 17 February 2025 to Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who chairs the ECCU Monetary Council, St Vincent and the Grenadines Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves objected to the EC$22 million spent on an official residence for Governor Timothy Antoine, calling the spending outrageous and the roughly 10,000 square foot house a mansion of veritable palace proportions. He wrote that the governor may wish to consider whether his continued occupancy of the office is tenable and that the spending invites disciplinary action, proposed that the Monetary Council sell the residence to the government of St Kitts and Nevis, and said he had supported Antoine's appointment but wanted suitable and comfortable accommodation for him instead. On 5 March 2025 Gonsalves told NBC Radio he would neither confirm nor deny sending the letter. The score for St Vincent and the Grenadines is 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence; the weakest part is corruption and secrecy around it, mainly laws that hide who owns money and money-laundering risk in its banks. De La Rue supplies the polymer the notes are made of and, by one report, printed the updated 2027 banknote family; PricewaterhouseCoopers Eastern Caribbean audits the accounts. The bank's 2020/2021 annual report says it continued its engagement with the World Bank's Reserves Advisory Management Partnership (RAMP), and that a second engagement was judged appropriate to go on building up its newly formed Risk and Analytics Unit, the unit that reports on the reserves portfolio; the same report says the investment guidelines for its external managers were reviewed and updated and that the foreign reserve portfolio had grown to about EC$4.6 billion. The annual report for 2024/2025 and the audited accounts to 31 March 2025 do not repeat the RAMP engagement, so it stands as a 2020/2021 fact. The careers of the people who have run the bank are published, and they reach Saint Vincent and the Grenadines through the union rather than through a central bank of its own. The ECCB's own pages on its former governors and deputy governors give dated careers. K Dwight Venner was Director of Finance and Planning in the Government of Saint Lucia from 1981 to 1989 and then governor from 1989 to 2015. Cecil Jacobs was appointed on transfer as Financial Secretary of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, having acted in that post in St Kitts from 1958 to 1961, and ran the institution from 1973 to 1989. Trevor Brathwaite was Permanent Secretary in Saint Lucia's Ministry of Finance, International Financial Services and Economic Affairs from 2002 to 2006 and deputy governor from 2006 to 2021; before entering the public sector in 1992 he was employed by KPMG Peat Marwick. Timothy Antoine had a 22-year career with the Government of Grenada, fourteen years of it as Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Finance, and advised the World Bank Group's executive director for Canada, Ireland and the Caribbean, before taking over as governor on 1 February 2016. Errol Allen, deputy governor from 1983, sits on the boards of the Bank of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and the National Commercial Bank of Anguilla and spent a year at the International Monetary Fund as a special appointee, and the page gives no years for those seats.

p:SYR: The Central Bank of Syria issues the Syrian pound, which moves within a band of about 5 percent against the US dollar. Basic Monetary Law No. 23 of 2002, issued in Damascus on 17 March 2002 by President Bashar al-Assad, places the bank and its policy-making council under the government. Article 1 has the Monetary and Credit Council work within the general economic directions of the state approved by the Council of Ministers. Article 8(3) has its decisions passed to the Minister of Economy and Foreign Trade, who may suspend for up to seven days any decision he considers contrary to the interest of the state and must refer a continuing disagreement to the Council of Ministers. Article 69 has the Governor appointed, and his service ended, by decree; article 2 puts the Council's non-bank seats, among them assistant ministers and the head of the State Planning Authority, in the gift of a decree; and article 71 has the Minister name the four supervising directors who sit with the Governor on the management committee. Government pressure was reported in 11 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, each time pressing the bank to ease and demanding that it print money. One case runs from 2005 to 2011: a Vienna court found that the Austrian banknote printer OeBS had overcharged the bank by 14 percent on banknote contracts and that the kickback returned to local decision makers. Prosecutors had told the court that former OeBS employees paid bribes to officials at Syrian and Azerbaijani banks in exchange for contracts to print money, an allegation as reported. OeBS managers were convicted in 2014 and again on retrial in 2018, and no Syrian official was named or tried. The governor appointed in May 2026, Safwat Raslan, came to the bank after a career largely in commercial banking abroad: he was a credit business manager at Deutsche Apotheker und Aerztebank in Germany, a consultant at EY and Capco, a banking expert at TARGOBANK and Deutsche Bank and a branch manager at Byblos Bank Syria, and his most recent post was director general of the Syrian Development Fund. No dates are given, and the ownership of those employers is not stated. Syria appoints no private audit firm: article 68(3) of the same law gives the auditing of the bank's records and accounts to the Central Organization for Financial Control, the state's own supreme audit institution. A circulating 500-pound note is printed by Goznak, the Russian state currency works. Syria scores 41 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:TJK: The National Bank of Tajikistan issues the somoni, which it keeps within a band of 2 per cent or less against the US dollar. The Law on the National Bank of Tajikistan, No. 722 of 28 June 2011, signed by President Emomali Rahmon, puts every seat on the bank's Board in the President's hands. Article 74(4) has the Chairman and his deputies appointed and released from office by presidential decree, with the decrees submitted to the lower house of parliament for approval; article 74(3) has the Board's three independent members approved by the President on the Chairman's proposal; and article 74(6) has the President set the salary of the Chairman and his deputies. One case is recorded, as an official finding: in March 2008 the International Monetary Fund's Executive Board found the bank had supplied inaccurate information on the cotton sector, international reserves, net domestic assets and credit policy, reporting reserves of about 450 million US dollars when they were roughly a third of that and concealing that reserves were pledged as collateral for cotton loans; Tajikistan was required to repay 47.4 million US dollars. No government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. Four career moves run in the same direction, all of them to one commercial bank, Spitamen Bank, whose charter names a single shareholder, the limited liability insurance and reinsurance company Spitamen Insurance, and calls the bank a commercial organisation; none of the four is an accusation. Navruz Samandarzoda, who had headed the bank's research and modelling department, joined Spitamen Bank in January 2018 and chairs its Management Board; Mahmud Hamralizoda, a leading specialist and then deputy head of the central bank's international relations department from 2018 to 2021, joined its Supervisory Board in January 2023; Sanovbar Dzhabirova, at the central bank from 1996 to 2008 and again from 2016 to 2021, latterly as head and then deputy director of its accounting department, joined the same Supervisory Board in January 2023; and Dilbar Khuseynova, head of the insurance control department from 2017 to 2024, joined it in October 2024, having worked at the Development Bank of Tajikistan and at Spitamen Bank itself before her years at the central bank as well as after. It has one swap line, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency: 3 billion yuan with China, signed on 3 September 2015 to run three years and extendable by agreement, drawn on for 1 million yuan in January 2016; whether it is in force is not known. Its commemorative 100-somoni note, circulated on 30 October 2025, was printed by Giesecke+Devrient of Germany, that note alone and not the regular series. RSM Tajikistan LLC signed the auditor's report on the 2023 statements; the firm holds a licence to audit banks issued by the National Bank itself, so the body being audited also licenses its auditor. Earlier audits were done by Deloitte and by Ernst & Young Ford Rhodes Sidat Hyder. Tajikistan scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed.
p:ATG: Antigua and Barbuda uses the East Caribbean dollar, issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, which sets monetary policy for eight members, among them Anguilla, Dominica, Grenada, Montserrat and Saint Lucia. p:BTN: Bhutan's central bank is the Royal Monetary Authority, which issues the ngultrum and keeps it pegged, or fixed, to the Indian rupee; the rupee circulates in the country as well. Its own law lets the government direct it: under the Royal Monetary Authority Act of Bhutan 2010, passed on 2 June 2010 and in force from 22 June 2010, section 149 lets the Royal Government issue such directives to the Authority as it considers necessary in the public interest, after consulting the Governor and reporting them to Parliament. Four of the Board's seven members are appointed by the Government, one of them from the Ministry of Finance, and the Royal Government sets the Governor's salary and the board members' fees. The Governor is appointed by the Druk Gyalpo on the Prime Minister's recommendation and may be removed the same way, but only on a committee finding of permanent incapacity, incapability of carrying out the duties or breach of the code of conduct. The Act repealed the 1982 Royal Monetary Authority Act, and the arrangement is standing, with no end date. An anonymous informer raised a case in October 2014, and the final findings of Bhutan's Anti-Corruption Commission, covering 2014 to 2016, said a former deputy governor had allegedly forged official documents, misused power and concealed earnings from World Bank and Asian Development Bank projects. Those allegations are unproven; the case was forwarded to the Office of the Attorney General, with no later outcome. Two career moves are recorded, and every post in them is a public one. Dasho Penjore began at the Royal Monetary Authority in 1987, was its Deputy Managing Director from 2003 to 2006, was appointed Chief Chamberlain to the King in 2006, was Chief Executive Officer of the National Pension and Provident Fund of Bhutan, a statutory pension body, and was appointed Governor of the Authority in December 2015. Damche Tenzin was Chief Legal Advisor and Company Secretary and then Chief Support Officer of Bank of Bhutan Limited from September 2008 to December 2014, then Chief General Counsel of the National Pension and Provident Fund until May 2016, and has been Chief General Counsel of the Royal Monetary Authority since 1 June 2016; Bank of Bhutan is 80 per cent owned by Druk Holding & Investments, a holding company owned by the government of Bhutan, with 20 per cent held by the State Bank of India, so that side of the move is public too. A commemorative 1,000-ngultrum note marking the Fourth King's seventieth birth anniversary was printed by De La Rue, and M/s P.K. Mitra & Company audited the accounts for 2003 and 2004. India opened a swap line, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency, of up to 100 million US dollars or its equivalent on 17 March 2016 under the Reserve Bank of India's SAARC framework; its three-year term ran out in March 2019. The bank scores 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:XKX: Kosovo has no currency of its own and uses the euro; its central bank is the Central Bank of the Republic of Kosovo. It used the Deutsche Mark from September 1999 and changed to the euro in 2002, the changeover finishing on 28 February 2002 in cooperation with the ECB. No exposure score is given, because too little data exists. In July 2010 European Union law enforcement officials arrested governor Hashim Rexhepi on suspicion of abuse of position, bribery, tax evasion, trading in influence and money laundering. A judge of the EU mission Eulex threw out all the charges on December 12, and in January 2012 Eulex said its prosecutor would take no further action after losing an appeal; he was acquitted. The bank has also joined the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, or RAMP. It describes that membership as building its own capacity in asset management, risk management and financial reporting rather than a handover of reserves; the World Bank, announcing an agreement signed on 16 April 2026 by Jorge Familiar and Governor Ahmet Ismaili, says a portion of the reserves will be managed from 2026.
p:PNG: The Bank of Papua New Guinea issues the kina, whose rate against the US dollar is shifted in small steps rather than left to the market, and the country scores 42 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. One case is on record. Court documents obtained by the journalism group OCCRP show that the National Fraud and Anti-Corruption Directorate searched the bank's offices in August and September 2023 in a money-laundering investigation into Genia, then acting governor; she won a temporary halt that was later dismissed, she has not been charged, and it remains under investigation and unproven. She had earlier been under fraud-squad investigation over a firearms deal for the bank's security team, and became governor in early 2024. The government had already put the bank's own law under review. On 13 May 2021 Treasurer Ian Ling-Stuckey, with the Prime Minister and the Ministerial Economic Committee of the National Executive Council, issued terms of reference for a review of the Central Banking Act 2000 that was told to examine whether the Governor should keep his sole power to decide monetary policy under section 10, and to reconsider the bank's governance and the length of senior management terms. In April 2024 the Prime Minister announced new board members, among them Sir Robin Fleming, former chief executive of the commercial bank Bank South Pacific, and Mark Baker, former country head of the commercial bank Australia and New Zealand Banking. The 2024 annual report names Pictet Asset Management as the weakest of the outside firms running part of the reserves that year, with DWS and BlackRock the strongest. Note Printing Australia listed the bank among its export orders in 2006 and 2007.
p:MKD: North Macedonia's money is the denar, issued by the National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia and held in practice at a fixed rate to the euro. Its notes are printed abroad, by three firms in turn. The French firm Oberthur Fiduciaire was contracted for 100-denar notes, reported on 8 May 2026, for 59,800,000 denars, about 972,358 euros; the Russian joint-stock company Goznak had the 100-denar notes in 2021 for about 400,000 euros, part of a 2.2 million euro reissue carrying the state's changed constitutional name; and three contracts with De La Rue International cover the 10, 500 and 1,000 denar notes, 45 million notes for 3.775 million euros, 20 million of them polymer. The state's own auditors have gone through the bank's books once. The State Audit Office examined the bank's 2003 financial statements, working on site from 12 October to 20 December 2004 under article 2 of the Law on State Audit, and its final report, number 11-107/8 of 4 March 2005, carries a section headed improper and unlawful use of funds. It found that the National Bank had guaranteed a domestic bank with foreign-currency deposits, and that in January 2004 the foreign banks drew 20,759,515 US dollars from the National Bank's guarantee deposit. It also found that 30,210 thousand denars of purchases, 35.61 per cent of the purchases audited, were made without following the Public Procurement Law, and it told the bank to give up commercial activities that article 83 of the Law on the National Bank does not allow it. In January 2025 a group of members of the Assembly moved on the bank's own money. Their bill, tabled under the shortened procedure, would rewrite article 15 of the Law on the National Bank so that the Council pays 30 per cent of the financial result into general reserves, 15 per cent once base capital is reached, and the remainder into the Budget of the Republic of North Macedonia, and it would oblige the bank to move the special reserves it had built up, which the bill puts at almost 27 million euros, into general reserves within 30 days and not to use them in the meantime. An amendment to that law was enacted as Sluzben vesnik 16/25, which the bank's own decisions cite from 4 February 2025, but the enacted text could not be read, so whether these are the provisions that passed is not confirmed. One case is recorded, running from 2017 to 2020, and it is unproven: an association of depositors of Eurostandard Bank said in a press release that the governor tipped off the finance minister and other large depositors so they could take their money out before the bank was put under administration, and that financial police reports were kept secret so it could keep operating. The association said Finance Minister Nina Angelovska withdrew more than 200,000 euros months before the central bank acted, and that over 60 million euros were lost; no charges and no official finding are reported. Two career moves are on record. Governor Anita Angelovska Bezhoska spent about eight years at the Ministry of Finance, ending as manager of the treasury department, was state secretary in 2003 and 2004, worked as an economist at the International Monetary Fund, and became governor in May 2018, a career with no private firm in it. Dimitar Bogov came from a commercial bank, as chief economist of Stopanska Banka AD Skopje, a member of the NBG Group, from 2002 to January 2007, then was vice governor and governor from 2011; no finding against him is reported. Grant Thornton DOO of Skopje signed the auditor's report on the 2023 accounts, with an opinion without qualifications, and the bank scores 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:BLZ: The Central Bank of Belize issues the Belize dollar, held at a fixed rate to the US dollar. The government money it keeps has twice been found not to add up. For 2011/2012 the Auditor General reported that the Treasury could not show that 25 government accounts held at the bank had been reconciled, and that the public debt records the bank manages did not match the Accountant General's statements. The National Assembly's Joint Public Accounts Committee, on the Auditor General's report for April 2016 to March 2017, made significant material differences between Central Bank and SmartStream balances a priority area, with gaps of 42 million, 19 million, 3 million and 1.4 million dollars; at hearings in March 2026 Auditor General Maria Rodriguez said the Central Bank accounts were not being reconciled. In August 2021 governor Gustavo Manuel Vasquez lost his post; Prime Minister John Briceno said the board had recommended he resign because of a lot of policy differences, and Vasquez wrote that his appointment was terminated on the instructions of the Ministry of Finance. De La Rue printed the 100-dollar note introduced on 4 August 2025. Belize scores 35 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and tells the public little, 4 of 15 in 2019. Two careers run out of the bank and back in, Kareem Michael's through the utility Belize Electricity Limited and Marina Laetitia Murillo's through private financial-sector management.
p:GIN: Guinea's money, the Guinean franc, is issued by the Central Bank of the Republic of Guinea. The country scores 30 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and the weakest part is corruption and secrecy around the bank. In December 2021 the country's military leader, Mamadi Doumbouya, dismissed Laounceny Kaba, who had run the bank for ten years, along with the two vice-governors, Baidy Aribot and Madjou Sow, and a younger economist, Karamo Kaba, replaced him; the report of 8 December 2021 puts the removal down to how long Kaba had held the post and to his closeness to the deposed president, Alpha Conde, and says, as a report rather than a confirmed fact, that he had tried without success to win the junta's confidence. Karamo Kaba, the bank's 16th governor, came to it from asset management: from 2003 to 2021 he was Economist Strategist and then Director of Economic Research at Ecofi Investissements, described as an asset management company and a subsidiary of the Credit Cooperatif group, and before that he was a portfolio manager and financial analyst at ACOFI Gestion and an economist at the agricultural cooperative union InVivo. On 23 June 2026 the appeals chamber of Guinea's CRIEF court convicted a former governor, Bah, in his absence of embezzlement of public funds and related offences, sentencing him to five years, ordering him to repay 10.5 million US dollars taken from the bank's coffers without trace, imposing a fine of 5 billion Guinean francs and confiscating assets; his defence said the money was released on the instruction of the highest state authorities for an international humanitarian organisation. Government pressure was reported in 4 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, each time to loosen policy and to print money. KPMG S.A. audits the accounts for 2023.
p:COM: The Central Bank of the Comoros issues the Comorian franc, and France stands behind it. A monetary cooperation agreement signed at Moroni and Paris on 23 November 1979 rests on an unlimited French guarantee of the currency the bank issues. It set the rate at 1 Comorian franc to 0.02 French francs; after a devaluation of 33 percent on 11 January 1994, the rate is now 1 euro to 491.968 Comorian francs. The bank must keep 65 percent of its foreign currency reserves on deposit with the French Treasury. Two governments also fill its board. Under statutes signed in Paris on 22 April 2008 it had at most eight members, half named by the French government and half by the government of the Union of the Comoros, with the Governor named by the President of the Union on the finance minister's proposal. Under statutes signed in Paris on 3 December 2024 and in force since March 2025, the board is six people, the governor plus three administrators named by the Comorian government and two named by the French government, and the French-appointed seats also take two of the four places on the committee that sets monetary policy and manages the reserves and two of the four on the banking supervision committee. Two cases are recorded, both findings of a parliamentary commission of inquiry into the programme that sold economic citizenship. Reporting in December 2017, it found that the programme's account TR0044 at the bank took in payments, including four cheques drawn by Comoro Gulf Holding on two commercial banks between March 2009 and April 2010, and that the bank booked money in without knowing the price the passports sold for; the bank's board noted in June 2014 that 6 million euros had been expected before the end of December 2013 while receipts since October 2013 came to only 2.670 million Comorian francs, which the inquiry called a shortfall of more than 2,900,000,000 Comorian francs. The account was closed on 1 September 2015. The same inquiry found that, according to his own collaborators, President Ikililou Dhoinine ordered that from January 2015 until the end of his term the funds no longer be paid into the bank and could not explain what became of them, so it concluded he was suspected of embezzling public money. The notes are printed at the Banque de France, which made the 10,000-franc note reported as introduced on 6 January 2026. It holds 0.02 tonnes of gold, 0.64 per cent of its reserves, recorded in its 2024 auditor's report as eighteen bars in the bank's own strongroom in Moroni. Mazars Fivoarana audited its 2024 accounts, and it scores 47 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed.
p:TKM: The Central Bank of Turkmenistan issues the manat. Its law leaves most of the power with the government: 0.41 of 1 on one independence index, where 1 means the bank holds the power, and 0.183 on another, ranking it 187 of 191. It scores 33 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, the largest part being corruption and secrecy around it, at 74. In March 2002 the prosecutor's office accused former central bank chairman Orazov of embezzling 120 million US dollars in German and Swiss loans. On 29 December 2002 the Supreme Court sentenced Orazov in absentia to 25 years over alleged involvement in the armed attack on President Niyazov of 25 November 2002, and the People's Council raised that to life imprisonment the next day; Amnesty International called the trial grossly unfair. That conviction is for the alleged attack, not the loan accusation, which remains unproven. In January 2014 President Gurbanguly Berdymukhamedov dismissed the bank's head, Tuvakmammet Japarov, for unspecified flaws in his work. Its notes are printed abroad by De La Rue, which printed the commemorative 200-manat polymer note introduced on 1 December 2025 for the thirtieth anniversary of permanent neutrality.
p:MRT: The Central Bank of Mauritania issues Mauritania's money, the ouguiya, and scores 30 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is corruption in the country and money-laundering risk in its banks. Central Banking reported on 30 July 2004 that President Maaouiya Ould Taya had sacked the chairman of the bank, the day after sacking his whole economic team, and that Zeine Ould Zeidane, formerly an adviser to the president, was installed in his place. The report names neither the sacked chairman nor any reason and gives no calendar date, saying only that it happened on the Monday. It rests on a single account relayed from IRIN, so it is reported rather than confirmed. One case is recorded, from 2020 and 2021, and it is still an investigation. In July 2020 police working under the Nouakchott-Ouest prosecutor arrested six people, one of them a bank employee, over foreign currency taken from the central bank; early reports put the amount at about 1 million US dollars and later reports at 2.4 million, plus 500,000 dollars in counterfeit notes. By March 2021 seven people were in pretrial detention, presumed to have taken about 1 million dollars, and supporters held a sit-in demanding a quick trial. No trial or verdict is reported. Two governors arrived from other public bodies. Abdel Aziz Ould Dahi was director general of the Caisse Nationale d'Assurance Maladie, the national health insurance fund, until he was made governor in January 2015, and he had been a minister under President Sidi Mohamed Ould Cheikh Abdallahi. Mohamed El Cheikh El Kebir Moulaye, governor since 21 January 2020, had held bank posts in studies, balance of payments and liquidity management, was deputy governor from 2014 to 2019, served as Minister of Employment and Vocational Training in 2007 and 2008 and was Minister of Economy and Industry from August 2019 until the appointment; he was also director general of PROCAPEC, the popular savings and credit funds. The bank signed an agreement with the World Bank treasury on foreign exchange reserve management, under which the treasury department provides technical assistance covering training of reserve staff, organisation of the relevant structures and the eventual setting up of a trading room; that is advice and training, not management of the money. Who prints the money is reported rather than confirmed by the bank: an industry body's profile says the 20-ouguiya polymer note launched on 28 November 2021 was made by the Canadian Bank Note Company, Limited, which is a third-party announcement rather than anything confirmed on the bank's own site. The 50-ouguiya note marking fifty years of the currency, introduced on 18 June 2023, came on three substrates, Durasafe composite by Landqart, paper with sisal by Oberthur and Hybrid by Louisenthal. It holds 1 tonne of gold, 4.3 per cent of its reserves.
p:ARE: The Central Bank of the United Arab Emirates issues the dirham and holds it at a fixed rate against the US dollar, an arrangement called a peg. It scores 30 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. On Saturday 29 August 2026 the bank said it had ordered a special and urgent examination of the UAE branches of Banque Misr, an Egyptian lender with five branches in the country, after the United States raised money-laundering concerns; the US Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network had proposed a rule that would revoke Banque Misr UAE's correspondent banking access to US financial institutions. The bank said the examination includes a forensic, in-depth lookback over the period covered by the US statement and focuses on transactions of the companies named in it, that it was studying options for the bank's status if the US special measure is formally imposed, and that it expects banks it licenses to avoid reputational risks to the financial system and to respect other countries' laws. Nothing has been proven against Banque Misr; these are concerns raised by the US authorities and an examination ordered by the UAE central bank. The same report noted that in June 2026 a foreign bank branch in the UAE, not named, was fined 20 million dirhams, about 5.44 million US dollars, for anti-money-laundering failures. No government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters surveyed between 2010 and 2018. Its law gives it middling independence, 0.685 of 1, and the cabinet's hold on it is written into that law. Under Decretal Federal Law No. 14 of 2018, board members are appointed by federal decree on the Cabinet's recommendation and their membership can be ended by federal decree with the Cabinet's approval, the exchange rate regime is set only on a board proposal with Cabinet approval, and the bank cannot withdraw a currency denomination from circulation without Cabinet approval. There is no episode and no end date: this is how the bank is arranged. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Its notes are printed by Oumolat Security Printing, which the Emirates Investment Authority started and owned before it was transferred to the central bank; a new 100 dirham polymer note printed by Oumolat was reported on 31 March 2025. Abdulhamid Saeed, made governor by federal decree on 2 April 2020, had been group chief executive of First Abu Dhabi Bank.
p:PAN: Panama has no central bank. Banco Nacional de Panamá is a state commercial bank, and the country uses the US dollar. The IMF lists Panama with Ecuador, El Salvador, the Marshall Islands, Micronesia, Palau and Timor-Leste as having no separate legal tender, with the US dollar as anchor. The US dollar is 89.08% of world currency trading, 56.7% of foreign reserves and 50.1% of Swift payments, and 16 places use it. No documented case at a central bank was found. The country has had 1 systemic banking crisis since 1970, and its financial secrecy score is 78.4 of 100. The exposure score is 53 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 fully exposed, which ranks 6 of 194; corruption and secrecy around it scores 67 and outside influence 39.
p:BDI: The Bank of the Republic of Burundi is the central bank of Burundi, which uses the Burundian franc. One case is recorded. In October 2023 the Ministry of Justice said that the dismissed governor, Dieudonné Murengerantwari, was being prosecuted for passive corruption (taking bribes), money laundering, misappropriation of public property and undermining the national economy. The prosecutor called this description of the facts provisional, and the governor was being questioned at the time of the report. He is charged, and nothing is reported as proven. The bank scores 34 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption in the country. President Evariste Ndayishimiye fired the governor, Dieudonne Murengerantwari, on Sunday 8 October 2023, thirteen months into a five-year term. The presidency gave no reasons; bank employees told Yaga Burundi the removal was linked to misappropriation of foreign currency. Edouard Normand Bigendako, a board member, replaced him and inherited the same shortage of foreign exchange. Murengerantwari was then held by the National Intelligence Service and charged with undermining the proper functioning of the national economy, passive corruption, money laundering and misappropriation of public assets, charges the justice ministry called provisional and which he had not answered. Under his thirteen months the bank had loosened exchange policy, lifting restrictions on instant transfers received from abroad and suspending a 2016 decision that barred diplomatic missions and international organisations from holding foreign currency accounts outside commercial banks. Civil society organisations criticise the bank for its lack of independence from political power. The bank's accounts are audited from outside the country by Forvis Mazars Cameroun SA, whose report on the year ended 30 June 2023 was signed at Bujumbura on 6 August 2026. One career move is recorded. Mathias Sinamenye ran the central bank from 1992 to 1998 and now sits on the board of Interbank Burundi, a commercial bank in Bujumbura, chairing its audit committee in 2022 and its credit committee by 2025. The bank states its own ownership in its annual report: the shareholding has been entirely private from the start, held by Burundians and foreigners of more than ten nationalities with staff taking part, and it calls itself one of the pioneers of private banking in Burundi. The governorship dates rest on an encyclopaedia entry rather than a primary record. Its notes are printed abroad by the French firm Oberthur Fiduciaire, which printed the 2,000-franc note dated 11 September 2023, a paper note carrying a green-to-gold pineapple in optically variable ink and a windowed thread showing a heifer's head.
p:ARM: Armenia uses the dram, issued by the Central Bank of Armenia, which scores 21 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. The dram is held on a pre-announced crawling peg against the US dollar, meaning the rate is moved in small announced steps. One case is recorded and it is unproven. In February 2022 Armbusinessbank's new ownership was registered as MFM Global Invest LLC of Switzerland with 74.998 per cent and Housing for Young Families, a refinancing credit organisation founded by the Central Bank of Armenia itself, with 25.001 per cent. Former labour minister Maneh Tandilyan called the deal non-transparent and a gross violation of the law that bars the regulator from interfering in the activities of commercial banks; the bank gave no comment to the news agency that reported it, and no inquiry or ruling has followed, so it stands as a claim rather than a finding. One career move runs both ways: Tigran Davtyan held managerial roles at the bank from 1994 to 1998 and later ran two commercial banks, as chief executive of Converse Bank from 2009 to 2016 and of Inecobank from 2018 to 2019, and has been an independent non-executive director of Ameriabank since July 2020. No government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters surveyed between 2010 and 2018. The bank has rejoined the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, having been a member from 2006 to 2014; what it gets is advice, onsite expertise and staff training rather than management of its assets. It has one swap line with China, an arrangement for two central banks to lend each other currency, for 77 billion drams and one billion yuan, dated March 2015, though whether it is still in force is not known. A bank representative says Giesecke+Devrient won the printing of its third banknote series after an evaluation of all offers. KPMG Armenia LLC audits the accounts.
p:CPV: The Bank of Cape Verde issues the escudo, and the government of Portugal guarantees it under a currency cooperation agreement signed on 13 March 1998. The rate is fixed at 110.265 Cape Verdean escudos to the euro, having started at 0.55 escudos to the Portuguese escudo. The Portuguese Treasury provides a short-term credit line of 27.5 million euros, which can rise to 45 million, with drawings capped at 5 million, and Cabo Verde must transfer reserves equal to 35 per cent of what it asks for; Banco de Portugal states the facility obliges neither it nor any euro-area institution to step in. The bank has also signed a technical assistance agreement with the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, becoming its 75th member, which is advisory work rather than management of its assets, and De La Rue printed the 1,000 and 2,000 escudo notes released on 15 April 2025. Its books are checked from outside by EY's Cape Verde member firm, which signed the auditor's report on the 2024 accounts and gave an opinion without qualifications on a balance sheet total of 99,898,332 thousand escudos and negative equity of 622,855 thousand escudos. The governor since 4 January 2021, Oscar Humberto Evora Santos, has moved back and forth between the bank and other public work: he joined the bank in 1991 in its studies and statistics department, worked from 1994 to 2000 on a World Bank vocational training project and then as coordinator of a UN-funded employment promotion project, returned to the bank from 2002 to 2013 as adviser and coordinator of the economic studies division, was Councillor for Finance and Business at the Municipality of Praia from 2008 to 2016 and Mayor of Praia from 2016 to 2020. No private employer is named. Who decides policy is written into its founding law, and that law was replaced in 2026: Lei n.º 70/X/2026 of 26 January 2026 revokes the 2002 Organic Law and states that the Government defines monetary and exchange rate policy with the bank collaborating, while the bank executes that policy on its own authority. The Council of Ministers appoints the Governor and Vice-Governor on the finance minister's proposal, and under article 51 they cannot be moved and may be dismissed only for ceasing to meet the requirements of office or for serious misconduct, with a right of appeal. Its law scores 0.518 of 1 for independence on a measure taken before that change, where 1 means the bank rather than the government holds the power. No case at the bank is documented, which is not proof none happened. It scores 51 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, more exposed than 97 per cent of the 194 places with a figure, with money issued, backed or fixed from abroad the main reason.
p:BRB: The Central Bank of Barbados issues the Barbados dollar and in practice holds it at a fixed rate against the United States dollar. Its founding governor, Sir Courtney Blackman, had been an economist at the Wall Street bank Irving Trust Company from 1968 to 1971 and led the bank from 1972 to 1987 across three terms, while also serving as Barbados' alternate governor to the International Monetary Fund until March 1987. Five cases are recorded, all findings by the Auditor General about government money held at the bank. His 2004 report found discrepancies with the Accountant General's records for the government current account between October 2000 and February 2004: unrecorded withdrawals above $1.8 million and unrecorded deposits above $6.8 million. The 2020 report found Treasury accounts unreconciled up to 31 March 2019, eight transfers of loan funds totalling $13.137 million made without the required signed memorandum, and the government's overdraft exceeding its statutory limit of 10 per cent of estimated revenue twice in 2018, each time by $10 million. The 2021 report found a $6,662,541.31 difference between Treasury and bank records for 22 September 2020 left unexplained. In 2017 Finance Minister Chris Sinckler dismissed Governor Delisle Worrell; the stated reason was the board's objection to his reported high-handed manner, some observers believed it was his refusal to keep financing the government with new money, and the Appeals Court upheld the minister's right to dismiss him. Otherwise no government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. De La Rue prints the five-dollar polymer note introduced in December 2022, PricewaterhouseCoopers SRL audits the accounts, and Barbados scores 35 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:SDN: The Central Bank of Sudan issues the Sudanese pound. It scores 45 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 85. On 9 February 2020 a body the transitional government had set up, the Empowerment Elimination, Anti-Corruption and Funds Recovery Committee, dissolved the bank's board of directors along with the boards of eleven other banks, and nine of the bank's managers were dismissed at the same time. The reason given was the bank's alleged links to the deposed government of Omar Al Bashir; that allegation is unproven, no individual board member was named and the evidence the committee relied on was not set out. In October 2025 Sovereignty Council head Abdel Fattah al-Burhan dismissed governor Burai Al-Siddiq Ali Ahmed after a dispute over the rules for buying and exporting gold, and appointed Amna Mirghani Hassan El Toum; deputy governor Mohamed Osman Ahmed Mohamed Khair was dismissed less than two weeks later. Three career moves are recorded.
