Ibrahim Mohammed Ali Nimir was general manager of the central bank from 1964 to 1967, then general manager of Elneilin Bank from 1970 to 1973, then returned as Governor and chairman of the board from 1973 to 1980; El Nilein's own group history says the bank, formed in 1963 out of a merger of Credit Lyonnais, the Arab Bank and the Red Sea Bank, was nationalised and became El Nilein Bank Group in 1970 and only became an independent entity in 2007, so that spell began in the year it passed into state hands. After his governorship he was general manager of National Bank from 1980 to 1982 and general manager of Workers National Bank from 1989 to 1992; Sudan nationalised its banks in 1970 and reversed course in stages afterwards, so those two legs are not settled either way. Mohamed Khair Ahmed Al-Zubair was Minister of Finance and National Economy from 2000 to 2001, held state minister and planning posts in the finance ministry through the 1980s and 1990s, was Vice President of the Bank of Sahel and Sahara Community, an intergovernmental bank, from 2002 to 2009, and became Governor of the Central Bank of Sudan in March 2011; the bank's own biography of him also lists former board seats, without dates, at the Saudi Sudanese Bank, where he was president of the board, the Financial Investment Bank and the Agricultural Bank of Sudan. Government pressure was reported in 2 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, both times pressing the bank to cut rates or ease and demanding that it print money. Its law scores 0.333 of 1 on one measure of independence, ranking 172 of 191, and it scores 1.5 of 15 on how much it tells the public. Its notes are made in the country: Dabanga reported in February 2019 that Sudan's new 200-pound banknote had gone into production at the Sudanese Company for Currency Printing, a domestic press the prime minister had visited that week. Who checks its books is the state rather than a firm: the bank's annual report presents its statement of financial position, profit and loss account, statement of changes in owner equity and cash flow statement for the year ended 31 December 2015 as audited by the National Audit Chamber, the body behind the Central Bank of Sudan Act 2002, which requires the accounts to be audited in accordance with the General Audit Chambers Act 1999 without naming an auditor. No documented case at the central bank was found, which is not proof none happened; Reporters Without Borders rates the situation for journalists here as very serious in its 2026 index, so the court reports a case would be found in may not exist or may not be publishable.
p:TTO: The Central Bank of Trinidad and Tobago issues the Trinidad and Tobago dollar and in practice holds it at a fixed rate against the US dollar. Both of its records come out of the collapse of the conglomerate CL Financial and of the Hindu Credit Union. The commission of enquiry into that collapse, set up in November 2010 under a single commissioner, Sir Anthony Colman, found the bank's powers to regulate insurers 'fundamentally deficient', tracing that to how narrowly the Insurance Act was drawn; it said the Inspector of financial institutions tried to use the limited tools then available but that Clico and CL Financial management largely ignored them, and that the collapse might have been avoided had powers in an unpassed Insurance Bill been in force by 2008. It blamed no named bank official. The enquiry sat from March 2011 to May 2013 at an estimated cost of 36.2 million dollars, including a 7 million dollar fee for Colman. At the same enquiry, on 6 December 2012, Queen's Counsel Peter Carter put it to former governor Ewart Williams that intervening in 2006 would have kept more than 10 billion Trinidad and Tobago dollars out of danger; Williams said the bank had seen early warning signs at CLICO that year but held off to avoid a run on the insurer, and intervened in 2009. That was the questioning of a witness rather than a finding, and the claim is unconfirmed. The bank is listed as a member of the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, which offers members advice, training and the management of assets without the listing saying which applies here. BDO T&T audited its accounts for 2024, De La Rue printed its 100-dollar plastic note of December 2019, and it holds 2 tonnes of gold. No government pressure was reported in any of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, and it scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. A governor was removed, though, for what he said in public. At the bank's Monetary Policy Forum on 4 December 2015, Governor Jwala Rambarran named the five largest users of the foreign exchange market by sector and the amounts they had used over three years, and said the country had entered a recession. The companies named complained to the finance minister and threatened to sue. On 22 December he was summoned to a meeting with the finance minister, Colm Imbert, and handed a bank press release recording the private and financial sectors' reaction; on 24 December 2015 the Acting President, on the advice of the Cabinet, revoked his appointment under the Central Bank Act, two and a half years before his five-year term was due to end. Imbert said he had broken several laws, and both Imbert and Prime Minister Keith Rowley said he had not backed the recession claim with government data. Rambarran said the law gave him the authority to release the names and that the public had a right to know how much foreign exchange was going to import and distribution. A deputy governor, Alvin Hilaire, replaced him. Hilaire, who was Governor from 2015 to 2025, had spent 11 years at the International Monetary Fund before that, as a senior economist and as IMF resident representative to Guinea and Sierra Leone, and worked on IMF programmes in Croatia, Colombia, Cameroon, Ecuador and Nicaragua. In June 2022 Justice Devindra Rampersad held the termination unlawful and in breach of his constitutional rights; the State appealed, and the case went on to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. The governor who replaced him was then removed for the opposite conduct. Alvin Hilaire was reappointed for three years in December 2020 and again in December 2023, with his final term due to end in December 2026; his appointment was revoked on 24 June 2025, about 18 months early, with no formal grounds stated. In the weeks before it, Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar publicly accused him of refusing to provide information about the country's largest users of foreign exchange, the same information Rambarran had been dismissed for disclosing. She said at a post-Cabinet news conference in June 2025 that getting information out of the bank was like a bed of thorns or pulling teeth, that Hilaire had failed to provide information to the Auditor General in 2024 and again in 2025, and that this was a blocker to the government's efforts to investigate the foreign exchange market. He challenged the revocation in court and a settlement out of court was reported in early November 2026, with the terms not described. Six of the bank's eleven governors since December 1964 have served fewer than five years, and these two are the ones who went to court over it.
p:QAT: The Qatar Central Bank issues the riyal, held at a fixed rate to the US dollar (a peg). Its law scores 0.607 of 1 on one independence index and 0.586 on another, where 1 means the bank holds the power. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters in 2010-2018, and no documented case at the bank was found. Where the bank sits is set out in its own law and has no end date. Under Law No. 13 of 2012, issued by the Emir, the bank is a corporate body with its own capital and budget and is under the direct control of the Emir; the Governor is appointed by Emiri decision for a renewable five-year term with the rank of a minister, and the board seats representatives of the ministries responsible for finance and for trade. The Governor, Sheikh Bandar bin Mohammed bin Saoud Al-Thani, has worked only in public bodies: an early career at the bank in the Credit and Banking Supervision Section and then the Investment Department as head of trading and managing the foreign exchange reserves, establishing and then leading the Qatar Credit Bureau as its chief executive, with the Banking Risk Department added in 2014, Head of the State Audit Bureau from 2015 to 2021, and then Governor. No bank, asset manager or other private financial firm is named. It has 4 swap lines, which are agreements to borrow another central bank's currency. They include 35 billion Chinese yuan with China, with a renewal agreement dated 14 October 2026, and 15 billion US dollars' worth of lira and riyal with Turkiye, amended in 2020, whose current status is not confirmed. It holds 116.2 tonnes of gold, 26.8 per cent of reserves. The exposure score is 29 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 fully exposed. De La Rue printed the 22-riyal commemorative note issued for the 2022 FIFA World Cup.
p:SLV: El Salvador's central bank is the Central Reserve Bank of El Salvador, and the currency is listed as both the colon and the US dollar. The IMF's 2023 classification puts the country among places with no separate legal tender of their own, using the US dollar as their anchor; legal changes made private acceptance of Bitcoin voluntary and tax payments payable only in US dollars, listed as steps taken before an IMF loan approved on 26 February 2025. One episode with parliament is recorded. In September 2020 Nicolas Martinez, president of the bank, answered a summons from a Legislative Assembly commission investigating the debt the government had taken on during the COVID-19 pandemic and how it was used, and resigned the day after appearing; no reason for the resignation is given. Deputies asked whether the release of banks' liquidity reserve was designed so banks could buy Treasury paper, and he answered that it was an autonomous decision of the banks. Two career moves are recorded. Rafael Barraza Dominguez held the presidency, the vice-presidency and the studies and economic policy management of the bank, with no dates given for any of them, and is now chief executive of Banco Agricola; a rating report filed with the Salvadoran stock exchange states that Banco Agricola's ultimate shareholder is Bancolombia, that the bank belongs to the Banagricola conglomerate owned by Bancolombia Panama, and that the three companies belong to the holding company Inversiones Financieras Banco Agricola, which is what makes this an employer with named corporate shareholders and no state holding. The other move stays within the public sector: Carlos Paredes came to the presidency of the bank from the Autonomous Port Executive Commission, the National Centre for Agricultural and Forestry Technology, the National Council for Science and Technology and the Ministry of Economy, with no dates given and no private financial employer named. No case at the bank is documented, which does not prove none happened; Reporters Without Borders rates the situation for journalists here as very serious in its 2026 index, so the court reports a case would be found in may not exist or may not be publishable. Written independence from government scores 0.789 of 1, and no government pressure was reported in any of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. On its reserves, the bank's own document on international reserves management says it joined the World Bank's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership in 2010, which it describes as advice on reserve management rather than managing a portfolio, and it names no external portfolio manager or custodian, referring only generally to external investment portfolio managers. The Corte de Cuentas de la Republica audits the accounts under a law still in force. El Salvador scores 39 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:HND: The Central Bank of Honduras issues the lempira, kept as of December 2025 at a set level against the US dollar and moved in small steps, an arrangement called a crawling peg. The man who runs it came from commercial banking: Wilfredo Rafael Cerrato Rodriguez was a credit officer at Banco Mercantil, S.A. from November 1993 to April 1996, a credit officer at Intermediaria Financiera, S.A. of Grupo FICOHSA from September to December 1996, and a credit officer and then agency manager at Banco FICOHSA from January 1997 to February 2003, ten years in Honduran commercial banking before his public career, and he became president of the central bank on 27 January 2018; Banco Ficohsa's audited financial statements state that it is 94.28% owned by Grupo Financiero Ficohsa S.A., domiciled in Panama, which is how the private shareholding of that employer is established, since the biography page itself states no ownership. Its accounts are checked from outside by Horwath Central America, for the 2023 financial year. The 200-lempira note is printed by Crane Currency Malta Limited, which won private tender 11/2023 by resolution 127-3/2024 of 14 March 2024, worth 1,284,000 US dollars at 6.42 US cents a note. One case is documented: on 3 June 2026 prosecutors charged 11 current and former employees, two of them serving managers, with 100 counts of negligent embezzlement over a scheme said to have removed public funds from the bank over several years, and they were arrested after the court admitted the case. The charges are unproven. Honduras scores 29 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, the heaviest part being corruption and secrecy around the bank, at 67.
p:STP: The Central Bank of Sao Tome and Principe issues the dobra, which is pegged to the euro. One episode is recorded. In June 2006 the cabinet dismissed the governor, Maria do Carmo Silveira, a former prime minister, together with her team, saying it had found irregularities in the construction of the new central bank building, a project valued at 8 million US dollars. No detail of those irregularities and no investigation finding was given, so the claim is unproven, and the report does not mention corruption or fraud. In early December 2022 the Council of Ministers replaced governor Americo Soares de Barros with Americo d'Oliveira dos Ramos, who had been Minister of Finance in Patrice Trovoada's government between 2014 and 2018, a move from one public post to another; no private employer is named. A commemorative 50-dobra note marking 50 years of independence, introduced on 26 August 2026, was produced by Royal Joh. Enschede in the Netherlands, as the bank's own launch communication states; that is the commemorative note, not the circulating series. The country has had two systemic banking crises since 1970, and it scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, with its weak point the corruption and secrecy around it, chiefly money-laundering risk in its banks.
p:BHR: The Central Bank of Bahrain, created in 1973, issues the Bahraini Dinar (BHD), held at a peg to the US dollar as of December 2025. Its exposure score is 30 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. The weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it (56): the country's laws hide who owns money, and financial secrecy scores 69 of 100. Written independence from government scores 0.515 of 1 on one index (rank 135 of 155) and 0.433 on another (rank 156 of 191). Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, and no documented case at the bank was found. The pressure here is built into the law instead, and it has no end date. Under the Central Bank of Bahrain and Financial Institutions Law of 2006, all seven board members, one of them a representative of the Ministry of Finance, hold office by Royal Decree for renewable four-year terms, and that decree names the chairman and vice chairman; the Governor, who has ministerial rank, is appointed by Royal Decree. Article 173 then has the Minister watch whether the bank is keeping to the general economic policy of the Kingdom, and where the Minister sees a conflict and the board holds to its own view, the Minister refers the disagreement to the Cabinet, which settles it by an order issued within thirty days. A swap line, which is an agreement to borrow another central bank's currency, runs both ways with the United Arab Emirates: BHD 2 billion (AED 20 billion), signed 8 April 2026, for up to 5 years. De La Rue printed the 20-dinar note. The bank's accounts are audited by KPMG Fakhro of Manama, which signed its report on the 2023 financial statements on 10 March 2024. Rasheed Mohammed Al Maraj has been Governor since January 2005; immediately before joining the bank he was General Manager and Chief Executive Officer of the Arab Petroleum Investments Company, APICORP, in Dammam, Saudi Arabia, and earlier he was Assistant Under-Secretary at Bahrain's Ministry of Finance and National Economy and Under-Secretary at the Ministry of Transportation.
p:TLS: Timor-Leste has its own central bank, the Banco Central de Timor-Leste, created in 2001, but not its own currency: it uses the US dollar. The International Monetary Fund's 2023 classification lists it among the places with no separate legal tender and the dollar as anchor. The bank is also the day-to-day manager of the country's Petroleum Fund, and it hires outside firms to run parts of that money. That arrangement is set by the Petroleum Fund Law, Law No. 9/2005 of 3 August, republished with amendments by Law No. 12/2011, and it leaves the decisions with the government. Article 11 says the Government is responsible for the overall management of the Fund, that the Minister of Finance takes the decisions on its investment strategy and management after first obtaining the opinion of the Investment Advisory Board, and that the Minister signs a contract with the central bank for the Fund's operational management. Article 12(5) requires an investment manager to act within any instructions the Minister issues and within that operational management contract, and Article 16(1)(b) has the Advisory Board advise the Minister on the investment instructions he gives. Ministerial Diploma No. 4/2019 of 1 March 2019 shows this version of the law still in force and names the bank as the Fund's Operational Manager. It covers the Petroleum Fund only: the law says nothing about who sets interest rates. Its quarterly report for 30 June 2025 sets out six managers and their mandates: the Bank for International Settlements on a hedged global developed-market sovereign bond mandate, State Street Global Advisors on an equity factor mandate and an international equity passive mandate, Schroders on an equity factor mandate, BlackRock on an international equity passive mandate, and Barings LLC and Franklin Templeton each on a 1-10 years US TIPS mandate. The report says the outside managers' investments stayed within their mandates during the quarter. One case is recorded. In its report and opinion on the 2019 General State Account, the country's Court of Accounts found that 6.6 million US dollars of European Union direct budget support, held in three bank accounts at the central bank, was not booked as state revenue, so 2019 state revenue was understated by that amount, and that the 2.3 million US dollars spent from those accounts was spent outside the state budget and the General State Account. The same report recorded a closing accounting balance of 4.4 million US dollars against a cash balance at the central bank of 5.2 million. One career move is recorded, every employer in it a public or multilateral body: Helder Lopes, governor from 2023 to 2029, had been Minister of Finance and Vice Minister of Finance, an adviser to the President and to the Ministry of Finance, and earlier a senior economist on the Asian Development Bank's private sector development initiative in Timor-Leste. Timor-Leste scores 37 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 71 percent of the 194 places with a figure. Its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, 57, with a Corruption Perceptions Index score of 44 of 100 for 2025. The independence the law gives the bank is comparatively strong, 0.777 of 1 and rank 50 of 191. Ernst & Young Audit & Associados - SROC, S.A. audited the 2023 accounts. The bank publishes a name, a title and a photograph for each of its seven board members and not one line of career, so what is known about its deputy governor Sara Lobo Brites comes from outside it: an encyclopaedia entry giving two posts and no dates beyond the five-year length of her central bank term, Vice-Governor of the bank and afterwards Deputy Minister of Finance in the VIII Constitutional Government. Both are public posts, so the move is listed here and not counted, and it rests on an encyclopaedia entry rather than a primary document.
p:GUY: The Bank of Guyana issues the Guyanese dollar, held at what is in practice a fixed rate to the US dollar as of December 2025. It scores 32 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 56, with the country scoring 40 of 100 on the Corruption Perceptions Index. Part of the bank's work is handed to ministers by the law itself, and that is a standing arrangement rather than a passing dispute: under section 29 of the Bank of Guyana Act, Chapter 85:02 (Act No. 19 of 1998, enacted 31 December 1998), the Minister, in consultation with the Bank, specifies the policies, principles and criteria of Guyana's exchange rate system, and the Bank is responsible only for the day-to-day administration of that system; section 14(2) lets the President terminate the appointment of the Governor, and the Minister terminate the appointment of any other Director, on stated grounds; section 3(1) describes the Bank as an autonomous institution governed by the Act. Independence written into its law scores 0.609 of 1, ranking 93 of 191, and no government pressure was reported in 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is recorded, and it ended in an official finding. The Auditor General, Deodat Sharma, reported in his 2013 report that eight accounts at the Bank of Guyana holding about 1.8 billion Guyana dollars had sat unused for more than five years, untouched since 2009: 474 million for UK Programme Aid-GEA, 371 million for the Infrastructural Development Fund, 280 million for the Agriculture Rehabilitation Project, 213 million for SIMAP Phase II, 172 million for the Financial Sector Reform Programme, 127 million for Accountant General-GEC Wartsila, 77 million for an Agriculture Loan and 55 million for UK Programme Aid-Rice. His Audit Office had reviewed eleven special accounts at the bank with balances of about 4.3 billion dollars in total; he said the money belonged in the Consolidated Fund and recommended the Ministry of Finance transfer it there as soon as possible, noting that on that basis the government's overall bank position would show a positive balance of 56 billion dollars. Two career moves are on record. The first is entirely within the public sector, so it is listed but not counted: governor Gobind Ganga directed the bank's research department from 1995 to November 2003, left to be an alternate executive director at the World Bank in Washington, returned as deputy governor in June 2005 and became governor on 2 December 2014, his earlier posts being academic, with no private employer anywhere in the career the bank publishes. The second runs the other way and into private banking: Demerara Bank Limited, which its own audited accounts describe as incorporated on 20 January 1992 as a private limited liability company, publishes a profile of its director Rajendra Rampersaud saying he has over two decades of central banking experience and served as a Director at the Bank of Guyana until 2018. Crane Currency is listed as having supplied banknotes, banknote paper and anti-counterfeiting features, though that comes from a client list in another body's announcement rather than a contract notice. The Auditor General audits the accounts.
p:AND: Andorra has no central bank; the Andorran Financial Authority oversees its finances, and the country uses the euro. Under its monetary agreement with the EU, Andorra may issue its own euro coins from July 2013. The IMF's 2023 classification lists Andorra and San Marino as having no separate legal tender, with the euro as anchor. Little else is scored: no overall exposure score exists, and independence and public transparency are not rated. Money-laundering risk is 3.48 of 10 (rank 171 of 177, where 1 is riskiest), and financial secrecy is 54.4 of 100. No documented case was found. The European Central Bank ran a temporary repo line, a lending arrangement, with Andorra from 15 December 2022 to 15 January 2024; it has expired.
p:UZB: The Central Bank of Uzbekistan, created in 1991, issues the country's money, held at a de facto crawling peg to the US dollar as of December 2025, meaning the rate is moved in small steps. It scores 25 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; outside influence scores 8 and corruption and secrecy around the bank 60. Written independence from government scores 0.862 of 1 on one index and 0.604 on another, and government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is on record, and the bank found it itself. In its own 2025 anti-corruption report the bank states that disciplinary measures were applied to 10 of its employees over shortcomings found in its 2025 monitoring, that three procurement counterparties were found to be affiliated with each other and their procurement processes were cancelled, and that two existing conflicts of interest among 2,152 declaring managers were resolved. The head of state has also moved against a chairman: on 11 December 2024 presidential press secretary Sherzod Asadov announced that President Shavkat Mirziyoyev had submitted a proposal to the Senate of the Oliy Majlis for Mamarizo Nurmuratov to leave his post as chairman of the bank, which he had held since June 2017, and the announcement gave no reason; under Uzbek law the Senate acts on the president's nomination, so the initiative came from the head of state. The man who took over that day has moved between the bank and the finance ministry: Timur Ishmetov started at the bank as an economist in 2000, worked through its foreign exchange and reserves departments, was First Deputy Chairman of the State Committee for Investments in April 2017, was the bank's First Deputy Chairman from June 2017 to 2019, left to be First Deputy Minister of Finance in May 2019, was Minister of Finance from February 2020 until the end of 2022, was First Deputy Adviser to the President on economic development, investment and foreign trade policy from December 2022, and became chairman of the bank with effect from 11 December 2024. Gold holdings are 431.7 tonnes, 87.5 per cent of reserves. A swap line, an agreement to borrow another central bank's currency, with China was set at 0.7 billion renminbi in April 2011; whether it is in force is not known. The notes are made by Davlat Belgisi, a state production association that the bank lists among its own subordinate organisations, taking in the Tashkent Printing Factory, the Tashkent Paper Factory and the Tashkent Mint.
p:SWZ: The Central Bank of Eswatini, set up in 1974, issues the country's currency, fixed at par to the South African rand under the Common Monetary Area. One licensing fight runs through two findings. In 2017 the bank's evaluations team recommended rejecting Farmers Bank's application for a commercial banking licence, warning it would tarnish the integrity of the bank's licensing policy, and it was turned down late that year. Governor Majozi Sithole said a royal command required him to attend a meeting about the venture on 14 July 2017, and in May 2018 finance minister Martin Dlamini told the bank that King Mswati III had ordered an investigation into its reluctance to license it. A conditional licence followed in September 2018 after a royal command. The bank revoked it on 5 October 2020 because the source of the seed capital was unexplained; an appeal chaired by commerce minister Manqoba Khumalo ruled in December 2020 that the licence should stand, and the bank reinstated it in January 2021 while objecting to procedural improprieties. A 2022 forensic report by Kroll, commissioned by the bank, said parties outside the bank had likely intervened and instructed it to proceed, and that 89 million rand of seed capital had gone from 2019 into silver bullion the bank could not verify existed. That finance minister had run the bank himself: Martin Dlamini was its Governor from July 1997 to November 2013, having worked there for 30 years in all, and was Minister of Finance from November 2013 to November 2018, which is the one career move documented here and names no commercial employer. In October 2023 the bank moved its portfolio of special drawing rights to Crown Agents Investment Management, which manages it and trains bank staff; Giesecke+Devrient of Germany printed the new 20 lilangeni note. Eswatini scores 36 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its written independence is 0.373 of 1 on the Cukierman method, where 1 means the bank holds the power. The bank's accounts are audited by SNG Grant Thornton Chartered Accountants (Eswatini) of Mbabane, which signed its report on the statements for the year ended 31 March 2026 on 26 August 2026. The state's own side of that licensing fight is documented too. Governor Majozi Sithole said a royal command required him to attend a meeting about the venture on 14 July 2017, and in May 2018 finance minister Martin Dlamini told the bank that King Mswati III had ordered an investigation into its reluctance to license Farmers Bank. A conditional licence followed in September 2018 after a royal command, and when the bank revoked it the appeal that overrode the revocation was chaired by a minister. What the officials were accused of stays with the two cases above; what the state did was to order an investigation into the bank's own supervisory decision and then override it.
p:HTI: The Bank of the Republic of Haiti, created in 1979, issues the gourde, held at a de facto peg to the US dollar as of December 2025; the dollar is also listed as a currency there. One case is recorded. In April 2004 justice minister Bernard Gousse barred Venel Joseph, a former governor of the bank, from leaving the country, naming him among 37 former officials to be kept available for investigations into crimes alleged against the government of ousted president Jean-Bertrand Aristide, and calling the travel ban an insurance policy. What conduct at the bank, if any, was being looked into is not reported, and no charge and no finding followed. The bank has also been called before parliament: the Senate's Economy and Finance commission summoned governor Charles Castel, with Ronald Baudin, Minister of Economy and Finance, to appear on Wednesday 1 June 2011 and answer questions about new taxes of 1.50 US dollars per money transfer and 5 cents a minute on incoming international calls. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. On the printing of the money, a Haitian news outlet reports that the bank ordered a reprint of 30 million 10-gourde notes from Oberthur Fiduciaire S.A.S. for 845,000 euros; that comes from the outlet rather than from any announcement by the bank, so it is reported rather than confirmed. KPMG S.A. and the firm Merove-Pierre - Cabinet d'Experts-Comptables audit the accounts jointly, their report covering the year ended 30 September 2021. Haiti's exposure score is 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, more exposed than 70 per cent of 194 places. Corruption and secrecy around the bank scores 82, with a Corruption Perceptions Index score of 16 of 100 and money-laundering risk of 8.12 of 10, rank 2 of 177 where 1 is riskiest. A World Bank speaker profile sets out the career of governor Charles Castel. It says he joined the bank as an advisor to the Governor in 1995, held the posts of General Counsel, Director of Banking Supervision and General Director, and was appointed Governor in 2007. Outside the bank it names only public employers: Executive Director of the Haitian Privatization Commission, where it says he led the government's first successful privatizations, of the Moulins d'Haiti flour mill and the Cimenterie Nationale cement works, a consultancy for the United Nations Development Program, and teaching at the State University of Haiti. It gives no dates for those posts and names no bank, insurer, asset manager or broker, so nothing in it is counted on the revolving-door layer.
p:CRI: The Central Bank of Costa Rica issues the country's money and, as of December 2025, keeps it within a moving band of plus or minus 2 percent against the US dollar. It scores 24 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence; outside influence alone scores 5, and the weak side is corruption and secrecy around the bank, at 52. Its notes are printed abroad: an international tender was opened in the second half of 2008 among the makers on the bank's supplier register for six new denominations, and Oberthur won it, with the 20,000-colon note of 2010 recorded as printed by Oberthur Technologies on cotton fibre paper at its plant in Rennes. That rests on Spanish Wikipedia and a numismatic blog rather than on a document from the bank. The independence written into its law is high, 0.826 of 1 on one index. Government pressure was reported in 1 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, and that instance was a threat to change the law. A later episode is on record: in January 2024 three serving cabinet ministers, for foreign trade, agriculture and tourism, each wrote to the bank's president demanding a revision of exchange-rate policy, and the President backed the approach at a press conference. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened. Semanario Universidad reports that the bank hired BlackRock in 2017 as a co-administrator of its international reserves and that BlackRock holds 5.5 percent of them, about 352 million US dollars, the bank telling the paper that hiring outside portfolio managers is usual practice in central banking. The Contraloria General de la Republica audits the accounts under the 1995 central bank law, which is in force. Rodrigo Cubero became president of the bank in 2018; La Republica reported on 6 August 2018, as he took over, that he had worked several years at the International Monetary Fund, most recently as deputy division chief at the IMF's Institute for Capacity Development, and that he had not taken part in the IMF reports that had advised the bank.
p:JOR: The Central Bank of Jordan issues the Jordanian dinar and holds it at a fixed rate against the US dollar, an arrangement called a peg. One case is documented, and it grew out of the collapse of a bank the central bank supervised. Governor Mohammed Said Nabulsi issued a decree requiring banks to hold 30 per cent of their foreign holdings as reserves at the central bank; Petra Bank was the only Jordanian bank unable to comply, which triggered an investigation and accusations of embezzlement and false accounting. Petra Bank collapsed on 2 August 1989 and was placed under government supervision with an audit of its books, the central bank announced a 350 million dollar bail-out of depositors, and Jordan's losses came to about 200 million dollars. A Jordanian military tribunal convicted Chalabi in absentia on 31 charges, including embezzlement, theft, misuse of depositor funds and currency speculation, and sentenced him to 22 years; he had fled the country about two weeks after the collapse, never served the sentence, and maintained that the prosecution was a politically motivated effort to discredit him. No government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters surveyed between 2010 and 2018. Parliament pushed once: in September 2003 members signed a petition urging Prime Minister Ali Abulragheb to remove governor Umayya Touqan, after Touqan froze all the bank accounts of six leaders of Hamas; whether the government acted on it is not known. One leader later crossed into private banking. Mohammed Said Mohammed Shahin, a former Governor and Chairman of the bank and earlier a deputy governor, became chairman of the Islamic International Arab Bank, a commercial bank, on 31 March 2017. Jordan scores 31 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weakest side corruption and secrecy around the bank.
p:SLB: The Solomon Islands dollar is issued by the Central Bank of Solomon Islands, created in 1976 and holding the currency at a crawling peg to the US dollar as of December 2025, meaning the rate is moved in small steps announced in advance. The Central Bank of Solomon Islands Act 2012 sets out how the government may steer it. Section 37 lets the Minister for Finance, with Cabinet's approval, give the bank written directions where he thinks the coordination of monetary and fiscal policies or the public interest requires it, and those directions must be published in the Gazette and laid before Parliament. Section 41(1) has the Governor appointed by the Governor-General on Cabinet's recommendation, and section 41(3) the other directors by the Minister after consulting the Governor. Section 44 protects them in office: they may be removed before their term ends only for permanent incapacity or serious misconduct, and the Governor only on a tribunal's recommendation. A 2023 amendment left all three sections untouched. One case is recorded: a former employee, Bobongi, was convicted on 39 counts of money laundering and two counts of larceny and embezzlement for stealing more than 1.7 million dollars in old banknotes in 2007 to 2009, while the bank was destroying them, and was sentenced to nine years. Note Printing Australia's customer list says it has produced and supplied polymer banknotes to the bank, with no date or value given. Crown Agents Investment Management manages about 95 percent of the bank's allocation of special drawing rights, a reserve asset issued by the International Monetary Fund, and the Auditor General's Office audits the accounts. The country scores 33 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and the bank is near the bottom of 112 places for what it tells the public, at 3 of 15. The bank's own board page gives its Deputy Governor, Raynold Moveni, a dated banking career before it: Research and Marketing Officer in the Research Department of the Development Bank of Solomon Islands in Honiara from January to December 1997, then Senior Research and Development Officer in the same department to October 1998, before he joined the central bank as a Senior Analyst in February 1999 and became Deputy Governor in 2020. The page says nothing about who owns the Development Bank of Solomon Islands, which is the country's national development bank, so the move is listed here and not counted on the revolving-door layer.
p:ABW: The Central Bank of Aruba, created in 1986, issues the Aruban florin and holds it at a peg to the US dollar as of December 2025. Its Central Bank Ordinance of 1991, amended through 2014, keeps the bank under the Governor of Aruba and the Minister of Finance. Section 18 has the Governor appoint the president and executive directors from a shortlist of three put up by the Supervisory Board, and suspend or dismiss them by state decree; section 19(3) allows general guidelines for their duties to be set by decree; section 23 gives him the appointment and dismissal of the supervisory directors; and section 27(1) has the Government Commissioner supervise the bank under the Minister's instructions. This is a standing arrangement with no end date. One case is recorded: the General Audit Chamber, reviewing the country's 2001-2004 accounts, found contributions paid into an earmarked account at the bank for the Fondo Desaroyo Aruba foundation were not accounted for completely, correctly and on time, with 16,898,503 florins paid in by the Netherlands left off the balance sheet out of a 19.3 million florin balance at the end of 2000. The president who held the post until the end of 2025 spent her working life in public bodies: Jeanette R. (Jane) Semeleer began as a management adviser at Aruba's Department of Economic Affairs, later worked at the Department of External Relations, joined the bank in 1990, was appointed Executive Director in 2000 and President in 2008, and retired on 1 December 2025; no private employer is named. Her successor arrives from commercial banking: Thomas Domhoff takes up the presidency on 1 July 2026, and his career, as reported on 1 April 2026, covers work on major projects at ING, ABN AMRO, Rabobank and Capgemini, a directorship at Banco Sicredi, a chief executive post at Castrolanda Agroindustrial and the restructuring of Girobank's legacy portfolio through GI-RO Settlement Holding; ING's own largest-investors page states that ING Group is a publicly-listed company and names BlackRock, which disclosed 7.3 per cent of its issued share capital, and Amundi Asset Management among holders above 3 per cent, which is how that employer's private ownership is established. Crane Currency is listed as having supplied new banknotes in 2019, on a client list in another organisation's announcement rather than a contract notice, so that is reported rather than confirmed by the bank. BNP Paribas Asset Management runs a fixed income mandate in US dollars and gives advice, and Ernst & Young audits the accounts. Aruba scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:MAC: Macao's money, the pataca, is issued by the Monetary Authority of Macao, and in December 2025 it was held at a fixed rate against the United States dollar. Its law leaves it little independence from government: 0.271 of 1 on one index, the lowest of 155 places, with its power to refuse lending to the government scored at zero, and the head of the executive appoints its board. That arrangement still stands. On 26 June 2025 Chief Executive Sam Hou Fai appointed Vong Sin Man, a worker of the Statistics and Census Service, to the board of directors for 1 July to 31 December 2025, under the Authority's statute approved by Decree-Law 14/96/M of 11 March 1996, with the pay borne by the Authority. One case is documented, and it is an administrative finding by a foreign regulator rather than a criminal conviction: on 15 September 2005 the US Treasury named Banco Delta Asia, a bank licensed and supervised in Macao, a primary money laundering concern under Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, and FinCEN proposed a rule cutting it off from US correspondent accounts. Treasury said the bank had served North Korean government agencies and front companies for more than 20 years, handled the bulk of North Korea's precious metal sales and serviced an account for a known international drug trafficker, and alleged that senior bank officials accepted large cash deposits, including counterfeit US currency, and agreed to put the notes into circulation; Under Secretary Stuart Levey said Macao needs significant improvement in its money laundering controls, and the bank denied wrongdoing. One career move is recorded. Antonio Jose Felix Pontes, an executive director of the Monetary Authority of Macao, Macao insurance commissioner and a member of the Authority's advisory council, is a non-executive director of Well Link Bank, Ltd., which its own history page describes as a fully licensed commercial bank registered in Macao, and a board director, executive committee member and chief compliance officer of A&P Investment Fund Management. The 1,000-pataca note of the Bank of China Macau series is printed by Hong Kong Note Printing Limited; the other note-issuing bank is BNU. It scores 34 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:OMN: The Central Bank of Oman, created in 1974, issues the Omani rial and holds it at a fixed rate, a peg, to the US dollar as of December 2025. No documented case at the bank was found, and no government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. Its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, with financial secrecy at 72.4 of 100. Independence written into its law scores 0.618 of 1 on one index and 0.46 on another, both measured on the law as it stood before 2025. That law has since been replaced. From 1 January 2025 Royal Decree 2/2025 issued a new Banking Law repealing the one of 2000, and Royal Decree 3/2025 issued the System of the Central Bank of Oman, a twenty-one article statute that serves as the bank's own governing act and is described as giving it legal, financial and administrative independence. The board is nonetheless made by decree: Royal Decree 4/2025 appointed a member of the ruling family as Chairman and made the Minister of Economy Deputy Chairman, with the Governor, the Undersecretary of the Ministry of Finance and the chairman of the Financial Services Authority among the members, and Royal Decree 5/2025 appointed the Governor with the rank of Minister. That Governor, Ahmed Al Musalmi, came to the bank in January 2025 from commercial banking: he had been chief executive of Sohar International Bank since 2018, and he replaced Tahir Al Amri. The appointment page does not state who owns Sohar International Bank; a separate shareholding breakdown for Sohar International Bank SAOG lists mixed ownership, with the state or government holding 11.6 per cent (Royal Court Affairs 11.6 per cent and Oman Investment Authority 4.53 per cent), private companies 17.3 per cent, public companies 11 per cent, institutions 15.6 per cent and the general public 44.5 per cent. It holds 6.7 tonnes of gold, 3.6 per cent of reserves. Oman's first polymer note, a 1-rial commemorative reported for introduction on 11 January 2026, was printed by Giesecke+Devrient; that is a commemorative, not the circulating series. Oman scores 29 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. The Independent Auditor's Report in the bank's Annual Report 2023 is signed by KPMG at Muscat on 7 May 2024.
p:SYC: The Central Bank of Seychelles, set up in 1983, issues the Seychelles rupee and, as of December 2025, holds it within a band of plus or minus 2 percent against the US dollar. It scores 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, below three-quarters of the places measured; its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 49, from laws that hide who owns money and money-laundering risk in its banks. One case is recorded and it rests on an anonymous accusation. Pierre Laporte left the governorship in March 2012 to become finance minister, and in September 2012 an anonymous letter accused him of drawing two salaries at once, one from the central bank and one from the government. He denied wrongdoing and said he had negotiated a severance package to offset the lower ministerial pay. No charge, inquiry or ruling is reported. Part of its foreign currency savings is handled by outsiders. The World Bank's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership runs a portfolio of its reserves, first funded with 100 million US dollars in 2019 and still held at the end of 2025, and during 2025 it also ran workshops and executive forums and paid for staff qualifications. Crown Agents Investment Management runs a bond portfolio split evenly between US dollars and Chinese renminbi, begun in 2014 with 25.0 million US dollars and topped up by another 25.0 million in April 2022. UBS Asset Management runs a money market fund holding part of the reserves, first funded with 10.0 million US dollars in 2017 and still held at the end of 2025, and has invited bank staff to its annual reserves seminar. A trade report says the bank's new family of banknotes was printed by the British printers De La Rue, giving no contract value, volume or term. The 2025 accounts were audited by the Auditor General of Seychelles, with the audit review carried out by Grant Thornton Audit and Accounting Limited in Abu Dhabi. The Seychelles Financial Services Authority's own page for its chief executive, Dr Steve Fanny, says he has sat on various boards including the Central Bank of Seychelles, and lists Nouvobanq among the others alongside Indian Ocean Tuna Ltd, the Seychelles Public Transport Corporation, Seychelles Petroleum Company and the Seychelles Investment Board. It also gives earlier posts as Principal Secretary of Trade in the Ministry of Finance and Special Advisor to the Ministry of Investment, Entrepreneurship Development and Business Innovation. The page gives no dates for any seat and makes no statement about who owns Nouvobanq, and an employer whose private ownership no source states is not counted on the revolving-door layer, so the move is listed here instead.
p:BHS: The Central Bank of The Bahamas issues the Bahamian dollar, which as of December 2025 is held at a fixed rate against the United States dollar. Its board and its exchange rate policy are in the finance minister's hands by statute: under the Central Bank of The Bahamas Act 2020, published on 27 July 2020, the Governor, both Deputy Governors and six other directors are appointed by the Governor-General on the Minister's advice after consulting the Board, and a director or Deputy Governor is removed the same way, while section 5(1)(f) makes the bank advise the Minister on exchange rate policy and implement the policy the Minister determines. The Central Bank of The Bahamas (Amendment) Act, 2023 left those provisions alone, and the arrangement has no end date. In December 2022 the Bahamian government drew down 232.3 million dollars of special drawing rights, the reserve asset the International Monetary Fund issues to member countries, held through the central bank. The opposition's finance spokesman, Kwasi Thompson, said the advance was contrary to section 21 of the Central Bank Act, which sets limits on how much the bank may lend or advance to the government; that is his assertion, and no finding establishes a breach. What is on record as fact is what followed: the government tabled a bill stating that section 21 would not apply to the transaction, deemed to have come into force on 1 December 2022, and Governor John Rolle said in early January that a memorandum of understanding between the bank and the Ministry of Finance stipulated a change to the Central Bank Act. Two career moves are recorded, neither of them an accusation. T. Baswell Donaldson, who had managed the Bahamas Monetary Authority from 1968 and chaired it from 1972, was appointed the bank's first Governor and Board Chairman on 1 June 1974 and served until May 1980; afterwards he chaired the commercial bank Commonwealth Bank, whose ownership is not stated, as well as the Securities Commission and the College of The Bahamas Council, both public bodies, and was ambassador to the United States. James H. Smith was governor from 1987 to 1997 and chairs CFAL, which describes itself as a leading independent investment management and advisory firm based in Nassau and as the investment arm of Colina Holdings Ltd, the only statement of its ownership either page gives; his public roles include senator and minister of state in the Ministry of Finance from 2002 to 2007 and the chairmanship of the government-owned Bahamas Development Bank. The Bahamas scores 29 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 fully exposed, its weak point secrecy: Bahamian law makes it hard to see who owns money there, scoring 75.4 of 100 for financial secrecy, ranked 32 of 141. No government pressure was reported in any of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. Giesecke+Devrient printed the bank's new 1-dollar note, introduced on 3 February 2025, and the auditors' report in the 2011 annual report carries two signature blocks, Deloitte & Touche and BDO, each signed as Chartered Accountants at Nassau on 16 April 2012.
p:DOM: The Dominican Republic's money is the peso, issued by the Central Bank of the Dominican Republic and held within a crawling band of 2 per cent or less against the US dollar as of December 2025. The bank scores 22 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, less exposed than 94 per cent of the 194 places with a figure. On a date the source does not give, the Directorate for the Prosecution of Administrative Corruption took former governor Jose Lois Malkun, former deputy governor Felix Calvo, former administrative director Cesar Apolinar Veloz and former legal counsel Manuel Rubio Cristoforis to court on charges including breach of trust and criminal association, over 18 missing promissory notes worth 10,663 million Dominican pesos said to have been handed fraudulently to the former banker Manuel Arturo Pellerano. Those charges are unproven. The bank neither complained nor joined the case, and a Monetary Board resolution signed by legal counsel Olga Morel said its authorities were negotiating the notes' return with Pellerano. One career move is recorded, and it is a move between public bodies rather than an accusation: George Manuel Hazoury sat on the Monetary Board, the bank's governing board, after serving as administrator of Banco de Reservas, which is the Dominican state's own bank, and he left the board in 2020 when decree 532-20 named the economists Arturo Martinez Moya and Eduardo Tejera to it for two years, alongside the departure of Manuel Garcia Arevalo, a former Minister of Industry and Commerce. The Polish Security Printing Works says it produced 55 million banknotes for the Dominican Republic in 2018, naming no counterparty and no contract value, and adds that most of its contracts are secret. KPMG audited the financial statements as at 31 December 2023.
p:URY: Uruguay's money is the peso, issued by the Central Bank of Uruguay and held within a moving band of 2 per cent or less against the US dollar as of December 2025. It scores 19 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 43, although the country scores 73 of 100 on the Corruption Perceptions Index. The constitution has given the executive a hold over the bank's board since 1967. Article 197 provides that where the Poder Ejecutivo, the executive branch, considers the management or acts of the directors of an ente autonomo, a self-governing state body, inconvenient or unlawful, it may make observations and suspend the acts observed, and that if the observations are disregarded it may order the rectifications, correctives or removals it sees fit, reporting them to the Senate. Article 198 adds that it may remove board members with the Senate's consent for ineptitude, omission or crime in office, that if the Senate does not rule within sixty days it may make the removal effective anyway, and that such removals give no right of appeal to the Tribunal de lo Contencioso Administrativo. The Banco Central del Uruguay is an ente autonomo, and article 14 of its charter designates its directors under that same chapter. One case is recorded, from 2017, and it was dismissed: prosecutor Rodrigo Morosoli, investigating the Cambio Nelson fraud at a currency exchange house, sought the formal indictment of Humberto Capote, a former president of the bank, for co-authorship of a continuing crime of misappropriation. Judge Marcelo Souto freed Capote at first instance, finding the evidence insufficient to prosecute him, and the prosecutor appealed in April 2017. No government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters surveyed from 2010 to 2018. Three people have moved between the bank and outside jobs. Guillermo Tolosa confirmed in December 2024 that he would preside over the bank once Yamandu Orsi took office as president of Uruguay; he had worked as an economist at the International Monetary Fund and as a consultant at Oxford Economics, with no years given for either, and was academic director of the research centre Ceres from 2018 to 2020. Washington Ribeiro spent 15 years on the bank's board, as director from June 2010 to March 2020, vice president from March 2020 to July 2024 and president from July 2024 to March 2025, and on 7 April 2026 he started as head of Uruguayan macro and sovereign strategy at the Uruguayan brokerage Latin Securities; no finding or complaint is attached to the move. Diego Labat, president of the bank from 2020 to 2024, was named general manager of the Bolsa Electronica de Valores by its board on 20 August 2025, replacing Eduardo Barbieri after 25 years in the post; the exchange was founded in January 1993 by 26 financial institutions operating in Uruguay, both public and private, so its ownership is mixed rather than plainly private. The accounts are audited by the Tribunal de Cuentas under the 1995 charter law. The bank is also named among the central bank clients of a fixed-income fund built around environmental and social standards, developed jointly by Amundi and the Latin American Reserve Fund; it invests in that fund rather than handing them its reserves to manage. Its notes are printed abroad by Oberthur Fiduciaire, which printed the revised 2,000-peso note dated 2015 that the bank introduced on 27 April 2016, carrying a holographic windowed security thread and a map of Uruguay.
p:TWN: The Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan) issues the New Taiwan dollar, and its notes are made by the Central Engraving and Printing Plant; a bank press release on the NT$200 note says that note was printed by China Engraving & Printing Works. Independence written into its law is low: 0.454 of 1 on one index and 0.194 on another, with the rules on lending to the government scored 0 and 0.03. No government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018, and no documented case at the bank was found. Where the bank sits is itself on record: under the revised Central Bank of China Act promulgated on 8 November 1979 it is a state bank and an agency under the Executive Yuan, the cabinet, rather than a body standing outside the executive branch, and its own official history records that it has been there since that reorganisation. The Act leaves rate and policy decisions with the bank's board, so what this describes is the institution's place in the machinery of government rather than a transfer of the policy power, and it has no end date. One overlap is recorded rather than a move: 陳思寬 (Chen Szu-kuan) sits on the bank's 21st Board of Directors for a term running from 27 January 2025 to 26 January 2030 while, by the bank's own list of directors, serving as chairman of SinoPac Financial Holdings Company Limited and of SinoPac Securities Investment Trust Company Limited; that list says nothing about who owns them. The bank holds 423.9 tonnes of gold. Taiwan scores 24 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weak point being corruption and secrecy around it.
p:MHL: The Marshall Islands has no central bank and uses the US dollar. The IMF's 2023 classification lists it among places with no separate legal tender, with the dollar as anchor. Too little is recorded to give an overall exposure score, and independence and transparency are not rated. Money-laundering risk is 4.89 of 10 (rank 109 of 177, where 1 is riskiest), and financial secrecy is 65.3 of 100. No documented case was found. The US dollar is used in 16 places and makes up 89.08% of world currency trading.
p:CUB: The Central Bank of Cuba issues the Cuban peso. Its exposure score is 35 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; that is more exposed than 66 per cent of 194 places. Corruption and secrecy around it scores 57, with a Corruption Perceptions Index score of 40 of 100. Written independence from government is low: 0.354 of 1 on one index, ranking 153 of 155, and 0.262 on another, ranking 180 of 191. On public transparency it scores 1.5 of 15. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, but the arrangement that matters here is in the law. Decree-Law 361 of 2018, issued by the Council of State and published in the Gaceta Oficial on 12 October 2018 in place of Decree-Law 172 of 1997, requires the bank to design monetary policy in step with the government's fiscal and macroeconomic aims, under an annual policy agreement signed by ministers. It has no end date. Its notes are printed by Goznak: the 200-peso note dated 2024 and the 50-peso note dated 2025 are recorded as carrying that printer, identified from the notes themselves rather than announced by the bank, so it is reported rather than confirmed. One career move is recorded. Joaquin Alonso Vazquez was announced on 16 February 2023 as Minister President of the bank, replacing Martha Sabina Wilson Gonzalez; he came from the presidency of CADECA S.A., the state currency-exchange entity, and before that held a series of posts at the state Banco Popular de Ahorro, as provincial deputy director in Havana, director of savings, director of credits and vice president for seven years to 2017, and he had been vice president of CUBALSE for economic and financial activity. One case is documented, and it is still under investigation: in late September 2026 an investigation in Santiago de Cuba concerned workers at two state banks, Banco Popular de Ahorro and BANDEC, both supervised by the Banco Central de Cuba, with reports saying the workers handed out cash in exchange for electronic transfers, charging commissions of between 30 and 50 per cent, acting together with self-employed people. Cash, banknote counting machines, magnetic cards and documents were reported seized, and no amounts, names or number of detainees were made public. The bank's Minister President, Juana Lilia Delgado Portal, issued an official note rejecting the conduct, ordering that any complaint be investigated without delay, and calling for administrative, labour and criminal responsibility to be established, internal controls strengthened and whistleblowers protected. No charges or outcomes had been announced.
p:DJI: The Central Bank of Djibouti, created in 1977, runs what is called a currency board: the Djibouti franc is held at a fixed rate of 1 US dollar to 177.721 francs and is backed entirely by US dollars, so the bank cannot issue francs without dollars behind them. The franc itself was created in March 1949, outside the franc zone. The executive fills the bank's board: under the statutes set by law no. 118/AN/11/6eme L of 22 January 2011, it is the Governor and six administrators appointed by decree, so every seat but the Governor's is a government appointment. The bank's own 2024 annual report sets out that composition, calls the board its supreme organ and cites the 2011 law, so the arrangement still stands. The independence written into its law scores 0.698 of 1, where 1 means the bank holds the power rather than the government, and four reforms since 1970 have all raised that score. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened; Reporters Without Borders rates the situation for journalists here as very serious in its 2026 index, so the court reports a case would be found in may not exist. It scores 60 of 100, the second highest of the 194 places with a figure, with money-laundering risk in its banks rated 6.93 of 10, the thirteenth riskiest of 177. Deloitte Cote d'Ivoire audited the 2021 accounts.
p:TUV: Tuvalu has no central bank and uses the Australian dollar. Its exposure score is 53 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; that is more exposed than 98% of 194 places, and its weakest side is outside influence (66) because its money is issued from abroad. Written independence from government scores 0.011 of 1, the lowest of 191. No documented case was found. The Australian dollar is used in 5 places and makes up 6.12% of world currency trading.
p:MCO: Monaco has no central bank and uses the euro. Under its monetary agreement with the EU, it may issue euro coins up to 1/500th of the quantity minted in France each year. Too little is recorded to give an overall exposure score, and independence and transparency are not rated. Financial secrecy is 72.7 of 100, and the World Bank control of corruption score is 72 of 100. No documented case was found. The euro is used in 28 places and makes up 28.54% of world currency trading.
p:FJI: The Reserve Bank of Fiji, created in 1973, issues the Fijian dollar and, as of December 2025, holds it at a pre-announced rate measured against the United States and Australian dollars. One removal is recorded. In April 2009 government officials removed governor Savenaca Narube and replaced him with deputy governor Sada Reddy, hours before the Fiji dollar was devalued by 20 percent; the new government had come to power the previous week and was led by the army. No official reason was given, and the report notes that Narube had recently warned about the economy and forecast a 0.3 percent contraction for 2009. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened. One career move is recorded: Inia Naiyaga spent 40 years as a central banker, 25 of them on the bank's executive management team, and retired as deputy governor in May 2014; he had advised the board of SUN Insurance since 2016, became an independent director in April 2018, and was appointed managing director from 6 June after chief executive Lolesh K. Sharma resigned. In 2006 the bank agreed with De La Rue International Limited of the United Kingdom to print a new design series, including a 100-dollar note for the first time, and KPMG audits the accounts. Fiji scores 33 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is corruption and secrecy, 56 of 100, mainly because the country's laws hide who owns money, at 77.4 of 100 on a financial secrecy measure. The independence the law gives the bank is thin, 0.435 of 1 and rank 154 of 191.
p:LIE: Liechtenstein has no central bank and uses the Swiss franc. A 1980 Currency Treaty with Switzerland declares the franc its official tender, and the Swiss National Bank serves as its national bank; certain Liechtenstein banks and investment undertakings report to the Swiss bank for monetary policy purposes. Too little is recorded to give an overall exposure score. Financial secrecy is 74.1 of 100 (rank 58 of 141) and money-laundering risk is 4.11 of 10. No documented case was found. The Swiss franc is used in 2 places and makes up 6.32% of world currency trading.
p:FSM: Micronesia has no central bank and uses the US dollar. The IMF's 2023 classification lists it among places with no separate legal tender, with the dollar as anchor. Little is recorded: no overall exposure score exists, and independence and transparency are not rated. The World Bank control of corruption score is 62 of 100. No documented case was found. The US dollar is used in 16 places and makes up 89.08% of world currency trading.
p:PLW: Palau has no central bank and uses the US dollar. The IMF's 2023 classification lists it among places with no separate legal tender, with the dollar as anchor. Little is recorded: no overall exposure score exists, and independence and transparency are not rated. The World Bank control of corruption score is 58 of 100. No documented case was found. The US dollar is used in 16 places and makes up 89.08% of world currency trading.
p:NRU: Nauru has no central bank of its own and uses the Australian dollar. The International Monetary Fund's 2023 classification lists Nauru, Kiribati and Tuvalu as having no separate legal tender, though its table does not name the currency. Five places use the Australian dollar. It accounts for 6.12% of world currency trading, 2.25% of foreign reserves and 1.64% of international payments sent through the Swift messaging network. Nauru is not given an overall score because there is too little data. Its control of corruption scores 57 of 100, higher meaning better.
p:WSM: The Central Bank of Samoa issues the Samoan currency, which as of December 2025 is kept within a crawling band of 2 per cent or less measured against the US and Australian dollars. Samoa scores 35 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 63 per cent of the 194 places with a figure. Its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around the bank, mainly because the country's laws hide who owns money and because of money-laundering risk in its banks. One finding is on record: a performance audit of government debt servicing carried out by the Samoa Audit Office in 2014 compared the due dates of government debt repayments with the dates the Central Bank of Samoa actually made them and found instances where repayments had been delayed. The same audit recorded that there was no formalised arrangement between the Ministry of Finance and the central bank, and its recommendations went to the Ministry of Finance, including that the two bodies formalise their responsibilities; no wrongdoing by any person is alleged in it. In April 2026 the government pressed ahead with changes to the bank's own law that would widen the Finance Minister's role and move some of the bank's rules into regulations. In a letter to the Attorney-General's office the bank said the changes had come as a surprise and warned they could weaken its independence, increase political influence and create legal uncertainty. The International Monetary Fund wrote to Finance Minister Mulipola Anarosa Ale Molio'o on 9 April 2026 warning that the reforms could weaken the bank's autonomy, and Prime Minister Laaulialemalietoa Leuatea Polataivao Schmidt rejected the warnings as outside interference. On 19 August 2026 parliament debated the second reading of the Central Bank of Samoa Amendment Bill 2026, which would stop the Governor chairing the bank's board, replacing her with an independent non-executive director, and would require the bank's executive committee to give the Minister of Finance quarterly reports on policy and to send the Minister the draft annual budget for comment within 14 working days. The Prime Minister said the two roles should be separated and that the central bank belongs to the government, and opposition leader Tuilaepa Sailele Malielegaoi said the government had not accepted the IMF's advice; the bill was not yet law when that was reported. The bank was created in 1984, and its law has been changed three times since 1970, each change giving it more independence. Note Printing Australia's customer list says it has produced and supplied polymer banknotes to the bank, and BDO Chartered Accountants audited the financial statements for the year ended 30 June 2025. Newsline Samoa reported on 31 July 2025 that the Pacific Catastrophe Risk Insurance Company had engaged a former Assistant Governor of the bank, Benjamin Pereira, to lead Samoa's contingency planning work. The article gives no dates for either post and says nothing about who owns the company. The World Bank's own programme paper says the facility was established in the Cook Islands as a foundation whose board of directors owns a group captive insurer, with a Council of Members made up of secretaries of finance from the participating Pacific Island countries, so the employer is publicly owned and the move is listed here rather than counted.
p:MDG: The Central Bank of Madagascar issues the country's money. Madagascar scores 32 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 fully exposed, which is less exposed than half of the 194 places with a figure. Its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 71, driven by corruption in the country and money-laundering risk in its banks, scored 6.77 of 10 with 1 the riskiest; the Corruption Perceptions Index puts the country at 25 of 100. Written independence from government scores 0.607 of 1; the bank was set up in 1973, and of four reforms since 1970, three raised independence and one lowered it. In February 2012 the transitional government dismissed governor Frederic Rasamoely. Bank employees staged a sit-in, saying the removal went against the bank's independence, and said their strike would continue while they challenged the new governor's appointment. The present governor, Aivo Handriatiana Andrianarivelo, was appointed by the Council of Ministers on 4 January 2023, coming from the International Monetary Fund, where he had been an Executive Director and board member representing 23 African countries; he had earlier been finance director at Catholic Relief Services, managing director of the state share-management body Fonds de Portage et de Privatisation and a technical adviser in the economy and finance ministry. His profile says only that he gained earlier experience at bank level, without naming the bank or giving dates, so no private financial employer is established. One case is on record, from 2026, and it is an allegation that remains unproven. During a period of popular demonstrations it was alleged that an unnamed senior official had pressured the bank to release funds. On 21 January 2026, at Antaninarenina, Andrianarivelo denied the allegation outright, saying the bank's only clients are the commercial banks, the public Treasury and international partner organisations working on major projects, that no individual can hold an account at the bank, himself included, and that requests for disbursement from the president, prime minister or ministers are not acted on because only the public Treasury can authorise a disbursement. No amount, no date for the alleged movement of funds and no name were given. He made the remarks while signing two agreements with the security forces on guarding bank sites and escorting cash between Toamasina, Antananarivo and the bank's eleven branches. The 20,000-ariary note is produced on Giesecke+Devrient's Louisenthal Hybrid substrate from Papierfabrik Louisenthal, which makes the material rather than printing the note; the printer is not named.
p:KIR: Kiribati has no central bank of its own and uses the Australian dollar. The International Monetary Fund's 2023 classification lists Kiribati, Nauru and Tuvalu as having no separate legal tender, though its table does not name the currency. Five places use the Australian dollar. It accounts for 6.12% of world currency trading, 2.25% of foreign reserves and 1.64% of international payments sent through the Swift messaging network. Kiribati is not given an overall score because there is too little data. Its control of corruption scores 54 of 100, higher meaning better.
p:BMU: Bermuda's money is the Bermudian dollar, issued by the Bermuda Monetary Authority, which is the central bank; as of December 2025 the dollar sat in a de facto peg to the US dollar, held at a fixed rate in practice. The Bermuda Monetary Authority Act 1969 places it under the finance minister. Section 21(2) lets the Minister give it written general directions that appear to him necessary in the public interest, which it shall act in accordance with; section 4(1)(d) has him appoint eleven members of the Board and section 4E(1) the Chairman, and section 4E(6) lets him end the Chairman's appointment if satisfied he is unable or unfit to discharge his functions. Independence written into law is almost absent, 0.06 of 1 and second from last of 191 places, with no reform since 1970. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened. One career move is recorded: Cheryl-Ann Lister, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer from 1999 through 2006, was appointed an independent director and audit committee member of AXIS Capital Holdings Limited, a Bermuda-based insurance and reinsurance group, in an announcement of 23 September 2008. The Office of the Auditor-General audits the accounts. The Authority announced on 30 October 2024 that its new 2 and 5 dollar notes, printed by De La Rue on polymer, would enter circulation that autumn, Bermuda's first polymer notes. Bermuda scores 36 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, with financial secrecy at 71.3 of 100.
p:ERI: The Bank of Eritrea issues the currency (ERN). Eritrea scores 56 of 100 on exposure (0 means shielded from outside influence, 100 means fully exposed), rank 2 of 194, more exposed than 99% of the 194 places with a figure. Outside influence scores 26 and corruption and secrecy around the bank 86, the weakest side, mainly from corruption in the country. The Corruption Perceptions Index is 13 of 100 (clean rank 177 of 182) and World Bank control of corruption is 16 of 100. No documented case at the central bank was found, which does not prove none happened. The law that governs the bank puts its appointments in one person's hands. Proclamation 93/1997 of 21 January 1997 keeps in being the bank created by Proclamation 32/1993 and gives the President the appointment of the Governor for a five-year term, with the legislature's approval, the appointment of the Deputy Governor, the Governor's pay on the Board's recommendation, the appointment of every nominated Board member, and approval of the fee a Board member is paid for each meeting attended; a director who resigns writes to the President and leaves only once the President accepts. The Board also seats a representative of the Ministry of Finance and the Auditor General. The same law says in Article 6 that the bank is not subject to instructions from the Government in performing its functions, determining its budget or setting its procedures, and that the Governor may be relieved only for just cause after the legislature is consulted, so what the record carries is control of the posts rather than a power to direct the bank's decisions. Who prints the nakfa is recorded only weakly: an encyclopaedia entry says the current series is printed by the German firm Giesecke+Devrient, and no document from the Bank of Eritrea confirming it was found, so that rests on the encyclopaedia alone. The country has had 1 systemic banking crisis since 1970. On the Cukierman method for independence written into law, the bank scores 0.423 of 1 (rank 160 of 191, 2023). It was created in 1993 and has had 2 reforms since 1970, both raising independence. In December 2025 the exchange rate was a dual market with parallel-market data missing, and no anchor was found. Gold holdings are 0 tonnes, 0% of reserves (117 of 122).
p:CYM: The Cayman Islands Monetary Authority acts as the central bank of the Cayman Islands, and the currency is the Cayman Islands dollar. The Monetary Authority Law (2020 Revision) puts the Authority under the Cabinet: section 33(1) lets the Cabinet give it written general directions that appear necessary in the public interest, which it shall act in accordance with; section 12(1) has the Cabinet appoint the directors, section 11(3) designate the chairperson and deputy chairperson, section 13(1) appoint the managing director, and section 14(3) terminate any director's appointment in the public interest. In June 2015 the Authority said it would commission an internal review of the involvement of local people and financial institutions in the FIFA corruption case, after the Caymanian businessman Jeffrey Webb was arrested in Switzerland on 27 May.
