The husband of its managing director Cindy Scotland, the former minister Mark Scotland, had worked for the Cayman Islands Football Association under Webb and was with Webb at the arrest; Gloria Glidden, deputy head of the banking division, is the wife of the former minister Cline Glidden, who was also in Switzerland with Webb. The chairman, George McCarthy, said Scotland would remain managing director and that there was no evidence any Cayman bank had done anything wrong. That review is still under investigation. One career move runs the other way, into the authority: its own board page says director Greg Swart was managing member and chief financial officer of Farallon Capital Management LLC, a global alternative asset management firm, from 2002 to 2019, and spent about twelve years at Goldman Sachs before that. A commemorative 70-dollar note introduced on 12 October 2023 was printed by De La Rue and is not part of the circulating series. The Auditor General, Patrick O. Smith, audits the accounts, and the authority scores 39 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:PSE: The Palestine Monetary Authority is the monetary authority of Palestine, which has no currency listed here; its exchange-rate classification reads no separate legal tender, or currency union. The head of state names its board. On 4 May 2026 President Mahmoud Abbas issued a decree reconstituting the board of directors, acting on a recommendation from the Cabinet and from the Authority's Governor. Three of the eight seats are held by virtue of law: the Governor as chairman, the Deputy Governor, and a representative of the Ministry of Finance, named as Majdi Al-Hassan; the report does not name the law that gives those seats. The Governor himself came to the Authority from finance, and that is the one career move recorded: Yahya Shunnar took over on 4 January 2025, succeeding Feras Milhem at the end of a four-year term, having held public and private sector roles in the Middle East and the United States, among them director at the Palestine Islamic Bank and vice-chairman of Tamkeen Insurance Company; the bank's own 2025 annual report names its shareholders above 5 per cent, the National Islamic Investment Company with 24.85 per cent, the Palestinian Pension Agency with 10.39 per cent, Razan Medical Center with 10.09 per cent, Mr Salah Al-Daghma with 9.59 per cent, Birzeit Pharmaceutical with 8.51 per cent, the Orphans Fund foundation with 7.01 per cent and Aswaq Investment with 5.45 per cent, which makes the shareholding mostly private with a public pension agency among the large holders. One case is recorded, and the Authority is on the receiving end of the money rather than the subject of the finding: in its 2020 annual report Palestine's Financial and Administrative Control Bureau qualified its audit of the Ministry of Finance's consolidated closing account, and one of its findings was that the ministry had not disclosed 2,130,918 dinars that it owed to the Palestine Monetary Authority. The law that created the Authority in 1997, with one reform since 1970, gives it a legal independence score of 0.435 of 1, ranking 155 of 191. Government pressure was reported in none of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018. The Authority scores 28 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption in the country.
p:JEY: Jersey has no central bank of its own and uses the pound sterling, which is issued by the Bank of England. Four places use sterling. It accounts for 10.16% of world currency trading, 4.57% of foreign reserves and 6.71% of international payments sent through the Swift messaging network. Jersey has no overall score because there is too little data. Its control of corruption scores 69 of 100, higher meaning better, and its financial secrecy score is 63.8 of 100, ranking 23 of 141, where a lower rank means more secrecy.
p:VIR: The U.S. Virgin Islands has no central bank of its own and uses the US dollar, which is issued under the Federal Reserve System. Sixteen places use the dollar. It accounts for 89.08% of world currency trading, 56.7% of foreign reserves and 50.1% of international payments sent through the Swift messaging network, first in each case. The territory has no overall score because there is too little data. Its control of corruption scores 47 of 100, higher meaning better, and its financial secrecy score is 70.2 of 100, ranking 109 of 141.

n:José Filomeno dos Santos: José Filomeno dos Santos is a person from Angola, tied to the National Bank of Angola through a court case. n:Cristina Fernández de Kirchner: Cristina Fernández de Kirchner is a former president of Argentina, based in Buenos Aires. Her government called on Martin Redrado, head of the Central Bank of the Argentine Republic, to resign on 6 January, saying he refused to back its decree calling for 6.6 billion US dollars of reserves; he refused to go, and on 7 January she issued a second decree firing him and accusing him of misconduct. On 8 January the courts suspended both decrees. Redrado resigned later that month; a page dated 30 January 2010 reports that an Argentine court held that she needed the approval of the full Congress to use the bank's reserves, and that the reserves stayed frozen while lawmakers were expected to take the matter up in March. She was later tried, with Vanoli, Pesce, former economy minister Kicillof and others, for defrauding the state through the central bank's sales of dollar futures between August and November 2015. On 13 April 2021 the Federal Court of Criminal Cassation unanimously dismissed the case against all fifteen defendants.

n:International Monetary Fund: The International Monetary Fund is an international lender based in Washington, United States, tied to 30 central banks and one other body. Most of those ties are careers rather than conduct: former Fund staff and officials have gone on to run or help run central banks in Kenya (Kamau Thugge and Patrick Njoroge), Mexico (Agustín Carstens, a former deputy managing director of the Fund, and Guillermo Ortiz), Pakistan (Reza Baqir, once chief of its Debt Policy Division), India (Raghuram Rajan, its former chief economist, and deputy governor Urjit Patel), Israel (Stanley Fischer, Jacob Frenkel and Karnit Flug), Bangladesh (Ahsan H Mansur), Mozambique, the Netherlands, Brazil, South Korea, Sweden, Malaysia, Colombia, Zambia, Trinidad and Tobago, Uruguay, Georgia, Costa Rica, Botswana, Suriname, North Macedonia, Madagascar, Curaçao, the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank and the Central Bank of West African States, and two Federal Reserve figures, Frederic S. Mishkin and Angel Ubide, also worked with the Fund. It sits on the Financial Stability Board, a body of regulators and central banks, represented by first deputy managing director Dan Katz. Four records concern money and reporting. In May 2023, an election year, Argentina's central bank passed a further 140 billion pesos to the Treasury as temporary advances, taking transfers since March to 370 billion pesos and using 99.2 per cent of the 372.8 billion peso first-half limit agreed with the Fund. The Bank of Ghana said in February 2023 that its claims on the government at December 2022 included a 37.9 billion cedi overdraft to cover auction shortfalls and maturing bonds, 7.2 billion cedis of treasury bonds bought from banks and 8.9 billion cedis of on-lent Fund money, after the government, the bank and the Fund had earlier adopted zero deficit financing. In December 2021 Malawi police arrested Kabambe and Mwanamvekha, saying they had procured and masterminded the falsification of reserve returns to make the Fund believe Malawi was meeting the conditions of its Extended Credit Facility; that allegation is unproven. In March 2008 the Fund's Executive Board found that the National Bank of Tajikistan had supplied inaccurate information on the cotton sector, international reserves, net domestic assets and credit policy, including reporting reserves of about 450 million dollars when they were roughly a third of that and concealing that reserves were pledged as collateral for loans to the cotton sector, and Tajikistan was required to repay 47.4 million dollars.
n:Securency: Securency is a banknote-material company in Melbourne, Australia, tied to six central banks. It was a 50-50 joint venture of the Reserve Bank of Australia and Innovia, and it is now called CCL Secure. It supplies the polymer plastic used for the Bank of Canada's banknotes that began circulating in 2011. In October 2011 Securency and Note Printing Australia pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to give benefits to foreign officials to win banknote business with the note-issuing authorities of Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam and Nepal. Securency paid a penalty of A$19,809,772. Its former chief financial officer received a suspended six-month sentence for false accounting in 2012, and its agent Radius Christanto a suspended two-year sentence in 2013. The officials who received the benefits are not named. In Nigeria, the anti-corruption agency EFCC questioned former governor Soludo around 2013 in a probe into whether Securency bribed Central Bank of Nigeria officials to win a contract to print polymer notes between 2006 and 2008. No outcome is given.
n:Note Printing Australia: Note Printing Australia prints banknotes at Craigieburn in Victoria, Australia, is wholly owned by the Reserve Bank of Australia and is tied to 20 central banks. In 2006/07 it produced 245 million notes for the Reserve Bank itself and filled export orders for the central banks of Chile, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, Brunei, Singapore and New Zealand; its customer list adds polymer notes produced and supplied for the central banks of Romania, Mexico, the Philippines, Bangladesh, Indonesia, Thailand, Kuwait, Samoa, the Solomon Islands, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Vanuatu and Vietnam. Three of those relationships carry a criminal case. In October 2011 Note Printing Australia and Securency, a joint venture half owned by the Reserve Bank, pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to provide benefits to foreign public officials in order to win banknote business from the note-issuing authorities of Indonesia (December 1999 to February 2001), Malaysia (October 2001 to December 2003), Nepal (February 2000 to May 2002) and Vietnam. The officials are not named. Securency paid 19,809,772 Australian dollars and Note Printing Australia 1,856,710 Australian dollars in proceeds-of-crime penalties, with fines of 480,000 and 450,000 Australian dollars; Securency's former chief financial officer received a suspended six-month sentence for false accounting in 2012 and its agent Radius Christanto a suspended two-year sentence in 2013. After the 2011 charges the Reserve Bank's board set up a special committee and commissioned an independent governance review by Cameron Ralph. Separately, a former Bank Negara Malaysia official, Mohamad Daud, was charged in July 2011 with receiving two bribes of 50,000 ringgit each in 2004 and 2005 linked to a 95 million ringgit contract for 5 ringgit polymer notes won by Note Printing Australia; the Shah Alam Sessions Court acquitted him on 6 December 2015 without calling his defence, and the Attorney-General withdrew the appeal in February 2016.

n:Anti-Corruption Commission (Bangladesh: The Anti-Corruption Commission is a government agency in Dhaka, Bangladesh, tied to Bangladesh Bank, the central bank. n:Federal Reserve Bank of New York: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York is a bank in New York, United States, that holds accounts and gold for other central banks, and it is tied to ten of them. De Nederlandsche Bank keeps 18.5 per cent of its gold there and the Bank of Finland 18 per cent, Sveriges Riksbank 13.2 tonnes or 10.5 per cent, and Danmarks Nationalbank around 0.5 per cent.
