On 21 October 2026, according to his lawyer, the bank's former governor Matolcsy was detained and taken to this office on suspicion of economic fraud causing significant financial damage and use of a forged private document. A lawyer and a businessman, among others, were also detained. These are suspicions only and nothing is proven.
n:Supreme Court of Victoria: This is a court in Melbourne, Australia, tied to four central banks: Bank Indonesia, Bank Negara Malaysia, Nepal Rastra Bank and the State Bank of Vietnam. In October 2011 Securency and Note Printing Australia (NPA), subsidiaries of the Reserve Bank of Australia, pleaded guilty there to conspiring to provide benefits to foreign public officials to win banknote business with the note-issuing authorities of these countries. The periods were 1999 to 2001 for Indonesia, 2001 to 2003 for Malaysia, 2000 to 2002 for Nepal (NPA only) and 2001 to 2004 for Vietnam (Securency only). The officials are not named.
n:Corruption Court (Jakarta): This is the anti-corruption court in Jakarta, Indonesia, tied to Bank Indonesia, the country's central bank. In October 2008 it sentenced former governor Burhanuddin Abdullah to five years for approving the use of 100 billion rupiah of bank funds in 2003 to pay legal fees for officials in a graft case and to bribe legislators over an amendment to the bank's law. The Jakarta High Court raised this to five and a half years in February 2009. In July 2014 it sentenced Budi Mulya to 10 years and a 500 million rupiah fine for corruption in a 2008 loan to Bank Century.
n:Jakarta High Court: This is an appeals court in Jakarta, Indonesia, tied to Bank Indonesia, the country's central bank. In October 2008 the Corruption Court sentenced former governor Burhanuddin Abdullah to five years for approving the use of 100 billion rupiah of bank funds in 2003 to pay legal fees for officials in a graft case and to bribe legislators over an amendment to the bank's law. In February 2009 the Jakarta High Court raised the sentence to five and a half years.
n:Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK: The KPK is Indonesia's anti-corruption agency, based in Jakarta, and is tied to Bank Indonesia, the central bank. In November 2008 it arrested four former deputy governors of the bank, including Aulia Pohan, after former governor Burhanuddin Abdullah was sentenced to five years that October. In August 2025 it named two members of parliament's House as suspects in the alleged misuse of corporate social responsibility (CSR) funds from Bank Indonesia and the Financial Services Authority. These are allegations and nothing is proven.
n:Indonesian legislators: This is the group of Indonesian lawmakers, in Jakarta, tied to Bank Indonesia, the central bank. In October 2008 the Corruption Court sentenced former governor Burhanuddin Abdullah to five years, raised to five and a half by the Jakarta High Court in February 2009. He was sentenced for approving the use of 100 billion rupiah of bank funds in 2003 to pay legal fees for officials in a graft case and to bribe legislators over an amendment to the bank's law. In November 2008 the anti-corruption commission arrested four former deputy governors.
n:Bank Century: Bank Century is a bank in Jakarta, Indonesia, tied to Bank Indonesia, the central bank. In 2008 Bank Indonesia granted it a short-term loan facility of 689.39 billion rupiah and declared it a failed bank with systemic impact. In July 2014 the anti-corruption court sentenced Bank Indonesia's Budi Mulya to 10 years and a 500 million rupiah fine for corruption over that loan. The court put state losses at 8.5 trillion rupiah, including a 6.7 trillion rupiah bailout.
n:Robert Tantular: Robert Tantular was the owner of Bank Century in Indonesia. Bank Indonesia, the country's central bank, granted Bank Century a loan facility of 689.39 billion rupiah in 2008. In July 2014 the anti-corruption court sentenced Budi Mulya of the central bank to 10 years and a 500 million rupiah fine for corruption over that loan. The court found Mulya received a loan of 1 billion rupiah from Tantular.
n:Bank Indonesia employees' foundation: This is a foundation for the employees of Bank Indonesia, the central bank of Indonesia, based in Jakarta. It appears in a corruption case from 2008, when the bank gave a 689.39 billion rupiah loan facility to Bank Century and declared it a failed bank. In July 2014 the anti-corruption court sentenced Budi Mulya to 10 years and a 500 million rupiah fine. The court found he acted partly to save 83 billion rupiah deposited by the foundation.
n:Heri Gunawan: Heri Gunawan is linked to Bank Indonesia, the central bank of Indonesia, through a case in Jakarta. In August 2025 the Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK) named two members of parliament's House as suspects in the alleged misuse of corporate social responsibility (CSR) funds from Bank Indonesia and the Financial Services Authority. The funds were channelled after closed-door budget discussions in 2020 to 2022 by the commission that approves the bank's budget. These are allegations and nothing is proven.
n:Satori: Satori is linked to Bank Indonesia, the central bank of Indonesia, through a case in Jakarta. In August 2025 the Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK) named two members of parliament's House as suspects in the alleged misuse of corporate social responsibility (CSR) funds from Bank Indonesia and the Financial Services Authority. The funds were channelled after closed-door budget discussions in 2020 to 2022 by the commission that approves the bank's budget. These are allegations and nothing is proven.
n:House of Representatives Commission XI: This is a committee of Indonesia's House of Representatives, in Jakarta, that approves the budget of Bank Indonesia, the central bank. In August 2025 the anti-corruption commission (KPK) named two House members as suspects in the alleged misuse of corporate social responsibility (CSR) funds from Bank Indonesia and the Financial Services Authority. The funds were channelled after closed-door budget discussions in 2020 to 2022 by this commission. These are allegations and nothing is proven.
n:Financial Services Authority (OJK): The Financial Services Authority (OJK) is an Indonesian agency in Jakarta tied to Bank Indonesia, the central bank. In August 2025 the anti-corruption commission (KPK) named two House members as suspects in the alleged misuse of corporate social responsibility (CSR) funds from Bank Indonesia and the OJK. The funds were channelled after closed-door budget discussions in 2020 to 2022 by the House commission that approves the central bank's budget. These are allegations and nothing is proven.
n:Central Bureau of Investigation (India: This is India's federal investigation agency, based in New Delhi, tied to the Reserve Bank of India, the central bank. In December 2016, while the country was withdrawing 500 and 1,000 rupee notes (demonetisation), it arrested RBI official K. Michael in Bangalore. He is accused of converting 15 million rupees (about 222,000 dollars) of withdrawn notes into 100 rupee notes without legal documentation, working with a state bank employee. This is an allegation and no outcome is reported.
n:Salar Aghakhani: Salar Aghakhani is a Tehran-based intermediary tied to the Central Bank of the Islamic Republic of Iran. In October 2021 a Tehran court sentenced him to 13 years over an illegal foreign-currency distribution scheme in 2017 and 2018. Former governor Seif got 10 years and former deputy Araghchi eight. According to Iran Times, the Supreme Court overturned the verdicts in 2023, citing insufficient evidence and authorisation by higher authorities. The judiciary dropped the prosecution of Seif and Araghchi in March 2025.
n:Tehran court: This is a court in Tehran, Iran, tied to the Central Bank of the Islamic Republic of Iran. In October 2021 it sentenced former governor Seif to 10 years for taking part in disrupting the financial system through illegal smuggling of foreign currency, former deputy Araghchi to eight years and intermediary Salar Aghakhani to 13 years, over a currency distribution scheme in 2017 and 2018. According to Iran Times, the Supreme Court overturned the verdicts in 2023, and the judiciary dropped the prosecution of Seif and Araghchi in March 2025.
n:Supreme Court of Iran: This is Iran's highest court, in Tehran, tied to the Central Bank of the Islamic Republic of Iran. In October 2021 a Tehran court sentenced former governor Seif to 10 years, former deputy Araghchi to eight and intermediary Salar Aghakhani to 13, over an illegal foreign-currency distribution scheme in 2017 and 2018. According to Iran Times, the Supreme Court overturned the verdicts in 2023, citing insufficient evidence and authorisation by higher authorities. The judiciary dropped the prosecution of Seif and Araghchi in March 2025.
n:Iranian judiciary: This is Iran's court system, based in Tehran, tied to the Central Bank of the Islamic Republic of Iran. In October 2021 a Tehran court sentenced former governor Seif to 10 years, former deputy Araghchi to eight and intermediary Salar Aghakhani to 13, over an illegal foreign-currency distribution scheme in 2017 and 2018. The judiciary said 10 people were identified in the scheme. The Supreme Court overturned the verdicts in 2023, according to Iran Times, and the judiciary dropped the prosecution of Seif and Araghchi in March 2025.
n:Cabinet of Iraq: This is the government cabinet of Iraq, in Baghdad, tied to the Central Bank of Iraq. In October 2012 it removed governor Sinan al-Shabibi after a parliamentary committee charged that bank officials were abusing the bank's dollar sales. A successor was named, and a committee member said arrest warrants had been issued for 30 people, including al-Shabibi and his deputy Mudher Saleh. The Supreme Judicial Council confirmed warrants without giving charges. His defence called the case politically motivated; a finance committee member also called it a political decision.
n:Supreme Judicial Council (Iraq): This is Iraq's top judicial body, in Baghdad, tied to the Central Bank of Iraq. In October 2012 the cabinet removed the bank's governor al-Shabibi after a parliamentary committee charged that bank officials were abusing the bank's dollar sales. The Supreme Judicial Council then confirmed arrest warrants for him and other officials without giving the charges. His defence called the case politically motivated.
n:Board of Supreme Audit (Iraq): This is Iraq's state audit agency, in Baghdad. Under Coalition Provisional Authority Order Number 56, the central bank law of 2004, it audits the accounts of the Central Bank of Iraq. In 2012 it investigated the central bank's daily dollar auctions and found that most transactions were based on fraudulent paperwork, and according to the US Special Inspector General for Iraq Reconstruction its top auditor told US officials that up to 800 million US dollars a week was leaving Iraq illegally.
n:Special Inspector General for Iraq Rec: This is a United States oversight agency for Iraq reconstruction, tied to the Central Bank of Iraq. It reported that in 2012 Iraq's Board of Supreme Audit investigated the central bank's daily dollar auctions and found most transactions were based on fraudulent paperwork. According to the agency, the top auditor told US officials that up to 800 million dollars a week was leaving Iraq illegally.
n:Special Investigation Commission (Icel: This is a commission set up by Iceland's parliament, based in Reykjavik, tied to the Central Bank of Iceland. In April 2010 it found that seven officials, including central bank head Oddsson and central bank officials Gudnason and Fridriksson, acted with gross negligence before the 2008 collapse of Iceland's three largest banks. It said they failed to act on information about the banks' condition.
n:Banca Popolare di Lodi: Banca Popolare di Lodi is a bank in Lodi, Italy, tied to the Bank of Italy, the country's central bank. In 2005 it attempted to take over another bank, Antonveneta. On 28 May 2011 a Milan court sentenced former Bank of Italy governor Fazio to four years in prison and a fine of 1.5 million euros for market rigging in that attempt. Prosecutors argued he repeatedly favoured Fiorani's bank over ABN Amro by speeding some authorisations and slowing others.
n:Gianpiero Fiorani: Gianpiero Fiorani is tied to the Bank of Italy, the country's central bank, through a case centred on Lodi. In the 2005 attempted takeover of Antonveneta by Banca Popolare di Lodi, prosecutors argued that former Bank of Italy governor Fazio favoured Fiorani's bank over ABN Amro by speeding some authorisations and slowing others. On 28 May 2011 a Milan court sentenced Fazio to four years in prison and a fine of 1.5 million euros for market rigging.
n:ABN Amro: ABN Amro is a bank based in Amsterdam, Netherlands, tied to four central banks. Three of the ties are careers. Lord Jitesh Gadhia, a Non-Executive Director of the Bank of England's Court, came from investment banking at Blackstone, Barclays Capital, ABN AMRO and Baring Brothers. Zsigmond Jarai was president and chief executive of ABN-AMRO Bank in Hungary from 1998, after posts at brokerages and banks in London and Budapest, and later led the Magyar Nemzeti Bank; no ethics finding is recorded. Thomas Domhoff took up the presidency of the Centrale Bank van Aruba from 1 July 2026, after project roles at ING, ABN AMRO, Rabobank and Capgemini and a directorship at Banco Sicredi. The fourth tie is a case at the Bank of Italy: on 28 May 2011 a Milan court sentenced former governor Fazio to four years in prison and a 1.5 million euro fine for market rigging in the 2005 attempted takeover of Antonveneta by Banca Popolare di Lodi, after prosecutors argued he had repeatedly favoured Fiorani's bank over ABN Amro by speeding some authorisations and slowing others.
n:Antonveneta: Antonveneta is a bank in Padua, Italy, tied to the Bank of Italy, the country's central bank. It was the target of an attempted takeover by Banca Popolare di Lodi in 2005. On 28 May 2011 a Milan court sentenced former Bank of Italy governor Fazio to four years in prison and a fine of 1.5 million euros for market rigging in that attempt. Prosecutors argued he favoured Lodi's bank over ABN Amro.
n:Milan court: This is a court in Milan, Italy, tied to the Bank of Italy, the country's central bank. On 28 May 2011 it sentenced former governor Fazio to four years in prison and a fine of 1.5 million euros for market rigging in the 2005 attempted takeover of Antonveneta by Banca Popolare di Lodi. In October 2011 Fazio was sentenced to three and a half years at first instance over Unipol's attempted 2005 takeover of BNL. On 30 May 2012 the Milan Court of Appeal acquitted him and 12 other defendants of market rigging.
n:Unipol: Unipol is an insurance and finance company in Bologna, Italy, tied to the Bank of Italy, the country's central bank. It attempted to take over the bank BNL in 2005. In October 2011 former Bank of Italy governor Fazio was sentenced to three and a half years at first instance over that attempt. On 30 May 2012 the Milan Court of Appeal acquitted him and 12 other defendants of market rigging.
n:BNL: BNL is a bank in Rome, Italy, tied to the Bank of Italy, the country's central bank. Unipol attempted to take it over in 2005. In October 2011 former Bank of Italy governor Fazio was sentenced to three and a half years at first instance over that attempt. On 30 May 2012 the Milan Court of Appeal acquitted him and 12 other defendants of market rigging.
n:Milan Court of Appeal: This is an appeals court in Milan, Italy, tied to the Bank of Italy, the country's central bank. Former governor Fazio was sentenced in October 2011 to three and a half years at first instance over Unipol's attempted 2005 takeover of the bank BNL. On 30 May 2012 the Milan Court of Appeal acquitted him and 12 other defendants of market rigging.
n:Yoshiaki Murakami: Yoshiaki Murakami is linked to the Bank of Japan, the country's central bank, through a fund he ran. In June 2006 Bank of Japan chief Fukui apologised and took a 30 percent pay cut for six months after disclosing he had kept an investment of 10 million yen, made in 1999, in that fund. Murakami was arrested for insider trading, and the stake had grown to 22 million yen. The bank said Fukui broke no law or internal rule, and he did not resign.
n:Wilfred Koinange: Wilfred Koinange, based in Nairobi, is named in the Goldenberg case involving the Central Bank of Kenya. The government paid cash subsidies for fictitious gold and diamond exports by Goldenberg International under President Moi. A judicial inquiry reported in February 2006. In March 2006 prosecutors indicted five people, including former governor Kotut and former deputy governor Riungu. Earlier proceedings against Riungu had been halted.
n:Kamlesh Pattni: Kamlesh Pattni is named in the Goldenberg case involving the Central Bank of Kenya. In that scandal the government paid cash subsidies for fictitious gold and diamond exports by Goldenberg International under President Moi. A judicial inquiry reported in February 2006. In March 2006 Kenyan prosecutors indicted five people, including former governor Kotut and former deputy governor Riungu. Earlier proceedings against Riungu had been halted.
n:Goldenberg International: Goldenberg International is a company in Nairobi, Kenya, named in a case involving the Central Bank of Kenya. Under President Moi, the government paid cash subsidies for fictitious gold and diamond exports by the company, in what became known as the Goldenberg scandal. A judicial inquiry reported in February 2006. In March 2006 Kenyan prosecutors indicted five people, including former governor Kotut and former deputy governor Riungu. Earlier proceedings against Riungu had been halted.
n:Daniel arap Moi: Daniel arap Moi was president of Kenya when, in the Goldenberg scandal, the government paid cash subsidies for fictitious gold and diamond exports by Goldenberg International. He is named in the case, which involves the Central Bank of Kenya. A judicial inquiry reported in February 2006. In March 2006 Kenyan prosecutors indicted five people, including former governor Kotut and former deputy governor Riungu. Earlier proceedings against Riungu had been halted.
n:Kenyan prosecutors: These are the state prosecutors of Kenya, based in Nairobi, tied to the Central Bank of Kenya. In March 2006 they indicted five people, including former governor Kotut and former deputy governor Riungu, over the Goldenberg scandal. In it, the government paid cash subsidies for fictitious gold and diamond exports by Goldenberg International under President Moi. A judicial inquiry had reported in February 2006. Earlier proceedings against Riungu had been halted.
n:Kenyan judicial inquiry: This is a judicial inquiry in Kenya, in Nairobi, tied to the Central Bank of Kenya. It reported in February 2006 on the Goldenberg scandal, in which the government paid cash subsidies for fictitious gold and diamond exports by Goldenberg International under President Moi. In March 2006 prosecutors indicted five people, including former central bank governor Kotut and former deputy governor Riungu. Earlier proceedings against Riungu had been halted.
n:Silla Mullei: Silla Mullei was governor of the Central Bank of Kenya. On 23 March 2006 he was charged with four counts of abuse of office. They included appointing his son as a bank consultant without following procurement procedures, with the son paid 2,619,154.85 shillings in fees, and improperly appointing three other consultants. He denied awarding 9 million shillings in contracts irregularly and was freed on 5 million shillings bail. The charges are unproven.
n:Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission: This is Kenya's anti-corruption agency, in Nairobi, tied to the Central Bank of Kenya. It said it was investigating former and current central bank officials over their role in the accounting fraud that brought down Imperial Bank. In August 2018 Imperial Bank's directors told a parliamentary committee that central bank officers took part in the 34 billion shilling embezzlement by manipulating the bank's IT systems. These are allegations and nothing is proven.
n:Imperial Bank: Imperial Bank was a bank in Nairobi, Kenya, that collapsed after an accounting fraud, and it is tied to the Central Bank of Kenya. In August 2018 its directors told a parliamentary committee that central bank officers took part in the 34 billion shilling embezzlement by manipulating the bank's IT systems. Kenya's Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission said it was investigating former and current central bank officials over their role. These are allegations and nothing is proven.
n:Kenyan National Assembly committee: This is a committee of Kenya's National Assembly, in Nairobi, tied to the Central Bank of Kenya. In August 2018 the directors of Imperial Bank, which had collapsed after an accounting fraud, told it that central bank officers took part in the 34 billion shilling embezzlement by manipulating the bank's IT systems. Kenya's Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission said it was investigating former and current central bank officials. These are allegations and nothing is proven.
n:Askar Akayev: Askar Akayev is the deposed president of Kyrgyzstan. In September 2005 prosecutors placed the governor of the National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic, Sarbanov, under house arrest, accusing him of abuse of power for handing out more than 400,000 dollars to Akayev in 1999. Sarbanov denied wrongdoing. No outcome is reported.
n:Kyrgyz prosecutors: These are the state prosecutors of Kyrgyzstan, based in Bishkek, tied to the National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic, the central bank. In September 2005 they placed governor Sarbanov under house arrest. They accused him of abuse of power for handing out more than 400,000 dollars to deposed president Askar Akayev in 1999. Sarbanov denied wrongdoing, and the accusation is unproven.
n:Vientiane People's Court: This is a court in Vientiane, Laos, tied to the Bank of the Lao P.D.R., the country's central bank. On 8 September 2026 it sentenced two former directors general of the bank to life imprisonment. One, Aod, was sentenced in his absence because he died during the proceedings. They were convicted of abusing their positions to withdraw foreign currency from the bank's reserves and exchange unlimited amounts. In a related case nine bank employees were convicted of corruption and money laundering, including trading currency at special rates. Losses across the cases exceeded 2.29 trillion kip (102.6 million dollars).
n:French prosecutors: These are state prosecutors in Paris, tied to Banque du Liban, Lebanon's central bank. Its governor for three decades until 2023, Riad Salameh, was investigated over allegations that more than 300 million dollars was siphoned off between 2002 and 2015 through Forry Associates, a company controlled by his brother Raja. In May 2023 they issued an arrest warrant after he failed to appear for questioning in a joint French, German and Luxembourg probe into illicit enrichment and alleged laundering of 330 million dollars. Germany issued a second warrant the following week. Salameh was later arrested in Beirut on charges of embezzlement, money laundering and fraud. He and his brother deny wrongdoing, and the charges are unproven.
n:German authorities: These are German state authorities tied to Banque du Liban, Lebanon's central bank. They took part in a joint French, German and Luxembourg probe into illicit enrichment and alleged laundering of 330 million dollars involving former governor Riad Salameh. In May 2023, the week after France issued an arrest warrant, Germany issued a second one on charges including corruption, forgery, money laundering and embezzlement. Salameh called the French warrant a violation of the law. He was later arrested in Beirut and denies wrongdoing. The charges are unproven.
n:Luxembourg authorities: These are Luxembourg state authorities tied to Banque du Liban, Lebanon's central bank. They took part in a joint French, German and Luxembourg judicial probe into illicit enrichment and alleged laundering of 330 million dollars involving former governor Riad Salameh. In May 2023 French prosecutors issued an arrest warrant for Salameh after he failed to appear for questioning, and Germany issued a second warrant the following week. Salameh called the French warrant a violation of the law.
n:Raja Salameh: Raja Salameh is the brother of Riad Salameh, who was governor of Banque du Liban, Lebanon's central bank, for three decades until 2023. Investigators allege that more than 300 million dollars was siphoned off between 2002 and 2015 through Forry Associates, a company Raja controlled, which is suspected of receiving commissions from commercial banks and transferring them abroad. Investigations are open in France, Germany, Switzerland and other countries. Both brothers deny wrongdoing, and nothing is proven.
n:Forry Associates: Forry Associates is a company based in Road Town, British Virgin Islands, controlled by Raja Salameh, brother of Riad Salameh, who was governor of Banque du Liban, Lebanon's central bank. Investigators allege that more than 300 million dollars was siphoned off between 2002 and 2015 through it. The company is suspected of receiving commissions from commercial banks and transferring them abroad. Investigations are open in France, Germany, Switzerland and other countries. Both brothers deny wrongdoing, and nothing is proven.
n:Lebanese state investigation: This is the Lebanese state investigation, in Beirut, into former Banque du Liban governor Riad Salameh. It covers allegations that more than 300 million dollars was siphoned off between 2002 and 2015 through Forry Associates, a company controlled by his brother Raja and suspected of receiving commissions from commercial banks and transferring them abroad. The central bank said it would act as principal plaintiff. Investigations are also open in France, Germany, Switzerland and other countries. Both brothers deny wrongdoing, and nothing is proven.
n:Swiss authorities: These are Swiss state authorities tied to Banque du Liban, Lebanon's central bank. Investigations into former governor Riad Salameh are open in Switzerland, as well as in France, Germany and other countries. They concern allegations that more than 300 million dollars was siphoned off between 2002 and 2015 through Forry Associates, a company controlled by his brother Raja and suspected of receiving commissions from commercial banks and transferring them abroad. Both brothers deny wrongdoing, and nothing is proven.
n:Marwan Issa el-Khoury: Marwan Issa el-Khoury, based in Beirut, is named in a case involving Banque du Liban, Lebanon's central bank. In January 2026 Beirut's indictment chamber indicted former governor Riad Salameh and two lawyers on charges including embezzlement of public funds, forgery and illicit enrichment. They are accused of embezzling 44.8 million dollars from a central bank consultancy account. Salameh was detained about 13 months and released in September 2025 on bail of more than 14 million dollars. He denies wrongdoing, and the charges are unproven.
n:Michel John Tueni: Michel John Tueni, based in Beirut, is named in a case involving Banque du Liban, Lebanon's central bank. In January 2026 Beirut's indictment chamber indicted former governor Riad Salameh and two lawyers on charges including embezzlement of public funds, forgery and illicit enrichment. They are accused of embezzling 44.8 million dollars from a central bank consultancy account. Salameh was detained about 13 months and released in September 2025 on bail of more than 14 million dollars. He denies wrongdoing, and the charges are unproven.
n:Beirut indictment chamber: This is the court in Beirut, Lebanon, that decides whether a criminal case goes to trial. In January 2026 it indicted Riad Salameh, the former head of Lebanon's central bank, Banque du Liban, and two lawyers. The charges include embezzlement of public funds, forgery and illicit enrichment. It accused them of taking 44.8 million dollars from a central bank "consultancy account". Salameh had been detained for about 13 months and was released in September 2025 on bail of more than 14 million dollars. He denies wrongdoing. The charges have not been proven.
n:Alvarez & Marsal: Alvarez & Marsal is a consulting firm based in New York, United States. In 2023 its forensic audit of Lebanon's central bank, Banque du Liban, found that the bank's foreign-currency position went from a 7.2 billion dollar surplus at the end of 2015 to a 50.7 billion dollar deficit at the end of 2020. The balance sheet showed no loss at all, because losses were netted or recorded in general accounts. The audit found that governor Riad Salameh set accounting standards that concealed the losses and chose which banks benefited from the bank's financial engineering. It also found that the bank's Central Council did not challenge him.
n:EY: EY, also written Ernst & Young, is an accounting and auditing firm based in London, United Kingdom, tied to 13 central banks. It audits the accounts of the Bank of England, where it signed the auditor's report in the 2026 annual report for the year to the end of February 2026, having been appointed from the year ending 28 February 2025; De Nederlandsche Bank in the Netherlands, approved for the financial years 2026 to 2032 by a European Union Council decision of 16 September 2025; the Bank of Canada for 2025, jointly with PricewaterhouseCoopers and appointed by the Governor-in-Council; Norges Bank in Norway for 2022 to 2027, engaged by its supervisory council, with Norway's national audit office also reviewing the oil fund audit; the South African Reserve Bank for 2025/26, jointly with BDO South Africa; the Bank of Cape Verde, where it gave an unqualified opinion for the year ended 31 December 2024 on a balance sheet total of 99,898,332 thousand escudos and negative equity of 622,855 thousand escudos; the Central Bank of Nigeria (2024); the Central Bank of Aruba (2025); the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe (2019); and the Central Bank of Yemen, where its appointment was announced on 7 February 2021. Three records go further. In Lebanon, Banque du Liban's 2018 audited accounts, signed off with qualifications by EY and Deloitte, carried a 6.82 billion dollar asset described as 'seigniorage on financial stability', inflating assets by more than 6 billion dollars while the bank helped fund a widening government deficit; the amount was determined each year by the governor. In Tanzania, an Ernst & Young audit of the Bank of Tanzania's External Payment Arrears account found about 133 billion shillings wrongly paid in 2005/06 to 22 local companies, many of them phoney or using fake documents; President Kikwete dismissed governor Ballali in January 2008, companies were ordered to refund the money and some lower-level defendants were jailed. In Portugal, the Bank of Portugal's ethics committee discussed at a meeting in April 2019 a request by governor Carlos Costa to be excused from matters concerning Caixa Geral de Depositos, after an EY audit of that bank's management. Costa had been on its board from 2004 to 2006 and may have sat on extended credit council meetings that approved operations which caused losses, while now heading the supervisor assessing former Caixa directors; vice-governor Elisa Ferreira did not recuse herself but told the committee of a possible conflict of interest relating to her husband's past role at La Seda. The committee's conclusions were not made public.
n:Deloitte: Deloitte is an accounting and auditing firm based in London, United Kingdom, tied to nine central banks. It audits the accounts of the Bank of France for the financial years 2024 to 2029, approved jointly with Mazars by a European Union Council decision of 16 July 2024; the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye, where its Turkish member firm signed the independent auditor's reports on the 2025 financial statements, the bank having used outside auditors since 2000; the Central Bank of Paraguay for 2025, 2026 and 2027, awarded by a board resolution of 7 November 2025 after an international public tender; the Bank of Italy for 2023 to 2027; Bank Al-Maghrib in Morocco, on a six-year non-renewable mandate for 2021 to 2026; the Central Bank of Libya (2021); and Banky Foiben'i Madagasikara, where its French member firm Deloitte & Associés signed the accounts to 31 December 2025 jointly with the Malagasy firm Auditeurs Associés CGA, the report dated in Antananarivo and Paris-La Défense together on 29 April 2026. Two further records are investigations. In Lebanon, Banque du Liban's 2018 audited accounts, signed off with qualifications by Deloitte and EY, carried a 6.82 billion dollar asset described as 'seigniorage on financial stability', inflating assets by more than 6 billion dollars; the amount was determined each year by the governor. In New Zealand, Deloitte was engaged by the Reserve Bank on 11 March 2016 and reported on 12 April that the leak of the 10 March Official Cash Rate decision came from a Mediaworks employee: a journalist in the bank's media lock-up emailed a draft story out of the room without the bank's approval shortly before 8am, and another employee who overheard colleagues discussing the rate cut emailed Michael Reddell at 8.04am, ahead of the 9am announcement. Reddell did not notify the bank until 9.08am, and Mediaworks reported itself on 5 April 2016. Deloitte judged the Minister of Finance's office unlikely to be the source. The Reserve Bank then ended embargoed lock-ups for news media and analysts.
n:Government of Lebanon: This is the national government of Lebanon, based in Beirut. It is tied to the country's central bank, Banque du Liban. The bank's 2018 audited accounts, signed off with qualifications by EY and Deloitte, recorded a 6.82 billion dollar asset described as "seigniorage on financial stability". That inflated the bank's assets by over 6 billion dollars. This happened while the bank helped fund a widening government deficit. The governor determined the amount each year.
n:Ali Ibrahim: Ali Ibrahim is a Lebanese prosecutor based in Beirut. On 14 May 2020 he ordered the arrest of Mazen Hamdan, the director of cash operations at Lebanon's central bank, Banque du Liban. On 18 May 2020 he charged Hamdan with illegally manipulating the exchange rate, according to a judicial source cited by AFP. No outcome of the charge is given.
n:Monrovia court: This court in Monrovia, Liberia, handled a case about missing banknotes at the Central Bank of Liberia. In March 2019 it ordered former deputy governor Sirleaf, former governor Weeks and official Hagba held for trial. The charges were economic sabotage, misuse of public money, theft or illegal disbursement of public money and criminal conspiracy. They concern Liberian dollar banknotes printed in 2016 to 2018 that could not be accounted for. AFP later reported that the Justice Minister dropped charges against Sirleaf and three others, while Weeks remained under indictment.
n:Ministry of Justice of Liberia: This is the justice ministry of Liberia, based in Monrovia. It is named in the case of Liberian dollar banknotes printed in 2016 to 2018 that the Central Bank of Liberia could not account for. In March 2019 a Monrovia court ordered former deputy governor Sirleaf, former governor Weeks and official Hagba held for trial on charges including economic sabotage, theft of public money and criminal conspiracy. AFP later reported that the Justice Minister dropped charges against Sirleaf and three others. Weeks remained under indictment.
n:Government of Liberia: This is the national government of Liberia, based in Monrovia. It is tied to the Central Bank of Liberia in two ways. A General Auditing Commission report on 2018 to 2023 found irregularities in the bank's lending to the government. These included more than 80 million dollars in apparently unauthorised financing for salary payments, irregular contract awards and spending above approved limits. In July 2024 the government then suspended the bank's governor, Tarlue, indefinitely. No later outcome is given.
n:General Auditing Commission (Liberia): This is the government audit agency of Liberia, based in Monrovia. It examined the Central Bank of Liberia for the years 2018 to 2023. Its report found irregularities in the bank's lending to the government, including more than 80 million dollars in apparently unauthorised financing for salary payments, irregular contract awards and management exceeding approved expenditure limits. In July 2024 Liberia suspended the bank's governor, Tarlue, indefinitely after the report. No later outcome is given.
n:Arjun Aloysius: Arjun Aloysius is a person tied to the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, with the marker placed at the country. He is listed as a recipient of money, favors or contracts from the bank. He is connected to the case over the February 2015 treasury bond auction, in which the Attorney General filed a 23-count indictment in June 2019 against former governor Mahendran and nine others. The Special High Court later issued an arrest warrant for Mahendran. No act by Aloysius himself is described here, and being tied to a case is not a finding of wrongdoing.
n:Perpetual Treasuries: Perpetual Treasuries is a company based in Colombo, Sri Lanka, listed as a recipient of money, favors or contracts from the Central Bank of Sri Lanka. It is connected to the case over the central bank's February 2015 treasury bond auction. In June 2019 the Attorney General filed a 23-count indictment against former governor Mahendran and nine others. The Special High Court later issued an arrest warrant for Mahendran. No act by the company itself is described here, and the tie is not a finding of wrongdoing.
n:Attorney General of Sri Lanka: This is the government's chief law officer in Sri Lanka, based in Colombo. In June 2019 the Attorney General filed an indictment with 23 counts under the Public Property Act and the Registered Stocks and Securities Ordinance. It named former Central Bank of Sri Lanka governor Mahendran and nine others, and concerned the February 2015 treasury bond auction. The case went before a three-judge Permanent High Court Trial-at-Bar. The Special High Court later issued an arrest warrant for Mahendran. The charges are unproven, and no verdict is given.
n:Permanent High Court Trial-at-Bar (Sri: This is a three-judge court in Colombo, Sri Lanka, that hears major criminal cases. In June 2019 the Attorney General filed an indictment before it with 23 counts under the Public Property Act and the Registered Stocks and Securities Ordinance. It named former Central Bank of Sri Lanka governor Mahendran and nine others over the February 2015 treasury bond auction. The Special High Court later issued an arrest warrant for Mahendran. The charges are unproven, and no verdict is given.
n:Supreme Court of Sri Lanka: This is the highest court of Sri Lanka, based in Colombo. On 14 November 2023 a majority of a five-judge bench ruled that the three Rajapaksa brothers, former Central Bank governors Cabraal and Lakshman, the former finance secretary, the former presidential secretary and members of the central bank's Monetary Board had violated the public trust. It found they breached Article 12(1) of the Constitution in their administration of the economy, which led to the 2022 economic crisis.
n:Gotabaya Rajapaksa: Gotabaya Rajapaksa is a person based in Colombo, Sri Lanka, named in a case involving the Central Bank of Sri Lanka. On 14 November 2023 a majority of a five-judge Supreme Court bench ruled that he, his brothers Mahinda and Basil, former central bank governors Cabraal and Lakshman, the former finance secretary, the former presidential secretary and members of the central bank's Monetary Board violated the public trust and breached Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The court said their administration of the economy led to the 2022 economic crisis.
n:Mahinda Rajapaksa: Mahinda Rajapaksa is a person based in Colombo, Sri Lanka, named in a case involving the Central Bank of Sri Lanka. On 14 November 2023 a majority of a five-judge Supreme Court bench ruled that he, his brothers Gotabaya and Basil, former central bank governors Cabraal and Lakshman, the former finance secretary, the former presidential secretary and members of the central bank's Monetary Board violated the public trust and breached Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The court said their administration of the economy led to the 2022 economic crisis.
n:Basil Rajapaksa: Basil Rajapaksa is a person based in Colombo, Sri Lanka, named in a case involving the Central Bank of Sri Lanka. On 14 November 2023 a majority of a five-judge Supreme Court bench ruled that he, his brothers Gotabaya and Mahinda, former central bank governors Cabraal and Lakshman, the former finance secretary, the former presidential secretary and members of the central bank's Monetary Board violated the public trust and breached Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The court said their administration of the economy led to the 2022 economic crisis.
n:Māris Martinsons: Māris Martinsons is a businessman tied to the Bank of Latvia, with the marker placed at the country. He was tried alongside Ilmārs Rimšēvičs, the bank's former governor. On 20 December 2023 the Riga District Court convicted Rimšēvičs of accepting a bribe and other material inducements and sentenced him to six years in prison with a five-year ban on public office. About 25,000 euros and several properties were confiscated. No verdict for Martinsons is given.
n:Riga District Court: This court in Riga, Latvia, tried the former governor of the Bank of Latvia, Rimšēvičs, alongside businessman Māris Martinsons. On 20 December 2023 it convicted Rimšēvičs of accepting a bribe and other material inducements. It sentenced him to six years in prison with a five-year ban on public office, and about 25,000 euros and several properties were confiscated.
n:Moldovan prosecutors: These are the prosecutors of Moldova, based in Chișinău. On 5 March 2020 they searched the National Bank of Moldova's headquarters and detained deputy governor Cincilei, former deputy governor Tăbîrţă and a division head. The suspicion was participation in fraud and money laundering linked to the theft of about 1 billion dollars from three banks, which surfaced in 2014 and 2015. The central bank had extended an emergency loan of 13 billion Moldovan lei, later converted into public debt. Prosecutors also moved to arrest former governor Drăguțanu. These are suspicions, and no outcome is given.
n:Andrés Manuel López Obrador: Andrés Manuel López Obrador was president of Mexico and is based in Mexico City. Two events tie him to the Bank of Mexico. On 23 March 2022 he announced the bank's unanimous interest rate rise from 6% to 6.5% before the bank published it. On 25 March he said the finance minister, who takes part in the bank's board meetings, had told him the previous evening. He apologised to the governor and accepted that they had violated the Banco de México law. Deputy governor Gerardo Esquivel called it an error, not a leak. Earlier, López Obrador withdrew his nomination of former finance minister Arturo Herrera as governor and nominated Victoria Rodríguez Ceja instead.
n:Rogelio Ramírez de la O: Rogelio Ramírez de la O is a person based in Mexico City, named in a case involving the Bank of Mexico. On 23 March 2022 President López Obrador announced the bank's unanimous interest rate rise from 6% to 6.5% before it was published. On 25 March the president said the finance minister, who takes part in the bank's board meetings, had told him the previous evening. He apologised to the governor and accepted that they had violated the Banco de México law. Deputy governor Gerardo Esquivel called it an error, not a leak.
n:Financial Crimes Commission (Mauritius: This is Mauritius's financial crimes agency, based in Port Louis. On 9 and 10 April 2025 it arrested Seegolam, former governor of the Bank of Mauritius, for "fraud by abuse of position". He was charged with fraud and released on bail. The investigation concerns the alleged embezzlement of 300 million rupees (6.7 million dollars) from the Mauritius Investment Corporation, a central bank-owned vehicle set up during the COVID pandemic. Seegolam and Padayachy deny wrongdoing. The charge is unproven.
n:Renganaden Padayachy: Renganaden Padayachy is a person based in Port Louis, Mauritius, named in a case involving the Bank of Mauritius. On 9 and 10 April 2025 Mauritius's Financial Crimes Commission arrested former governor Seegolam, who was charged with fraud and released on bail. The case concerns the alleged embezzlement of 300 million rupees (6.7 million dollars) from the Mauritius Investment Corporation, a central bank-owned vehicle set up during the COVID pandemic. Seegolam and Padayachy deny wrongdoing. Being named in the case is not a finding against him.
n:Mauritius Investment Corporation: The Mauritius Investment Corporation is a company in Port Louis, Mauritius, owned by the Bank of Mauritius and set up during the COVID pandemic. It is named in an investigation into the alleged embezzlement of 300 million rupees (6.7 million dollars) from it. On 9 and 10 April 2025 the Financial Crimes Commission arrested former governor Seegolam, who was charged with fraud and released on bail. Seegolam and Padayachy deny wrongdoing. The allegation is unproven.
n:FDH Bank: FDH Bank is a bank based in Blantyre, Malawi, tied to the Reserve Bank of Malawi. A forensic audit of the central bank's payments between January 2019 and June 2020 led the state to charge four people, including Kabambe. They were charged with abuse of office, negligence, money laundering and causing loss of public funds. The state alleges the central bank paid 4.3 billion kwacha to FDH Bank without board approval. Pleas were not taken because the charges were subject to change. The charges are unproven.
n:Malawi prosecutors: These are the state prosecutors of Malawi, based in Lilongwe. After a forensic audit of Reserve Bank of Malawi payments between January 2019 and June 2020, they charged four people, including Kabambe, with abuse of office, negligence, money laundering and causing loss of public funds. They allege the central bank paid 4.3 billion kwacha to FDH Bank without board approval. Pleas were not taken because the charges were subject to change. The charges are unproven.
n:Joseph Mwanamvekha: Joseph Mwanamvekha is a person based in Lilongwe, Malawi, named in a case involving the Reserve Bank of Malawi. In December 2021 Malawi police arrested him and Kabambe. Police said they procured and masterminded the falsification of Gross Liability and Net Reserve Base returns, to make the International Monetary Fund believe Malawi was meeting the conditions of its Extended Credit Facility, a lending arrangement. This is an allegation by police, and no outcome is given.
n:Malawi Police Service: This is Malawi's national police force, based in Lilongwe. In December 2021 it arrested Kabambe and Joseph Mwanamvekha in a case involving the Reserve Bank of Malawi. Police said they procured and masterminded the falsification of Gross Liability and Net Reserve Base returns, to make the International Monetary Fund believe Malawi was meeting the conditions of its Extended Credit Facility, a lending arrangement. The claim is unproven, and no outcome is given.
n:Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission: This is Malaysia's anti-corruption agency, based in Putrajaya. In July 2011 it charged former Bank Negara Malaysia official Mohamad Daud with receiving two bribes of 50,000 ringgit each in 2004 and 2005. They were linked to the 95 million ringgit contract for the RM5 polymer banknote, won by Note Printing Australia. The Shah Alam Sessions Court acquitted him without calling his defence on 6 December 2015. The Attorney-General withdrew the appeal in February 2016.
n:Shah Alam Sessions Court: This court in Shah Alam, Malaysia, heard the case of former Bank Negara Malaysia official Mohamad Daud. The Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission charged him in July 2011 with receiving two bribes of 50,000 ringgit each in 2004 and 2005, linked to the 95 million ringgit RM5 polymer banknote contract won by Note Printing Australia. The court acquitted him without calling his defence on 6 December 2015. The Attorney-General withdrew the appeal in February 2016.
n:Attorney-General of Malaysia: This is the government's chief legal officer in Malaysia, based in Putrajaya. It is named in the case of former Bank Negara Malaysia official Mohamad Daud, charged in July 2011 with receiving two bribes of 50,000 ringgit each in 2004 and 2005, linked to the 95 million ringgit RM5 polymer banknote contract won by Note Printing Australia. The Shah Alam Sessions Court acquitted him on 6 December 2015 without calling his defence. The Attorney-General withdrew the appeal in February 2016.
n:Economic and Financial Crimes Commissi: The EFCC is Nigeria's financial crimes agency, based in Abuja, and has pursued several matters at the Central Bank of Nigeria. Around 2013 it said it had questioned former governor Soludo in a probe into whether Securency, part-owned by the Reserve Bank of Australia, bribed bank officials to win the 2006 to 2008 polymer banknote printing contract. In January 2024 it re-arraigned former governor Emefiele on 20 counts, including conspiracy, criminal breach of trust and forgery. He pleaded not guilty. In April 2024 it filed a 26-count charge alleging he directed 2,136,391,737.33 dollars of foreign exchange without bids. It also filed a four-count charge over printing 684,590,000 banknotes at a cost of 18.96 billion naira in the 2022 to 2023 redesign. A bank clerk and a Wema Bank employee were sentenced to three years each after a plea bargain, in an 8 billion naira currency mutilation scam. The charges against Emefiele are unproven.
n:Jim Obazee: Jim Obazee is a person based in Nigeria, appointed as special investigator of the Central Bank of Nigeria. His December 2023 report to President Tinubu said former governor Emefiele kept billions of naira in 593 bank accounts in the United States, United Kingdom and China. It also said he placed 543,482,213 pounds in UK fixed deposits without approval from the central bank's board or investment committee. These are findings of the report, and no outcome is given.
n:Bola Tinubu: Bola Tinubu is the president of Nigeria and is based in Abuja. On 10 June 2023 he suspended Central Bank of Nigeria governor Godwin Emefiele with immediate effect, citing an ongoing investigation, and named Deputy Governor Folashodun Shonubi acting governor. In December 2023 special investigator Jim Obazee submitted a report to him saying Emefiele kept billions of naira in 593 bank accounts in the United States, United Kingdom and China, and placed 543,482,213 pounds in UK fixed deposits without board approval. These are findings of the report, and no outcome is given.
n:Federal Capital Territory High Court: This court in Abuja, Nigeria, is named in the case of former Central Bank of Nigeria governor Godwin Emefiele. In January 2024 the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission re-arraigned him on 20 counts, including conspiracy, criminal breach of trust, forgery and obtaining money by false pretences. The counts include awarding a 2018 contract for Toyota Hilux vehicles to a company linked to bank staff, and obtaining over 6 million dollars by falsely claiming the president directed an advance. He pleaded not guilty. The charges are unproven.
n:Henry Isioma Omole: Henry Isioma Omole is a person based in Lagos, Nigeria, named in a case involving the Central Bank of Nigeria. In April 2024 the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission filed a 26-count charge in Lagos alleging former governor Emefiele directed allocation of 2,136,391,737.33 dollars of foreign exchange without bids in 2020 and 2021. Omole is a co-defendant, accused of receiving a 110,000 dollar bribe on Emefiele's behalf for favourable allocations. The charge is unproven, and no outcome is given.
n:Wema Bank: Wema Bank is a bank based in Lagos, Nigeria, named in a case involving the Central Bank of Nigeria. A senior clerk at the central bank and a Wema Bank employee were each sentenced to three years in prison after a plea bargain with the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission. They faced six counts of stealing and conspiracy, part of an 8 billion naira currency mutilation scam at the central bank's Ibadan branch.
n:Commission for the Investigation of Ab: This is a Nepali anti-corruption body based in Kathmandu. In 2007 it charged Nepal Rastra Bank's sitting governor Bhattarai and executive director Pradhan with embezzlement over the hiring of American consultants for the second phase of the Financial Sector Reform Program. Bhattarai was suspended. The Supreme Court later cleared both, which allowed Bhattarai's reinstatement. A confidential World Bank report, reported in 2014, named a private banker as the main figure behind the scandal.
n:Supreme Court of Nepal: This is the highest court of Nepal, based in Kathmandu, and it ruled in two cases involving Nepal Rastra Bank. In 2007 the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority charged governor Bhattarai and executive director Pradhan with embezzlement over hiring American consultants, and Bhattarai was suspended. The Supreme Court later cleared both, allowing his reinstatement. On 8 April 2022 the government suspended governor Adhikari over charges of leaking sensitive information about government decisions and not fulfilling his responsibilities. On 19 April 2022 the Supreme Court stayed the suspension and he returned to work.
n:World Bank: The World Bank is an international lender based in Washington, United States, tied to 18 central banks and one other body. Most of the ties are careers. People have gone from the Bank into central banks: Ishrat Husain to the State Bank of Pakistan; Stanley Fischer, a former chief economist, to the Bank of Israel from 2005 to 2013; Duvvuri Subbarao, a former lead economist, to the Reserve Bank of India from 2008 to 2013; Mario Marcel from a Bank director post to the council of the Central Bank of Chile, approved in September 2015; Hwang Geon-il, a former executive director, to the Bank of Korea's monetary policy committee; Adriana D. Kugler from United States executive director at the World Bank Group to a governorship of the Federal Reserve System, held from 13 September 2023 to 8 August 2025; Mario Draghi from executive director, 1984 to 1990, to the Italian Treasury and later the governorship of the Bank of Italy; Denny Kalyalya to the Bank of Zambia in February 2015; Mamo Mihretu to the National Bank of Ethiopia in January 2023; Marouane Abassi, the Bank's representative in Libya, to the Central Bank of Tunisia, approved by parliament in February 2018; Óscar Évora Santos to the Bank of Cape Verde on 4 January 2021; and B. Lkhagvasuren into the Bank of Mongolia as adviser to the governor in 2000, later its governor, where Enkhjargal Danzanbaljir also moved out to the World Bank and other development banks and back to the supervisory board. Similar moves are recorded at the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank (Sir K Dwight Venner and Timothy N. J. Antoine), the Central Bank of West African States (Jean-Claude Kassi Brou), the Bank of Guyana (Gobind Ganga) and the National Reserve Bank of Tonga (Tatafu Moeaki); Frederic S. Mishkin consulted for the Bank around his time as a Federal Reserve governor. The World Bank also sits on the Financial Stability Board, a body of regulators and central banks, represented by Pablo Saavedra. One tie is not a career at all: the Banco Central de Honduras states in Nota 4.2 of its audited accounts at 31 December 2024 that the World Bank administers a portfolio of 26,691,806,174 lempiras of its investments, the larger of two externally administered portfolios, the auditor Horwath Central America noting that part of the portfolio is managed outside the bank through international institutions specialising in portfolio management. One record is a case. In 2007 Nepal's Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority charged Nepal Rastra Bank's sitting governor, Bhattarai, and executive director Pradhan with embezzlement over the hiring of American consultants for the second phase of the Financial Sector Reform Program, and Bhattarai was suspended; the Supreme Court later cleared both, and a confidential World Bank report, reported in 2014, named a private banker as the main figure behind the scandal.
n:MSIF INC: MSIF INC is a company based in the United States, with the marker placed at the country. It is listed as a recipient of money, favors or contracts from Nepal Rastra Bank. This ties it to a 2007 case in which a Nepali commission charged the sitting governor Bhattarai and executive director Pradhan with embezzlement over the hiring of American consultants for a financial sector reform program. Bhattarai was suspended. The Supreme Court later cleared both, and he was reinstated. No act by the company itself is described here.
n:Rajan Singh Bhandari: Rajan Singh Bhandari is a person based in Kathmandu, Nepal, named in a case involving Nepal Rastra Bank. In 2007 Nepal's Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority charged the bank's sitting governor Bhattarai and executive director Pradhan with embezzlement over the hiring of American consultants for a financial sector reform program. Bhattarai was suspended. The Supreme Court later cleared both, allowing his reinstatement. A confidential World Bank report, reported in 2014, named a private banker as the main figure behind the scandal. Being named in the case is not a finding against him.
n:IEF Incorporated: IEF Incorporated is a company based in the United States, with the marker placed at the country. It is listed as a recipient of money, favors or contracts from Nepal Rastra Bank. This ties it to a 2007 case in which a Nepali commission charged the sitting governor Bhattarai and executive director Pradhan with embezzlement over the hiring of American consultants for a financial sector reform program. Bhattarai was suspended. The Supreme Court later cleared both, and he was reinstated. No act by the company itself is described here.
n:KPMG: KPMG is an accounting and auditing firm based in London, United Kingdom, tied to 15 central banks. It audits the accounts of 14 of them. It signed the independent auditors' report on the Federal Reserve Banks' combined financial statements for 2025. It is external auditor of the Bank of Spain for the financial years 2023 to 2027, approved by a European Union Council decision of 19 September 2023. It has audited the Swiss National Bank since 2015, was re-elected by the general meeting of 25 April 2025 and is proposed for 2026 and 2027. It audits the Reserve Bank of Australia, and Note Printing Australia, under a contract with the national audit office, so the Reserve Bank does not choose the audit partner. It also audits the Central Bank of Malta (for 2019 to 2025), the Bank of Ghana (2025), the State Bank of Pakistan (the year ended 30 June 2026, in a report dated 27 August 2026), the Central Bank of the Dominican Republic (statements as at 31 December 2023), the Reserve Bank of Fiji (2022), Banque du Liban in Lebanon (from 2020), the Central Bank of Oman (2023), the National Bank of Angola (2021) and the Central Bank of Jordan (the year ended 31 December 2018, in a report dated 28 March 2019). It audited the Bank of England up to the financial year ended 29 February 2024, after which the Bank appointed Ernst and Young. The firm is also named in a Nepalese case. In 2007 Nepal's Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority charged the sitting governor of Nepal Rastra Bank, Bhattarai, and executive director Pradhan with embezzlement over the hiring of American consultants for the second phase of the Financial Sector Reform Program, and Bhattarai was suspended; the Supreme Court later cleared both, allowing his reinstatement, and a confidential World Bank report, reported in 2014, named a private banker as the main figure behind the scandal.
n:Krishnan R: Krishnan R is a person linked to Sri Lanka and named in a case involving Nepal Rastra Bank, Nepal's central bank. In 2007 Nepal's Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority charged the sitting governor, Bhattarai, and executive director Pradhan with embezzlement over the hiring of American consultants for the second phase of the Financial Sector Reform Program. Bhattarai was suspended. The Supreme Court later cleared both men and allowed Bhattarai to return. A confidential World Bank report, reported in 2014, named a private banker as the main figure behind the scandal. Being named in the case is a tie, not a finding against Krishnan R.
n:Government of Nepal: The Government of Nepal is tied to Nepal Rastra Bank, the country's central bank. On 8 April 2022 it suspended governor Adhikari over charges of leaking sensitive information about government decisions and not fulfilling his responsibilities, and it set up a three-member probe committee headed by a former Supreme Court judge. On 19 April 2022 the Supreme Court stayed the suspension, and Adhikari went back to work.
n:National Fraud and Anti-Corruption Dir: The National Fraud and Anti-Corruption Directorate is an agency based in Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea. Court documents obtained by the reporting group OCCRP show it searched Bank of Papua New Guinea offices in August and September 2023 in a money-laundering investigation into the then-acting governor, Genia. She obtained a temporary stay, which was later dismissed. She was appointed governor in early 2024 and has not been charged. She had earlier been under fraud-squad investigation over a firearms deal for the bank's security team.
n:Sorin Ovidiu Vântu: Sorin Ovidiu Vântu is a businessman linked to Romania. In 2014 Romania's High Court of Cassation and Justice placed Olteanu, a deputy governor of the National Bank of Romania, under 30 days of house arrest. The National Anticorruption Directorate alleged that in 2008, while parliament speaker, Olteanu asked for and received a 1 million euro bribe from Vântu. Olteanu's lawyer said he would resign from the bank. The result of the trial is not given, so the allegation is unproven.
n:National Anticorruption Directorate (R: The National Anticorruption Directorate is a prosecution agency based in Bucharest, Romania. In 2014 it brought a case alleging that Olteanu, then a deputy governor of the National Bank of Romania, asked for and received a 1 million euro bribe in 2008 from businessman Sorin Ovidiu Vântu while Olteanu was parliament speaker. Romania's High Court of Cassation and Justice placed him under 30 days of house arrest, and his lawyer said he would resign from the bank. The outcome of the trial is not given, so the allegation is unproven.
n:High Court of Cassation and Justice (R: The High Court of Cassation and Justice is Romania's top court, based in Bucharest. In 2014 it placed Olteanu, a deputy governor of the National Bank of Romania, under 30 days of house arrest. This came in a case brought by the National Anticorruption Directorate, which alleged that he asked for and received a 1 million euro bribe in 2008, while parliament speaker, from businessman Sorin Ovidiu Vântu. His lawyer said he would resign from the bank. The outcome of the trial is not given, so the allegation is unproven.
n:Oleg Alexeyev: Oleg Alexeyev is a person linked to Russia and named in a case involving the Bank of Russia, the country's central bank. On 19 October 2005 the Moscow prosecutor's office indicted Alexei Mishin, chief legal expert at the central bank's Moscow directorate, and a deputy department head of the Federal Tax Service. They were accused of accepting a 1 million dollar bribe, according to the news agency Interfax. No outcome is given, so the charge is unproven. Being named in the case is a tie, not a finding against Alexeyev.
n:Moscow prosecutor's office: The Moscow prosecutor's office is a state prosecution agency based in Moscow, Russia. On 19 October 2005 it indicted Alexei Mishin, chief legal expert at the Bank of Russia's Moscow directorate, and a deputy department head of the Federal Tax Service for accepting a 1 million dollar bribe, according to the news agency Interfax. No outcome is given, so the charge is unproven.
n:UN Monitoring Group for Somalia and Er: The UN Monitoring Group for Somalia and Eritrea is a United Nations expert body based in New York, United States. Its July 2013 report on the Central Bank of Somalia said 80 percent of withdrawals from the bank were made for private purposes and that the governor was key to the irregularities. It also said 12 million dollars of 16.9 million dollars transferred by PricewaterhouseCoopers could not be traced. The central bank rejected the allegations.
n:Shulman Rogers: Shulman Rogers is a law firm based in Potomac, United States. It is named in a case involving the Central Bank of Somalia. Governor Abrar resigned after seven weeks and wrote to the president that since her appointment she had 'continuously been asked to sanction deals and violate my fiduciary responsibility'. She said she had refused to sanction a contract over frozen government assets with Shulman Rogers. The firm denied wrongdoing.
n:Serbian police: Serbian police are the national police, based in Belgrade. In January 2006 they arrested Dejan Simić, vice-governor of the National Bank of Serbia, on suspicion of taking bribes, according to the news agency Mina. No outcome is given, so the suspicion is unproven.
n:De La Rue: De La Rue is a banknote printer based in Basingstoke, United Kingdom, tied to 38 central banks. It prints or supplies notes for most of them. The Bank of England awarded it a 500 million pound printing contract on 29 September 2014, worked at the Bank's Debden site in Essex, and later triggered a three-year extension of its polymer banknote contract to 2028. The Central Bank of Kenya gave it an 18 billion shilling contract for new-look currency, made at the Ruaraka plant it co-owns with the Kenyan government, ahead of Giesecke & Devrient, Crane Currency and Oberthur Fiduciaire; Crane AB disputed that award before the procurement review board. Sveriges Riksbank signed with it on 19 September 2018 for just over three years, replacing Crane, and Danmarks Nationalbank has signed for the new Danish series launching in 2028, for a minimum of six years. The National Bank of Ethiopia gave it 187 million birr of a 206 million birr deal, for the 100 birr note, and the national bank of North Macedonia three contracts for 45 million notes worth 3.775 million euros. Printing or supply is also recorded for Libya, South Sudan, Tanzania, Ghana, Albania, Lesotho, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, the Gambia, Namibia, Botswana, Seychelles, Mauritius, Cape Verde, Iceland, Fiji, Tonga, the Maldives, Bhutan, Jamaica, Belize, Barbados, Trinidad and Tobago, Bermuda, the Cayman Islands, the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, Bahrain, Qatar, Turkmenistan and Iraq. Two records concern conduct. A United Nations Human Rights Council commission report said the firm transferred about 1.4 million dollars between 2016 and September 2017 to a Nairobi account held by a Bank of South Sudan consultant, against a banknote contract worth about 144 million dollars, and noted 'suspected corruption'; the United Kingdom's Serious Fraud Office opened an investigation in July 2019 and closed it in June 2020, saying the case did not meet the test for prosecution. In September 2010 De La Rue said some employees had deliberately falsified banknote paper specification test certificates for a limited number of customers, which was followed by the suspension of supply to the Reserve Bank of India. At the trial of former Central Bank of Nigeria governor Godwin Emefiele over the alleged unlawful printing of redesigned naira notes in 2022, an allegation that is unproven, a prosecution witness said original naira designs had historically been handled by De La Rue while the new notes were printed locally.
n:Equity Bank: Equity Bank is a bank based in Nairobi, Kenya. It is named in a case involving the Bank of South Sudan. A UN Human Rights Council commission report said the banknote printer De La Rue transferred about 1.4 million dollars to an Equity Bank account in Nairobi held by a Bank of South Sudan consultant between 2016 and September 2017. The transfers were set against a banknote contract worth about 144 million dollars, and the report noted 'suspected corruption'. The UK Serious Fraud Office closed its own investigation into De La Rue in June 2020 without charges.
n:UN Commission on Human Rights in South: The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan is a United Nations body based in Geneva, Switzerland. Its report to the UN Human Rights Council said the banknote printer De La Rue transferred about 1.4 million dollars to an Equity Bank account in Nairobi held by a Bank of South Sudan consultant between 2016 and September 2017. The transfers were set against a banknote contract worth about 144 million dollars, and the report noted 'suspected corruption'. The UK Serious Fraud Office closed its own investigation into De La Rue in June 2020 without charges.
n:South Sudan security forces: South Sudan's security forces are based in Juba. n:Surinamese court: The Surinamese court is a criminal court in Paramaribo, Suriname, that heard two cases tied to the Central Bank of Suriname. It gave him eight years and the same fine, and the bank's legal director and others were also convicted. On appeal in January 2026 Hoefdraad's term became 10 years and van Trikt's became six. n:Jakaya Kikwete: Jakaya Kikwete was president of Tanzania. n:Office of the Auditor General (Uganda): The Auditor General of Uganda is the state audit office, and it does two things on this map. It has also examined how the bank behaved. A confidential 2018 report from this office to parliament said Bank of Uganda managers, including governor Mutebile, acted without guidelines, regulations or policies and may have intentionally neglected aspects of the closure and sale of at least seven commercial banks, including Crane Bank, in 2016 and 2017.

n:National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukr: The National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine is the country's main anti-graft agency, based in Kyiv. On 11 November 2019 it detained seven people, including Pysaruk, a former first deputy governor of the National Bank of Ukraine, and current and former bank officials. The suspicion is that they embezzled 1.2 billion hryvnia (about 49 million dollars) of a 2014 stabilisation loan from the bank to VAB Bank, which was declared insolvent in November 2014. No outcome is given, so the suspicion is unproven.
n:VAB Bank: VAB Bank is a bank based in Kyiv, Ukraine. In 2014 it received a stabilisation loan from the National Bank of Ukraine, and it was declared insolvent in November 2014. n:Medley Global Advisors: Medley Global Advisors is a company based in New York, United States. In April 2017 Lacker resigned with immediate effect as head of the Richmond Federal Reserve Bank. He said that in October 2012 he spoke with a Medley analyst who held confidential information on options discussed at the September 2012 meeting of the Fed's policy committee, and that he may have confirmed it. He said he had not disclosed this in a 2012 internal inquiry. His lawyer said the investigation was complete and no charges would be brought.
n:Federal Reserve Office of Inspector Ge: The Federal Reserve Office of Inspector General is the Fed's internal watchdog, based in Washington. A report issued on 11 September 2024 found that trades made on Bostic's behalf from 2017 for about five years, including several during blackout periods before policy meetings, violated Fed ethics policies and created the appearance of acting on confidential information. It found no violation of insider trading or conflict of interest laws. It found no evidence that Powell's December 2019 trades or Clarida's 2020 trades broke laws, rules or policies then in effect, and made no law enforcement referral. Its January 2024 report said Kaplan's 2020 trading gave an appearance of acting on confidential information, and that Rosengren failed to report multiple trades. A 15 November 2025 ethics office report on Kugler's 2024 stock trades followed a Fed referral to it.
n:US Office of Government Ethics: The US Office of Government Ethics is a federal agency based in Washington. After a Federal Reserve referral to its inspector general, it released a report on 15 November 2025 on Kugler, a former Fed governor. Kugler's 2024 financial disclosure listed more than a dozen individual stock trades, several during blackout periods before policy meetings. The report said these violated Fed rules barring officials from holding individual stocks. The largest was an April 2024 Apple purchase of 100,000 to 250,000 dollars.
n:Apple: Apple is a technology company based in Cupertino, United States. It is tied to the Federal Reserve through stock held by an official. n:UN Panel of Experts on Yemen: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen is a United Nations expert body based in New York, United States. Its January 2021 report said the Aden-based Central Bank of Yemen broke its foreign-exchange rules and laundered a substantial part of a 2 billion dollar Saudi deposit, giving traders a 423 million dollar windfall. The bank rejected the claims. On 25 March 2021, after an internal review, the panel told the government it had withdrawn the money-laundering and corruption accusations, according to a Yemeni official quoted by Arab News.
n:Saudi Arabia: Saudi Arabia is a country whose government is based in Riyadh. It is tied to the Central Bank of Yemen through a 2 billion dollar Saudi deposit. n:Bankorp: Bankorp is a bank in South Africa. It is tied to the South African Reserve Bank, the country's central bank, through an apartheid-era rescue loan the Reserve Bank gave it. In June 2017 the Public Protector, a state watchdog, ordered Absa, the bank that later took over Bankorp, to repay 1.125 billion rand for that rescue. On 16 February 2018 the Pretoria High Court set aside the Public Protector's report and its orders, after the Reserve Bank and Absa asked for a review. The court also ordered the Public Protector to pay part of the Reserve Bank's costs personally.
n:Public Protector (South Africa): The Public Protector is a state agency in Pretoria, South Africa. n:Robert Mugabe: Robert Mugabe, based in Harare, was president of Zimbabwe. He is named in a case involving the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, the country's central bank. Under its governor Gono, the bank ran what are called quasi-fiscal activities, meaning spending that normally belongs to the government. These included cash for state enterprises and farm equipment handed out at events presided over by Mugabe. The bank also raided private foreign-currency accounts to fund state operations, leaving debts of close to 1.3 billion dollars. In 2014 the government tabled a bill to move that debt to taxpayers.
n:Government of Zimbabwe: The Government of Zimbabwe sits in Harare. It is tied to the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, the country's central bank, as a recipient of its money. These included cash for state enterprises and farm equipment handed out at events presided over by President Mugabe. The bank also raided private foreign-currency accounts to fund state operations, leaving debts of close to 1.3 billion dollars. In 2014 the government tabled the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe (Debt Assumption) Bill to move the debt to taxpayers.
n:Sakunda Holdings: Sakunda Holdings is a company in Harare, Zimbabwe, owned by Kudakwashe Tagwirei, who is described as an ally of the president. It received money from the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, the country's central bank. At a September 2019 parliamentary Public Accounts Committee hearing, deputy governor Mlambo confirmed the bank issued 663.8 million dollars in Treasury Bills to Sakunda in 2017 and 2018 for the Command Agriculture programme, on instruction from the Finance Ministry. The committee also cited a 1.37 billion dollar overdraft issued by December 2017 without parliamentary approval. It could not get an explanation for 2.9 billion dollars paid from unallocated reserves in 2017.
